**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-33) Surat al-Baqarah
Madaniyyah (Medinan), and its verses number two hundred and eighty-seven.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾. All the other letter-names by which the letters are spelled out are names whose referents (musammayat) are the letters (huruf) from which words are composed, because they fall under the definition of a noun (ism) and take on what is specific to nouns: definiteness, indefiniteness, plurality, diminutive form, and the like. This is what al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) stated explicitly.

As for what Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, reported, that he (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites a letter from the Book of Allah, he has a good deed, and a good deed is multiplied tenfold. I do not say that Alif-Lam-Mim is one letter; rather, Alif is a letter, Lam is a letter, and Mim is a letter," then the word "letter" here means other than the meaning it has been conventionally given, since restricting it to that is a later convention. Rather, it is used in its linguistic sense, and perhaps he named it by the name of what it denotes.

Since their referents are individual letters while the names themselves are compound, they are placed at the beginning so that their pronunciation by way of the referent is the first thing that strikes the ear. The hamzah is used in place of the alif, because it is impossible to begin with the alif. The hamzah is, when no governing words precede it, pause-form and free of inflection because there is no cause or requirement for inflection; yet it is capable of inflection and open to it, since it does not fit the basic form of the letter. For this reason it is said of Sad and Qaf, when they are combined, that they are "between two sakin (quiescent) letters," and they are not treated like the words ayna (where) and ha'ula' (these).

Furthermore, since their referents are the essential elements of speech and its simple components from which it is composed, the surah opens with a group of them, as a way of alerting those who were challenged by the Qur'an and as an indication that the origin of what is recited to them is speech arranged of the same kind of material they use to arrange their own speech. Had it come from other than Allah, they would not have been unable, all of them together, despite their solidarity and the strength of their eloquence, to produce anything approaching it. And so that it is the first thing to strike the ears as standing independently with a type of inimitability (i'jaz). The pronunciation of the names of the letters is restricted to one who has written and studied; as for one who is unlettered (ummi) and has not mixed with the Book, it is improbable, strange, and a departure from habit, like writing and reciting. This is especially so since in this he has observed what the skilled and accomplished man of letters, the supreme master of his art, cannot achieve: he has brought forth in these openings fourteen names, which are half of the names of the letters of the alphabet, if the alif is not counted as a separate letter, across twenty-nine surahs by their number, if the original alif is counted, comprising half of each of their categories.

Thus he mentioned from the voiceless (al-mahmusah), which are those whose point of articulation has weak reliance, and whose mnemonic is (سَتَشْحَثُكَ خَصَفَهُ), half of them: ha', kaf, ha', sad, sin, and kaf. From the remaining voiced (al-majhurah) letters, half of them, collected in (لَنْ يُقْطَعَ أمْرٌ). From the eight strong (al-shadidah) letters, collected in (أجَدْتَ طَبَقَكَ), four, collected in (أقَطَكَ). From the remaining soft (al-rakhwah) letters, ten, collected in "khamsun" (five) on the pattern of "nasrihi"; from the closed (al-mutbaqah) letters, which are sad, dad, ta', and za', half of them; from the remaining open (al-munfatihah) letters, half of them; from the echoing (al-qalqalah) letters, which are letters that vibrate when they are pronounced and are collected in (قد طبج), the lesser half, because they are few; from the two soft letters (al-layyinatan), the ya', since it is the lightest in weight; from the elevated (al-mustali'ah) letters, which are those where the voice rises toward the upper palate, and they are seven: qaf, sad, ta', kha', ghayn, dad, and za', the lesser half; from the remaining lowered (al-munkhafidah) letters, half of them; from the letters of substitution (huruf al-badal), which are eleven according to what Sibawayh mentioned and Ibn Jinni chose, and they are collected in (أجِدُ طَوَيْتُ), of which the six common and well-known ones are those collected in (أهطمين). Some have added seven others: lam in (أصِيلالَ), sad and za' in (صِراطٍ وزِراطٍ), fa' in (أجْدافٍ), 'ayn in (أعَنَ), tha' in (ثروغ الدَّلْو), and ba' in (بِاسْمِكَ), until they reach eighteen. Of these, nine are mentioned: the six mentioned, (p-34) plus lam, sad, and 'ayn.

Among the letters that are assimilated into their like but not into their near-equivals, there are fifteen: hamzah, ha', 'ayn, sad, ta', mim, ya', kha', ghayn, dad, fa', za' (ظ), shin, za', and waw, the lesser half of them. Among those into which these two groups are assimilated, the remaining thirteen, the greater half: ha' (ح), qaf, kaf, ra', sin, lam, and nun, because of the lightness and eloquence in assimilation. From the four letters that are not assimilated into what is near them, and into which their near-equivalents are assimilated, which are mim, za', sin, and fa', half of them.

Since the articulated letters (al-huruf al-dhaqliyyah), which are relied on by the tip of the tongue, are six, collected in (رُبَّ مُنَفَّلٍ), and the guttural letters (al-halqiyyah), which are ha' (ح), kha', 'ayn, ghayn, ha' (ه), and hamzah, are frequent in speech, he mentioned two-thirds of them. Since the patterns of augmentation (abniyat al-mazid) do not exceed the quadriliteral-plus-augmentation form, he mentioned from the ten augmentation letters, which are collected in (اليَوْمَ تَنْساهُ), seven of its letters, as an indication of this. If you were to survey words and their compounds, you would find the letters left out of each category to be heavily represented by those mentioned. Then he mentioned them as single letters, as pairs, as triples, as quadruples, and as quintuples, signaling that the challenged-with thing is composed of their words, whose roots are single words, and composed of two or more letters up to five. He mentioned three single-letter forms in three surahs, because they occur in the three categories: noun (ism), verb (fi'l), and particle (harf). And four two-letter forms, because they occur in the particle without deletion (like بَلْ), in the verb with deletion of a heavy element (like قُلْ), and in the noun without deletion (like مَنَ), and with (like دَمٍ) in nine surahs, because each of them occurs in each of the three categories in three ways. Among nouns: مَن, إذْ, and ذُو. Among verbs: قُلْ, بِعْ, and خِفْ. Among particles: مِن, إنْ, and مُذْ, according to the dialect of one who has tested it. And three three-letter forms, because they come in the three categories in thirteen surahs, as an indication that the basic patterns in use are thirteen: ten of them for nouns, three for verbs, and quadriliteral and quintiliteral forms, as an indication that each of these has a basic form, like جَعْفَرَ and سَفَرْجَلَ, and a derived form (mulhaq), like قَرْدَدَ and جَحَنْفَلَ. Perhaps they were distributed among the surahs and not all counted at the beginning of the Qur'an for this benefit, along with the renewed challenge, the repetition of the admonition, and the emphasis upon it.

The meaning is that this thing challenged with is composed of the same kind as these letters, or composed of them. This is what has been said. It has also been said that they are names of the surahs, and most scholars agree on this. They were named with them as an indication that they are words of known composition, so that had they not been revelation from Allah, the opponents' capacity would not have fallen short of opposing them. It has been argued in support of this that if they did not convey meaning, the address through them would be like addressing someone with meaningless sounds, or speaking Zanji (a non-Arabic language) to an Arab, and the whole Qur'an would not be a clarification and guidance. Since the challenge could be made with it even though they convey meaning, then either it is intended that they are the surahs in whose beginning they stand, as their titles, or it is something else. The second is false, because either what is intended is what they were assigned to in the language of the Arabs, which is obviously not the case, or something other than that, which is also false, because the Qur'an was revealed in their language, according to His saying: ﴿in clear Arabic tongue﴾. So it should not be interpreted as something not in their language.

It may be objected: why could they not be extra letters for alerting, or indicating the end of one speech and the beginning of another, as Qutrub said, or allusions to words of which they are the beginnings, with the speaker restricting himself to them, like the poet's saying:

I said to her, "Stop!" and she said, "Qaf!"

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "Alif is the blessings (alaa') of Allah, Lam is His utterance (lafzuhu), and Mim is His kingdom (mulkuhu)." And from him: that "Ra," "Ha Mim," and "Nun" together form "al-Rahman." And from him: that "Alif-Lam-Mim" means: "I am Allah, the All-Knowing," and similarly for the rest of the openings. And from him: that Alif is from Allah, Lam is from Jibril, and Mim is from Muhammad, meaning: the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, through the tongue of Jibril, upon Muhammad, may the blessings and peace of both be upon them. Or it refers to the durations of peoples and terms, by the reckoning of the abjad (numerical value of letters), as Abu al-'Aliyah said, relying on what has been narrated: "When the Jews came to him (ﷺ), he recited to them Alif-Lam-Mim of al-Baqarah. They counted it and said: 'How do we enter a religion whose duration is seventy-one years?' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) smiled, and they said: 'Is there anything else?' He said: 'Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad, Alif-Lam-Ra, and Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra.' They said: 'You have confused us, and we do not know which of them to take.'" His recitation of them to them in this order, and his affirming them in their derivation, is evidence of this. And this indication, although it is not Arabic, is by its prevalence among people, including the Arabs, classed among the Arabicized loanwords, like mishkat (niche), sijjil (baked clay), and qistas (balance). Or it is an indication of the simple letters, with Allah swearing by them for their nobility, since they are the simple elements of Allah's names and the material of His address.

Furthermore, the claim that they are names of the surahs excludes them from what is not in the language of the Arabs, because naming with three or more names is considered objectionable among them, and it leads to the unity of the name and the named, and it entails the part coming after the whole, since the name is posterior to the named in rank. We reply: these expressions were not known to be used as additions for alerting or for indicating the cessation and resumption that applies to them and to other things, insofar as they are the openings of surahs, and this does not require that they have no meaning within their context, nor that they were not used as abbreviations of specific words in their language. As for the poetry, it is an anomaly. As for Ibn 'Abbas's saying, it is an alert that these letters are the source of names and the origins of address, and an illustration with good examples. Do you not see that he counted each letter as standing for distinct words with no interpretation? And he restricted them to these meanings rather than others, since there is no restrictor, either lexically or semantically, nor by the reckoning of the abjad, for otherwise they would be classed with Arabicized loanwords. The hadith contains no proof, since it is possible that he (ﷺ) smiled out of wonder at their ignorance. And making them a means of swearing is not impossible, but it requires supposing things for which there is no evidence. Naming with three names is only prohibited when they are compounded and made into one name, following the pattern of Ba'labakk. As for when they are listed as numerals are listed, there is no objection. And consider Sibawayh's equating of naming by a sentence or a line of poetry with a group of names of the letters of the alphabet. The named (musammaa) is the whole surah, and the name is a part of it, so there is no unity. And it is prior in its essence and posterior in respect of being a name, so there is no circularity, since the two aspects differ. The first view is closer to verification, more suitable to the subtleties of the revelation, and safer from the necessity of transfer (naql) and the occurrence of homonymy in proper names from a single imposer, for that would return by way of contradiction to what is intended by being a proper name.

It has been said that they are names of the Qur'an, and for this reason it is informed about with "the Book" and "the Qur'an."

It has been said that they are names of Allah the Exalted. What indicates this is that 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, used to say: "O Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad," and "O Ha-Mim-'Ayn-Sin-Qaf," and perhaps he meant: "O Revealer of these two."

It has been said: the Alif is from the furthest part of the throat, which is the origin of the points of articulation; the Lam is from the tip of the tongue, which is the middle of them; and the Mim is from the lips, which is the last of them. He combined them, as a sign that the servant should make the beginning, middle, and end of his speech the remembrance of Allah the Exalted.

It has been said: it is a secret that Allah has kept to Himself. Something close to this has been reported from the Four Caliphs and others of the Companions. Perhaps they meant that they are secrets between Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, and symbols which He did not intend to convey to anyone else, since address with what conveys nothing would be far-fetched.

If you take them as names of God, or of the Qur'an, or of the surahs, then they have a place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). They may be in the nominative, either as a subject (mubtada', "inchoative") or as a predicate (khabar). Or they may be in the accusative, by supposing the verb of oath (fi'l al-qasam) in the manner of "By God, I will certainly do it" (la-af'alanna), with the accusative or otherwise, as has been mentioned. Or they may be in the genitive, by supposing the particle of oath (harf al-qasam) to be elided.

Grammatical inflection (i'rab) is possible in pronunciation, and hikaya (reporting the letters as they are spoken, without inflection) applies to those that are standing alone or that are balanced with a single word, such as (ḥā mīm) ḥ-m, since it is like Habil (Hābīl). Hikaya applies to nothing other than that. The discussion of this will return to you in detail, God willing.

If you keep them in their own meanings, then if they are considered as forming a composition from these letters, they fall within the scope of the nominative, as subject or predicate, as already explained. If you take them as things sworn by, then each word among them is in the accusative or genitive according to the two dialects, as in "By God, I will certainly do it," and the whole is a sworn sentence by the verb supposed for it.

If you take them as fragments of words, or as sounds placed in the position of letters of alerting (huruf al-tanbih), then they have no place in i'rab, like independent sentences and enumerated single words. They are paused upon with a complete pause (waqf al-tamam) when they are supposed to be such that they do not need what follows them. None of them is a verse according to other than the Kufans. As for them, then alif-lam-mim in its places, and alif-lam-mim-sad, kaf-ha-ya-'ayn-sad, ta-ha, ta-sin-mim, ta-sin, ya-sin, and ha-mim are a verse, and ha-mim 'ayn-sin-qaf are two verses, and the rest are not verses. This is a matter of revelation (tawqif), with no room for analogy (qiyas) in it.

﴿That is the Book﴾. "That" is a demonstrative referring to (Alif-Lam-Mim), if it is interpreted as the composition made of these letters, or explained as the sura or the Qur'an. Since it has been spoken and recited, or since it has reached the addressee from the sender, it has become distant, so it is pointed to with the word used for something distant (p-36), and [it is] masculine. When (Alif-Lam-Mim) is intended as the sura, the demonstrative is used to refer to "the Book," and it is its predicate or its attribute, which is that very thing. Or it refers to "the Book," in which case it is its attribute, and what is meant is the Book promised to be sent down, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We will cast upon you a weighty word﴾. Or [it refers to the Book] among the earlier scriptures. "Kitab" is a verbal noun (masdar) that has been used as a name for the thing written, for emphasis.

It has been said that "kitab" is on the pattern fi'al in the sense of maf'ul, like libas (garment). Then it was applied to the composed speech before it is written, because it is among the things that are written. The root meaning of kutub is gathering together, and from it comes katibah (a military unit).

﴿There is no doubt in it﴾. Its meaning is that, because of its clarity and the brilliance of its proof, a rational person, after proper reflection, will not doubt that it is a revelation that has reached the limit of inimitability. It does not mean that no one at all doubts it. Do you not see His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾, to the end of the verse? He did not remove doubt from them, but rather showed them the way that would relieve it, which is that they should strive to produce something comparable to one of its chapters and exert their utmost effort in that; when they are unable to do so, it becomes clear to them that there is no room for suspicion and no entry for doubt in it.

It has been said: its meaning is "there is no doubt in it for the God-fearing." ﴿Guidance﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in the genitive, and the element governing it is the adverbial phrase that functions as an attribute of the negated noun. "Rayb" originally is the verbal noun of "rabani al-shay'," when a thing produces rayb in you, and rayb is the restlessness and agitation of the soul; the word was applied to doubt because it unsettles the soul and removes tranquility.

In a hadith: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt," for doubt is unease, and truthfulness is tranquility. From the same root comes rayb al-zaman (the misfortunes of time), for its calamities.

﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾: it guides them to the truth. "Huda" (guidance) is originally a verbal noun like al-suraa and al-tuqa, and its meaning is indication.

It has been said: it is the indication that conveys one to the desired goal, because it has been set in opposition to misguidance in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, either we or you are upon guidance or in clear error﴾, and because one is not called "guided" (mahdi) except one who has reached the sought objective. Its being specific to the God-fearing is because they are the ones guided by it and benefit from its text, although its indication is general for every observer, Muslim or disbeliever; and on this basis He said, exalted is He: ﴿guidance for mankind﴾. Or [it is specific to the God-fearing] because no one benefits from reflecting upon it except one who has polished the intellect and used it in contemplating the signs, examining the miracles, and recognizing prophethood. For it is like a food suitable for preserving health: it brings no benefit unless health is already present. To this He alluded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾. What the Qur'an contains of the general (mujmal) and the ambiguous (mutashabih) does not undermine its being guidance, because it is never free of an explanation that specifies what is meant by it.

"Muttaqi" is an active participle from their saying "waqahu, fa-ittaqa," and "wiqaya" is the utmost protection. In the usage of the Law (shar'), it is a name for one who guards himself from what harms him in the Hereafter, and it has three levels:

The first: guarding oneself from the eternal punishment by disavowing polytheism, and to this refers His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He made them hold to the word of piety﴾.

The second: avoiding everything that is sinful, whether an act or an omission, even minor sins according to some, and this is what is commonly known as taqwa in the Law, and it is what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been God-fearing﴾.

The third: that one purifies oneself from whatever occupies one's inner self away from the Truth, and devotes oneself to Him wholeheartedly; this is true taqwa, which is what is required by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear God with the fear due to Him﴾. He has interpreted His saying ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾ here according to all three aspects.

Know that the verse admits several aspects of i'rab (grammatical analysis, the study of case endings and syntactic function): that (Alif-Lam-Mim) be a subject (mubtada'), on the basis that it is a name for the Qur'an or the sura, or that it is implicitly "the composition made of them," and "that" is its predicate, even though it is more specific than "composition" in general. The principle is that the more specific is not to be understood as the more general, because what is meant by it is the composition complete in its arrangement, reaching the utmost degree of eloquence and the ranks of rhetorical excellence, and "the Book" is an attribute of that.

And that (Alif-Lam-Mim) be the predicate of an omitted subject, and "that" a second predicate or an appositive (badal), and ﴿the Book﴾ its attribute, and ﴿there is no doubt﴾: according to the well-known reading it is indeclinable (mabni) because it contains the meaning of min (from), and it is in the accusative position as the subject of the generic negating "la" which operates like "inna." This is because it is the opposite of affirmation and is required to be followed by nouns just as it is required. In the reading of Abu al-Sha'tha' it is nominative, governed by "la" in the sense of "laysa" (is not), and "fihi" is its predicate; it was not fronted as it was fronted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in it there is no intoxication﴾, because the intention was not to restrict the negation of doubt to it among the other books, as was intended there. [In this reading] "fihi" may also be its attribute, and ﴿for the God-fearing﴾ its predicate. ﴿Guidance﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), or its predicate is omitted, as in "la dayr" (no harm). For this reason the pause is made at ﴿there is no doubt﴾, and [also] because "fihi" is the predicate of "guidance," which was fronted over it because it is indefinite; the estimated sense is: "there is no doubt in it; in it is guidance." And that "that" be a subject and ﴿the Book﴾ its predicate, meaning: it is the complete Book that deserves to be called a book; or [﴿the Book﴾] is its attribute, and what follows is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾.

The best view is that these are four harmonious sentences, in which each subsequent one establishes the preceding one; for this reason the conjunction is not placed between them. So ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ is a sentence showing that the challenge is directed to a composition of the same kind as that from which they compose their speech. ﴿That is the Book﴾ is a second sentence establishing the aspect of the challenge. ﴿There is no doubt in it﴾ is a third sentence bearing witness to its perfection, that the Book described with the utmost perfection, since there is no perfection higher than that which belongs to truth and certainty. ﴿Guidance for the God-fearing﴾, with what is estimated as its subject, is the beginning of a fourth sentence that confirms that it is truth around which doubt does not hover, by [stating] that it is ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾; or the preceding sentences entail the following one as evidence entails what it proves. Its explanation is that when attention was first drawn to the inimitability of the challenge, in that it is of the same kind as their speech and they were unable to produce a counterpart to it, it was inferred from this that it is the Book that has reached the limit of perfection, and that this entails that doubt cannot cling to its edges, since nothing is more deficient than what is subject to suspicion and uncertainty; and whatever is like that is necessarily ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾. In each of these there is a refined point of eloquence: in the first, there is omission and allusion to the intended meaning together with a reason given; in the second, the grandeur of the definite article; in the third, the postponement of the adverbial phrase lest falsehood be suggested; in the fourth, the omission and the description with a verbal noun for emphasis, and its indefinite form to exalt it; and restricting guidance to the God-fearing, by considering the end result, is calling those who are approaching taqwa "God-fearing," for brevity and to magnify their state.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 3:**

﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾. This may be a relative clause (mawsul) attached to *al-muttaqin* (the God-conscious), in which case it is a genitive descriptive qualifier (sifah majrurah) that specifies it, if *taqwa* (God-consciousness) is interpreted as abstention from what is not fitting. It is then consequent upon it in the manner of adornment following clearing away, and of polishing following refinement. Or it is an explanatory clause (muwaddihah), if *taqwa* is interpreted as encompassing the doing of good deeds and the avoidance of evil deeds, because it includes what is the root of deeds and the foundation of good deeds: faith, prayer and almsgiving. These are the "mothers" (ummahat) of the inner acts, and of the bodily and financial acts of worship, which generally entail all other acts of obedience and the avoidance of sins. Do you not see the saying of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾? And the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Prayer is the pillar of religion, and zakat is the bridge of Islam." Or it is brought for the purpose of praise by what the word *al-muttaqin* contains. The singling out of faith in the unseen, establishing prayer and giving zakat by mention is a demonstration of their excellence over the rest of what falls under the name of *taqwa*. Or it is in the accusative as a praise (madh) or in the nominative by an implied elision: "I mean" or "they are those who". Or it is separated from what precedes it, in the nominative as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿those are upon guidance﴾, so the pause upon *al-muttaqin* is complete.

Faith (*iman*) linguistically is an expression for assent (*tasdiq*), derived from security (*amn*), as if the one who assents secures the one assented to from denial and opposition. Its transitivity by *ba'* (with) is because it includes the meaning of acknowledgment (*i'tiraf*). It is also used in the sense of trust (*wuthuq*), insofar as the one who trusts in a thing becomes secure from it. From this is the saying: "I did not feel secure that I would find a companion." Both senses are good in ﴿they believe in the unseen﴾.

As for its legal (shar'i) meaning: it is assent to what is known by necessity to be from the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), such as monotheism (*tawhid*), prophethood, resurrection and recompense. It is the combination of three matters: holding the truth as belief (*i'tiqad*), affirming it verbally (*iqrar*), and acting in accordance with its requirements. This is the position of the majority of the hadith scholars (*muhaddithun*), the Mu'tazilites and the Kharijites.

Whoever neglects belief alone is a hypocrite (*munafiq*). Whoever neglects affirmation is an unbeliever (*kafir*). Whoever neglects action is a sinner (*fasiq*) by consensus, an unbeliever according to the Kharijites, and outside of faith but not within unbelief according to the Mu'tazilites. What indicates that it is assent alone is that the Glorified and Exalted attributed faith to the heart, saying: ﴿Those - He has written faith in their hearts﴾; ﴿while his heart is at rest with faith﴾; (p-38) ﴿and their hearts have not believed﴾; ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾. Righteous deeds are conjoined with it in countless places, and He paired it with sins, saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾; ﴿O you who believe, retribution is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾; ﴿those who believe and have not mixed their belief with injustice﴾. This is in addition to the fact that it involves less alteration, as it is closer to the original, and it is definitively the intended meaning in the verse, since the transitive form with *ba'* is by consensus assent.

Then it is disputed whether mere assent of the heart is sufficient, because it is the aim, or whether affirmation must be added for the one able to do it. The truth is perhaps the second, because He (Exalted) censured the obstinate more than He censured the ignorant who fell short. The one who opposes this may make the censure to be for denial, not for the absence of affirmation by one able to do it.

The word *ghayb* (the unseen) is a verbal noun (masdar) which is described by it for emphasis, like *al-shahadah* (the witnessed) in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. The Arabs call a depression in the ground *ghayb*, and the hollow next to the kidney as well. Or it is the form *fa'il* lightened like *qil*. What is meant by it is the hidden which is not perceived by the senses, nor required by the immediate intellect. It is of two kinds: a kind for which there is no evidence, which is what is meant by the saying of the Most High: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but Him﴾; and a kind for which an established proof has been set up, such as the Creator, His attributes, the Last Day and its conditions. This is what is meant in this verse. This is when you make it a complement of *iman* and place it in the position of the direct object. If you make it a circumstantial state (hal), on the supposition of "those who are associated with the unseen," it would mean absence and concealment. The meaning is that they believe while absent from you, unlike the hypocrites who, when they ﴿meet those who believe, say: "We believe," but when they are alone with their devils, say: "Indeed we are with you; we were only mocking"﴾. Or it means "from the one believed in", because it is narrated that Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "By He other than whom there is no god, no one has believed with a faith more excellent than faith in the unseen," and then he recited this verse.

It has been said that what is meant by *ghayb* is the heart, because it is hidden. The meaning is that they believe with their hearts, not like those who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. So the *ba'* is for transitivity according to the first view, for accompaniment according to the second, and for instrumentality according to the third.

﴿And they establish prayer﴾: that is, they straighten its pillars and guard it against any deviation occurring in its acts. From *aqama al-'awd* (he straightened the stick) when he made it straight. Or they persist in it, from *qamat al-suq* (the market became brisk) when it was in demand, and *aqamtuha* (I made it brisk) when you made it in demand. Someone said:

*"Ghazalah made the market of blows brisk / for the people of the two Iraqs, a whole year, bound up."*

For when it is guarded, it is like the goods in demand, and when it is neglected, it is like the stagnant goods that are shunned. Or they strive for its performance without slackness or idleness, from the expression "he stood to the matter" (*qama bi al-amr*) and "he established it" (*aqamahu*) when he worked hard at it and bore its burden. Its opposite is "he sat back from the matter" (*qa'ada 'an al-amr*) and "he held back" (*taqa'ada*). Or they perform it. He expressed performance by establishment because it involves standing, just as He expressed it by *qunut* (devout obedience), bowing, prostration and glorification. The first is more apparent, because it is more widely known, closer to the literal reality, and more beneficial, since it includes the warning that the one truly deserving of praise is the one who observes its outward limits of obligations and sunnas, and its inner rights of humility and turning the heart toward Allah the Most High. Not those who pray but are heedless of their prayer. For this reason He mentioned in the context of praise "those who establish prayer", and in the context of blame "woe to the worshippers." Prayer (*salah*) is a form (*fa'lah*) from *sallá* (he supplicated), like zakat (*zakah*) from *zakka* (he purified). They were written with a *waw* according to the pronunciation of the emphatic form. The specific act was named *salah* because it includes supplication.

It has been said: the origin of *sallá* is "he moved the two *salawayn*" (the two sides of the hip), because the one praying does it in his bowing and prostration. The fame of this word in the second meaning, along with its lack of fame in the first, does not detract from its being transferred from it. The supplicant was named a worshipper (*musalli*) by way of likening him in his humility to the one who bows and prostrates.

﴿And from what We have provided for them they spend﴾. *Al-rizq* (provision) linguistically means portion. The Most High said: ﴿and you make your provision that you deny [it]﴾. By custom it is specified as the designation of a thing given to a living being for its benefit and for enabling it to have it.

As for the Mu'tazilites: since they held it impossible for Allah the Most High to enable someone with what is unlawful, because He forbade its benefit and commanded to refrain from it, they said: the unlawful is not provision. Do you not see that He attributed provision here to Himself, as a notification that they spend only what is wholly lawful?

Yet spending what is unlawful does not merit praise. He censured the polytheists for forbidding some of what Allah had given them as provision, by His saying: (p-39) ﴿Say: "Have you considered what Allah has sent down to you of provision, and you made from it what is unlawful and lawful?"﴾. Our companions (the Ash'arites) held that the attribution is for magnification and encouragement to spend, and that the censure is for forbidding what was not forbidden. The restriction of "what We have provided them" to the lawful is by the indicator of context. They relied for the inclusion of the unlawful in provision on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of 'Amr ibn Qurrah: "Allah has provided you with what is good, and you chose what Allah has forbidden you of His provision instead of what Allah has permitted you of His lawful things." And because if it were not provision, the one who nourishes himself with it throughout his life would not be called one provided for; but this is not so, by the saying of the Most High: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾.

*Anfaqa al-shay'* (he spent the thing) and *anfadahu* (he exhausted it) are two siblings (close in meaning). If you survey the words, you will find that every root whose first radical is *nun* and whose middle radical is *fa'* indicates the meaning of going away and departing. The apparent meaning of this *infaq* is the disbursement of wealth in the path of good, whether obligatory or voluntary. Whoever interpreted it as zakat mentions its best type and its foundation, or restricts it to it because it is associated with what is its counterpart. The fronting of the object is for emphasis upon it and to preserve the rhyme-endings of the verses. The introduction of *min* (from) which indicates partiality upon it is to prevent the one obligated from extravagance, which is prohibited. It is possible that what is intended by it is spending from all the blessings Allah has given them, outward and inward. This is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Knowledge that is not acted upon is like a treasure that is not spent from." This is the view of the one who said: "And from what We have specially bestowed upon them of the lights of gnosis, they overflow."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 4:

﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾ are the believers among the People of the Book, such as ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, and his like. They are conjoined to ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾, and they are included with them in the category of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) as two more specific groups within a more general one. The meaning of ﴿those﴾ is those who came to faith having turned from polytheism and denial, and the meaning of ﴿these﴾ is their counterparts. Thus the two verses are a detailed explanation of the God-fearing. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Alternatively, they are conjoined to the God-fearing, as though he had said, "a guidance for the God-fearing" who turn away from polytheism, and "those who believe" are from among the adherents of the various religious communities. It is possible that by them is meant the first group themselves, and the conjunction has been placed in the middle, as it is placed in the middle in the line of poetry:

"To the mighty king and son of the hero, and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."

And in his saying:

"Alas for Dhuʾaba, for al-Harith the sa'ih, then al-Ghanim, then al-Ayib."

The sense is that they are those who combine belief in what reason grasps in general terms with the performance of what it confirms of bodily and financial acts of worship, and belief in what has no route to knowledge except through revelation (al-sam'). He repeated the relative pronoun to draw attention to the difference between the two categories and the divergence between the two paths.

Or [they are] a group from among them, namely the believers among the People of the Book, whom he mentioned singling them out from the general category, like the mention of Gabriel and Michael after the angels, to exalt their station and to encourage others like them.

Revelation (al-inzal) is the transferring of a thing from above to below. It attaches meanings only through their attachment to the bearing substances that carry them. Perhaps the descent of the divine books upon the messengers occurs by the angel receiving it from Allah, the Exalted, in a spiritual reception, or by his taking it from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), so that it descends with him and he conveys it to the Messenger. What is meant by ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾ is the entire Qur'an and the whole Sharia. He expressed it with the past tense even though some of it was yet to be revealed, by giving precedence to what exists over what does not yet exist (taghlib). Or [it is] treating the awaited as if it had already occurred. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book sent down after Moses﴾. For the jinn did not hear all of it, and the whole Book was not yet revealed at that time. What is meant by ﴿what was sent down before you﴾ is the Torah, the Gospel, and all the earlier books. Belief in them in general is an individual obligation (fard ʿayn). With regard to the first [the Qur'an] belief in it in detail, rather than the second, is because we are bound to its particulars, which is an obligation, but it is an obligation of sufficiency (fard kifaya). This is because its being obligatory upon every individual would entail hardship and the corruption of livelihood.

﴿And in the Hereafter they are certain﴾: that is, they are certain with a certainty that removed what they had been upon, namely the belief that Paradise would be entered only by one who is a Jew or a Christian, and that the Fire would touch them only for a few counted days; and their disagreement over the bliss of Paradise, whether it is of the same kind as the bliss of this world or other than it, and over whether it is lasting or ends. The placing of the prepositional phrase first and the construction of "they are certain" with ﴿they﴾ is a pointed reference to others among the People of the Book, and to the fact that their belief regarding the matter of the Hereafter is neither accurate nor issuing from true certainty. Certainty (al-yaqin) is the perfecting of knowledge by removing doubt and suspicion from it, through reflection and inference. For this reason it is not applied to the knowledge of the Creator, nor to necessary knowledge (al-ʿulum al-darurIyya). "Al-akhira" is the feminine of "al-akhir," an attribute of the abode, as shown by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is the Last Abode﴾, so it became predominant as a noun, like "al-dunya." It is reported from Nafiʿ that he lightened it by deleting the hamza and placing its vowel on the lam. "Yuqinun" has also been read with the waw changed to a hamza because the preceding letter is dammed, treating it as if it were a damma-vowelled letter, in several instances, such as "wuqitu." A parallel to this is:

"For the love of al-Mu'qid, if (I am) toward Musa... and Ja'dah, when the flame lit up both of them."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 5:

﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord.﴾ The clause is in the place of a nominative (raf') if one of the two relative pronouns (ulaika... alladhina) is considered separated from "the God-fearing" (al-muttaqin), with it being the predicate of that. It is as if, when it was said, ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾, it was asked: "What is the matter with them, that they were singled out for this?" So it was answered with His words: ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ to the end of the verses. Otherwise, it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) with no place in the i'rab, as if it were the result of the rulings and attributes mentioned before. Or it is the answer to a questioner who said: "What is it for those described by these attributes that they are singled out for guidance?" Its parallel is: "I have done good to Zayd, your old friend, who is worthy of kindness," for the demonstrative here is like restating the described subject with its mentioned attributes, and this is more eloquent than starting a new sentence by repeating the noun alone, because it contains the explanation and summary of the cause, since the attaching of the ruling to the attribute indicates that it is what necessitates it. The meaning of elevation (al-isti'la') in ﴿upon guidance﴾ is an image of their being firmly established in guidance and settled upon it, by the condition of one who has mounted a thing and ridden it. They have expressed this in their saying: "He mounted ignorance and went astray, and sat upon the back of desire." This is only attained through exhausting thought, persistently reflecting on the proofs that have been set up, and being constant in holding oneself accountable in action. "Guidance" is indefinite (nukkira) for magnification (lil-ta'zim), as if it were intended as a kind that its reality cannot be fully reached and its measure cannot be grasped. Its parallel is the saying of the Hudhali poet:

"By the father of the bird that feeds its young in the morning... upon Khalid, you have indeed fallen upon the flesh."

Its magnification is further emphasized by the fact that Allah Most High is the One who bestows it and grants success in it. The nun (in "min rabbihim") has been assimilated into the ra' with nasal resonance (ghunna) and without nasal resonance.

﴿And those are the successful (al-muflihun).﴾ He repeated the demonstrative here to draw attention to the fact that their possession of those attributes necessitates each of the two effects, and that each of them is sufficient to distinguish them from others. He placed the conjunction (al-'atif) in the middle because the meanings of the two sentences differ here, unlike His saying: ﴿Those are like cattle; nay, they are further astray; those are the heedless﴾, for recording them as heedless and likening them to beasts are one and the same thing, so the second sentence confirms the first and therefore the conjunction is not appropriate. "Hum" is a separating pronoun (fasl) which separates the predicate from the description and emphasizes the attribution, and it conveys the restriction of the predicated subject; or it is a subject (mubtada') and "al-muflihun" is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of "ulaika." "Al-muflih" with ha' and jim means one who attains the sought object, as if he is one for whom the faces of victory have been opened. This structure, and what shares with it in the first and middle letters, such as falaqa, faladha and falia, indicates splitting (al-shaqq). Opening (al-fath) and the definiteness of "al-muflihin" serve to indicate that the God-fearing are the people whom you have heard are the successful in the Hereafter, or the reference is to what every person knows of the reality of the successful and their particular characteristics.

Caution: Consider how He, glory be to Him and exalted, drew attention to the God-fearing being singled out for attaining what not everyone attains, from various aspects: building the speech upon the demonstrative for causation together with brevity, repeating it, defining the predicate, and placing the separating pronoun in the middle, all to manifest their rank and to encourage following in their footsteps. The Wa'idiyya have held onto this regarding the eternal punishment of sinners among the people of the qibla. It is answered that what is meant by "the successful" is those who are complete in success, and this implies the absence of complete success for one who does not have their attributes, not the total absence of success for him.

(p-41) ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾. When He mentioned His special servants and the elite of His allies by the attributes that qualified them for guidance and success, He followed them with their opposites, the obstinate rebels, for whom guidance is of no benefit and for whom signs and warnings are of no avail. He did not conjoin their story to the story of the believers, as He conjoined them in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ ﴿and indeed, the wicked will be in the Blazing Fire﴾, because of the difference between them in purpose. The first was brought to mention the Book and explain its status, while the second is aimed at explaining their defiance and their immersion in misguidance. And *inna* (indeed) is among the particles that resemble the verb in the number of letters, in being built on the fatha, in being restricted to nouns, and in giving its meanings, and especially the transitive verb in that it enters upon two nouns. Therefore it operates in the secondary manner of verbs, which is putting the first part in the accusative and raising the second, signalling that it is a branch in operation and an intruder into it.

The Kufans said: the predicate before its entry was nominative by virtue of being a predicate, and that quality remains after its entry. It is required by the principle of continuity (*istishab*), so the particle does not make it nominative. It is answered that the predicate's requirement of the nominative is conditional on being unaffected, because it deviates from that in the predicate of *kana*, and that condition has ceased with its entry, so the operation of the particle is determined. Its benefit is emphasising and confirming the attribution, and for this reason an oath is introduced with it and it begins answers. It is also mentioned in contexts of doubt, like His words: ﴿And they ask you about Dhul-Qarnayn. Say: I will recite to you from him a mention﴾ ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾, and ﴿And Moses said: O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: your saying *'Abd Allah qā'im* (Abdullah is standing) is an information about his standing; *inna 'Abd Allah qā'im* is an answer to one asking about his standing; and *inna 'Abd Allah la-qā'im* is an answer to one denying his standing.

The definiteness of the relative pronoun (*al-ladhīna*) is either for a specific reference (*al-'ahd*), in which case it means particular persons such as Abu Lahab, Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and the rabbis of the Jews; or it is for the category (*al-jins*), encompassing whoever is set upon disbelief and others. From among them, He excluded those who were not persistent with what was attributed to them. Disbelief (*kufr*) linguistically means concealing a blessing. Its origin is *kafr* with a fatha, which means covering, and from it the farmer is called *kāfir*, and night is called *kāfir*, and the sheath of a fruit is called *kāfūr*. In the Sharia, it is denying what is known by necessity to be what the Messenger ﷺ brought. The wearing of the *ghiyār* (the distinctive belt) and the tightening of the *zunnār* (the sacred cord) and the like are counted as disbelief because they indicate denial, for whoever believes in the Messenger ﷺ does not dare to do them openly. This is not because they are disbelief in themselves.

The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) argued from what came in the Qur'an in the past tense as proof that it was created, since such a tense requires a prior informant of the thing reported. It is answered that this is required by the relation (*ta'alluq*), and its occurrence does not necessitate the occurrence of speech, as in the case of knowledge.

﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. This is the predicate of *inna*. *Sawā'* is a noun meaning equality, and it is used as a description, just as verbal nouns are used as descriptions. God Most High said: ﴿Come to a word that is equal between us and you﴾. It is in the nominative because it is the predicate of *inna*, and what follows it is raised by it as its subject, as if it were said: indeed those who disbelieve, your warning and its absence are equal for them. Or it is a predicate of what follows it, meaning: your warning and its absence are equal regarding them. A verb is only prevented from being predicated when it is meant in its complete sense. But if it is used and meant as the word itself, or as the general sense of the event implied by it through extension, then it is like a noun in being annexed and attributed, as in His words: ﴿And when it is said to them: believe﴾, and ﴿those who are truthful, their truthfulness﴾, and their saying: "Hearing of Mu'aydi is better than seeing him."

Here He turned from the verbal noun to the verb because the verb implies renewal, and because the interrogative hamza fits well with it, and *am* (or) follows it to establish and confirm the meaning of equality. Both were stripped of the meaning of interrogation for the sake of mere equality, just as the vocative particles were stripped of the meaning of request for the sake of mere specification, as in their saying: "O Allah, forgive us, O company."

The warning (*indhār*) is frightening, and it is meant as frightening from the punishment of God. He limited it to this without glad tidings because it strikes the heart more and has a stronger effect on the soul, since averting harm is more important than bringing benefit. So when warning does not benefit them, glad tidings would be even less fitting.

It was read as ﴿*a-anzarta-hum*﴾ with the two hamzas both realised, and with the second softened to a sound between the two (*bayna bayna*), and changed to an alif. The last of these is a solecism, because a moving letter is not changed, and because it leads to joining two sukuns against its rule. It was also read with an alif inserted between them, both realised; with that alif and the second hamza softened between the two; with the interrogative hamza dropped; and with it dropped and its vowel transferred onto the preceding unvowelled letter.

﴿They will not believe﴾. This is a sentence explaining the generality of what precedes it regarding what equality applies to, so it has no place in grammatical analysis (*i'rāb*). Or it is an emphatic circumstantial clause. Or it is a substitute. Or it is the predicate of *inna*, and the sentence before it is an interjection stating the cause of the ruling.

This verse is among the proofs used by those who permit charging people with what is impossible. He, glorified and exalted, informed about them that they will not believe, and He commanded them to believe. So if they believed, His report would become false, and their belief would include belief that they will not believe, so the two opposites would combine. The truth is that charging with what is impossible in itself, though rationally permissible, since rulings do not require a purpose, especially compliance, nevertheless does not occur, as shown by induction. Informing about the occurrence or non-occurrence of a thing does not negate the capacity to do it, just as His informing about what He does, or what the servant does by his own choice. The benefit of warning after knowing that it will not benefit them is establishing the proof against them, and the Messenger gaining the merit of conveying the message. For this reason He said "It is the same for them," and did not say "the same for you," just as He said to the idol worshippers: ﴿It is the same for you whether you call upon them or you are silent﴾.

In the verse there is information about the unseen as it actually is, if by the relative pronoun are meant particular persons. In that case it is among the miracles.

﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering.﴾ This is an explanation of the preceding judgment and a statement of what it entails.

Al-khatm (الختم) means al-katm (الكتم, concealment). The term was applied to securing something by pressing a seal (al-khatam) upon it, because it conceals the thing. Al-bulugh (البلوغ, reaching) is its end, in view of the fact that it is the last act performed in securing it. Al-ghishawah (الغشاوة) is on the pattern of fi'alah, from ghashahu, meaning he covered it. The pattern denotes that which envelops a thing, like al-'isabah (the head-band) and al-'imamah (the turban). Neither sealing nor covering is literal. What is meant by them is that Allah produces in their souls a state that trains them to prefer disbelief and sins, and to find faith and acts of obedience repugnant, because of their misguidance, their immersion in blind imitation (taqlid), and their turning away from sound reflection. Thus their hearts are made such that the truth cannot penetrate them, and their hearing recoils from listening to it, so that it is as if it were sealed. Their eyes do not perceive the signs set out for them in themselves and in the horizons as the eyes of those who see clearly perceive them, so it is as if they were covered over, and a barrier is placed between them and seeing. He called this, by way of metaphor, a seal and a covering. Or, he likened their hearts and their sense faculties, which are impaired, to things upon which a barrier was placed between them and their benefit, and called it a seal and a covering.

He expressed the production of this state by sealing (al-tab') in His saying, ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts and their hearing and their sight﴾. He expressed it by neglect (al-ighfal) in His saying, ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made neglectful of Our remembrance﴾, and by hardening (al-iqsa') in His saying, ﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾. This is because all contingent things are ultimately dependent upon Allah, the Exalted, and occur by His power, so they are ascribed to Him. And it is also because these things are caused by what they have committed, as evidenced by His saying, ﴿Rather, Allah has sealed upon them because of their disbelief﴾, and His saying, ﴿That is because they believed and then disbelieved, so their hearts were sealed﴾. The verse came in condemning them for the abomination of their attribute and the grimness of their outcome.

The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) were perplexed by this verse and mentioned several interpretive possibilities:

First: when these people turned away from the truth and this became firmly rooted in their hearts until it became like a natural disposition for them, it was likened to an innate, created attribute upon which they were constituted.

Second: what is meant is a depiction of the state of their hearts as the hearts of beasts, which Allah created devoid of understanding. Or, the hearts are presumed to have a seal set upon them by Allah. A parallel to this is the expression "the valley carried him off" (sala bihi al-wadi), meaning he perished, and "the phoenix carried him off" (tarat bihi al-'anqa'), meaning his absence was prolonged.

Third: in reality that act is the doing of the devil or the disbeliever, but since its emanation from him is by Allah's empowering him to do it, it is attributed to Allah in the manner of ascribing an act to the one who causes it.

Fourth: when their roots (a'raq) became firmly entrenched in disbelief and so solidified that no path remained to attaining their faith except compulsion and coercion, and then He did not compel them, preserving the purpose of obligation (taklif), He expressed His abandoning of them by the word "seal," for it blocks their faith. This carries an indication of the continuation of their affair in error and the extremity of their immersion in misguidance and transgression.

Fifth: that it is a report of what the disbelievers used to say, namely: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings from what you call us to, and in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a barrier﴾, mocking them and deriding them, like His saying, ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not...﴾, the verse.

Sixth: that this refers to the Hereafter, and it is reported in the past tense because of its certainty and the assurance of its occurrence. His saying supports this: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind and mute and deaf﴾.

Seventh: that what is meant by the seal is marking their hearts with a mark that the angels recognize, so they hate them and turn away from them. On this method is our discourse and their discourse regarding what is ascribed to Allah, the Exalted, of sealing, misguidance, and the like.

﴿And upon their hearing﴾ is conjoined to "upon their hearts," on the basis of His saying, ﴿And Allah sealed upon his hearing and his heart﴾, and for the consensus (al-wifaq) on pausing upon it. Also, because the two (hearing and heart) share in perception from all directions, He made what prevents them from their specific function a seal, which prevents from all directions. The sight's perception of what is specific to the direction of facing, He made what prevents it from its function a covering specific to that direction. He repeated the preposition (al-jarr) to make it more indicative of the intensity of the seal in both places and of the independence of each of them in the ruling. He made "hearing" singular (al-sam') for safety from confusion and in consideration of the origin, for it is a verbal noun in its root, and verbal nouns are not pluralized. Or, there is an elided modifier, as in "and upon the faculties of their hearing."

Al-absar (الأبصار) is the plural of basar, which is the perception of the eye. It may be used metaphorically for the faculty of sight, and for the organ, and likewise hearing (al-sam'). Perhaps what is meant by them in the verse is the organ, because it is more suitable to sealing and covering. By "heart" is meant that which is the locus of knowledge, and it may also be used to mean intellect and understanding, as He said, ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾. The inclination of the sad (al-sad) toward the ya' (in pronunciation of the letters) was permitted because the kasra on the ra' overcomes the elevated (al-musta'liyah) letter due to the repetition (al-takrir) it contains.

Ghishawatun (غشاوة) is in the nominative by being the subject (al-ibtida') according to Sibawayh, and in the nominative by the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) according to al-Akhfash. Its being conjoined to the verbal sentence supports this. It was also read in the accusative, on the assumption of "and He made upon their eyes a covering," or by eliding the preposition and attaching the seal directly to it, meaning: "and He sealed upon their eyes with a covering." It was read with a damma and raf', and with a fatha and nasb, and both are dialectal forms of it. The reading "ghishwatun" with a kasra is nominative, and with a fatha is nominative and accusative. The reading "'ashawatun" with an unpointed 'ayn is also attested.

﴿And for them is a great punishment﴾ is a threat and an explanation of what they deserve. Al-'adhab (العذاب, punishment) is like al-nakal (النكال, deterrent punishment) in pattern and meaning. One says: "'adhaba 'an al-shay'" and "nakala 'anhu" when he refrained from it. From this comes "al-ma' al-'adhb" (sweet water), because it quells thirst and restrains it, and for this reason it is called "nuqakh" and "furat." Then the usage broadened and it was applied to every harmful pain even if it is not a deterrent, that is, a punishment that deters the offender from repetition. So it is more general than both. It is said that its derivation is from ta'dhib, which is the removal of sweetness, like ta'diyah (rendering something impure) and tamrid (causing sickness). Al-'azim (العظيم, great) is the opposite of al-haqir (the contemptible), and al-kabir (the big) is the opposite of al-saghir (the small). Just as the contemptible is below the small, the great is above the big. The description of a thing with it means that when it is compared with all that is of its kind, all of them fall short of it and are diminished in comparison to it. The indefiniteness (al-tankir) in the verse means that over their eyes is a kind of covering that is not what people commonly know, namely, blindness to the signs. And for them is a kind of great pain whose true nature none knows except Allah.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 8:

﴿And among the people are those who say, "We believe in God and the Last Day,"﴾ When He, glory be to Him and exalted, began by describing the state of the Book and proceeded to explain it, He mentioned the believers who sincerely devoted their religion to God, whose hearts agreed with their tongues in it. He then followed them with their opposites, those who purely embraced disbelief, outwardly and inwardly, and did not turn toward faith in the slightest. Then He mentioned a third category, the wavering between the two categories, and they are those who believed with their mouths while their hearts did not believe. This completes the division. They are the most wicked of the disbelievers and the most hateful to God, because they disguised disbelief and mixed it with deception and mockery. For this reason He lengthened the description of their wickedness and ignorance, mocked them, scorned their deeds, marked their blindness and transgression, struck examples for them, and revealed concerning them ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾. Their whole story is joined to the story of the persistent disbelievers.

The word *al-nās* (the people) originally was *unās*, based on their saying *insān*, *anas* and *anāsī*. The hamza was dropped, as in the word *lawaqah*, and the definite article was substituted for it, which is why the two are hardly ever combined. As for the line of poetry: (p-44) "Indeed the fates look down upon the people who are secure," it is anomalous. *Al-nās* here is a collective noun like *rijāl*, since the pattern *fa‘āl* is not established among the patterns of plurals. It is derived from *anisa* (to be sociable), because they keep company with their like, or from *ānasa* (to perceive), because they are visible and observant. For this reason they were named *bashar* (human beings), just as the jinn were named *jinn* because they are hidden. The *alif-lām* in *al-nās* is for the category, and *min* is descriptive, since there is no specific reference. So it is as if He said: "And among the people are people who say..." Or the *alif-lām* is for a known reference, and the known are those who disbelieved. *Man* is then a relative pronoun, meaning Ibn Ubayy, his companions and his peers. Insofar as they were determined upon hypocrisy, they entered the ranks of the disbelievers whose hearts are sealed. Their being singled out by additions they made to disbelief does not prevent their inclusion under this category, since categories are diversified by additions in which their parts differ. On this view, the verse is a division of the second category.

The specific mention of belief in God and the Last Day singles out what is the greatest aim of faith, and it is a claim that they had obtained faith from both its sides and encompassed its two ends. It also indicates that they are hypocrites even in what they think is their sincere belief, so how much more so in what they intend as hypocrisy. The people were Jews, and they believed in God and the Last Day with a belief that was no belief at all, because they held to anthropomorphism, the taking of a son (for God), that no one but themselves would enter Paradise, and that the Fire would touch them only for a few counted days, and similar notions. They regarded the believers as having believed in the same way as they did. This is a clarification of the multiplication of their wickedness and their excess in disbelief, because what they said, if it had come from them not in the manner of deception and hypocrisy, while their creed was their creed, would not have been belief. How much more so when they said it as disguise over the Muslims and as mockery of them. In the repetition of the *bāʾ* (in *bi-llāhi* and *bi-l-yawmi*) there is a claim of belief in each one in an original and firm manner.

*Al-qawl* (saying) is the uttering of what conveys meaning. It is also used to mean the thing said, to mean the concept in the soul that is expressed by the word, and, metaphorically, to mean an opinion or a doctrine. *Al-yawm al-ākhir* (the Last Day) is meant as the period from the gathering (*al-ḥashr*) onward without end, or until the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, since that is the last of the limited periods.

﴿But they are not believers﴾ This is a denial of what they claimed and a negation of what they professed to affirm. The original form would have been *wa-mā āmanū* (and they did not believe), to match their statement in its explicit reference to the act rather than the agent. But He reversed it for emphasis, or for intensity in denial, because removing their very selves from the ranks of believers is more forceful than negating faith from them in the past tense. For this reason He emphasized the negation with the *bāʾ* and stated faith absolutely, to mean that they have no share in faith whatsoever. It is also possible that it be restricted by what they were restricted by, since it is the answer to it.

The verse indicates that whoever claims faith while his heart contradicts his tongue regarding belief is not a believer, because whoever utters the two testimonies while his heart is empty of what agrees with them or contradicts them is not a believer. The disagreement with the Karramiyya (a sect) concerns the second point, so it is not a valid proof against them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 9:

﴿They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe﴾. Al-khud' (deception) is that you make another person imagine something contrary to what you conceal of harm, in order to divert him from what he is engaged in and from what he is about to do, from the saying of the Arabs: "The dabb (lizard) deceived (khada'a)," when it hides itself in its burrow; and a dabb is khadi' and khidi' when it makes the hunter (al-harish) imagine that it is facing him, and then it comes out from another door. Its root meaning is concealment, and from it come al-makhda' (the inner chamber of a storehouse) and al-akhda'an (the two hidden veins in the neck). Al-mukhadaʿa (mutual deception) occurs between two parties.

Their deceiving Allah is not in its literal sense, because nothing hidden is concealed from Him, and because they did not intend to deceive Him. Rather, the meaning is either: deceiving His Messenger, with the omission of the noun (al-mudaf) being understood; or that dealing with the Messenger is dealing with Allah, insofar as he is His deputy, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ and ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are pledging allegiance only to Allah﴾. Or: the form of their conduct toward Allah, the Exalted, is the display of faith and the concealment of disbelief, while Allah's treatment of them is to apply to them the rulings of the Muslims, though they are in His sight the most wicked of the disbelievers and the people of the lowest level of the Fire, as a gradual leading on (istidraj) for them, and in obedience to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers' obedience to the command of Allah regarding concealing their state and applying to them the ruling of Islam, matching them in their conduct, the form of the conduct of those who deceive one another.

It is possible that ﴿yukhadi'una﴾ is meant as yakhda'una (they deceive), since it serves as an explanation of "they say," or as a resumption (istinaf) mentioning the purpose behind it. However, it was expressed in the pattern of فاعل (fa'ala) for mughalaba (contest), since the pattern was for contest, and an action, when it is contested, is more forceful than when it occurs without the opposition of an opponent or rival; the pattern retained that sense. This is supported by the reading of those who read (yakhda'una). Their purpose in this was to ward off from themselves what the other disbelievers might inflict upon them, to receive the honour and gifts given to the believers, to mix with the Muslims so that they might learn their secrets and spread them to their enemies, and other aims and intentions.

(And they deceive none but themselves) is the reading of Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr. The meaning: the circle of deception returns to them, and its harm falls upon them. Or: in this they deceived themselves, since they deluded themselves by it. And their own selves deceived them, when they whispered to them empty hopes and drove them to deceive the One from whom no hidden thing is concealed.

The rest read ﴿wa-ma yakhda'una﴾, because deception cannot be conceived except between two parties. It was also read yakh'da'una from khada'a, and yukhda'una meaning yakhtadi'una, and yukhda'una and yukhadi'una in the passive voice. The word (anfusahum) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition. Al-nafs is the essence and reality of a thing. Then it was applied to the spirit, because the life of a living being is by it; to the heart, because it is the locus of the spirit or what is attached to it; to the blood, because the body's subsistence is by it; to water, because of the intense need for it; and to opinion, in the saying of people: "So-and-so consults his nafs," because it emanates from it, or because it resembles an entity that commands him and advises him. The intended meaning of al-anfus here is their very selves, though it is possible to take them as their spirits and opinions.

﴿And they perceive not﴾ means they do not sense this, because of the persistence of their heedlessness. He made the reaching of the calamity of deception and the return of its harm to them, in its manifestness, like the perceptible thing that is hidden only from one whose senses are defective. Al-shu'ur is perception (al-ihsas), and the senses of a human being are his mashaʿir, and its root is al-shi'r (poetry, i.e. subtle perception), and from it comes al-shi'ar (the distinctive sign or emblem).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 10:

﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah has increased their disease﴾ Al-maraḍ (disease) is literally that which befalls the body, taking it out of the balance proper to it and causing disorder in its functions. It is used figuratively for the psychological conditions that impair their perfection, such as ignorance, corrupt belief, envy, rancour, and love of sins, because these prevent the attainment of virtues or lead to the loss of the true, eternal life. The noble verse admits both meanings: their hearts were in pain, burning over what had escaped them of leadership, and envious of what they saw of the firm establishment of the Messenger's affair (ﷺ) and the elevation of his station day by day. Allah increased their grief by what He increased of the elevation of his affair and the exaltation of his remembrance. Their souls were characterised by disbelief, corrupt belief, enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ), and the like, and Allah, glorified and exalted is He, increased that by the seal (of hearts). Or (the increase is) by the multiplication of obligations, the repetition of revelation, and the multiplication of victory. The attribution of the increase to Allah, the Exalted, is because He is the cause of the one who does it, and its attribution to the surah in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿so it increased them in filth﴾, is because it was the means.

It is possible that the disease means what entered their hearts of cowardice and weakness when they witnessed the strength of the Muslims and the support Allah, the Exalted, gave them with the angels, and He cast terror into their hearts. Its increase is by the multiplication of what was increased for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in victory over the enemies and expansion in the lands.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ That is, painful. It is said: alima (he suffered pain), so he is alim (painful), like wajia (he was hurt), so he is wajiʿ (wounded). The punishment is described with it for emphasis, as in his saying:

*Their greeting among them is a painful blow*

following the manner of their saying: "jadda jadduhu" (his fortune was great). ﴿Because they used to lie﴾ ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī recited it (as "yukdhibūna" in the sense of "kānū yakdhibūna"? no: "kānū kadhabū" form) — the meaning being "because of their lying," or "in exchange for it," as a recompense for them, which is their saying, "We believe." The rest recited ﴿yakdhibūna﴾, from kadhdhabahu, because they used to deny the Messenger (peace be upon him) in their hearts, and when they were alone with their devils. Or from kadhdhaba, which is for emphasis or multiplication, like bayyana al-shayʾ (he made the thing clear) and mawwatat al-bahaʾim (he made the animals die). Or from kadhaba, as a wild animal does when it runs a course and stops to look behind it, for the hypocrite is perplexed and hesitant.

Lying (kadhib) is reporting something contrary to how it actually is. It is entirely forbidden, because it is the cause given for deserving punishment, being ordered upon it (p-46). What is narrated, that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) told three lies, is to be understood as allusion (taʿrīḍ). However, since it resembled lying in its form, it was named by it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 11:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾ is conjoined with ﴿they lie﴾ or with (they say). As for what is narrated from Salman (may Allah be pleased with him), that the people of this verse have not yet come, perhaps he meant by it that its people are not only those who existed at that time, but that there will also come after them those whose condition is their condition, because the verse is connected to what precedes it by the pronoun within it. Corruption (al-fasad) is the departure of a thing from balance (al-i'tidal). Its opposite is righteousness (al-salah), and both encompass every harmful and beneficial thing.

Among their corruption on the earth was the stirring up of wars and strife by deceiving the Muslims, and aiding the disbelievers against them by divulging secrets to them, for that leads to the corruption of what is on the earth of people, animals and tilth.

Among it also is the public display of sins and the belittling of the religion, for neglecting the laws and turning away from them necessitates chaos and disorder (al-haraj wa'l-maraj) and disrupts the order of the world. The speaker is Allah the Exalted, or the Messenger (ﷺ), or some of the believers. Al-Kisa'i and Hisham read (qila) with the isham of the first damma (a partial rounding of the vowel).

﴿They say, "We are only reformers."﴾ This is the answer to (idha, "when"), a rejection of the one giving counsel, by way of emphasis. The meaning is that it is not valid to address us with that, for our business is nothing but reform, and our state is purely free of any admixture of corruption, because (innama, "only") restricts what it precedes to what follows it, like: innama Zayd munṭaliq ("Zayd is only departing") and innama yanṭaliq Zayd ("only Zayd departs"). They said that only because they perceived corruption in the form of reform due to the sickness in their hearts, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Is one whose evil deed has been made attractive to him, so that he sees it as good...?﴾

Verily they are the corruptors, but they do not perceive. ﴿ألا إنَّهم هُمُ المُفْسِدُونَ ولَكِنْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ is a rebuttal of what they claimed, the most emphatic rebuttal. It begins with a resumptive construction and is introduced with two particles of emphasis (ta'kid):

(ألا) is the alerting particle, which signals the certainty of what follows. When the hamza of interrogation (istifham) used for denial (inkar) enters upon a negation, it conveys affirmation. A parallel is ﴿ألَيْسَ ذَلِكَ بِقادِرٍ﴾ ("Is not He able to do that?"). For this reason, a sentence after it hardly ever occurs except when introduced by what oaths are introduced with. Its sister is (أمّا), which is among the forerunners of the oath. (إنَّ) affirms the attribution. The definite predicate (ta'rif al-khabar) and the interposed separating pronoun (damir al-fasl) serve to refute what is implied in their statement ﴿إنَّما نَحْنُ مُصْلِحُونَ﴾ ("We are only reformers"), namely an implicit insinuation against the believers. The corrective contrast (istidrak) with ﴿لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ ("but they do not perceive") completes the refutation.
