﴿وَإذا قِيلَ لَهم آمِنُوا﴾ مِن تَمامِ النُّصْحِ والإرْشادِ فَإنَّ كَمالَ الإيمانِ بِمَجْمُوعِ الأمْرَيْنِ: الإعْراضِ عَمّا لا يَنْبَغِي وهو المَقْصُودُ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿لا تُفْسِدُوا﴾، والإتْيانِ بِما يَنْبَغِي وهو المَطْلُوبُ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿آمِنُوا﴾.

﴿كَما آمَنَ النّاسُ﴾ في حَيِّزِ النَّصْبِ عَلى المَصْدَرِ (the accusative of the verbal noun, masdar), وما مَصْدَرِيَّةٌ أوْ كافَّةٌ مِثْلُها في رُبَّما (ma is either verbal, forming a masdar, or restrictive, like it in rubba-ma), واللّامُ في النّاسِ لِلْجِنْسِ (the lam of genus) والمُرادُ بِهِ الكامِلُونَ في الإنْسانِيَّةِ العامِلُونَ بِقَضِيَّةِ العَقْلِ، فَإنَّ اسْمَ الجِنْسِ كَما يُسْتَعْمَلُ لِمُسَمّاهُ مُطْلَقًا يُسْتَعْمَلُ لِما يَسْتَجْمِعُ المَعانِيَ المَخْصُوصَةَ بِهِ والمَقْصُودَةَ مِنهُ، ولِذَلِكَ يُسْلَبُ عَنْ غَيْرِهِ فَيُقالُ: زَيْدٌ لَيْسَ بِإنْسانٍ، ومِن هَذا البابِ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ ونَحْوُهُ وقَدْ جَمَعَهُما الشّاعِرُ في قَوْلِهِ:

؎ إذِ النّاسُ ناسٌ والزَّمانُ زَمانُ

أوْ لِلْعَهْدِ (the lam of a known referent), والمُرادُ بِهِ الرَّسُولُ ﷺ ومَن مَعَهُ. أوْ مَن آمَنَ مِن أهْلِ جِلْدَتِهِمْ كابْنِ سَلامِ وأصْحابِهِ، (p-47)والمَعْنى آمَنُوا إيمانًا مَقْرُونًا بِالإخْلاصِ مُتَمَحِّضًا عَنْ شَوائِبِ النِّفاقِ مُماثِلًا لِإيمانِهِمْ، واسْتَدَلَّ بِهِ عَلى قَبُولِ تَوْبَةِ الزِّنْدِيقِ وأنَّ الإقْرارَ بِاللِّسانِ إيمانٌ وإنْ لَمْ يُفِدِ التَّقْيِيدَ.

﴿قالُوا أنُؤْمِنُ كَما آمَنَ السُّفَهاءُ﴾ الهَمْزَةُ فِيهِ لِلْإنْكارِ، واللّامُ مُشارٌ بِها إلى النّاسِ، أوِ الجِنْسِ بِأسْرِهِ وهم مُنْدَرِجُونَ فِيهِ عَلى زَعْمِهِمْ، وإنَّما سَفَّهُوهم لِاعْتِقادِهِمْ فَسادَ رَأْيِهِمْ، أوْ لِتَحْقِيرِ شَأْنِهِمْ، فَإنَّ أكْثَرَ المُؤْمِنِينَ كانُوا فُقَراءَ ومِنهم مَوالِي: كَصُهَيْبٍ وبِلالٍ، أوْ لِلتَّجَلُّدِ وعَدَمِ المُبالاةِ بِمَن آمَنُ مِنهم إنْ فُسِّرَ النّاسُ بِعَبْدِ اللَّهِ بْنِ سَلامٍ وأشْياعِهِ. والسَّفَهُ: خِفَّةٌ وسَخافَةُ رَأْيٍ يَقْتَضِيهِما نُقْصانُ العَقْلِ، والحِلْمُ يُقابِلُهُ.

﴿أَلا إنَّهم هُمُ السُّفَهاءُ ولَكِنْ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ رَدٌّ ومُبالَغَةٌ في تَجْهِيلِهِمْ، فَإنَّ الجاهِلَ بِجَهْلِهِ الجازِمِ عَلى خِلافِ ما هو الواقِعُ أعْظَمُ ضَلالَةً وأتَمُّ جَهالَةً مِنَ المُتَوَقِّفِ المُعْتَرِفِ بِجَهْلِهِ، فَإنَّهُ رُبَّما يُعْذَرُ وتَنْفَعُهُ الآياتُ والنُّذُرُ، وإنَّما فُصِّلَتِ الآيَةُ بِ﴿لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ والَّتِي قَبْلَها بِ﴿لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ لِأنَّهُ أكْثَرُ طِباقًا لِذِكْرِ السَّفَهِ، ولِأنَّ الوُقُوفَ عَلى أمْرِ الدِّينِ والتَّمْيِيزَ بَيْنَ الحَقِّ والباطِلِ مِمّا يَفْتَقِرُ إلى نَظَرٍ وفِكْرٍ. وأمّا النِّفاقُ وما فِيهِ مِنَ الفِتَنِ والفَسادِ فَإنَّما يُدْرَكُ بِأدْنى تَفَطُّنٍ وتَأمُّلٍ فِيما يُشاهَدُ مِن أقْوالِهِمْ وأفْعالِهِمْ.

**Al-Baydawi, Anwar al-Tanzil, on surah 2, verse 14:**

﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe."﴾ This explains how they deal with the believers and with the disbelievers. What the story opened with (the statement about the hypocrites' condition) is here presented to explain their creed and to prepare the ground for their hypocrisy (nifaq, the outward display of faith concealing disbelief), so it is not a repetition.

It is narrated that Ibn Ubayy and his companions met a group of the Companions. He said to his people: "Watch how I will turn these fools away from you." He took the hand of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "Welcome to the Sincere One (al-Siddiq), the master of the Banu Taym, the elder of Islam, the second of the Messenger of Allah in the cave, the one who gave his soul and his wealth to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Then he took the hand of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "Welcome to the master of the Banu 'Adi, al-Faruq (the Distinguisher), strong in his religion, the one who gave his soul and his wealth to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Then he took the hand of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "Welcome, O cousin of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his son-in-law, master of the Banu Hashim, except for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." Then the verse was revealed.

Al-liqa' (meeting) means encountering and coming upon. One says laqitahu and laqa'tuhu (both forms of the verb لَقِيتُهُ and لاقَيْتُهُ) when you come upon him and face him. From the same root is alqaytuhu, when you cast him down, because by casting him down you put him in a place where he is met.

﴿And when they go apart to their shayatin (satans, here meaning their leaders)﴾: from khalawtu bi-fulan and khalawtu ilayhi (the verbs خَلَوْتُ بِفُلانٍ وإلَيْهِ), meaning when you are alone with him. Or it derives from khalaka dhamm, meaning "he passed you by and left you," and from it comes "the past generations" (al-qurun al-khaliyah). Or it derives from khalawtu bihi, meaning "I mocked him," and it takes ila because it implies the sense of reporting (al-infa'). The meaning of "their shayatin" is those who matched Satan in their defiance. These are the ones who openly display their disbelief. Attributing them to "their" indicates partnership in disbelief. Or it means the senior hypocrites and those who had the junior ones say so.

Sibawayh treated its nun (ن in shayatin) as sometimes original, deriving the word from shatana (شَطَنَ), meaning "to be far away," since such a person is far from righteousness; their saying tashaytana (تَشَيْطَنَ, "he acted like a satan") supports this. Other times it is taken as an added letter, deriving the word from shata (شاطَ), meaning "to be void," and among its names is al-batil (falsehood).

﴿They say, "Indeed we are with you."﴾ That is, in religion and belief. They addressed the believers with a verbal sentence (al-jumlah al-fi'liyyah, a sentence built on a verb) and the satans with a nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah, a sentence built on a noun and predicate) emphasized with inna (إنّا). This is because with the first they intended to claim that they had newly produced faith, and with the second they intended to confirm their steadfastness in what they had been upon. Also, they had no motive from conviction or sincere desire for what they said to the believers, and the claim of perfect faith was not likely to be accepted by the believers among the Muhajirun and the Ansar, unlike what they said to the disbelievers.

﴿We are only mockers.﴾ This is an emphasis of what came before, because one who mocks something and treats it lightly persists in its opposite. Or it is a substitute (badal) for it, because whoever belittles Islam has magnified disbelief. Or it is a new independent statement (isti'naf), as if the satans said to them, after they said "Indeed we are with you": "If that is true, then why do you agree with the believers and claim faith?" And they answered with this.

Al-istihza' (mockery) is ridicule and making light of something. One says haziʼtu and istahzaʼtu (هَزِئْتُ واسْتَهْزَأْتُ) with the same meaning, like ajibtu and istajabtu. Its root meaning is lightness, from al-hazʼ, which is quick killing. One says hazaʼa fulan when he dies on the spot, and his she-camel tahza' bihi, meaning she hastens and moves lightly.(p-48)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 15:

﴿Allah mocks them﴾: He requites them for their mockery. The requital of mockery is named by its name, just as the requital of an evil deed is called an evil deed, either for the sake of matching word with word, or because it is similar to it in measure, or because the harm of the mockery returns upon them, so that He is as one who mocks them, or because He inflicts upon them the abasement and humiliation that are the necessary consequence of mockery, or the purpose of it; or He treats them as one who mocks is treated. In this world, this is by applying to them the rulings of the Muslims, and by drawing them on gradually (istidraj) through respite and an increase in blessings while they persist in transgression. In the Hereafter, it is by opening for them, while they are in the Fire, a door to the Garden, so that they hasten toward it; when they reach it, the door is shut upon them. This is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾. It was phrased as a new sentence (isti'naf) and not joined by a conjunction, to show that Allah, exalted is He, took upon Himself their requital, and did not make the believers need to oppose them, and that their mockery is of no account in comparison with what Allah, exalted is He, does to them. Perhaps He did not say "Allah is a mocker of them" so as to correspond to their saying, indicating that the mockery occurs moment by moment and is renewed from time to time; and thus were Allah's inflictions upon them, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not see that they are tried every year once or twice?﴾.

﴿And He extends for them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾: from madda al-jaysh and amadda-hu, when he increased it and strengthened it; and from it: "madadtu al-siraja" and "al-arda," when you improve them with oil and manure. It is not from the extension (madd) in lifespan, for that is transitive with the preposition "lam," as in amla lahu. The reading of Ibn Kathir supports this: ﴿wa-yamuddu-hum﴾. As for the Mu'tazilah, since it was impossible for them to keep the speech on its apparent meaning, they said: when Allah, exalted is He, withheld from them His favours which He bestows upon the believers, and forsook them because of their disbelief and persistence, and blocked the paths of success for themselves, their hearts increased in rust and darkness because of it, just as the hearts of the believers increase in expansion and light; and the Satan was enabled to lead them astray, so he increased them in transgression. This was ascribed to Allah, exalted is He, as the ascription of an act to its cause, metaphorically; and He attributed the transgression to them, lest it be supposed that the ascription of the act to Him is literal. The proof of this is that when He ascribed the extension to the devils, He made the error absolute, saying: ﴿and their brothers extend them in error﴾. Or its origin is "yamuddu lahum," meaning "yumli lahum" (He gives them respite), and "yamuddu fi a'marihim" (He extends their lifespans), so that they might take heed and obey; but they only increased in transgression and blindness. So the "lam" was omitted and the verb was made transitive by itself, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Musa chose his people﴾. Or the estimate is: He extends for them for their betterment, and yet they wander blindly in their transgression. Transgression, with a damma or kasra, is like luqyan; and transgression is going beyond the limit in obstinacy and excess in disbelief, and its origin is passing a thing beyond its place. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, when the water overflowed, We carried you﴾. Blindness (al-'amah) in insight is like blindness (al-'ama) in sight, and it is bewilderment in a matter; one says: "a man 'amih and 'amih," and "a land 'amha' with no landmark in it." He said:

"Blind to guidance among the ignorant, the bewildered"

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 16:

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance.﴾ They chose it over it and substituted it for it. Its root meaning is the paying of a price to obtain what is sought of concrete goods. If one of the two exchanged items is cash (naḍḍ, i.e., gold or silver coin), it is determined that it is the price, since it is not sought for its own sake to be a price; paying it is shira' (purchase). Otherwise, whichever of the two exchanged items you conceive in the form of the price, the one who pays it is the buyer (mushtari) and the one who takes it is the seller (bA'i'). For this reason the two words (shira' and bay') are counted among the antonyms (al-aḍdad, words with opposite meanings). Then the word was borrowed for turning away from what is in one's hand while obtaining something else by it, whether the thing is an abstract meaning or a concrete object. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I took the whole head, bald-patched, and with the clear, gapped front teeth,
And with the long-lived, the long life of Jayдar, as the Muslim bought when he became a Christian."

Then its usage was extended so that it is employed for desiring to turn away from a thing in hope of something else. The meaning is that they neglected the guidance which Allah had placed for them through the natural disposition (fitrah) upon which He created mankind, while obtaining the error to which they went. Or: they chose error and preferred it over guidance. (p-49) ﴿So their commerce did not profit.﴾ This is a tarshih (nurturing) of the metaphor: when he used "purchase" for their dealings, he followed it with what resembles it, as an illustration of their loss. Similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"When I saw the eagle overpowering Ibn Da'yah, and nesting in its two nests, my chest was stirred for him."

Commerce (tijarah) is seeking profit through buying and selling. Profit (ribh) is the surplus over the capital, and for this reason it is called shaff. Attributing it to commerce, though it belongs to its practitioners, is an extended usage because it is connected to the doer, or because commerce resembles it in that it is the cause of profit and loss.

﴿Nor were they guided﴾ to the paths of commerce, for the purpose of commerce is the safety of the capital and the profit. These people have lost both aims, because their capital was the sound natural disposition and pure reason. When they held these errors as beliefs, their readiness was nullified, their reason was corrupted, and they had no capital left by which to reach the discovery of truth and the attainment of perfection. Thus they remained losers, despairing of profit, having lost the principal.

**﴿Their similitude is that of one who kindled a fire﴾**. When He had described the reality of their state, He followed it with a parable (ḍarb al-mathal) to add clarity and confirmation, for it has a stronger effect on the heart and more effectively silences the most stubborn opponent, since it shows you the imagined made real and the intelligible made sensible. For this reason God has multiplied parables in His Books, and they are widespread in the speech of the prophets and the wise. The word *mathal* originally means "counterpart" (*naẓīr*), as in *mathal*, *mithl*, and *mathīl*, like *shabah*, *shibh*, and *shabīh*. Then the term was applied to a well-known saying whose occasion of use is well known, and only something strange is used as a parable. For this reason it has been preserved from alteration. It was then borrowed for any state, story, or attribute that is significant and has something strange about it, as in His saying, ﴿The similitude of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, and His saying, ﴿And to God belongs the highest similitude﴾.

The meaning is: their state, which is wondrous in its matter, is like the state of one who kindled a fire. *Alladhī* means *alladhīna* (those who), as in His saying, ﴿and you plunged as those who plunged﴾, if the pronoun in *bi-nūrihim* is taken to refer to the group. The reason this is permissible, while it is not permissible to put the singular active participle in place of the plural, is that the relative (*alladhī*) is not itself the object of description; rather, the clause that follows it, its *ṣila* (relative clause), is what serves as the link to describing the definiteness. It is not a complete noun but is like a part of one. Its rule is that it is not pluralized, just as its sisters (the other relative pronouns) are not pluralized. It is used identically for singular and plural. *Alladhīna* is not its sound plural (*jam' muṣaḥḥaḥ*); rather, it is a form with an added element, added for the sake of added meaning. For this reason it always takes the *yā'* in the eloquent dialect in which the revelation was sent down. Because it is extended by its relative clause, it deserves lightening, and for this reason it was carried to excess: its *yā'* was deleted and then the vowel was made a kasra, and then it was restricted to the *lām* in the forms of the active and passive participles. Or it is intended to denote the genus of those who kindle, or the group that kindled. *Al-istiqād* means seeking fuel and striving to obtain it, and it is the blazing of fire and the rising of its flame. The derivation of *nār* (fire) is from *nāra yanūru nawran*, meaning "to move about," because there is motion and agitation in it.

**﴿So when it lit up what was around him﴾**. That is, the fire lit up what was around the one who kindled it, if you make it transitive (*muta'addiyah*). Otherwise, it is possible for it to be attributed to *mā* (what), and the feminine form is because "what was around him" refers to things and places; or it is attributed to the pronoun of the fire. *Mā* is a relative pronoun in the sense of "places," in the accusative as an adverbial of place, or it is superfluous (*mazīdah*). *Ḥawlahu* is an adverbial of place. The formation of *ḥawl* is for turning around, and a year is called *ḥawl* because it revolves.

**﴿God took away their light﴾**. This is the answer to *lammā* (when). The pronoun refers to *alladhī*, and it is plural for the sake of conveying its meaning. On this basis, He said *bi-nūrihim* ("their light") and did not say *bi-nārihim* ("their fire"), because light is what is intended by kindling it. Or it is a resumptive clause (*isti'nāf*), answering the objection of a questioner who says: "What is the matter with them, that their state has been likened to the state of one who kindled a fire whose fire went out?" Or it is an explanatory substitute (*badal*) for the parabolic clause by way of elucidation. The pronoun, on both views, refers to the hypocrites, and the answer (apodosis) is omitted, as in His saying, ﴿So when they went with him﴾, for brevity and because there is no risk of ambiguity. The attribution of the going away to God, the Exalted, is either because everything is by His act, or because the extinguishing came about through a hidden cause or a heavenly matter such as wind or rain, or for emphasis. For this reason the verb was made transitive with *bi* rather than with the *hamza* (causative), because of the meaning of retention and holding fast contained in it. It is said: "The ruler took away his wealth," meaning he seized it. What God seizes and holds back, none can release. For this reason He turned away from *ḍaw'* (brightness), which is what the wording would normally require, to *nūr* (light). For if it had been said, "God took away their brightness," it would have allowed for His taking away whatever excess is in brightness, while what is called light would remain. The purpose is the removal of light from them altogether. Do you not see how He established and confirmed that by His saying, ﴿and left them in darkness, unable to see﴾? So He mentioned the darkness which is the absence of light and the complete obliteration of it, and He made it plural, indefinite, and described it as pure darkness in which no two shapes can be seen. *Taraka* originally means "to cast off and leave," and it has one object, so it was given the meaning of *ṣayyara* (to make), and it went in the manner of the verbs of the heart, as in His saying, ﴿and He left them in darkness﴾.

And as the poet says:

*So I left him as prey for wild beasts, which tear at him, devouring the beauty of his hand and wrist.*

The word *ẓulmah* (darkness) is derived from their saying, "What prevented you (*mā ẓalamaka*) from doing such-and-such?", meaning "what prevented you," because it blocks the sight and prevents seeing.

**﴿And their darknesses﴾**: the darkness of disbelief, the darkness of hypocrisy, and the darkness of the Day of Resurrection, ﴿the Day when you will see the believing men and women, their light running before them and on their right﴾. Or the darkness of misguidance, the darkness of God's wrath, and the darkness of everlasting punishment. Or an intense darkness, as if it were a piled-up darkness. The object of ﴿they do not see﴾ is of the kind of the omitted and abandoned object, so the verb is as if it were intransitive.

The verse is a parable God set forth for one who was given a kind of guidance and then wasted it, and was not brought thereby to everlasting bliss, so he remains bewildered and full of regret. It is a confirmation and clarification of what the first verse contained. Included in its generality are these hypocrites, for they wasted what their tongues had uttered of the truth, by concealing disbelief and displaying it when they were alone with their devils. Also included is whoever prefers misguidance to the guidance placed in him by his nature, or who apostatizes from his religion after believing, or whoever has the states of desire (*irādah*) sound in him and then claims the states of love (*maḥabbah*), so God takes away what the lights of desire had shone upon him. Or it is a parable for their faith in terms of the fact that it returns to them with the preservation of their blood, the safety of their property and children, and their sharing in the spoils with the Muslims. The judgement is by the kindled fire for illumination, and by the going away of its effect and the obliteration of its light through their destruction and the exposure of their condition, by God's extinguishing it and taking away its light.

**﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾**. When they stopped their ears against giving heed to the truth, and refused to let their tongues speak it, or let their eyes contemplate the signs, they were treated as though their faculties had been struck with paralysis and their powers had been removed, as in his saying:

*They are deaf when they hear good spoken of me,*
*but when evil of me is mentioned in their presence, they are all ears.*

And as in his saying:

*I am deaf to whatever I do not wish to hear,*
*yet I am the most attentive of God's creatures when I wish to listen.*

Applying these terms to them is by way of *tamthil* (illustrative analogy), not *isti'ara* (metaphor). For metaphor requires that the thing represented be omitted, such that the speech could be taken literally as the borrowed term were it not for an indicator. An example is Zuhayr's saying:

*In the presence of a lion, armed and thrust forth,*
*with a mane, whose claws have not been trimmed.*

This is why skilled eloquent poets, when they imagine a comparison, turn away from it entirely, as Abu Tammam al-Ta'i said:

*He rises until the ignorant man thinks*
*that he has some business in the sky.*

Here, although the subject is omitted by elision, it is in the status of something explicitly stated. Its parallel is:

*A lion against me, yet in wars an ostrich,*
*a broad-winged bird that flees at the whistle of the whistler.*

(p-51) This holds if you take the pronoun as referring to the hypocrites, with the verse being a *fadhlaka* (summarizing conclusion) and result of the analogy. If you take the pronoun as referring to those who kindled the fire, then the words are literal. The meaning is: when they kindled a fire, God took away their light and left them in terrible darkness, which so bewildered them that their senses were disordered and their faculties diminished. All three words (*deaf, dumb, blind*) have been read in the accusative as circumstantial states (*ḥāl*) of the object of *taraka* ("left"). *Ṣamam* (deafness) originally means hardness arising from the compactness of parts; hence a stone is called *aṣamm* and a spear-shaft *ṣammā*, and the stopper of a bottle is *ṣimām*. The loss of the sense of hearing is named after this, because its cause is that the inner part of the ear canal is compact with no hollow in it, so that it cannot hold air that carries sound by its vibration. *Bakam* means muteness. *ʿAmā* (blindness) is the absence of sight in what should be able to see, and it may also be said of the absence of insight.

**﴿Therefore they do not return﴾**: they do not revert to the guidance which they sold and wasted, or to the error which they purchased; or, they are bewildered and do not know whether to advance or to retreat, and how they could return to the place from which they began. The *fa'* (therefore) indicates that their being characterized by the previously mentioned attributes is the cause of their bewilderment and being held back.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 19:

﴿Or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "the one who kindled a fire", meaning: "like the case of people with a rain-cloud", on account of His saying: ﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾. The particle "aw" (or) is originally for equivalence in doubt, then its use was extended to be for equivalence without doubt, as in: "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin", and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not obey from among them any sinner or ungrateful one﴾. For it indicates equivalence in the goodness of sitting in their company and the obligation of disobeying them. Of this kind is His saying: ﴿or like a rain-cloud﴾, and its meaning is that the story of the hypocrites is likened to these two stories, and that they are equal in the validity of likening to them, and you have the choice of illustrating with them or with whichever of them you wish. And ṣayyib is on the pattern fayʿal, from ṣawb, which is descending, and it is said of rain and of cloud. Al-Shammakh said:

A dark, low-hanging cloud, true of thunder, pouring rain

In the verse it may bear either meaning, and its being indefinite is because a particular kind of heavy rain is intended. The definiteness of "the sky" (al-samāʾ) is to indicate that the cloud is overspreading, seizing all the horizons of the sky, for every horizon of it is called a sky, just as every layer of it is a sky. And [a poet] said:

And between us and the sky, after the earth

It gave to it what is in ṣayyib of intensity in terms of its root, its form, and its indefiniteness. It has also been said that by "the sky" is meant the clouds, so the "al" is for defining the reality (li-taʿrīf al-māhiyya).

﴿In it are darknesses, thunder and lightning﴾. If by ṣayyib is meant the rain, then its darknesses are the darkness of its density through the successive falling of drops, and the darkness of its cloud together with the darkness of the night. He made it the place of the thunder and lightning, because they are at its top and its descent, joined to it. If by it is meant the cloud, then its darknesses are its blackness and its covering together with the darkness of the night. Their being in the nominative through the adverbial phrase is in agreement, because it depends on a described noun. Thunder (raʿd) is a sound heard from the cloud. The well-known view is that its cause is the agitation of the bodies of the clouds and their collision when the wind drives them, from trembling. Lightning (barq) is what shines from the cloud, from "baraqa al-shayʾu bariqan" (the thing gleamed, a gleam). Both are verbal nouns (maṣdar) in origin, and for this reason neither is pluralized.

﴿they put their fingers in their ears﴾. The pronoun refers to the people of the rain-cloud. Although its explicit mention is omitted and ṣayyib is placed in its position, its meaning remains, so it is permissible to rely upon it, just as Hassan relied upon it in his saying:

They give to drink whoever comes to al-Barīṣ upon them... Barada flowing with pure sealed wine

where he mentioned the pronoun, because the meaning is "water of Barada". The clause is a resumptive (istiʾnāf), as if, when he mentioned what signals severity and terror, it was said: "How then is their state with such as this?" and it was answered with it. He used "fingers" in place of "fingertips" only for emphasis.

﴿because of the thunderbolts﴾ is connected to "they put", meaning: on account of them they put (their fingers), like the saying "he gave him to drink because of the cloud". The ṣāʿiqa is a crash of terrible thunder accompanied by fire that passes over nothing without consuming it, from al-ṣaʿq, which is intensity of sound. It may also be applied to any terrifying thing that is heard or seen. One says: "the thunderbolt struck him" (ṣaʿaqathu al-ṣāʿiqa) when it destroyed him by burning or by intensity of sound. It was also read as "al-ṣawāqiʿ", which is not a transposition of "al-ṣawāʿiq", since both patterns are equally used in conjugation: one says ṣaqaʿa al-dīk (the rooster crowed), khaṭīb miṣqaʿ (an eloquent orator), and ṣaqaʿathu al-ṣāqiʿa. Originally it is either an adjective for a crash of thunder or for thunder. The tāʾ (in ṣāʿiqa) is for emphasis, as in "al-riwāya" (the transmission), or it is a verbal noun like "al-ʿāfiya" and "al-kādhiba".

﴿for fear of death﴾ is in the accusative as a reason (mafʿūl li-ajlihi), like His saying:

And I overlook the faults of the noble, saving them for later... and I pardon the abuse of the base out of generosity

Death (al-mawt) is the cessation of life. It has been said that it is an accident opposed to it, based on His saying: ﴿He created death and life﴾. This was rejected on the ground that "creation" means determination, and that non-existence is determined.

﴿And Allah encompasses the disbelievers﴾: they cannot escape Him, just as the encompassed cannot escape the encompasser. Deception and stratagems do not save them. The sentence is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya) and has no place in the i'rab.

The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. This is a second resumed sentence, as if it were an answer to someone who asks: what is their condition with those thunderbolts? *Kāda* (كاد) is one of the verbs of approximation (*af'āl al-muqārabah*). It is used to express that a report is close to occurring, because its cause has arisen, but it did not occur, either because a condition is missing or because an impediment is present. *ʿAsā* (عسى) is used to express hope. Thus *ʿasā* is a pure predicate verb, which is why it is conjugated in all its forms, unlike *ʿasā*. The predicate of *kāda* must be an imperfect verb, to indicate that the approach itself is what is intended, without *an*, in order to emphasise the nearness through the indication of the present. It may also take *an*, by analogy with *ʿasā*, just as it is analogised with *ʿasā* in omitting its predicate, because the two share the basic meaning of approximation.

*Al-khaṭf* means taking quickly. It is read *yakhṭifu* with a kasra on the ṭāʾ; *yakhtaṭafu*, on the basis that it is *yakhtaṭif*, so the fatḥah of the tāʾ was transferred to the khāʾ and then it was assimilated into the ṭāʾ; *yakhṭifu* with a kasra on the khāʾ, because of the meeting of two quiescent letters and the following of the yāʾ for it; *yakhaṭṭifu* and *yatakhaṭṭafu*.

Whenever it shines for them, they walk in it; and when it darkens over them, they stand still. This is a third resumed sentence, as if it were asked: what do they do during the two intervals of the flashing of the lightning and its concealment? So it was answered with this. *Aḍāʾa* (أضاء) may be transitive, with the object omitted, meaning: whenever it illuminates for them a place of walking, they take it; or intransitive in meaning: whenever it flashes for them, they walk in the place of its light. Likewise *aḍlama* (أظلم), which came transitive, transferred from the darkness of the night. This is supported by the reading *uḍlima* in the passive voice, and by the verse of Abu Tammam:

*They two darkened my two states, and there became clear*
*their darkness from the face of a beardless, grey-haired one.*

Although he is among the later poets, he is one of the scholars of Arabic, so it is not far-fetched to treat what he says as on the level of what he transmits. The reason he said *kullamā* with illumination and *idhā* with darkening is that they are eager to walk, so whenever they find an opportunity from it, they seize it, and this is not the case with stopping. The meaning of *qāmū* (قاموا) is they stood still, as in the expression *qāmati al-sūq* when the market became stagnant, and *qāma al-māʾ* when the water froze.

And if God had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight. That is: if God had willed to take away their hearing by the crash of the thunder and their sight by the flash of the lightning, He would have taken them away. The object has been omitted because the answer indicates it. Its omission has become very common with *shāʾa* (شاء) and *arāda* (أراد), to the point that it is hardly mentioned except in a remarkable matter, as in his saying:

*If I willed to weep blood, I would have wept it.*

*Law* (ولو) is one of the particles of condition. Its apparent meaning is the indication of the non-occurrence of the first because of the non-occurrence of the second, since the necessitated is non-existent when its necessity is non-existent. It was read *la-adhhaba bi-asmāʿihim*, with the addition of the *bāʾ*, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾.

The benefit of this conditional statement is to show the impediment to the taking away of their hearing and sight, even though what requires it is present, and to draw attention to the fact that the effect of causes on their effects is conditional upon the will of God, exalted is He, and that their existence, though linked to their causes, occurs by His power and His word.

Indeed God is over all things Powerful. This is as if it were an explicit statement of it and an affirmation of it. The word *shayʾ* (شيء) is specific to what exists, because originally it is the verbal noun of *shāʾa*. It has been used with the meaning of *shāʾa* at times, and in that case it encompasses the Creator, exalted is He, as He said: ﴿Say: What thing is greatest as testimony? Say: God is witness﴾. And it has another meaning, *mushiʾ* (مشيء), that is, one who wills its existence; and what God wills to exist exists in general. On this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God is over all things Powerful﴾. And ﴿God is the Creator of all things﴾. So both are upon their generality without any exception. The Muʿtazilah, since they said that *shayʾ* is what can be brought into existence, and this encompasses the necessary and the possible, or what can be known and reported about, and so it encompasses the impossible as well, were obliged to restrict it to the possible in both places, on the basis of rational proof.

*Al-qudrah* (power) is: the ability to bring a thing into existence. It has been said that it is an attribute that necessitates capability. It has been said that the power of a human is a state by which one is enabled to act. The power of God, exalted is He, is an expression of the negation of incapacity from Him. The one who is capable (*al-qādir*) is the one who, if he wills, acts, and if he does not will, does not act. The one who is *qadīr* (powerful) is the doer of what He wills, in the manner He wills; therefore this word is rarely applied to anyone other than the Creator, exalted is He. The derivation of *qudrah* is from *qadar*, because the capable one brings the act into being according to the measure of his strength, or according to the measure that his will requires. In this is evidence that the originated thing, at the moment of its origination, and the possible thing, at the moment of its continuance, are both objects of power, and that the servant's object of power is an object of power for God, exalted is He, because it is a thing, and every thing is an object of power for God, exalted is He.

The apparent view is that the two similitudes are of the kind of composite similitudes, which is to liken a condition abstracted from a totality whose parts are joined and adhering until they become one thing, to another like it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not bear it﴾ up to the end of the verse. For this is a comparison of the condition of the Jews in their ignorance with what they had of the Torah, to the condition of a donkey in its ignorance of what it carries of books of wisdom. The purpose of both is to depict the condition of the hypocrites in their bewilderment and distress, by comparison with one who suffers when his fire has gone out after being kindled, in darkness, or with one whom the sky has seized on a dark night with a crashing thunder, a flashing lightning, and fear of thunderbolts.

It is also possible to take the two as being of the kind of individual similitude, which is to take separate things and liken each to its counterparts, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the blind and the seeing are not equal﴾, ﴿nor are the darknesses and the light﴾, ﴿nor the shade and the heat﴾, and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if the hearts of birds, moist and dry,*
*by their nests are the 'unnāb fruit and the decayed dry husk.*

In the first, the selves of the hypocrites are likened to those who kindle a fire; their display of faith to the kindling of the fire; what they benefit from it, such as the preservation of blood, the safety of property and children, and other things, to the illumination of what is around those who kindle the fire; and the cessation of that from them soon, by their destruction and the exposure of their condition, and their remaining in perpetual loss and everlasting punishment, to the extinguishing of their fire and the going away of their light.

In the second, their selves are likened to the people of the downpour, and their faith mixed with unbelief and deception to a downpour in which there are darknesses, thunder and lightning; in that although it is beneficial in itself, when it has been found in this form its benefit turns into harm; and their hypocrisy is a precaution against the blows of the believers, and against what other unbelievers may attack them with, by placing their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts out of fear of death; in that it does not turn back anything of God's decree, nor does it save them from the harms He intends for them. Their bewilderment is due to the severity of the matter and their ignorance of what they are doing. They are described as doing this because whenever they meet a flash of lightning they seize it as an opportunity, with fear that it may snatch away their sight, so they take a few small steps; then when it becomes hidden and its brightness fades, they remain stationary, not moving.

It has also been said: the faith, the Qur'an, and the rest of the knowledge given to humans, which is the cause of eternal life, are likened to the downpour through which the earth lives; and the doubts that are committed with them, and the objections that stand between them and that, which cause confusion, are likened to the darknesses. The promise and threat within it are likened to thunder, and the manifest signs within it to lightning. Their deafness to what they hear of the threat is likened to the condition of one whom thunder terrifies, so he fears its thunderbolts and stops his ears against them, although there is no escape for them from them. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾. Their being stirred by what flashes for them of guidance they perceive, or of provision to which their sight aspires, by their walking in the place of the lightning's light whenever it shines for them, and their bewilderment and hesitation in the matter when a doubt confronts them or a calamity afflicts them, by their standing still when it becomes dark over them.

By His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if God had willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾, He has drawn attention to the fact that He made for them hearing and sight (p-54) so that they might use them as a means to guidance and success; then they turned them toward immediate pleasures and blocked them from the delayed benefits. Had God willed, He would have placed them in the condition they have made for themselves, for He is Powerful over whatever He wills.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 21:**

﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾. When he had enumerated the groups of the legally accountable (*mukallafin*) and mentioned their distinguishing characteristics and the ways their affairs are directed, he turned to them in direct address, by way of *iltifat* (a shift from third person to second person), to stir the listener, to animate him, to draw attention to the matter of worship, to magnify its importance, and to compensate for the hardship of worship with the pleasure of being addressed. *Ya* (يا) is a particle established for calling the distant, though the near may also be addressed with it, treating them as if they were distant. This is either because of the greatness of the one addressed, as in the words of the supplicant, "O Lord" and "O Allah," for He is nearer to him than his jugular vein, or because of the heedlessness and poor understanding of the one addressed, or for the sake of giving attention to the one called for and intensifying the exhortation to it. The particle together with the vocative noun forms a complete sentence, since it stands in the place of the verb "I call." *Ayyu* (أيّ) is used as a link to the vocative of what is defined by *al-* (the definite article), since it is impossible to add *ya* directly to it, because two particles of definition cannot be combined. It is then given the rule of the vocative, and what is intended by the call is described by a clarifying qualifier, and its being obligatorily in the nominative case indicates that it is the intended one. The *ha'* of alerting (هاء التنبيه) is inserted between them for emphasis and as a substitute for what it deserves, namely the genitive complement. The calling in this manner occurs frequently in the Qur'an because it is self-sufficient with several aspects of emphasis. Everything for which Allah calls His servants is a matter of great importance, deserving that they take notice of it and direct their hearts toward it, and most of them are heedless of it. It is fitting that it be called for with the most emphatic and eloquent form. Plurals and their collective nouns preceded by *al-* are general where there is no specific reference, as is shown by the validity of an exception made from them. Or the generality is emphasized by something that conveys generality, as in His words, "So the angels prostrated, all of them together." The Companions' use of its generality is widespread and well known. Thus "*an-nas*" (mankind) includes both those present at the time of revelation in terms of the wording and those who will exist later, because it is firmly established from his religion (ﷺ) that the implication of his address and his rulings encompasses both groups and remains valid until the Hour, except what the evidence has specified. As for what is related from 'Alqama and al-Hasan, that everything in which "O mankind" occurs is Meccan and everything in which "O you who believe" occurs is Medinan, even if its attribution to the Prophet is sound, it does not require restricting it to the disbelievers, nor does it mean that they were not commanded to worship. For what is commanded is the common element between the beginning of worship, its increase, and perseverance in it. What is required of the disbelievers is therefore to begin it after bringing what must come first, namely knowledge and acknowledgment of the Creator, for it is among the necessary consequences of the obligation of something that whatever it cannot be completed without is also obligatory. Just as ritual impurity does not prevent the obligation of prayer, so disbelief does not prevent the obligation of worship; rather, it is obligatory to remove it and to occupy oneself with worship immediately after. For believers, the requirement is increase and steadfastness in it. He said "your Lord" to alert that what makes worship obligatory is lordship (*rububiyya*).

﴿who created you﴾. This is a qualifier applied to Him, may He be exalted, for magnification and for giving the reason. It may be restrictive and explanatory if the address is specific to the polytheists, and "Lord" is taken in a broader sense than the true Lord, including the deities they call lords. *Khalq* (الخلق) is the bringing of a thing into existence with measure and proportion; its root meaning is measuring, as in the saying "he created the sandal" when he measured it and fashioned it by the gauge.

﴿and those before you﴾. This includes everything that precedes a person, either in essence or in time. It is in the accusative, coordinated with the pronoun in the accusative in "created you." The clause is presented as something already established among them, either because they acknowledge it, as Allah the Exalted said, "If you asked them who created them, they would surely say, 'Allah,'" or because they are able to know it with the slightest reflection. It has been recited as "*man qablakum*" (مَن قَبْلَكم) with the second relative pronoun inserted between the first and its relative clause for emphasis, just as Jarir inserted in his verse:

*O Taym, Taym of ʿAdi, may you have no father,*

the second "Taym" between the first and what is added to it.

﴿so that you may be God-fearing﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in "worship," as if he said: worship your Lord, hoping that you will be enrolled among the God-fearing, who are successful in guidance and salvation, deserving the protection of Allah the Exalted. By this He indicated that God-fearing (*taqwa*) is the ultimate of the stages of those who travel the spiritual path, namely disassociation from everything other than Allah the Exalted in turning to Allah, and that the worshipper should not be deceived by his worship, but should be one who has fear (p-55) and hope. Allah the Exalted said, "They call upon their Lord in fear and hope," and "They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment." Or it may be taken as connected to the object of "created you" and what is coordinated with it, in the sense that He created you and those before you in the form of those from whom God-fearing is hoped, because their affair is weighted by the gathering of its causes and the multitude of motives toward it. The addressees are given precedence over the absent in wording, while the meaning includes all of them. It has also been said that it is a reason for creation, meaning: He created you so that you might be God-fearing, as He said, "I did not create jinn and humankind except that they might worship Me." But this is weak, since no such usage is established in the language.

The verse indicates that the path to knowing Allah the Exalted, to knowing His oneness and His deserving of worship, is reflection on His handiwork and inference from His acts. It also indicates that the servant does not deserve a reward from Allah for his worship, for since it is obligatory upon him as gratitude for the previous blessings Allah has enumerated, he is like a hired worker who took his wage before doing the work.

The Creator who made the earth a resting place for you﴾ is a second qualifier (ṣifa thāniya), or an object of praise in the accusative, or in the nominative, or a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿So do not set up﴾. The verb ﴿made﴾ (jaʿala) is among the general verbs and comes in three senses. In the sense of "became" or "began," it takes no object, as in the verse of poetry:

*Surely the young she-camel of the Banu Suhayl has made, from the saddlebags, its pasture near.*

In the sense of "brought into being" (awjada), it takes one object, as in God's words: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾. In the sense of "rendered" (ṣayyara), it takes two objects, as in God's words: ﴿who made for you the earth a bed﴾. Rendering something into a state can occur by action at one time and by speech or contract at another.

The meaning of making it a bed is that He made some of its surfaces prominent and visible above the water, despite its nature of being encompassed by water. He rendered it intermediate between hardness and softness, until it became prepared for you to sit and sleep upon it like a spread bed. This does not require that it be flat, since the roundness of its shape together with the greatness of its mass and the vastness of its body does not preclude spreading out upon it.

﴿and the heaven a building﴾: a dome erected over you. "Heaven" (samāʾ) is a collective noun that applies to the singular and the plural, like "dinar" and "dirham." It is said to be the plural of samāʾa. "Building" (bināʾ) is a verbal noun, and the built structure is named by it, whether a house, a dome or a tent. From the same root comes "he consummated the marriage with his wife" (banā ʿalā imraʾatihi), because when they married they erected a new tent over her.

﴿And He sent down from the heaven water, and brought forth thereby fruits as a provision for you﴾ is conjoined to ﴿made﴾. The emergence of fruits is by God's power and will. But the making of water mixed with earth to be a cause for their emergence and a material for them is like the drop of seed for animals. He established His custom of bestowing their forms and qualities upon the material formed from both of them. Or He placed in the water an active power and in the earth a receptive power, from whose union the kinds of fruits come into being. He is able to bring all things into existence without causes and materials, just as He originated the souls of causes and materials. But in their production, passing gradually from state to state, He has crafts and wisdoms by which He renews for those with insight lessons and assurance of His great power. In bringing them into being there is no single instant.

"From" (min) in ﴿from the heaven﴾ is used for the starting point (ibtidāʾ). This holds whether "heaven" means the clouds, since whatever is above you is a heaven, or the sphere (falak), since rain begins from the heaven to the clouds and from there to the earth, as the apparent evidence indicates. Or it refers to celestial causes that stir the moist particles from the depths of the earth into the atmosphere, where they condense into rain-bearing cloud.

The second "from" (min) in ﴿of the fruits﴾ is partitive (tabʿīḍ), as shown by God's words: ﴿so We brought forth with it fruits﴾. It also accords with the deniers' associating with it, namely water and provision. It is as if He had said: "We sent down from the heaven some of the water and brought forth with it some of the fruits, so that they would be some of your provision." So it is in reality, since He did not send down all of the water from the heaven, nor did He bring forth with the rain all fruits, nor did He make all that is provided for fruit. Or it is explanatory (tabyīn), and "provision" (rizq) is an object in the sense of "what is provided," as when you say, "I spent a thousand of the dirhams."

The plural "fruits" (thamarāt) is permissible even though the context implies multiplicity, because by "fruits" is meant the plural of "fruit" (thamara) as in your saying, "I picked the fruit of his orchard." This is supported by the reading of one who recited "min al-thamara" in the singular.

Or the plural forms are interchangeable, as in God's words: ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind﴾, and in His words: ﴿three periods﴾. Or, since the plural is defined by the article (al-), it has left the limit of paucity.

﴿for you﴾ is an attribute of "provision" if "provision" means what is provided, and its object if it means the verbal noun, as though He had said: "a provision for you."

﴿So do not set up rivals to God﴾ is connected to ﴿worship﴾, as a prohibition conjoined to it. Or it is a negation in the subjunctive, governed by an implied "that" (an), with the response (jawāb) to it. Or it is governed by "perhaps" (laʿalla), in the way that the subjunctive of ﴿that I may fulfil the means﴾ governs ﴿the means of the heavens, and look upon﴾. This is by analogy with the six things, because they share the characteristic of not being obligatory. The meaning is: if you fear God, do not set up rivals to Him. Or, with what was made, if it is taken as a new sentence in the sense of a prohibition that stands as a predicate in the sense of "it is said of it: do not set up." The "fa" (so) is causal (sababiyya), placed upon it because the subject includes the meaning of a condition. The meaning is that whoever has singled you out with these great blessings and mighty signs ought not to be associated with Him.

A rival (nidd) is a hostile equal. Jarir said:

*Do you Taym set up a rival against me? / Yet Taym is no equal to one of noble descent.*

It comes from "nadda yandudda nudūdan," meaning to flee, and "nādadtu al-rajul" means I opposed the man. The term is specific to an opponent who is similar in essence, just as "equal" (musāwī) is specific to one similar in measure. The naming of what the polytheists worship besides God as "rivals" does not mean they claimed these were equal to Him in essence or attributes, nor that they opposed Him in His acts. Rather, since they abandoned His worship for the worship of these, and called them gods, their condition resembled that of one who believes them to be necessary beings by essence, able to avert from them God's punishment and grant them what God has not willed for them of good. So He mocked them and reproached them, by making them set up rivals to one who cannot have a rival.

For this reason Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl, the monotheist of the pre-Islamic period, said:

*Lord one, or a thousand lords / I worship when affairs are divided?*

*I have abandoned al-Lat and al-ʿUzza entirely; / thus does the discerning man act.*

﴿while you know﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿so do not﴾. The object of "you know" is omitted, meaning: your condition is that you are of the people of knowledge, reflection and sound judgment. If you reflected with even the least reflection, your intellect would be compelled to affirm a single Originator of possible things, sole in necessary existence, exalted above resemblance to created things. Or the object is intended but unstated, namely that they do not resemble Him and cannot do what He does, as in God's words, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ On this reading the purpose is reproach and rebuke, not restricting the ruling to this alone, since the one who knows and the ignorant one who has the capacity for knowledge are equal in the obligation.

Know that the content of the two verses is the command to worship God, glorified and exalted be He, and the prohibition of associating anything with Him, exalted be He, along with an indication of what is the cause and the requirement. Its explanation is that He ordered worship in connection with the attribute of lordship, indicating that lordship is the cause of its obligation. Then He clarified His lordship by stating that He, exalted be He, is their Creator and the Creator of their roots, and of what they need for their livelihood, such as shelter, shade, foods and clothing. The fruit is more general than food, and provision is more general than what is eaten and drunk. Then, since these matters, which no one other than Him can control, bear witness to His oneness, exalted be He, He placed the prohibition of associating anything with Him upon them. Perhaps, glorified be He, He intended from the last verse, along with what the outward meaning indicates and the discourse was directed towards, an allusion to the detailed creation of the human being and what He poured upon him of meanings and qualities, by way of parable. So He likened the body to the earth, the soul to the heaven, and the intellect to the water. He likened the practical and theoretical virtues poured upon him, which are acquired through the intellect's use of the senses, and the pairing of the soulish and bodily powers, to the fruits produced by the pairing of the active heavenly powers and the receptive earthly powers, by the power of the free agent. For every verse has an outward and an inner meaning, and for every limit there is a vantage point.

(p-57) ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant, then produce a surah﴾. When (al-Baydawi) established His oneness, exalted is He, and explained the path that leads to knowledge of it, he mentioned right after it the proof of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the Qur'an, miraculous through its eloquence, which surpasses the eloquence of every logician (mantiq), and which silenced those who were challenged to oppose it from among the most eloquent orators of the pure Arabs, despite their great numbers, their excessive hostility and harm, and their eagerness for contention and opposition. He also described what makes its miraculousness known and makes certain that it is from God, as he claims.

He said ﴿what We have sent down﴾ because its revelation came in installments according to events, which is what the people of poetry and oratory regard as a cause of doubt, as God related about them when He said: ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?"﴾. So it was obligatory to challenge them in this manner, to remove the doubt and to establish the proof. He attributed the word "servant" to Himself, exalted is He, to honor the mention of him and to indicate that he is specially chosen and submits to His command, exalted is He. It was also read as ʿibādinā ("Our servants"), meaning Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community.

The surah (sūrah) is a section of the Qur'an that is delimited, the least of which is three verses. If its waw is taken as original, it is derived from the "surahs" of a city (sūr al-madīnah), because it encloses a section of the Qur'an separated and set apart on its own; or because it contains kinds of knowledge in the way the walls of a city contain what is within them; or from the surah meaning rank (rutbah). Al-Nabigha said:

"And for the clan of Harrāb and Qadd there is a surah in glory, whose crow does not fly away."

Because surahs are like stations and ranks through which the reader ascends, they differ in length and brevity, in merit and nobility, and in the reward of recitation. If its hamzah is taken as a substitution, then it is from the surah meaning remnant and piece of a thing. The wisdom in dividing the Qur'an into surahs is: distinguishing the types, the succession of forms, the harmony of arrangement, the energizing of the reader, facilitating memorization, and encouraging it. For when one finishes a surah, that relieves him, like the traveler who knows that he has covered a mile or traversed a stage; and when the memorizer completes it, he believes he has taken a complete portion of the Qur'an and gained a defined and self-contained section, so that this becomes great in his eyes and he rejoices in it, along with other benefits.

﴿from the like of it﴾ is an attribute of surah, meaning: a surah existing from the like of it. The pronoun refers to what We have sent down, and ﴿from﴾ is for partition or for specification. It is superfluous according to al-Akhfash, meaning a surah similar to the Great Qur'an in eloquence and excellence of arrangement. Or the pronoun refers to Our servant, and ﴿from﴾ is for origin, meaning: a surah existing from one who is in his condition, peace and blessings be upon him, in that he was a human, unlettered, who had not read books nor learned sciences.

Or it is connected to ﴿then produce﴾, and the pronoun refers to the servant (ﷺ). Yet returning it to the one who sent it down is more appropriate, because it corresponds to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then produce a surah from the like of it﴾, and to the rest of the verses of challenge; and because the discourse is about it, not about the one to whom it was sent down, so its due is not to be separated from it, in order that the order and arrangement be coherent; and because addressing a vast multitude to produce the like of what one man from their own kin has produced is more eloquent in the challenge than being told: "Let him produce something like what this other man, his like, produced." And because it is miraculous in itself, not in relation to him, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "If mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like."﴾. And because returning it to "Our servant" would give the impression that it could come from one who was not of his description, and His saying, exalted is He, does not suit that.

﴿And call your witnesses besides God﴾, for He commanded them to seek help from everyone who would support and assist them. The word "witnesses" (shuhadāʾ) is the plural of shahīd, meaning one present, or one who gives testimony, or a helper, or a leader. It may have been named so because he attends the assemblies, and affairs are settled in his presence, since the root implies presence, either physically or in imagination. From it is said of one slain in the cause of God: shahīd, because he was present at what he was hoping for, or because the angels were present with him. The meaning of ﴿besides﴾ (dūn) is the nearest place to a thing, and from it comes tadwīn of books, because it is bringing one part near another. "Dūnaka hādhā" means: take it from the nearest place to you. Then it was borrowed for ranks, so it is said: "Zayd is dūn ʿAmr," meaning in nobility. From it comes "the base thing" (al-shayʾ al-dūn). Then its usage broadened to mean every transgression of one limit to another and every passing over of one matter to another. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The believers should not take the disbelievers as allies besides the believers﴾, meaning they should not go beyond the guardianship of the believers to the guardianship of the disbelievers. Umayya said:

"O soul, what protection do you have besides God?"

That is, if you go beyond the protection of God, nothing else will shield you. The word ﴿from﴾ is connected to "call." The meaning is: ﴿and call﴾ for opposition whomever is present to you, or whose help you hope for, from your humans, your jinn, and your gods besides God, exalted is He, for none can produce its like except God. Or: ﴿and call﴾ besides God witnesses who will testify for you that what you have produced is its like, and do not call upon God as witness, for that is the habit of the one confounded and unable to establish proof. Or the meaning is by "your witnesses," that is, those whom you have taken besides God as allies and gods, and whom you claimed would testify for you on the Day of Resurrection; or those who would testify for you before God, exalted is He, according to your assumption, from the words of al-Aʿshā:

"It shows you the mote, besides it, while it is beneath it."

So that they may help you, and in their command to seek support from inanimate things in opposing the Mighty Qur'an, there is the utmost rebuke and mockery of them. It was also said: ﴿besides God﴾ means besides His allies, meaning the eloquent Arabs and the notable spectators, so that they may testify for you that what you have produced is its like, for a sensible person does not consent to testify to the soundness of what has clearly been shown to be corrupt and whose defect is manifest.

﴿if you are truthful﴾ that it is from the speech of humans. Its answer is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. Truthfulness (ṣidq) is a statement that corresponds to reality. It was also said: together with the speaker's belief that it is so, based on evidence or sign. For God, exalted is He, declared the hypocrites liars in their saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the Messenger of God﴾, since they did not believe in its correspondence. And it was rejected by directing the accusation of lying to their saying "we testify," because testimony is a report of what one knows, and they were not knowing of it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 24:

﴿And if you do not, and you will never do, then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾. When He had made clear to them what by which they might recognize the matter of the Messenger ﷺ and what he brought, and had distinguished for them the truth from falsehood, He arranged upon it what is like a summation of it, namely that if you strive to oppose him and all of you are unable to produce anything equal to it or approaching it, it becomes apparent that it is inimitable (mu'jiz), and belief in it is obligatory; so believe in it and fear the punishment prepared for those who deny. He expressed the producing of it in a qualified manner by the verb that encompasses producing it and other than it, for brevity. The necessary consequence of the recompense was made to take its place by way of metonymy (kinaya), to establish what is alluded to, to magnify the gravity of obstinacy, and to state the threat explicitly with brevity. He introduced the conditional with in (إن), which is for doubt, while the situation calls for idha (إذا), which is for certainty, since the Speaker, glorified and exalted is He, was not doubtful of their inability; for this reason He negated their producing it, placing it parenthetically between the condition and the consequence, mocking them and addressing them according to their own supposition, since inability before reflection was not established in their minds. And ﴿tafalu﴾ (تفعلوا) is apocopated by ﴿lam﴾ (لم) because it is obligatory in its operation, specific to the imperfect, and joined to its object; and because when it makes the verb past, it becomes like a part of it, and the conditional particle is like one entering upon the whole, so it is as if he said: "if you have left off the action." For this reason their combination is permissible. ﴿Wa-lan﴾ (ولن) is like "lan" in negating the future, except that it is more emphatic; it is a particle of reduction (muqtadab) according to Sibawayh and al-Khalil in one of two narrations from him, and in the other narration its origin is lan (لا أن); according to al-Farra' its origin is la (لا), so its alif was replaced by a nun. And ﴿wuqud﴾ (الوَقُود) with a fatha is that by which the fire is kindled; with a damma it is the verbal noun. The verbal noun has also come with a fatha; Sibawayh said: "We have heard someone say: the fire kindled a high kindling (وقودا عاليا)." The noun with a damma is perhaps a verbal noun named as such, as it is said: "So-and-so is the pride of his people and the ornament of his land." It has also been read with it. The apparent meaning is that the intended sense is the noun; if the verbal noun is intended, then it is by elision of a modifier, i.e., its fuel is the burning of men. And ﴿al-hijara﴾ (الحِجارَة) is the plural of hajar (حَجَر), like jimala, the plural of jamal; this is rare and not a regular pattern. What is meant by them are the idols which they carved and associated with themselves, and worshipped, hoping for their intercession, for benefit from them, and for repelling harms by their status. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾. They were punished by that which is the source of their sin, just as the disbelievers were punished by what they hoarded, or by the opposite of what they expected, as an increase in their regret. It has been said: it is gold and silver which they used to hoard and be deceived by. On this view, there is no point in specifying this kind of punishment for the disbelievers. It has been said: stones of sulphur, but this is specification without evidence and a nullification of the purpose, since the aim is to magnify its state and the intensity of its flame so that it is kindled by what does not kindle other fires, while sulphur kindles every fire however weak. If this is authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, then perhaps he meant that all stones are for that fire as sulphur stones are for the other fires. Since the verse is Medinan, and before it was revealed at Mecca His saying in Surat al-Tahrim: ﴿a fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾ had been sent down, and they had heard it, the definiteness of "the Fire" is valid. The clause's occurring as a relative clause "beside it" (bi-izaihā) is because it must be a known matter.

﴿Prepared for the disbelievers﴾: it was made ready for them and made a provision for their punishment. It has been read "u'tuddat" (اعْتُدَّتْ), from al-'atad (العَتاد) in the sense of 'uddah (provision). The clause is a resumption, or a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied, referring to the Fire, not to the pronoun in ﴿wuquduha﴾, even if you make it a verbal noun, separating the two by the predicate. In the two verses there is what indicates prophethood in several respects:

First: what they contain of challenge and incitement to earnest effort and exhausting one's capacity in opposing him, by reproach and threat, and by making the threat contingent on not producing anything that opposes the shortest surah of the Qur'an. Then, despite their numbers and their renown for eloquence and their eagerness for opposition, they did not confront him by opposing him, and they resorted to leaving their homeland and expending their lives.

Second: that they contain information about the unseen as it actually is, for if they had opposed him with something, its concealment would ordinarily have been impossible, especially as those who attacked him were more numerous than those who defended him in every age.

Third: that if he ﷺ had doubted his matter, he would not have called them to opposition with this exaggeration, for fear that he might be opposed and his proof be refuted. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿prepared for the disbelievers﴾ indicates that the Fire is created and now prepared for them.

And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them are gardens ﴿وَبَشِّرِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وعَمِلُوا الصّالِحاتِ أنَّ لَهم جَنّاتٍ﴾. It is conjoined (ʿaṭf, coordination) to the preceding sentence. The purpose is to set the state of the one who believes in the Mighty Qur'an, and the description of his reward, against the state of the one who disbelieves in it and the manner of his punishment. This follows the divine custom of pairing encouragement (targhib) with warning (tarhib), to energize the acquisition of what saves and to deter from committing what destroys. It is not that the act itself is conjoined, such that something of the same kind as a command or prohibition would have to be sought for it, to be conjoined to it or to ﴿فاتَّقُوا﴾ (so fear [the Fire]). For when they do not produce anything that opposes it after the challenge, its inimitability becomes manifest. And when that is manifest, whoever disbelieves in it deserves punishment, and whoever believes in it deserves reward. That requires warning these and giving good news to those. The Messenger (ﷺ), or the scholar of every age, or anyone able to give good news, is commanded to give them good tidings. He did not address them with the good news as he addressed the disbelievers, in exalting their status and announcing that they are worthy of being given good tidings and congratulated on what has been prepared for them.

It is also read as ﴿وَبُشِّرَ﴾ in the passive voice, conjoined to ﴿أُعِدَّتْ﴾ (was prepared), in which case it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new independent sentence). Al-bishara (good news) is the news that brings joy, for the effect of joy appears on the skin's surface (al-bashra). For this reason the jurists said: good news is the first report. So if a man says to his slaves, "Whoever gives me the good news of my son's arrival is free," and they inform him one by one, the first of them is freed; but if he says, "Whoever informs me," they are all freed. As for His statement, exalted is He, ﴿فَبَشِّرْهم بِعَذابٍ ألِيمٍ﴾ (so give them the good news of a painful punishment), it is sarcastic (tahakkum), or in the manner of the saying: "Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

﴿الصّالِحاتِ﴾ (al-ṣāliḥāt, the righteous deeds) is the plural of ṣāliḥa, which is one of the adjectives that have become predominant and function as nouns, like ḥasana (good). Ḥuṭayʾa said:

"How shall I satirize, when there keeps coming to me, in my absence, a good one from the family of Lam?"

It denotes the deeds that the Law has sanctioned and deemed good. Its feminine form is according to the interpretation of "quality" (khaṣla) or "trait" (khalla), and the lām in it is for the genus. He conjoined the deed to faith, giving the ruling for both, to indicate that the cause for deserving this good news is the combination of the two matters (the combining of the two descriptions). Faith, which is an expression for verification and affirmation, is a foundation (ussun), and righteous deeds are like the building upon it; there is no benefit in a foundation with no building on it. For this reason they are rarely mentioned separately. In this there is evidence that the deeds lie outside the designation of faith, for the principle is that a thing is not conjoined to itself nor to what is included within it.

﴿أنَّ لَهُمْ﴾ (that for them) is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, the verb reaching it directly, or it is in the genitive by an implied preposition, like: "By Allah, I will surely do it." 

Al-janna (the garden) is the single instance of al-jann, which is the verbal noun of janna-hu, meaning he covered it, and the root's core is concealment. It was named by this for the tree that shades, because its branches intertwine, in intensification, as if it covers what is beneath it with a single covering. Zuhayr said:

"As if my two eyes, at the two sides of a female camel-carrier [that is] among the water-carriers, were watering a tall, dense garden of palms."

That is, tall palm trees. Then the orchard (bustan) was called so because of its thick, shaded trees, and then the abode of reward, because of the gardens in it. It is said that it was named so because in this world it concealed what had been prepared in it for mankind of the branches of blessings, as He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿فَلا تَعْلَمُ نَفْسٌ ما أُخْفِيَ لَهم مِن قُرَّةِ أعْيُنٍ﴾ (no soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for the eyes). Its plural and indefiniteness (in the text) are because the gardens, according to what Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned, are seven: the Paradise of Firdaws, the Garden of ʿAdn, the Garden of Bliss, the Abode of Eternity, the Garden of Refuge, the Abode of Peace, and ʿIlliyyun. Within each of them there are levels and degrees differing according to the differences in deeds and doers.

The lām in ﴿لَهُمْ﴾ (for them) indicates their entitlement to them, because of what is consequent upon it of faith and righteous deed, not for its own essence. For it does not repay the previous blessings, let alone require reward and recompense for what is to come. Rather, it is by the Lawgiver's making, and by the requirement of His promise, exalted is He, not unconditionally, but on condition that one persists in it until death while believing, due to His statement, exalted is He: ﴿وَمَن يَرْتَدِدْ مِنكم عَنْ دِينِهِ فَيَمُتْ وهو كافِرٌ فَأُولَئِكَ حَبِطَتْ أعْمالُهُمْ﴾ (And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless), and His statement to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿لَئِنْ أشْرَكْتَ لَيَحْبَطَنَّ عَمَلُكَ﴾ (If you associate, your deed will surely become worthless), and similar verses. Perhaps He, glorified and exalted, did not restrict it here, being content with those (other verses).

﴿تَجْرِي مِن تَحْتِها الأنْهارُ﴾ (beneath which rivers flow) means: from beneath their trees, just as you see them flowing beneath the trees growing on their banks. It is reported from Masruq: the rivers of Paradise flow without a trench. The lām in al-anhar (the rivers) is for the genus, as in your saying to someone: "A garden by the flowing water." Or it is for the known referent: they are the rivers mentioned in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿فِيها أنْهارٌ مِن ماءٍ غَيْرِ آسِنٍ﴾ (therein are rivers of water unchanging). Al-nahr, with a fatḥa and sukūn, is the wide watercourse above the small canal and below the sea, like the Nile and the Euphrates. The root carries the sense of width. The intended meaning of it is its water, by an implied meaning, or by figurative usage (majaz, non-literal usage), or the channels themselves. Attributing the flowing to them is figurative, as in His statement: ﴿وَأخْرَجَتِ الأرْضُ أثْقالَها﴾ (and the earth will bring out its burdens).

﴿كُلَّما رُزِقُوا مِنها مِن ثَمَرَةٍ رِزْقًا قالُوا هَذا الَّذِي رُزِقْنا﴾ (Whenever they are provided with a provision of its fruit, they say: "This is what we were provided with") is a second attribute of ﴿جَنّاتٍ﴾ (gardens), or the predicate of an omitted subject, or a resumptive sentence. It is as if, when it was said, "for them are gardens," it came into the hearer's mind that their fruits are like the fruits of this world, or of other kinds, so this was removed by that. ﴿كُلَّما﴾ (whenever) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and ﴿رِزْقًا﴾ (a provision) is the object. The two instances of ﴿مِنْ﴾ (from) indicate origin, and they stand in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The original structure and meaning of the speech is: each time they were provided with a provision (that is) originating from the gardens, [the provision being] originating from a fruit. He restricted the provision by its being originating from the gardens, and its origination from them by its origination from a fruit. So the first circumstantial referent is ﴿رِزْقًا﴾ and the second circumstantial referent is the pronoun hidden in the circumstantial clause. It is possible that ﴿مِن ثَمَرِهِ﴾ (of its fruit) is an explanatory clarification placed before, as in your saying: "I saw from you a lion." And ﴿هَذا﴾ (this) is a pointer to the kind of what they were provided with, like your saying, pointing to a flowing river, "This water does not cease," for you do not mean by it the particular visible water, but the known kind that is continuous through the succession of its flow. Even though the pointing is to its particular instance, the meaning is: "This is like our provision." But because the resemblance between them is strong, he made its essence [identical to] its essence, as in your saying: "Abu Yusuf is Abu Hanifa."

﴿مِن قَبْلُ﴾ (from before) means: from before this, in this world. He made the fruit of Paradise of the same kind as the fruit of this world, so that the soul would incline towards it at first sight, for natures incline towards what is familiar and recoil from other things. Then its excellence and the true nature of the blessing in it become clear to them, for if it were of a kind they had not known, they would think that it could only be like that. Or [the meaning is]: in Paradise, because their food resembles itself in appearance, as Ibn Kathir reported from al-Ḥasan, may Allah be pleased with them both: that one of them is brought a dish, and he eats from it, then another is brought to him, and he sees it like the first, and says that; the angel says: "Eat, for the color is one but the taste differs." Or as is reported that he (ﷺ) said: "By Him in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, a man of the people of Paradise will reach out to take a fruit to eat it, but it does not reach his mouth until Allah, exalted is He, replaces it with one like it." So perhaps, when they see it in its first form, they say that. The first is more apparent, because it preserves the generality of ﴿كُلَّما﴾ (whenever), for it indicates their repeating this saying each time they are provided.
