What prompts them to it is the extreme of their astonishment and their delight in what they find of the great difference in pleasure and the precise resemblance in appearance.

﴿وَأُتُوا بِهِ مُتَشابِهًا﴾ (and they are brought it in resemblance) is a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ) that confirms that. The pronoun, according to the first view, refers to what they were provided with in both abodes, for it is implied by the words of the Mighty, the Majestic: ﴿هَذا الَّذِي رُزِقْنا مِن قَبْلُ﴾. A parallel to it is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿إنْ يَكُنْ غَنِيًّا أوْ فَقِيرًا فاللَّهُ أوْلى بِهِما﴾ (If he is rich or poor, Allah is more deserving of both), meaning of the two kinds, rich and poor. According to the second view, it refers to the provision. If it is said: resemblance is similarity in attribute, and this is absent between the fruits of this world and the Hereafter, as Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "There is nothing in Paradise of the foods of this world except the names." I say: the resemblance between them is present in the form, which is the basis of the name, not in the quantity or the taste, and that suffices for the application of the term "resemblance." Moreover, the noble verse has another interpretation: that the delights of the people of Paradise, in exchange for what they were provided in this world of knowledge and acts of obedience, vary in pleasure according to their variation. So it is possible that what is meant by ﴿هَذا الَّذِي رُزِقْنا﴾ is that it is their reward. Their resemblance is the equality of the two in nobility, excellence, and high rank. Thus this in the promise is like His statement: ﴿ذُوقُوا ما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ﴾ (taste what you used to do) in the threat.

﴿وَلَهم فِيها أزْواجٌ مُطَهَّرَةٌ﴾ (and for them therein are purified spouses) are purified from what is found repugnant in women and blamed in their conditions, such as menstruation, filth, the uncleanness of nature, and bad character. For purification (tatahhur) is used of bodies, characters, and actions. It is also read as ﴿مُطَهَّراتٌ﴾ (purified, feminine plural), and both are eloquent dialects. It is said: "the women did" in the form fa'alat and fa'alna, and they are fā'ila and fawā'il. He said:

"And when the virgins are veiled in smoke and hasten to set the cooking pots, and grow weary."

So the plural is according to the wording, and the singular is according to the interpretation of the group. ﴿مُطَهَّرَةٌ﴾ with a doubled ṭā' and a kasra on the hā' means the same as mutaṭahhira (purifying themselves), and muṭahhara is more emphatic than ṭāhira (pure). It is also muṭahhara to indicate that a purifier has purified them, and there is none but Allah, the Mighty, the Majestic. The word zawj (spouse) is said of the male and the female, and originally it refers to what has a counterpart of its own kind, like a pair of a shoe. If it is said: the benefit of food is nourishment and removing the harm of hunger, and the benefit of marriage is procreation and preserving the species, and these are dispensed with in Paradise. I say: the foods, marriages, and all other conditions of Paradise share with their worldly counterparts only some attributes and considerations, and are named by their names by way of metaphor and analogy. They do not share in the full reality, so as to entail all that goes with it and yield the very same benefit.

﴿وَهم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ (and they therein are abiding) means: remaining forever. Al-khuld and al-khulūd originally mean lasting for a long time, whether it endures or not. For this reason the stones of the hearth and the boulders are called khawālid, and the part of a human that remains in its state as long as he lives is called khald. If it were coined for perpetuity, the restriction by "forever" in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿خالِدِينَ فِيها أبَدًا﴾ (abiding therein forever) would be superfluous, and its use where there is no perpetuity, as in their saying "a long-standing pause" (waqafa mukhalladun), would entail either homonymy (ishtirak) or figurative usage (majaz). The basic principle negates both. This is unlike the case in which it was coined for something more general than it, and then used in it with that consideration, like the use of "body" (jism) for a human, as in His statement: ﴿وَما جَعَلْنا لِبَشَرٍ مِن قَبْلِكَ الخُلْدَ﴾ (And We did not grant to any human before you eternity). However, what is meant here is perpetuity according to the majority of scholars, due to the verses and traditions that bear witness to it.

If it is said: bodies are composed of parts of opposite qualities, subject to transformations that lead to disintegration and dissolution, so how is their eternity in the Gardens conceivable? I say: He, exalted is He, will restore them in such a way that transformation does not affect them, by making their parts, for example, mutually balanced in quality, equal in strength, so that none of them can overpower another to transform it, intertwined and mutually entailing, such that some of them never separate from others, as is observed in some minerals.

Moreover, measuring that world and its conditions by what we find and observe is a sign of deficiency of reason and weakness of insight. Know that since most sensory pleasures are confined to: dwellings, foods, and marriages, as induction (istiqrāʾ) shows, the criterion of all of that is permanence and stability. For every great blessing, when fear of its loss accompanies it, becomes troubled and impure, not free of the taints of pain. So He gave good news to the believers of these, and illustrated what He has prepared for them in the Hereafter with the most splendid of what is enjoyed of them, and removed from them the fear of their passing by the promise of eternity, so that it would indicate their perfection in delight and joy.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 26:

﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a mosquito﴾. Since the preceding verses contained various kinds of parable (tamthil, a figurative comparison or similitude), he followed this with an explanation of its excellence, of what its true standard is, and of its condition. That condition is that it must correspond to the thing being illustrated in the respect in which the illustration is made, in greatness, smallness, lowliness and nobility, and not to the illustrating object itself. A parable is only resorted to in order to reveal the meaning being illustrated, to lift the veil from it, and to bring it out in the form of something perceived by the senses, so that the imagination (wahm) may assist the intellect ('aql) and reconcile it to that meaning. Pure abstract meaning is grasped by the intellect only with some resistance from the imagination, because it is in the imagination's nature to incline toward the sensible and to love imitation. For this reason, parables became widespread in the divine books and spread through the expressions of eloquent people and the allusions of the wise. The lowly is illustrated by the lowly, just as the great is illustrated by the great, even though the parable may be greater than every great thing. Thus, in the Gospel, the rancour of hearts was illustrated by chaff, and hard hearts by a pebble, and addressing fools was illustrated by stirring up wasps. And in the speech of the Arabs it has come: "More attentive than a tick, more flighty than a butterfly, and more precious than the brain of a mosquito." This is not what the ignorant among the disbelievers said: "When Allah illustrated the state of the hypocrites by the state of those who kindle a fire," and "the people of the rain-cloud," and the worship of idols in weakness and frailty by "the spider's house"? And [they said that] He made [these creatures] less than the fly and of baser worth than it? Allah, glorified and exalted, is too high and too majestic to set forth parables and mention the fly and the spider.

Furthermore, when He guided them to what indicates that the thing by which He challenged them is a revealed inspiration, and ordained upon it the threat for whoever disbelieves in it and the promise for whoever believes in it after its matter had become manifest, He began to answer what they had criticised in it, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed﴾, meaning: He does not abandon setting forth a parable with the mosquito as one abandons it who is ashamed to illustrate with it because of its insignificance. Haya' (shame, modesty) is the withdrawal of the soul from what is ugly for fear of blame, and it is the mean between shamelessness (waqaha), which is boldness toward ugly things and indifference to them, and bashfulness (khajal), which is the confinement of the soul from acting at all.

Its derivation is from life (hayah), for it is a breaking that affects the animal faculty and turns it back from its actions. It is said: "hayiya al-rajul" (the man became shy), just as one says "nasiya" (he forgot) and "hashiya" (he became numb), when his faculties of memory and feeling are affected. When it is ascribed to the Creator, may He be exalted, as in the hadith: "Indeed Allah is ashamed before a Muslim grey-haired man to punish him," and "Indeed Allah is living and generous; He is ashamed, when a servant raises his hands to Him, to return them empty until He places good in them." So what is meant by it is the necessary consequence of withdrawal, just as what is meant by His mercy and His wrath is the attainment of the good and the disliked, which are the necessary consequences of those two meanings. A similar example is the saying of one who describes camels:

"When they are thirsty and the water presents itself to them, they drink from it in a stream like rose-water."

He turned away from the expression "tark" (abandoning) to this one because of what it contains of illustration and emphasis. The verse may especially admit that its coming is in contrast to what occurred in the speech of the disbelievers. The verb "daraba mathalan" (to set forth a parable) is derived from "daraba al-khatim" (striking the seal), and its origin is the falling of one thing upon another. "An" with its clause is in the genitive position according to al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad), with an implied "min" (from), and in the accusative according to Sibawayh, by the verb reaching it after the deletion of the particle.

"Ma" here is indefinite (ibhamiyyah), which increases the indefinite noun in indefiniteness and generality and blocks off the ways of restriction, like your saying: "Give me a book, any (ma) book," that is, whatever book it may be. Or it is an added particle for emphasis, like the one in His saying: ﴿So by a mercy from Allah﴾. By "added" we do not mean idle and wasted [material], for the whole Qur'an is guidance and clarification. Rather [it is an added element] that was not placed to express a meaning intended by it, but was placed so that it would be mentioned together with other things and would thereby lend them firmness and strength; and this is an increase in guidance that does not detract from it.

"Ba'udah" (a mosquito) is an explanatory apposition to "mathalan" (an example). Or it is the object of "yadriba" (He sets forth), and "mathalan" is a circumstantial accusative placed before it because it is indefinite. Or both are its two objects, because the verb includes the meaning of "making" (ja'l). It has also been read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject. On this reading there are other possibilities: it may be a relative (mawsulah) whose antecedent of the relative clause is omitted, as in His saying: ﴿Completion upon the one who did well﴾; or it may be a qualifying (mawsufah) with a similar qualification, and its position is accusative by way of substitution (badaliyyah) in both cases. Or it may be an interrogative (istifhamiyyah) which is the subject, as if, when He answered their amazement that Allah sets forth parables, He said afterwards: "What is the mosquito and what is above it," so that He would not set forth a parable with it, but rather might illustrate with something even more insignificant than that. Compare the saying: "So-and-so does not mind what he gives away: a dinar or two dinars."

"Ba'ud" (mosquitoes) is of the form fa'ul from "al-ba'd" (cutting off), which is like "al-bad'" and "al-'adb," and it became particularly applied to this kind, just as "khumush" (insects) is applied generally to small creatures.

﴿And what is above it﴾ is coordinated with "ba'udah" (mosquito), or with "ma" (what) if it is made a noun. Its meaning is whatever exceeds it in body, such as the fly and the spider, as if he intended by this to answer what they had found objectionable. The meaning is: He is not ashamed to set forth a parable with a mosquito, let alone with what is larger than it; or [the meaning is] in the respect in which it was made a parable, namely smallness and insignificance, such as its wing. For indeed, upon him be prayer and peace, he set forth the mosquito's wing as a parable for this world. A comparable example in the two possibilities is what is narrated: a man in Mina fell upon the rope of a tent, and 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'No Muslim is pricked by a thorn or anything greater than it, except that a degree is written for him by it and a sin is erased from him by it.'" This may include what exceeds the thorn in pain, such as falling, and what exceeds it in smallness, such as the bite of an ant, because of his saying, upon him be prayer and peace: "Whatever befalls the believer of distress is an expiation for his sins, even to the bite of an ant."

﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾. "Amma" (as for) is a particle of detailing: it details what was stated in general, emphasises what it introduces, and contains the sense of a condition, which is why it is answered by "fa" (then). Sibawayh said: "Amma Zayd fa-dhahib" means: "Whatever may be the case concerning Zayd, he is going," that is, he is going without doubt, and it is a firm resolve from him. The original was that the "fa" would enter upon the clause, since it is the consequent, but they disliked placing it directly after the conditional particle, so they put it upon the predicate, and they made the subject a substitute for the condition verbally. In beginning the two clauses with this particle there is a praise of the state of the believers and a considering of their knowledge as significant, and an eloquent censure of the disbelievers for their saying. The pronoun in "annahu" (that it) refers to the parable, or to "an yudraba" (that it be set forth). And "al-haqq" (the truth) is that which is firm and cannot be legitimately denied; it encompasses established entities, correct actions and true statements, from their saying "haqqa al-amr" (the matter became established), when it becomes firm. From it comes "thawb muhaqqaq" (a cloth of firm weave), that is, well-made in its weaving.

﴿And as for those who disbelieve, they say﴾. It would have been proper to say: "And as for those who disbelieve, they do not know," so that it would correspond to its counterpart and face its contrasting half. But since their saying this was a clear proof of the complete extent of their ignorance, He turned to it by way of metonymy (kinayah), so that it would serve as evidence against them.

﴿What did Allah intend by this as a parable?﴾ This admits two possibilities: that "ma" is an interrogative and "dha" means "alladhi" (who/which) with what follows it as its relative clause, and the whole is the predicate of "ma"; or that "ma" together with "dha" is one word meaning "what thing," in the accusative position as object, like "ma arada Allah" (what Allah intended). The better answer to it is the nominative on the first analysis and the accusative on the second, so that the answer corresponds to the question.

Irada (will, intention) is the inclination of the soul and its tendency toward an act, to the point where it moves it to that act; it is also said of the faculty which is the source of this inclination. The first meaning together with the act, and the second before it, are both unimaginable as attributes of the Creator, may He be exalted. For this reason it has been disputed what His will means. It has been said: His will concerning His own acts is that He is neither heedless nor compelled, and concerning the acts of others, that He commanded them. On this view, acts of disobedience are not by His will. It has also been said: it is His knowledge that the matter comprises the most perfect order and the most beneficial aspect, so that it calls the capable one to bring it about. The truth, however, is that it is the preponderance of one of two possibilities over the other, and specifying it with one aspect rather than another, or with a meaning that necessitates this preponderance. It is more general than choice (ikhtiyar), for choice is an inclination together with preference. In this question there is an implication of belittlement and disdain. "Mathalan" (as a parable) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) or as a circumstantial accusative, like His saying: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾.

﴿He leads many astray by it and He guides many by it﴾. This is the answer to "ma dha" (what this is), that is: the misleading of many and the guidance of many. The verb is placed in the position of the verbal noun to indicate occurrence and renewal. Or it is an explanation of the two clauses introduced by "amma", and a recording that knowledge of its being the truth is guidance and clarification, and that the disbelievers' taking it as an object of censure and denial, in disregard of the good of its purpose, is misguidance and wickedness. The multitude of each of the two groups is considered with regard to themselves, not in comparison with their opposites, for those who are guided are few compared with the people of misguidance, as He, exalted, said: (p-64) ﴿And few are they﴾, and ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾. It is possible that the multitude of the misguided is in terms of number, and the multitude of the guided is in terms of excellence and nobility, as the poet said:

"They are few when counted, but many when they gather in strength."

And he said:

"Indeed the noble are many in the lands, even if they are few; just as others are few, even if they are many."

﴿And He does not lead astray by it except the defiant﴾, that is, those who have gone out of the bounds of faith, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed the hypocrites, they are the defiant﴾, from their saying: "fasaqat al-rutabah 'an qishriha" (the date slipped out of its skin) when it came out. The root of fisq (defiance) is going out from the path. Ru'bah said:

"Defiant, deviating from their course, veering aside."

In the Law, the fasiq (defiant one) is the one who goes out from the command of Allah by committing a major sin, and it has three degrees:

The first: negligence (taghabi), which is committing it at times while regarding it as ugly.

The second: persistence (infimak), which is becoming accustomed to committing it, unconcerned with it.

The third: denial (juhud), which is committing it while considering it right. When one approaches this station and oversteps its limits, he removes the noose of faith from his neck and clothes himself in disbelief. As long as he remains in the degree of negligence or persistence, the name of believer is not removed from him, because he is characterised by affirmation (tasdiq), which is what the name of faith signifies, and because of His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾. The Mu'tazilah (Mu'tazilites), when they said: faith is an expression for the combination of affirmation, verbal profession and action, and disbelief is the denial and rejection of the truth, made it a third category standing between the two stations of the believer and the disbeliever, because it shares with each of them some of the rulings. The restriction of misguidance to them, arranged upon the attribute of defiance, indicates that it is this [defiance] which prepared them for misguidance and brought them to error. This is because their disbelief, their deviation from the truth and their persistence in falsehood turned the faces of their thinking away from the wisdom of the parable toward the lowliness of what was used as the illustration, until their ignorance became firmly rooted through it and their error increased, so they denied it and mocked it.

It has been read ﴿yudallu﴾ in the passive voice, and "al-fasiquna" (the defiant ones) in the nominative.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 27:

﴿Those who break the covenant of God﴾ is a qualifier of *al-fasiqin* (the defiantly disobedient, *fasiq* being one who transgresses God's command), serving to censure them and to confirm their transgression. *Al-naqd* (breaking) means undoing the structure of a thing. Its original sense is the unwinding of the strands of a rope. Its use for annulling a covenant is because a covenant is figuratively described as a rope, since it binds one of the two parties to the other. If "rope" is mentioned alone, this is *tarshih* (a figurative device that develops a metaphor). If it is mentioned together with "covenant," it is an allusion (*ramz*) to what accompanies it, namely that the covenant is a rope in the firmness of the bond between the two parties to it. This is like your saying, "a brave man who devours his rivals" and "a scholar from whom people part ways," for in this there is an indication that he is a lion in his bravery and a sea in terms of the benefit he gives.

*Al-ahd* (covenant) is a firm pledge. It is used for that which must be observed and kept, such as a bequest and an oath. It is also applied to a dwelling (*al-dar*), in that it is kept up by returning to it, and to history (*al-tarikh*), because it preserves events.

This covenant is either the covenant taken by reason, which is the proof established against His servants, indicating His oneness, the necessity of His existence, and the truthfulness of His messenger. To this refers His saying, ﴿And He made them bear witness concerning themselves﴾ (7:172). Or it is the covenant taken through the messengers from the nations, that when a messenger came to them, confirmed by miracles, they would confirm him, follow him, not conceal his matter, and not oppose his judgment. To this he alludes with His saying, ﴿And [recall] when God took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾ (3:187) and its like. It has been said that God's covenants are three: a covenant He took from all the descendants of Adam, that they acknowledge His lordship; a covenant He took from the prophets, that they establish the religion and not divide over it; and a covenant He took from the scholars, that they make the truth clear and not conceal it.

﴿After its binding﴾: the pronoun refers to the covenant. *Al-mithaq* (binding agreement) is the name for that by which firm binding occurs, and *al-wathaqa* means firmness. What is meant by it is what God bound His covenant with, of signs and scriptures, or what they bound themselves with, of commitment and acceptance. It may also be that it carries the sense of a verbal noun. The particle *min* (from/after) here indicates the starting point, since the beginning of the breaking is after the binding.

﴿And they sever what God has commanded to be joined﴾ includes every severance that God does not approve of, such as severing the ties of kinship, turning away from allegiance to the believers, making distinctions between the prophets (peace be upon them) and the scriptures in their confirmation, abandoning the obligatory congregations, and all else that involves rejecting good. Or it is engaging in evil, for this severs the connection between God and the servant, which is the intended purpose in itself of every joining and separating. *Al-amr* (command) is the speech that demands an action. It was said: with superiority; it was also said: with dominance. By this, the matter (*amr*) which is one of the affairs was named, a designation of the object by the verbal noun, for it is among the things that are commanded. As it has been said, it has a matter (*sha'n*), which is the demand and intention. One says *sha'antu sha'nahu*, meaning "I intended his intention." The clause ﴿that it be joined﴾ may be in the accusative or genitive case, as a substitute for *ma* (what) or for its pronoun. The second is better in wording and meaning.

﴿And they cause corruption in the earth﴾ by preventing [people] from faith and mocking the truth, and by cutting the ties by which the order and well-being of the world are maintained.

﴿Those are the losers﴾: those who lost by neglecting the intellect from reflection, by failing to seize what would grant them eternal life, by exchanging denial and disparagement of the signs for faith in them and reflection upon their realities and drawing from their lights, by buying breaking for fulfilment, corruption for righteousness, and punishment for reward.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 28:**

﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ This is an interrogative (istikhbar) carrying a denial and an expression of wonder at their disbelief. It denies that there is any state in which their disbelief could occur, by way of demonstrative reasoning (al-tariq al-burhani). Their existence cannot be separated from some state and attribute. So when he denies that their disbelief has any state in which it could exist, this necessarily entails the denial of its existence. This is more emphatic and stronger in denying disbelief than "Do you disbelieve?" (atakfurun), and it better suits what follows of the circumstantial clause (al-hal). The address is directed at those who disbelieve. When He described them with disbelief, evil speech and corrupt deeds, He addressed them by way of iltifat (a shift from third person to second person) and rebuked them for their disbelief, though they knew their own condition, which requires the opposite of that. The meaning is: tell me, in what state do you disbelieve?

﴿And you were dead⦆ That is, bodies without life: elements, nourishments, humours, drops of semen, and lumps of flesh, formed and unformed.

﴿Then He gave you life⦆ by creating the souls and breathing them into you. He joined it with "then" (fa) because it is directly connected to what precedes it, not separated from it by an interval, unlike the rest.

﴿Then He causes you to die⦆ when your terms are fulfilled. ﴿Then He will bring you back to life⦆ at the resurrection on the day the Trumpet is blown, or for the questioning in the graves. ﴿Then to Him you will be returned⦆ after the gathering, and He will recompense you for your deeds. Or, you will be raised up to Him from your graves for reckoning. So how strange is your disbelief, given your knowledge of this condition of yours!

If it is said: if they knew that they were dead, then He gave them life, then He causes them to die, they did not know that He will give them life again and that to Him they will be returned. I say: their being able to know both of these, through the proofs He has set up for them, is treated as equivalent to their knowledge in terms of removing excuse. Especially since the verse contains an indication of what proves the validity of both, namely: when He, exalted is He, was able to give them life at first, He is able to give them life a second time, for originating creation is no easier for Him than its repetition.

Or, the address is to both groups (the believers and the disbelievers). When He, exalted and glorified is He, had explained the proofs of monotheism and prophethood, promised reward for faith and threatened punishment for disbelief, He reinforced this by enumerating for them the general and particular blessings, and deemed the emergence of disbelief from them ugly and unlikely given those magnificent blessings, for the greatness of blessings necessitates the greatness of disobedience toward the Benefactor.

If it is said: how is death counted among the blessings that require gratitude? I say: since it is a means to the second life, which is the true life, as God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed the Last Abode, that is the true life⦆, it is among the great blessings. (p-66) Although what is counted as a blessing for them is the meaning drawn from the whole narrative together, just as the circumstantial clause (al-hal) is the knowledge of it, not each single sentence, for some of its sentences are past and some are future, and neither of these can validly serve as a circumstantial clause.

Or the address is to the believers specifically, to affirm the favour upon them and to place disbelief far from them, in the sense: how can disbelief be imagined from you when you were dead, ignorant, and He gave you life through the knowledge and faith He bestowed upon you, then He causes you to die the known death, then He gives you life, the true life, then to Him you will be returned, and He will reward you with what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.

Life is literally (haqiqah) the sensitive faculty, or what requires it, and by it the animal is called "hayawan" (animal). It is used metaphorically for the nutritive faculty, since it is among its first stages and preliminaries. And for what concerns man among the virtues, such as reason, knowledge and faith, insofar as these are his perfection and final end. Death, in opposition to these, is applied to whatever is opposed to them at each level. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: God gives you life, then causes you to die﴾. And He said: ﴿Know that God gives life to the earth after its death﴾, and He said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among people...﴾. When the Creator, exalted is He, is described with it, what is meant is the validity of His being characterised by the knowledge and power that are necessary for this faculty in us, or a meaning subsisting in His essence that requires that, by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

Ya'qub read "turja'un" (you will be returned) with a fatha on the ta' throughout the Qur'an.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 29:**

﴿It is He who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it.﴾ This explains another blessing, ordered after the first. Creating them as living beings able to act, time after time, is one thing, and creating what their survival depends on and through which their livelihood is completed is another. The meaning of ﴿for you﴾ is: for your sake and for your benefit in this world, by your making use of these things for the welfare of your bodies, whether through an intermediary or without one, and for your religion, through inference (istidlal), consideration (i'tibar) and recognition (ta'arruf) of what suits them of the pleasures and pains of the Hereafter. This is not meant as a purpose (gharad) in the strict sense, since the agent who acts for a purpose is thereby perfected. Rather, it is as though it were a purpose, in that it is the outcome (aqibah) and consequence (muaddah) of the act. This implies the permissibility of beneficial things, and it does not preclude that some of them are specifically assigned to some people because of incidental causes. For it indicates that the whole is for the whole, not that each one is for each one. What is meant by ﴿whatever is on the earth﴾ is all of it, unless by "the earth" is meant the direction of the lower part, just as "the sky" is meant as the direction of the upper part. ﴿Jami'an﴾ (all of it) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the second relative pronoun (al-mawsul al-thani).

﴿Then He turned to the sky.﴾ He intended it by His will, from the expression istawa ilayhi ka-l-sahm al-mursal ("he turned toward it like a released arrow"), when one aims at it in a straight line without turning aside from anything. The basic meaning of istiwa' is seeking equality (talab al-sawa'), and its application to uprightness (i'tidal) is because of the equalizing of the arrangement of its parts. It cannot be taken in that sense here, because that is a property of bodies. It has also been said that istawa means "he prevailed and took possession," as the poet said:

*"Bishr has prevailed over Iraq... without sword or spilled blood."*

The first meaning is more faithful to the root, to the preposition with which the verb is construed, and to the equalizing (taswiyah) that follows it with the particle fa' (then). What is meant by ﴿the sky﴾ is these heavenly bodies, or the directions of height. The particle ﴿thumma﴾ (then) is perhaps for the difference between the two creations and the superiority of the creation of the sky over the creation of the earth, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then he was among those who believed﴾. It is not for delay in time, since that would contradict the apparent sense of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the earth after that He spread out﴾, which indicates that the spreading of the earth, which preceded the creation of what is in it, was delayed beyond the creation of the sky and its equalizing. Unless one resumes with ﴿dahaha﴾ (He spread it), with the earth in the accusative governed by an implied verb indicated by ﴿Are you more difficult to create?﴾, as if to say: "Consider the earth and reflect upon its affair after that." But this is contrary to the apparent sense.

﴿So He completed them﴾: He made them balanced and created them preserved from crookedness and fissures. The pronoun ﴿hunna﴾ (them) refers to the sky if it is interpreted as the heavenly bodies, since it is plural. Or it has the sense of plurality. Otherwise it is an ambiguous pronoun (mubham) explained by what follows it, as in the expression "rubbahu rajulan" (how often a man...).

﴿Seven heavens﴾ is either a substitute (badal) or an explanation (tafsir). If it is said: Do not the astronomers (ashab al-arsad) affirm nine spheres? I say: There are doubts about what they have mentioned. And even if it is correct, the verse does not negate anything beyond them. Moreover, if the Throne and the Footstool are added to them, no disagreement remains.

﴿And He is Knowing of all things﴾: This contains a causal explanation, as though He said: Because He knows the reality of all things, He created what He created in this most perfect pattern and most beneficial manner. It is also an argument that whoever's act is in this wondrous order and beautiful arrangement is knowing. For the perfecting of acts, their firm construction, and their specification in the best and most beneficial way can be conceived only from a knowing, wise and merciful one. It also removes what troubles their hearts, namely that after bodies have been scattered and their parts crumbled, and have joined with what resembles them, how can the parts of each body be gathered a second time such that nothing of them is missing and nothing is added that was not with them, so that it is restored as it was? Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He is Knowing of every creation﴾.

Know that the soundness of the resurrection (hashr) rests on three premises, and these two verses provide proof for them. As for the first, it is that the matter of bodies is receptive to gathering and life, and He pointed to the proof of it in His saying: ﴿and you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die﴾. For the successive alternation of dispersal and gathering, and of death and life, upon them indicates that they are by their very nature receptive to these, and what is essential does not accept ceasing or changing. As for the second and third, He, mighty and majestic, knows them and their places, and is able to gather them and bring them to life. He pointed to the basis for affirming these two by saying that He, exalted is He, is able to originate them and to originate what is greater in creation and more wondrous in making. Therefore He is more able to restore them and bring them back to life. And He, exalted is He, created what He created as a creation that is equal, firm, without disparity or disorder, in which He took account of their interests and met their needs.

This is evidence of the completeness of His knowledge and the perfection of His wisdom; His power is exalted and His wisdom is subtle. Nafi', Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i made the ha' in forms like ﴿fa-huwa﴾ and ﴿huwa﴾ quiescent, likening it to ʿadud (the arm), as a comparison to that.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 30:**

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am placing on the earth a khalifah (successor)"﴾. This is an enumeration of a third blessing that encompasses all people, for the creation of Adam, his honouring, and his being preferred over the angels by commanding them to prostrate to him, is a favour that encompasses his offspring. *Idh* (إذ) is an adverb (*zarf*) placed for the time of a past relation in which another relation occurred, just as *idha* (إذا) is placed for the time of a future relation in which another relation occurs. For this reason both must be construed with sentences (*jumal*), like *haythu* (حيث) for place. Both are indeclinable (*mabni*), being likened to relative pronouns, and both are used to express causation and conditionality. Their position in the sentence is always accusative by virtue of being adverbial, since they are among the adverbs that do not vary in form, for the reason we have mentioned. As for the words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿And mention the brother of ʿAd, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf﴾ and similar verses, they are understood as meaning "mention the event when it was the case that...", so the event is omitted and the adverb is put in its place. Its governing verb in this verse is "they said" (qalu), or "mention" (udhkur) according to the interpretation mentioned, since it occurs as an explicit object in the Qur'an many times, or it is an implied verb indicated by the meaning of the preceding verse, like "and He began your creation when He said..." On this view the sentence is coordinated with "He created for you" and is included in the scope of the relative clause. It is reported from Maʿmar that the particle is superfluous (*zaʾid*).

*Al-malaʾika* (الملائكة, the angels) is the plural of *malʾak* according to the original form, like *al-shamaʾil* the plural of *shamʾal*, and the *ta* is for the feminization of the plural. It is an inverted form of *malʾak* from *al-alukah* (الألوكة), which means "message", because they are intermediaries between God, Exalted is He, and people, so they are the messengers of God, or they are like messengers to them. Scholars differed about their reality, after agreeing that they are existing beings that subsist by themselves. The majority of Muslims hold that they are subtle bodies capable of taking various forms, citing that the messengers used to see them in that way. A group of Christians said they are the excellent human souls separated from bodies. The philosophers claimed that they are simple substances (*jawahir mujarrada*) differing in reality from the rational souls, divided into two kinds: one kind whose concern is total immersion in knowledge of the Truth, majestic is His majesty, and transcendence above occupation with anything else, as He described them in His well-established revelation, saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They glorify Him night and day; they never tire﴾, and they are the *ʿIlliyyun* and the angels brought near. The other kind manages the affair from the heaven to the earth according to what has been decreed and what the divine pen has written, ﴿They do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾, and they are the ones who manage affairs, some of them celestial and some of them terrestrial, according to a detail I have set out in the book *al-Tawali* (الطوالع).

As for those addressed, "the angels" means all of them, because of the generality of the wording and the absence of any specifier. It was said: the angels of the earth. It was said: Iblis and those with him in fighting the jinn, for God, Exalted is He, first settled them on the earth, and they caused corruption in it, so He sent Iblis to them with an army of angels, and he destroyed them and scattered them among the islands and mountains.

*Jaʿil* (جاعل) is from *jaʿala*, which takes two objects, and these are *fi al-ardi* (in the earth) and *khalifah* (successor), and it operates on both, because it has the meaning of the future and relies on a subject. It may also mean "creator" (*khaliq*).

The *khalifah* is one who succeeds another and takes his place. The *ha* in it is for intensification (*mubalaghah*). The intended referent is Adam, peace be upon him, because he was the khalifah of God on His earth. Likewise every prophet whom God appointed as successor for the cultivation of the earth, the governance of people, the perfecting of their souls, and the execution of His command among them. This is not because God has any need of one to stand in for Him, but because of the inadequacy of the one appointed to receive His overflow (*faydh*) and to take His command without an intermediary. For this reason He did not make a prophet of an angel, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man﴾. Do you not see that when the prophets' strength was great and their disposition was kindled, so that its oil nearly shines even though no fire touches it, He sent the angels to them, and the one among them of highest rank He addressed without intermediary, as He addressed Moses, peace be upon him, at the appointed time, and Muhammad ﷺ on the night of the Ascension. A parallel in nature is this: when the bone was unable to receive nourishment from the flesh because of the distance between them, the Creator, Exalted is He, in His wisdom placed between them the cartilage (*ghudrūf*) suitable for both, so that it takes from this and gives to that.

Or the meaning is "successor of the one who dwelt on the earth before him", or it means him and his offspring, because they succeed those before them, or some of them succeed others. The singular wording is either because mention of him suffices without mention of his sons, just as mention of the tribe's ancestor suffices in their saying "Mudar" and "Hashim", or it is interpreted as "one who will succeed you", or "a successor who will replace you."

The purpose of God's saying this to the angels is to teach consultation and to magnify the status of the one appointed: the Mighty and Majestic announced the existence of the inhabitants of His kingdom, and named him "successor" before creating him, and He showed his superior merit over the defects that are in him, by their question and His answer, and by explaining that wisdom requires bringing into being what its good outweighs, for abandoning abundant good for the sake of little evil is great evil, and so on.

﴿They said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption in it and sheds blood?"﴾ This is an expression of wonder that He should appoint for cultivating and reforming the earth one who would corrupt it, or that He would substitute for the people of obedience the people of disobedience. It is also a request to uncover what was hidden from them of the wisdom that overcame those corruptions and nullified them, and an inquiry about what would guide them and remove their doubt, like a student asking his teacher about what troubles his chest. It is not an objection against God, majestic is His power, nor a slander against the children of Adam by way of backbiting, for they are too exalted for such a thought to be attributed to them, given His saying, ﴿Rather, they are honoured servants. They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾. They knew this either by information from God, Exalted is He, or by receiving it from the Preserved Tablet, or by deduction from what was fixed in their intellects that infallibility is among the special qualities of the angels, or by analogy of one of the two species (jinn and humans) to the other.

*Al-safk* (السفك), *al-sabk* (السبك), *al-safh* (السفح) and *al-shann* (الشن) are kinds of pouring. *Al-safk* is said of blood and tears; *al-sabk* of molten jewels; *al-safh* of pouring from above; and *al-shann* of pouring from the mouth of a waterskin or the like. Likewise *al-sann*. It is recited as *yusfaku* (يُسفَك, passive voice), in which case the returning pronoun to *man* (من), whether it is taken as a relative pronoun or as a deleted qualifying noun, is implied, meaning: blood is shed among them.

﴿And we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾. This is a clarifying circumstantial clause (*hal muqarrirah*) for the aspect of the difficulty, like your saying, "Do you do good to your enemies while I am the old, needy friend?" The meaning is: "Will You appoint rebels while we are infallible and deserving of that?" The intended purpose is an inquiry into what has preferred them, along with what is expected from them, as opposed to the infallible angels concerning the appointment, not vanity or boasting. It is as if they knew that the one appointed as khalifah would have three powers on which his affair depends: an appetitive power and an irascible power, which lead him to corruption and the shedding of blood, and a rational power, which calls him to knowledge and obedience. They looked at these individually and said: what is the wisdom in appointing him, when, considering those two powers, wisdom does not require bringing him into being, let alone appointing him as successor; and as for the rational power, we establish what is expected from it, free from the opposition of those corruptions. They overlooked the excellence of each of the two powers when they become refined, obedient to the intellect, habituated to good, such as chastity, courage, striving against desire, and fairness. They did not know that composition yields what individual units fall short of, such as comprehension of particulars, deriving crafts, and extracting the benefits of existing things, moving from potentiality to actuality, which is the purpose of the appointment. To this God, Exalted is He, alluded in summary by His saying: (p-69) ﴿He said, "Indeed I know what you do not know."﴾

*Al-tasbih* (التسبيح, glorification) is the removal of God, Exalted is He, from evil, and likewise *al-taqdis* (التقديس, sanctification), from *sabaha* in the land and water, and *qadusa* in the land when one goes far away in it. It is said *qadusa* when one becomes pure, because the one who purifies a thing removes it far from filth. "With Your praise" (بحمدك) is in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: "clothed in Your praise for what You have inspired us to know of You and enabled us to glorify You with." By this they corrected what the attribution of glorification to themselves might suggest. "And we sanctify You" means "we purify our souls from sins for Your sake." It is as though they set against the corruption, which was explained as shirk according to some, the glorification, and against the shedding of blood, which is the greatest of blameworthy acts, the purification of souls from sins. It was also said: "we sanctify You," and the *lam* is superfluous.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 31:

﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾. This is either by creating in him a necessary knowledge (ʿilm ḍarūrī) of them, or by casting them into his heart (ilqāʾ fī raʿihi). It does not require a prior convention (iṣṭilāḥ) so that it would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul). Teaching (taʿlīm) is an act which usually results in knowledge, and for this reason one says ʿallamtuhu fa-lam yataʿallam ("I taught him, but he did not learn"). Ādam is a non-Arabic name (ism aʿjamī), like Āzar and Shālikh. Its derivation is from al-udmah or al-admah, meaning "the pattern/exemplar" (al-uswah), or from adīm al-arḍ ("the surface of the earth"), in accordance with what has been narrated from him, upon him be prayers and peace, that "God, exalted is He, took a handful from the entire earth, its plain and its hard ground, and created Adam from it."

Therefore his descendants come in varying dispositions (akhyāf). Or it is from al-udm or al-udmah, meaning "affection" (al-ulfah). This is a strained derivation (taʿassuf), like deriving Idrīs from al-dars, Yaʿqūb from al-ʿaqb, and Iblīs from al-iblās. The noun (ism), considered from the standpoint of derivation (ishtiqāq), is that which serves as a sign of a thing and an indication which raises it to the mind, along with words, attributes and verbs. Its customary usage is for a word established to denote a meaning, whether it is compound or simple, whether it is a subject of predication, a predicate, or a connective between them. Technically (iṣṭilāḥan), in the case of the simple noun, it is that which signifies a meaning in itself, not connected with any of the three tenses.

What is meant in the verse is either the first or the second, and the second entails the first, because knowledge of words in terms of their signification depends on knowledge of meanings. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, created him from different parts and divergent faculties, prepared to perceive the various kinds of perceptible things, both intelligibles and sensibles, and imaginables and estimables. He inspired him with knowledge of the essences of things, their properties, their names, the principles of the sciences, the laws of crafts, and the manner of their instruments.

﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾. The pronoun in ʿaraḍahum refers to the named things (al-musammayāt), which are implied, since the sense is "the names of the named things." The genitive complement has been omitted because the governing noun indicates it, and the article (al-lām) has been substituted for it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the head has blazed with gray hair﴾ [19:4]. This is because presenting (ʿarḍ) is for asking about the names of the things presented, so the thing presented is not the very things themselves, especially if by it is meant the words. What is meant by it is the essences of things, or the signifieds of words. The masculine form of the pronoun is used so that those among the rational beings (ʿuqalāʾ) contained in it predominate. It was also read ʿaraḍahunna and ʿaraḍahā, in the sense of "he presented their named things" or "her named things."

﴿He said: "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful"﴾. This is a rebuke (tabkīt) of them and an alerting to their incapacity for the matter of vicegerency (khilāfah), for disposing and managing affairs requires establishing justice before the realization of knowledge, and comprehending the ranks of capacities and the measure of rights is impossible. This is not an obligation, so that it would fall under the obligation of the impossible. And inbāʾ (informing) is a report that includes an imparting of knowledge (iʿlām); for this reason it works in the manner of each of the two (i.e., khabar and iʿlām).

﴿If you are truthful﴾: in your claim that you are deserving of vicegerency because of your infallibility (ʿiṣmah), or that their creation, their installation as vicegerents, and their attribute (which is what you describe) are not befitting to the All-Wise. Although they did not state this explicitly, it is entailed by their speech. Truthfulness (taṣdīq) may apply to speech with regard to its explicit content, and it may also apply to it by supposing what its implied meaning (madlūl) entails of reports. By this consideration it also applies to performatives (inshāʾāt).

﴿They said: Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us.﴾ This is an acknowledgment of incapacity and deficiency, and an indication that their question was an inquiry (istifsar) and not an objection (i'tiraḍ). It also shows that what had been hidden from them of the excellence of man and the wisdom in his creation had become clear to them, and it is an expression of gratitude for His favor in having made them know and having revealed to them what had been obscure to them, and an observance of courtesy (adab) by entrusting all knowledge to Him. "Subhana" (Glory be to Him, tasbih) is a verbal noun like "ghufran," and it is hardly ever used except in the construction of an annexed noun and in the accusative, with its verb suppressed, as in "ma'adhallah" (God forbid). It has been used as a proper name for tasbih (glorification, i.e., declaring God free of imperfection, tanzih) irregularly, in the line of poetry: "Glory be to Alqama al-Fakhir." Opening the speech with it is an apology for the inquiry and for ignorance of the reality of the situation. For this reason it was made the key to repentance: Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Glory be to You! I have repented to You﴾, and Yunus said: ﴿Glory be to You! Indeed I was among the wrongdoers﴾.

﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing﴾ Who nothing hidden is concealed from. ﴿the All-Wise﴾ Who perfects His creatures, Who does nothing except that in it is far-reaching wisdom. And "You" (anta) is a separating pronoun (fasl). It has also been said that it is an emphasis for the kaf (you) as in your saying: "I passed by you, you," though "I passed by anta" is not permissible, since the follower (tabi') admits what the followed (matbu') does not. For this reason "ya hadha al-rajul" (O this man) is permissible, but "ya al-rajul" is not. It has also been said that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is what follows it, and the sentence is the predicate of "inna."

﴿He said: "O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ That is, teach them. It is also recited with the hamzah (the glottal-stop letter) changed to a yāʾ, and with it dropped, with a kasrah on the hāʾ in both readings.

﴿So when he had informed them of their names, He said: "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you conceal?"﴾ This recalls His saying, ﴿Indeed, I know what you do not know﴾ (2:30), but it is stated in a more expanded form so that it serves as a proof against them. When He knew what was hidden from them of the affairs of the heavens and the earth, and what was apparent to them of their outward and inward states, He knew what they did not know. There is also an implicit rebuke for them for leaving what was better, which was to hold back, awaiting clarification for themselves. It has been said that "what you reveal" refers to their saying, ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾ (2:30), and "what you conceal" refers to their inner conviction that they were worthy of the vicegerency (khilafah) and that God would not create a creature more excellent than them. It has also been said that "what you reveal" is the obedience they displayed, and "what you conceal" is the disobedience that Iblis concealed among them. The hamzah here is for denial (al-inkar); it entered upon a negative particle, and so it conveys affirmation and confirmation.

Know that these verses indicate the nobility of man, the superiority of knowledge and its excellence over worship, and that knowledge is a condition for the vicegerency, indeed its foundation. They also indicate that teaching may rightly be attributed to God Most High, even though it is not proper to call Him "teacher" (muʿallim), since that name is specific to those who practise teaching as a profession. They indicate that languages are divinely prescribed (tawqifiyyah), for names indicate words either specifically or generally, and teaching them clearly involves imparting them to the learner while explaining their meanings to him; this requires a prior act of designation, and the default assumption negates that this designation came from anyone before Adam, so it must have come from God, glorified and exalted is He. They also indicate that the concept of wisdom (ḥikmah) is additional to the concept of knowledge, for otherwise His saying ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knowing, the Wise﴾ (2:32) would be repetitive. They indicate that the knowledge and perfections of the angels admit of increase. The philosophers (ḥukamāʾ) denied this for the highest rank among them, and interpreted by it His saying, ﴿There is not among us any but that he has a known station﴾ (37:164). They indicate that Adam is more excellent than these angels because he is more knowledgeable than them, and the more knowledgeable is more excellent, based on His saying, ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ (39:9). And they indicate that God Most High knows things before they come into being.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 34:**

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam."﴾ When He informed them of their names and taught them what they did not know, He commanded them to prostrate to him, acknowledging his excellence, discharging his right, and apologizing for what they had said about him. It is also said that He commanded them before He had perfected his creation, based on His words, exalted is He: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration﴾, as a test for them and a manifestation of his excellence. The conjunction (al-'atif) is a coordination of the temporal clause upon the preceding temporal clause if you take it as governed by a hidden verb. Otherwise, it is coordinated with what is supposed to govern it upon the preceding sentence. Rather, the whole story is coordinated upon the other story, and it is the fourth blessing He enumerated for them.

Sujud (prostration) originally means humbling oneself with lowering. The poet said:

*You see the hills in it prostrating before the hooves.*

And another said:

*They said to him: "Prostrate to Layla," so he prostrated.*

He means the camel when it lowers its head. In the Shari'a (sacred law), it means placing the forehead on the ground with the intention of worship. The thing commanded is either the legal meaning, in which case the one actually prostrated to is God, Exalted is He, and Adam was made a qibla (direction of prayer) for their prostration to magnify his station; or Adam was a cause for its obligation. It is as though, when He created him in such a way that he would be a model for all originated beings, indeed for all existents in their entirety, and a copy of what is in the spiritual and corporeal world, and a means for the angels to attain the perfections decreed for them, and a link to the manifestation of the ranks and degrees in which they differ, He commanded them to prostrate, in humility before what they saw in him of the greatness of His power and the dazzling nature of His signs, and in gratitude for what He bestowed upon them through him. So the lam in it is like the lam in the words of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

*Was he not the first to pray towards your qibla, and the most knowledgeable of people in the Qur'an and the sunan?*

Or in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾.

As for the linguistic meaning, which is humility toward Adam as a greeting and an honoring of him, like the prostration of Joseph's brothers to him; or humbling oneself and submitting by striving to obtain that upon which their livelihood depends and by which their perfection is completed. The discussion of whether those commanded to prostrate were all the angels or a group among them has already preceded.

﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis. He refused and was arrogant.﴾ He refrained from what he was commanded, out of arrogance at taking him as a means in the worship of his Lord, or at honoring him and receiving him with greeting, or at serving him and striving in what is good and righteous for him. Ibaa' (refusal) is abstention by choice. Takabbur (haughtiness) is that a man sees himself as greater than others. Istikbar (arrogance) is seeking that through affectation.

﴿And he was among the disbelievers﴾, meaning in God's knowledge, or he became one of them by considering God's command to him to prostrate to Adam as a disgrace, believing that he was better than him; and the better does not befit being commanded to humble himself before the lesser and to seek a means through him, as His words indicated: ﴿I am better than him﴾, in answer to His words: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My hands? Were you arrogant, or were you among the exalted?﴾. Not merely by abandoning an obligation alone. The verse indicates that Adam, peace be upon him, is more excellent than the angels commanded to prostrate to him, at least in some respect; and that Iblis was among the angels, for otherwise the command would not have included him, and his exception from them would not be valid. This is not refuted by His words, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn﴾, because it is permissible to say that he was of the jinn in deed and of the angels in kind. Also, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, related that among the angels there is a type who reproduce, called the jinn, and Iblis is among them. As for one who claims he was not of the angels, he may say that he was a jinn who grew up among the angels and was overwhelmed by thousands of them, so they prevailed over him; or that the jinn were also commanded along with the angels, but He dispensed with mentioning them by mentioning the angels, for when it is known that the great ones are commanded to humble themselves before someone and to seek a means through him, it is known that the lesser ones are also commanded to do so. The pronoun in ﴿So they prostrated﴾ refers to both groups, as though He said: "So those commanded to prostrate prostrated, except Iblis." And among the angels there is one who is not infallible ('isma), though the majority of them are infallible, just as among humans there are infallible ones while the majority of them are not infallible. Perhaps a type of angel does not oppose the devils in essence, but opposes them only in accidental attributes and qualities, like the righteous and the sinners among humans and jinn, which includes both.

Iblis was of this category, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. Therefore it is valid for him to change from his state and to fall from his station, as He indicated, Mighty and Exalted is He, saying: ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn, so he defied the command of his Lord﴾. It is not said: How is that valid, when the angels were created from light and the jinn from fire? Because 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, related that he, peace be upon him, said: "The angels were created from light, and the jinn were created from a smokeless fire." It is like an illustration of what we have mentioned, for what is meant by light is a luminous substance, and fire is likewise, except that its light is turbid, overwhelmed by smoke, and guarded against because of the extreme heat and burning that accompany it. When it becomes refined and purified, it is pure light; and whenever it reverts, it returns to its first state, fresh, and it continues to increase until its light is extinguished and pure smoke remains. This is closer to the correct view and more in harmony with reconciling the texts. And knowledge is with Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

Among the benefits of the verse: the condemnation of arrogance, and that it may lead its possessor to disbelief; the encouragement to comply with His command and to refrain from delving into its secret; that the command indicates obligation; and that the one whom Allah, exalted is He, knew of his state that he would die in disbelief is in reality the disbeliever, since what matters is the ending, even if by outward judgment he was a believer. This is the view of al-muwafah (the ending of life determines faith) attributed to our shaykh Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, may Allah have mercy on him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 35:

﴿And We said: O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾. Al-sukna (dwelling) is from al-sukun (stillness), since it is settledness and remaining. The ﴿you﴾ is an emphatic that emphasizes the concealed pronoun (al-mustakinn) so that the conjunction with it is valid. He did not address the two of them at first, as an alert that he (Adam) is the intended one of the ruling, and the one conjoined to him is a follower of him. Al-Jannah (the Garden) is the abode of reward, because the lam (the definite article) is for prior reference (al-'ahd), and there is no prior referent other than it.

As for one who claims that it has not yet been created, he said it is a garden that was in the land of Palestine, or between Fars and Kerman, which Allah the Exalted created as a test for Adam. He took the ihbat (descent) to mean moving from it to the land of India, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Go down to a city﴾. And ﴿abundant, wide, and comfortable﴾ (raghadan) is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (masdar).

﴿Wherever you wish﴾: in whatever place of the Garden you two wish. He widened the matter for them, removing the cause (of prohibition). The excuse regarding eating from the forbidden tree, out of its many trees, is that the forbidden one is singled out by restriction (lil-hasr).

﴿And do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers﴾. In it there are several intensifications: linking the prohibition to approaching, which is among the preliminaries of eating, as an intensification of its prohibition and of the obligation to avoid it; and an alert that nearness to a thing produces an incitement and an inclination that seizes the core of the heart and distracts it from what reason and the Law require, as it was narrated: "Your love of a thing makes you blind and deaf."

Therefore, they should not hover around what Allah has forbidden them, out of fear that they would fall into it, and He made it a cause for them to be among the wrongdoers who wronged themselves by committing sins, or by diminishing their share through doing what harms honor and bliss. The fa' (so) indicates causation, whether it is taken as conjoining to the prohibition or as an answer to it. The tree is wheat, or the vine, or the fig, or a tree whoever eats from it becomes impure (ahdatha); and it is better not to specify it without a decisive proof, just as it was not specified in the verse, since what is intended does not depend on it. It is read with a kasra on the shin (ash-shajarih), "taqraba" with a kasra on the ta' (taqrabā), and "hadhi" with a ya' (hadhi).

﴿Fa-azallahumā al-shayṭānu ʿanhā﴾ He caused them to slip from it (from the tree), and induced them to commit the slip because of it. The ʿan here is similar to its use in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَمَا فَعَلْتُهُ عَنْ أَمْرِي﴾ ("I did it not of my own accord" (Q. 18:82)). Or, he caused them to slip from the Garden, in the sense of removing them. This is supported by the reading of Ḥamzah, ﴿fa-azālahumā﴾ ("he removed them"). The two are close in meaning, except that azalla implies a stumble together with removal. Among his causing them to slip is his saying: ﴿هَلْ أَدُلُّكَ عَلَى شَجَرَةِ الْخُلْدِ وَمُلْكٍ لَا يَبْلَى﴾ ("Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?" (Q. 20:120)), and his saying: ﴿مَا نَهَاكُمَا رَبُّكُمَا عَنْ هَذِهِ الشَّجَرَةِ إِلَّا أَنْ تَكُونَا مَلَكَيْنِ أَوْ تَكُونَا مِنَ الْخَالِدِينَ﴾ ("Your Lord has forbidden you this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortals" (Q. 7:20)), and his swearing to them with the words: ﴿إِنِّي لَكُمَا لَمِنَ النَّاصِحِينَ﴾ ("Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisers" (Q. 7:21)).

It is disputed whether he appeared to them and spoke with them thus, or cast it to them by way of whispering (waswasah), and how he managed to cause them to slip after it had been said to him: ﴿فَاخْرُجْ مِنْهَا فَإِنَّكَ رَجِيمٌ﴾ ("Then get out of it, for you are accursed" (Q. 15:34)).

(It is said: he was prevented from entering in the manner of honour, as he used to enter with the angels, but he was not prevented from entering for the purpose of whispering, as a trial for Adam and Eve.

It is said: he stood at the door and called out to them. It is said: he appeared in the form of an animal and entered, and the guardians did not recognise him. It is said: he entered into the mouth of the serpent (p-73) until it entered with him. It is said: he sent some of his followers and they caused them to slip. And knowledge is with God, Glorified and Exalted.)

﴿Fa-akhrajahumā mimmā kānā fīhi﴾ That is, from the honour and bounty.

﴿Wa-qulnā ihbiṭū﴾ ("And We said: Go down") is addressed to Adam, upon him be peace, and Eve, in accordance with His saying, Glorified and Exalted: ﴿قَالَ اهْبِطَا مِنْهَا جَمِيعًا﴾ ("He said: Go down from it, both of you together" (Q. 20:123)). The pronoun is in the plural because the two of them are the origin of the species, so it is as though they were all of mankind. Or, it is them and Iblis, who was expelled from it a second time after he had been entering it for the purpose of whispering; or he entered it secretly, or it refers to descent from the heaven.

﴿Baʿḍukum li-baʿḍin ʿaduwwun﴾ ("Some of you are enemies to others") is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), in which the conjunction wāw is dispensed with in favour of the pronoun. The meaning is: mutually hostile, some of you oppressing others by misguiding them.

﴿Wa-lakum fī al-arḍi mustaqarrun﴾ ("And for you on the earth is a dwelling place"): a place of settling (mawḍiʿ istiqrār), or the act of settling (istiqrār).

﴿Wa-matāʿun﴾ ("and enjoyment"): enjoyment (tamattuʿ). ﴿Ilā ḥīnin﴾ ("for a time"): he means by it the time of death, or the Resurrection.

**Verse 2:37:** ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words,﴾ he welcomed them by accepting them, consenting to them, and acting upon them when he came to know them. Ibn Kathir read *Adam* in the accusative and *the words* in the nominative, on the basis that the words reached him and came to him, and they are His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ to the end of the verse. It was also said that they were: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. Blessed is Your name and exalted is Your majesty. There is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins except You." And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "O Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, did Your mercy not precede Your wrath?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Did You not make me dwell in Your garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "O Lord, if I repent and make amends, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes." The root of *kalimah* (word) is *kalim*, which is an impact perceived by one of the two senses, hearing or sight, such as speech, a wound, or a movement.

﴿So He turned toward him﴾ He returned to him with mercy and accepted his repentance. He connected this with the particle *fa* (then) to the receiving of the words because it includes the meaning of repentance, which is acknowledgment of the sin, regret over it, and resolve never to return to it. Only Adam is mentioned because Hawwa' (Eve) was subordinate to him in the ruling, and for this reason the mention of women is omitted in most of the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

﴿Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance﴾ the One who returns repeatedly to His servants with forgiveness, or the One who greatly helps them to repent. The root of *tawbah* (repentance) is return. When it is attributed to the servant, it is a return from disobedience; when it is attributed to the Creator, exalted is He, it means a return from punishment to forgiveness.

﴿the Most Merciful﴾ the one who intensifies in mercy. Combining the two attributes is a promise to the penitent of kindness together with pardon.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 38:**

﴿We said, "Descend from it, all of you."﴾ It is repeated for emphasis (ta'kid), or because the intended meaning differs. The first mention indicates that their descent is to a house of trial, in which they will be hostile to one another and will not remain forever. The second indicates that they were sent down for moral responsibility (taklif). So whoever follows the guidance (al-huda) will be saved, and whoever strays from it will perish. The point of this is that the fear of descent, when it is linked to either one of these two matters alone, is enough for a resolute person to keep him from opposing the command of God, glorified and exalted be He. How much more so when it is linked to both of them. But (Adam) forgot and We found in him no resolve. And each one of these two matters is sufficient as a deterrent for whoever wishes to take heed.

It has been said that the first descent is from the Garden to the lowest heaven, and the second is from it to the earth. But this, as you see, is weak.

﴿jamī'an﴾ ("all of you") is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) in wording, but an emphasis (ta'kid) in meaning, as if it were said: "Descend, you all together." Therefore, it does not require that they gather for the descent at one time, just as your saying "They came, all of them" does not require that they came at one time.

﴿Then if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ The second conditional clause, together with its response, is the response to the first conditional clause. The particle ما (mā) is an added element (mazīdah), and it is used to emphasize إنّ (in), which is why the verb is emphasized with the nūn of emphasis (nūn al-tawkid), even though there is no sense of demand in it. The meaning is: if guidance comes to you from Me, by revelation or by sending a messenger, then whoever among you follows it will be saved and succeed.

The particle of doubt (ḥarf al-shakk) is used here, although the coming of guidance is certain to happen, because in itself it is a possibility and not necessary by reason. The word "guidance" (al-huda) is repeated rather than replaced by a pronoun, because by the second mention he intends something more general than the first. This is what the messengers brought and what reason requires. That is, whoever follows what has come to him, observing in it what reason testifies to, then there is no fear for them, let alone that something disliked should befall them, nor will something beloved escape them so that they grieve over it. Fear concerns what is expected, and grief concerns what has happened. Thus he has negated punishment for them and affirmed reward for them in the most emphatic and most eloquent manner.

It is recited as "hudan" (هُدًى) according to the dialect of Hudhayl, and "lā khawfa" (لا خَوْفَ) with a fatḥah.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 39:**

﴿Those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with ﴿whoever follows﴾ and what follows it to the end, and it is its counterpart (qasīm). It is as if He said: "And whoever does not follow, but disbelieves in Allah and denies His signs." Or [it means]: they disbelieve in the signs in their hearts (jannan) and deny them with their tongues, so that both verbs are directed at the prepositional phrase (al-jār wa-al-majrūr).

The word āyah (sign) originally means a manifest indication. It is applied to created things insofar as they point to the existence of the Creator, His knowledge and His power. It is also applied to each section of the Qur'an's words that is distinguished from others by a separation. Its derivation is from āy, because it makes clear one thing from another (āyan min ay), or from awā ilayhi (to take refuge in it). Its original form is ʾayah or awyah, like tamrah, and its ʿayn was replaced by an alif contrary to analogy. Or it is ʾayiyah, or awaya like ramakah, and it was then treated by the rules of ʿillah (morphological weakening). Or it is āʾiyah like qāʾilah, and the hamzah was deleted for ease of pronunciation.

The intended meaning of ﴿Our signs﴾ is the revealed verses, or what includes them and the rational signs.

The Hashwiyya (a term for literalist, anthropomorphist traditionalists) have clung to this story as proof that the prophets are not protected from sin (ʿişmah, infallibility), in several respects:

First: Adam, upon him be the blessings of Allah, was a prophet, and he committed what was forbidden, and whoever commits what is forbidden is a sinner.

Second: By his transgression he became one of the wrongdoers (ẓālimīn), and the wrongdoer is cursed, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers.﴾

Third: He, exalted is He, attributed disobedience to him, saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾

Fourth: He, exalted is He, taught him repentance (tawbah), which is turning back from sin and feeling remorse for it.

Fifth: His acknowledgment that he was a loser (khāsir) unless Allah forgave him, by His saying: ﴿And if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers.﴾ And the loser is one who has committed a grave sin.

Sixth: Had he not sinned, what befell him would not have befallen him.

The answer to these is in several respects.

First: He was not a prophet at that time, and the one making the claim must prove it.

Second: The prohibition was for tanzīh (advisory discouragement, not a binding prohibition), and he was called a wrongdoer and a loser only because he wronged himself and lost his share through abandoning what was better for him (tark al-awlā). As for the attribution of error (ghayy) and disobedience (ʿişyān) to him, the answer to that will come in its proper place, if Allah wills. He was commanded to repent only to make up for what he had missed, and what befell him was a rebuke for his abandonment of what was better, and a fulfilment of what he had said to the angels before his creation.

Third: He did it forgetfully, according to His saying, glorified is He and exalted is He: ﴿But he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾ However, he was rebuked for not guarding himself against the causes of forgetfulness. It is possible that although this was lifted from the community (ummah), it was not lifted from the prophets, because of their great rank, as he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "The people most severely tested are the prophets, then the righteous saints, then the best of people, and then those next best to them." Or his act led to what befell him through a hypothetical causal path (al-sababiyyah al-muqaddarah, causation assumed for the sake of argument), without being held accountable for his consumption of it, like the consumption of poison by one who is ignorant of its nature. It cannot be said that this is false because of His saying: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you only from this tree﴾ and ﴿And he swore to them both﴾ (the two verses), because there is nothing in them indicating that his eating occurred at the time when Iblis spoke to him. Perhaps his speech produced in him a natural inclination, then he restrained himself from it out of regard for the command of Allah, until he forgot that, the obstacle was removed, and his nature moved him to it.
