Fourth: He, peace be upon him, undertook it on account of an ijtihād (independent legal reasoning) in which he erred. He thought that the prohibition was for tanzīh, or that it referred to this very tree, so that it would permit eating from other trees of its kind, whereas what was meant was a reference to the species. This is like what is reported, that he, upon him be blessings and peace, took silk and gold in his hand and said: "These two are forbidden to the males of my community and lawful to its females." And what befell him befell him in order to magnify the gravity of sin, so that his descendants would avoid it. In this story there is evidence that Paradise is created, that it is in a high direction, that repentance is accepted, that whoever follows guidance is safe in the outcome, that the punishment of the Fire is everlasting, that the disbeliever abides in it forever, and that others do not abide in it, by the implication (mafhūm) of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will abide therein forever.﴾

Know that when He, glorified is He and exalted is He, mentioned the proofs of tawḥīd (oneness of God), prophethood and the return (maʿād), and followed them with an enumeration of general blessings as confirmation and emphasis, insofar as these are firmly established events that indicate a wise Originator, to whom alone belong creation and command, with no partner; and insofar as the report of them, as they are recorded in earlier scriptures, comes from one who did not learn them and did not engage in any of them, is a report of the unseen that is miraculous and indicates the prophethood of the one who reports it; and insofar as they include the creation of man and his origins and what is greater than that, they indicate that He is able to restore him as He was able to originate him, He addressed the People of Knowledge and the Book among them, and commanded them to remember the blessings of Allah upon them, and to fulfil His covenant in following the truth and adhering to the proofs, so that they would be the first to believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and what was sent down to him. So He said:

﴿O Children of Israel﴾, i.e., the descendants of Ya'qub (Jacob). The word *ibn* (son) is derived from *binā'* (building), because the son is the building of his father. For this reason, a made thing is attributed to its maker, so one says *abu al-harb* ("father of war") and *bint al-fikr* ("daughter of thought"). Isrā'īl is the epithet (*laqab*) of Ya'qub, peace be upon him, and its meaning in Hebrew is "the chosen one of God." It is also said to mean "servant of God." It has also been read as *Isrā'il* with the yā' dropped, as *Isrāl* with both dropped, and as *Isrā'yīl* with the hamza changed into a yā'.

﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾, i.e., by reflecting upon it and giving thanks for it. The favour is restricted to them because man is by nature jealous and envious. When he looks at what God has bestowed upon others, jealousy and envy move him toward ingratitude and discontent; but if he looks at what God has bestowed upon him, the love of blessing moves him toward contentment and gratitude. It is also said that by it is meant what God bestowed upon their forefathers: deliverance from Pharaoh and from drowning, and pardon for taking the calf; and what was bestowed upon them: attaining the time of Muhammad ﷺ. It is also read *ādhdhakirū* (with the *dhāl* doubled), and the original form is *idhtakirū*. *Ni'matī* (with the yā' sukūn in pause and its dropping in continuous speech) is the view of those who do not vowel the yā' when the letter before it is kasra.

﴿And fulfil My covenant﴾, by faith and obedience.

﴿I shall fulfil your covenant﴾, by good recompense. The word *'ahd* (covenant) is attributed both to the one who makes the covenant and to the one with whom it is made. It is likely that the first is attributed to the agent and the second to the object, for He, exalted is He, made a covenant with them concerning faith and righteous deeds by setting up proofs and sending down books, and He promised them reward for their good deeds. The fulfilment of these two covenants is a broad matter. The first stage of fulfilment from us is the utterance of the two words of testimony, and from God, the protection of blood and property. The last stage from us is immersion in the ocean of tawhid to such a degree that one forgets oneself, let alone others, and from God, the attainment of perpetual meeting with Him. What has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, is: "Fulfil My covenant" in following Muhammad ﷺ; "I shall fulfil your covenant" in the removal of burdens and fetters. From others it is related: "Fulfil by performing the obligations and avoiding the grave sins; I shall fulfil by forgiveness and reward." Or: "Fulfil by remaining steadfast upon the straight path; I shall fulfil by honour and everlasting bliss." These are views according to the intermediaries. It is also said that both are attributed to the object, and the meaning is: "Fulfil what you have pledged to Me of faith and undertaking obedience; I shall fulfil what I have pledged to you of good recompense." The details of the two covenants are in Surat al-Ma'ida in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And We will surely admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. It is also read *ūfi* (with shadda) for emphasis.

﴿And fear Me alone﴾ in what you do and what you leave undone, and especially in breaking the covenant. It is more emphatic in restricting meaning than *iyyāka* in ﴿You alone do we worship﴾, because of what it contains of the repetition of the object together with fronting, and the *fā'* of consequence, which indicates that the statement contains the meaning of a condition, as if it were said: "If you are fearful of anything, then fear Me." *Rahba* (dread) is fear together with caution. The verse contains both promise and warning, and indicates the obligation of gratitude and of fulfilling the covenant, and that the believer should fear none but God, exalted is He.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 41:**

﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾. This singles out belief (*iman*) for command and exhortation, because it is the aim and the foundation for fulfilling covenants. The qualification of the revelation as confirming what is with them of the divine books is either because it descends in the manner described in those books, or because it agrees with them in narratives, promises, calling to monotheism, commanding worship and justice among people, forbidding sins and abominations. As for its disagreement with them in particular rulings, this is due to the differences of eras in what is beneficial, since each of them is true relative to its own time, and takes into account the welfare of those addressed by it. Even if an earlier revelation descended in the days of a later one, it would descend in accordance with it. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If Moses were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me."

It is a reminder that following them (the revelations) does not contradict belief in him, but rather necessitates it. For this reason, he alluded to it with his words:

﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾. The implication is that what is required is that they be the first to believe in it. Also, they were the people who considered its miracles, who had knowledge of its matter, who sought its opening (victory) through it, and who gave good tidings of its time. The phrase ﴿the first to disbelieve in it﴾ comes as a predicate of the plural pronoun, with the implied meaning: "the first group or party," or by interpretation: "let not each one of you be the first to disbelieve in it," like your saying, "He clothed us in a robe." If it is asked: how were they forbidden to be first in disbelief when the polytheists of the Arabs preceded them? I say: what is meant by it is an allusion, not a direct indication of what the apparent wording states, like your saying, "As for me, I am not ignorant," or "Do not be the first to disbelieve in it" from among the People of the Book, or from among those who disbelieved in what is with him, for whoever disbelieves in the Qur'an has disbelieved in what confirms it, or like those of the polytheists of Mecca who disbelieved.

The word ﴿first﴾ (*awwal*) is an elative form (*af'al*) that has no positive form of its own. It was said that its origin is *awwal* from *wa-ʾa-l*, whose hamza was changed to a waw for lightening, in a non-analogical way; or that it is *ʾawʾal* from *ʾal*, whose hamza was changed to a waw and then assimilated.

﴿And do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾. Do not substitute for belief in them and following them the worldly portions, for these, however great, are small and base in comparison with what you miss of the portions of the Hereafter by abandoning belief. It was said: they had leadership among their people, along with customary dues and gifts from them, so they feared losing these if they followed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and so they chose them over him. It was also said: they used to take bribes, so they would distort the truth and conceal it.

﴿And fear Me, so be mindful of Me﴾ by belief, following the truth, and turning away from the world. Since the preceding verse included what is like the preliminaries to what is in the second verse, it was detailed with reverence, which is the prelude to piety; and because the address with it (the first command) encompassed both the scholar and the imitator (*muqallid*), He commanded them with reverence, which is the starting point of conduct. And the address with the second, when it was specific to the people of knowledge, He commanded them with piety, which is its endpoint.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 42:

﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾ is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with what precedes it. *Al-labs* (confusion, mixing) means mixing, and it may also entail making one thing appear similar to another. The meaning is: do not mix the truth that has been revealed to you with the falsehood that you invent and conceal, so that the two cannot be distinguished. Or: do not make the truth ambiguous through the mixing in of the falsehood that you write within it or mention in its interpretation.

﴿And conceal the truth﴾ is a jussive (*jazm*) that falls under the ruling of the prohibition, as if they were commanded to believe and to abandon error, and forbidden to mislead by confusing those who have heard the truth and by concealing it from those who have not heard it. Alternatively, it is in the accusative (*nuṣiba*) by the implied *an*, on the basis that the *waw* is for conjunction in the sense of "with," meaning: do not combine the mixing of truth with falsehood and the concealing of it. Supporting this is that in the *mushaf* (codex) of Ibn Masʿud it reads "*wa-taktumūna*" (and you conceal), meaning *wa-antum taktumūna* (while you conceal), with *taktumūna* in the sense of *kātimīn* (concealers). This implies that the abhorrence of confusion is due to what accompanies it of concealing the truth.

﴿while you know﴾ means knowing that you are confusing and concealing. This is more grievous, since the ignorant person may be excused.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 43:

﴿And establish the prayer and give the zakat﴾. He means the prayer of the Muslims and their zakat, for other than these is neither prayer nor zakat. He commanded them with the branches of Islam after having commanded them with its roots, and in this there is evidence that the disbelievers are addressed by them (i.e., by the branches of the law). Zakat is from "zakā al-zar‘" (zakāt, the crop grew), when it increases, for giving it out draws blessing into one's wealth and brings forth for the soul the virtue of generosity. Or it is from zakāt meaning purity (ṭahārah), for it purifies wealth from impurity and the soul from miserliness.

﴿And bow with those who bow﴾, i.e., in their congregation, for the congregational prayer surpasses the prayer of one alone by twenty-seven degrees, because of the mutual support of souls in it. He expressed the prayer by bowing (rukū‘) as a safeguard against the prayer of the Jews. It has been said that rukū‘ means submission and compliance with what the Lawgiver obliges them to. Al-Adba' al-Sa‘di said:

؎ Do not humiliate the weak, lest you bow (tarka‘) one day while time has raised him up.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 44:

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people﴾ is a rebuke couched as a question, with astonishment. Al-birr (righteousness, piety) means the abundance of good, derived from al-birr, which is the wide open expanse; it encompasses every good. For this reason it has been said that al-birr is of three kinds: righteousness in the worship of God, Exalted is He; righteousness in regard to one's relatives; and righteousness in dealing with strangers.

﴿And you forget yourselves﴾ and leave them out of righteousness, as though they were forgotten. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning the rabbis of Madinah, who would secretly enjoin those they advised to follow Muhammad (ﷺ) while they themselves did not follow him. It has also been said: they used to enjoin giving charity while they themselves did not give charity. ﴿While you recite the Book﴾ is a reproach, like His saying: ﴿while you know﴾, that is, you recite the Torah, and in it is the warning against obstinacy, the abandoning of righteousness, and the contradiction of speech with action.

﴿Will you not then use reason?﴾ that is, [will you not reflect on] the ugliness of your conduct so that it would restrain you from it; or, do you have no reason that would prevent you from what you know to be the grave consequence of it?

Al-ʿaql (reason, intellect) originally means restraint. The human faculty of perception is named after it, because it restrains a person from what is reprehensible and guides him toward what is good; then the faculty by which the soul perceives this perception is also called by that name. The verse rebukes the one who admonishes others yet is not admonished by his own bad conduct and the corruption of his soul, and whose action is the action of one ignorant of the Law or a fool devoid of reason, for the one who combines both of these is restrained by his own character from it. The intent of this is to urge the admonisher to purify the soul and to attend to it with perfecting it, so that it may stand and thereby set others upright, not to prevent the sinner from admonishing, for failing to fulfil one of the two commanded matters does not necessitate failing the other.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 45:

﴿Seek help through patience and prayer.﴾ It is connected to what precedes it, as if, when they were commanded to do what is burdensome for them, because of its hardship, its requiring them to give up leadership, and their turning away from wealth, they were treated with this remedy. The meaning is: seek help for your needs by waiting for success and relief, relying upon God. Or (seek help) through fasting, which is patience in abstaining from things that break the fast, because it breaks the appetite and purifies the soul. Seeking help through prayer, and taking refuge in it, is because it comprises all kinds of acts of worship, both of the soul and of the body: purity, covering the private parts, and spending wealth on these two, facing the Ka'ba, devoting oneself to worship, showing humility through the limbs, sincerity of intention in the heart, struggling against Satan, intimate conversation with the Truth, reciting the Qur'an, pronouncing the two testimonies of faith, and restraining the self from what is pleasurable, until you are answered in attaining your aims and having your calamities relieved.

It is narrated that "when a matter distressed him, he (ﷺ) would turn to prayer." It is also permissible that by "them" (prayer and patience) what is meant is supplication (p-78): ﴿and indeed it⦁﴾, that is, indeed seeking help through these two, or through prayer, and singling it out by returning the pronoun to it, because of its great status and because it combines many kinds of patience. Or (the pronoun refers to) the whole of what they were commanded to do and forbidden from.

﴿is indeed burdensome﴾, that is, heavy and difficult, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Hard upon the polytheists is that to which you call them﴾.

﴿except for those who are humble﴾, that is, those who are submissive (al-mukhbitin). Khushu' is ikhbat (humble submission), and from it comes khush'a, meaning a low, flattened patch of sand. Khudu' is gentleness and compliance; for this reason it is said that khushu' is with the limbs and khudu' is with the heart.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 46:

﴿Those who expect that they will meet their Lord, and that they will return to Him.﴾ That is, they anticipate meeting Allah, the Exalted, and attaining what is with Him; or they are certain that they will be gathered to Allah, and He will recompense them. This is supported by the fact that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is "يَعْلَمُونَ" (ya'lamun, "they know"). It seems that, since ẓann (ẓann, "supposition/assumption") resembles 'ilm (ʿilm, "knowledge") in being a stronger likelihood, it was applied to it because it includes the meaning of expectation. Aws ibn Hajar said:

﴿Then I sent it forth, certain in its supposition that it... is piercing what lies between the ribs and the lower chest.﴾

It is only that it does not weigh upon them as it weighs upon others, because their souls are trained by its like, and they anticipate in exchange for it what makes its hardships seem small and its toils pleasant. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer."

O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you (ﷺ? no) —

Let me correct and translate properly:

O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you. He repeated it for emphasis and to remind them of the particular favor, which is especially the greatest of favors, and He linked it to a severe threat, as a warning to those who neglected it and fell short in its rights.

﴿And that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ It is coordinated with "My favor."

﴿Over the worlds﴾ means the worlds of their time. By this is intended the preference of their forefathers who lived in the era of Musa, upon him be peace, and after him, before they were corrupted by what Allah the Exalted had granted them of knowledge, faith and righteous deeds, and made them prophets and just kings. It has been cited as evidence for the preference of humans over angels, though this argument is weak.

Surah 2, verse 48, from al-Baydawi's commentary (Anwar al-Tanzil):

﴿And guard yourselves against a Day﴾ i.e., against what it contains of reckoning and punishment.

﴿on which no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾ it will not discharge on its behalf any of the rights (owed), or any of the recompense; so its accusative case is as an infinitive (maṣdar). It was also read as lā tujzi'u, from ajza'a 'anhu, meaning "to suffice for him" when it suffices; and on this reading it is necessarily an infinitive. Its being indefinite, along with the indefiniteness of the two "souls," is for generality and for complete despair. The clause is an attributive (ṣifah) of "a Day," and its returning pronoun is omitted, its estimated form being lā tajzī fīhi ("will not avail in it"). Whoever does not permit the omission of a returning pronoun governed by a preposition says: the matter was extended, so the preposition was dropped and the word was treated as a direct object, and then it was omitted, just as it was omitted in His saying: "am mālun aṣābū" (or wealth they have gained).

﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾ i.e., from the second, disobedient soul, or from the first. It seems that the verse is meant to negate that anyone can ward off punishment from anyone in any possible way, for it is either by compulsion or otherwise. The first is by help (nuṣrah), and the second is either gratuitous or otherwise. The first is that intercession be made for him, and the second is either by discharging what was upon him, which is that one suffices on his behalf, or by something else, which is that a ransom (ʿadl) be given on his behalf. Intercession (shafā'ah) is from shaf' (pair), as if the one for whom intercession is made was a single unit, and the intercessor made him a pair by adding himself to him. The ʿadl is the ransom. It was said: the substitute; its root meaning is equalization, and it was named for the ransom because it was made equal to the one being ransomed. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read wa-lā tuqbalu with a tā' (feminine).

﴿nor will they be helped﴾ they will not be protected from the punishment of God. The pronoun refers to what the indefinite second "soul" implies, which occurs in the context of "soul" among many souls, and its masculine form is by the sense of "servants" or "humans." Naṣr (help) is more specific than maʿūnah (assistance), because it is specific to averting harm. The Mu'tazilah have held onto this verse to negate intercession for the people of major sins. It is answered that it is specific to the disbelievers, on account of the verses and hadiths that come concerning intercession, and it is supported by the fact that the address is with them, and the verse was revealed as a refutation of what the Jews used to claim, that their fathers would intercede for them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 49:

﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ is an elaboration of what was summarized in His saying: ﴿Remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. It is conjoined to ﴿My favour﴾ in the manner of the conjunction of (Jibril) and (Mika'il) to (the angels). It is also read as «anjaynakum» (with the first person). The original form of Al (ʾāl) is Ahl (family), since its diminutive is Uhayl; it was specifically used with reference to those of high standing, such as prophets and kings. Fir'awn (Pharaoh) is a title for whoever ruled the Amalekites, like Kisra and Qayṣar for the kings of Persia and Byzantium. From their arrogance was derived the verb tafarʿana al-rajul, meaning a man who transgressed and became tyrannical. The Pharaoh of Musa was Mus'ab ibn Rayyan, and it is said that he was his son al-Walid, from the remnants of 'Ad. The Pharaoh of Yusuf, peace be upon him, was Rayyan, and between them were more than four hundred years.

﴿They afflicted you﴾: they sought (yabghunakum), from sama-hu khasfan, when he inflicted injustice upon him. The root of al-sawm is going forth in pursuit of something.

﴿with the worst of torment﴾: the most grievous of it, for it is foul in comparison with the rest. Al-su' is a verbal noun of sa'a yasu'u, and it is in the accusative as an object of yasumunakum. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in najjaynakum, or from "the people of Pharaoh," or from both together, since each of them contains a pronoun referring to the other.

﴿They slaughtered your sons and spared your women﴾ is an explanation of yasumunakum; for this reason it is not joined by a conjunction. It is also read yadhbahuna with the light (non-doubled) form.

They did this to them because Pharaoh saw in a dream, or the soothsayers told him, that a male would be born among them who would take away his kingdom; but their scheming did not avert anything from the decree of God.

﴿And in that was a trial﴾: an ordeal, if "that" refers to their action, and a blessing if it refers to the deliverance. Its original sense is testing, but since God's testing of His servants is sometimes by affliction and sometimes by bounty, the term was applied to both. It is also permissible that "that" refers to the whole event, and that by it is meant the common testing between them.

﴿from your Lord﴾: through their being empowered over you, or through the sending of Musa, peace be upon him, and his success in delivering you, or through both. ﴿Great﴾ is an adjective of trial. The verse contains an admonition that whatever befalls the servant of good or evil is a test from God Most High; therefore he must give thanks for what pleases him and be patient with what harms him, so that he may be among the best of those who are tested.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 50:

﴿And when We divided the sea for you﴾: We split it and separated its parts from one another, until paths came into being in it through your passing along them. Or it means "because of your deliverance," or "mingled with you," as in his saying:

*"They trample us over skulls and dust."*

It is also recited as "faraqna" (with the intensive, *tafʿīl*, form, meaning "We divided thoroughly"), because the paths were twelve, according to the number of the tribes (*asbāt*).

﴿So We delivered you and drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾: By this he means Pharaoh and his people. He mentioned only them because it was known that they were the more deserving of it. (p-80) It is also said that it refers to his person. This is as it is narrated that al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Muhammad," meaning his person, and mention of him was sufficient without mention of his followers.

﴿While you were looking on﴾: at that, that is, at their drowning and the sea closing over them; or at the splitting of the sea into dry, smooth paths; or at their bodies which the sea cast onto the shore; or it means that some of you were looking at others.

It is narrated that Allah commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to set out by night with the Children of Israel. He went out with them, and Pharaoh and his armies overtook them at dawn, and they met them on the shore of the sea. Allah revealed to him: "Strike the sea with your staff." He struck it, and twelve dry paths appeared in it, and they walked along them. They said: "O Moses, we fear that some of us will drown and we will not know." So Allah opened in them openings (*kuwan*), and they could see and hear one another until they had crossed the sea. Then, when Pharaoh reached it and saw it split, he plunged into it with his armies, and it closed over them and drowned them all.

Know that this event is among the greatest of the blessings Allah bestowed upon the Children of Israel, and among the signs that compel knowledge of the existence of the Wise Creator and the truthfulness of Moses, peace be upon him. Yet after that they took the calf and said: ﴿We will not believe you until we see Allah plainly﴾, and the like of that. Thus they were far removed, in intelligence, acuteness, soundness of disposition and good following, from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Moreover, the miracles of his that have been transmitted by continuous report are matters of reasoning, such as the Qur'an, its challenge (to produce its like), and the excellences gathered in it which bear witness to the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), subtle matters that only the intelligent perceive; and his (ﷺ) reporting of them, peace be upon him, is among his miracles, as has passed in their explanation.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 51:

﴿And [remember] when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ When they returned to Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, God promised Moses that He would give him the Torah, and He set for him an appointed time: the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten [days] of Dhu al-Hijjah. He expressed it in terms of nights, because they are the beginnings of the months (ghurar al-shuhur).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿wa-'adna﴾ (We appointed), because God promised him the revelation. Moses, peace be upon him, promised to come to the appointed place at Mount Sinai (al-Tur).

﴿Then you took the calf﴾ as a god or an object of worship.

﴿after him﴾ after Moses, peace be upon him, or after his departure.

﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾ by your associating partners with God.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 52–53:

﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ after you repented, and al-'afw (pardon) is the erasure of the offence, from ʿafā, meaning "it effaced" (daras, "it wore away"). ﴿After that﴾, i.e., after the taking (of the calf as a deity), ﴿so that you might give thanks﴾, i.e., in order that you might give thanks for His pardon.

﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾: this means the Torah, which combines being a revealed Book with being a proof (ḥujja) that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. It has been said that by al-furqān ("the Criterion") he meant his miracles, which distinguish between the one who is truthful and the one who is false in his claim, or between disbelief and faith. It has also been said that it is the law (al-sharʿ) that distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful, or the victory by which He separated him from his enemy, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿on the day of the Criterion﴾, meaning the Day of Badr.

﴿So that you might be guided﴾, i.e., in order that you might be guided by reflecting upon the Book and contemplating the signs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 52–53:

﴿Then We pardoned you﴾ after you repented, and al-'afw (pardon) is the erasure of the offence, from ʿafā, meaning "it effaced" (daras, "it wore away"). ﴿After that﴾, i.e., after the taking (of the calf as a deity), ﴿so that you might give thanks﴾, i.e., in order that you might give thanks for His pardon.

﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾: this means the Torah, which combines being a revealed Book with being a proof (ḥujja) that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. It has been said that by al-furqān ("the Criterion") he meant his miracles, which distinguish between the one who is truthful and the one who is false in his claim, or between disbelief and faith. It has also been said that it is the law (al-sharʿ) that distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful, or the victory by which He separated him from his enemy, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿on the day of the Criterion﴾, meaning the Day of Badr.

﴿So that you might be guided﴾, i.e., in order that you might be guided by reflecting upon the Book and contemplating the signs.

And [remember] when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf [for worship], so turn in repentance to your Creator (bari')." Then resolve (fa'azimu) upon repentance and returning to the One who created you free from disparity (bura'a min al-tafawut), and who distinguishes some of you from others by different forms and shapes. The root of the word (al-tarkib, here meaning the root form) is for the purity of a thing from other things, either in the sense of thorough removal, as in their saying "the patient was cured (bara'a) of his illness" and "the debtor was cleared (bara'a) of his debt," or in the sense of origination (al-insha'), as in their saying "God created (bara'a) Adam from clay." Or [it may be read as] "so repent (fatubu)."

"So kill yourselves (faqtulu anfusakum)," as completion of your repentance by self-exhaustion (al-bakh'), or by cutting off desires, as it has been said: "Whoever does not punish his self does not give it comfort, and whoever does not kill it does not give it life." It has also been said that they were commanded that some of them should kill others. And it has been said that those who had not worshipped the calf were commanded to kill the worshippers.

It is reported that a man would see his father, his son, or his relative [among the worshippers] and could not bring himself to proceed with God's command. So God sent a mist and a black cloud, so that they could not see one another. They began to fight one another from morning until evening, until Moses and Aaron prayed, and the cloud was lifted and the repentance was granted. The number of those killed was seventy thousand. The first fa' (ف) is for causation (al-tasabbub), and the second fa' is for sequence (al-ta'qib).

"That is better for you with your Creator (dhalikum khayrun lakum 'inda bari'ikum)," in that it is a purification from polytheism, and a means of reaching eternal life and everlasting joy.

"So He turned to you (fa-taba 'alaykum)" is linked to something omitted, if you take it as the speech of Moses (peace be upon him) to them; its implied sense is: "If you do what you were commanded, then He has turned to you in forgiveness." Or it is conjoined to an omitted element, if you take it as an address from God Most High to them, in the manner of iltifat (a shift from one grammatical person to another), as if He said: "So you did what you were commanded, and your Creator turned to you in forgiveness." Mentioning the Creator (al-bari') and placing the command upon Him indicates that they had reached the utmost ignorance and foolishness, to the extent that they abandoned the worship of their wise Creator for the worship of cows, which are a proverb for foolishness. It also indicates that whoever does not recognize the right of his benefactor deserves that the favor not be taken back from him. For this reason they were commanded to kill and to dismantle the composition (fakk al-tarkib).

"Indeed He is the Oft-Returning (al-tawwab), the Most Merciful (al-rahim)," to the one who greatly grants success in repentance, or accepts it from sinners, and exceeds in bestowing favor upon them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 55:

﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will not believe you until we see Allah openly."⁠﴾ That is, on account of your saying, or: "we will not acknowledge you."

﴿Until we see Allah openly⁠﴾: visibly, face to face. Its original sense is the verbal noun of your saying "jahartu bil-qira'ah" (I recited aloud), and it was borrowed for direct observation (al-mu'aynah). It is put in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is a type of seeing, or as a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject or the object. It has also been read as jahratan with a fatha, as a verbal noun like al-ghalabah, or as the plural of jahir like al-katabah, in which case it is definitely a circumstantial state of the subject. Those who spoke were the seventy whom Musa, peace be upon him, chose for the appointed time. It is also said they were ten thousand of his people, and the one who believed in him said: indeed Allah, who gave you the Torah and spoke to you, or indeed you are a prophet.

﴿So the thunderbolt seized you⁠﴾ because of their extreme obstinacy, their description of Allah, and their demand for the impossible. They thought that He, exalted is He, resembles bodies, so they asked to see Him with the seeing of bodies in directions and in places facing the one who sees, and that is impossible. Rather, what is possible is that He be seen with a vision free of modality, and that is for the believers in the Hereafter and for certain individuals among the prophets in some states in this world. It was said that a fire came down from the sky and burned them. It was said it was a cry. It was said it was troops who heard its rustle, so they fell down, struck dead, for a day and a night.

﴿And you were looking⁠﴾ at what befell you, either by its very self or by its effect.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 56–57:

﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾ through the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa). It is a qualifier for "resurrection" (al-ba'th), because it may have been after a fainting spell or sleep, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We raised them up﴾ (p-82).

﴿So that you may give thanks﴾ for the blessing of being raised up, or for what you had disbelieved when you saw the might of Allah in the thunderbolt.

﴿And We shaded you with clouds﴾: God subjected the clouds to them, shading them from the sun when they were in the wilderness (al-tih).

﴿And We sent down upon you manna and quails﴾: al-taranjabin (honey-dew) and al-sumani (quails). It is said that manna would descend upon them like snow from dawn until sunrise, and the south wind would bring quails to them; and at night a pillar of fire would descend, by whose light they travelled, and their garments would neither become soiled nor wear out.

﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾, understood as an implied "saying" (qawl).

﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾: there is an ellipsis here, and the original is: "So they wronged, by disbelieving these blessings, and they did not wrong Us."

﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ by ingratitude, because its harm does not pass beyond them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 56–57:

﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾ through the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa). It is a qualifier for "resurrection" (al-ba'th), because it may have been after a fainting spell or sleep, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We raised them up﴾ (p-82).

﴿So that you may give thanks﴾ for the blessing of being raised up, or for what you had disbelieved when you saw the might of Allah in the thunderbolt.

﴿And We shaded you with clouds﴾: God subjected the clouds to them, shading them from the sun when they were in the wilderness (al-tih).

It is said that manna would descend upon them like snow from dawn until sunrise, and the south wind would bring quails to them; and at night a pillar of fire would descend, by whose light they travelled, and their garments would neither become soiled nor wear out.

﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾, understood as an implied "saying" (qawl).

﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾: there is an ellipsis here, and the original is: "So they wronged, by disbelieving these blessings, and they did not wrong Us."

﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ by ingratitude, because its harm does not pass beyond them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 58:

﴿And when We said: Enter this town﴾ — meaning Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It is also said it was Jericho (Arihā); they were commanded to enter it after the wandering (al-tih).

﴿and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance﴾ — raghadan: wide, plentiful. It is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the waw (of the verb "eat").

﴿And enter the gate﴾ — i.e., the gate of the town, or the dome toward which they used to pray. For they did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis during the lifetime of Moses, peace be upon him.

﴿in prostration﴾ — humbly bowing low, or prostrating to God in gratitude for bringing them out of the wandering.

﴿and say: Ḥiṭṭah﴾ — i.e., our request, or your command is ḥiṭṭah. It is a form (fi'lah) from al-ḥaṭṭ (lowering), like al-jilsah (a sitting). It was also read in the accusative according to the original form, meaning: "Remove from us our sins, a removal (ḥiṭṭatan)," or as the object of qūlū, i.e., "say this word." It is also said its meaning is: our command is ḥiṭṭah, i.e., that we should settle in this town and dwell in it.

﴿We will forgive you your wrongs﴾ — for your prostration and your supplication. Nāfi' read it with the yā' (naghfir, "We will forgive"), and Ibn ʿĀmir with the tā' (tughfar, "will be forgiven"), in the passive form.

Khaṭāyā: its original form is khaṭāyi'u, like khaṭāyi'a. According to Sībawayh, the added yā' was replaced by a hamzah because it came after an alif, and two hamzahs came together, so the second was replaced by a yā', then turned into an alif, and the hamzah was between two alifs, so it was replaced by a yā'. According to al-Khalīl, the hamzah was moved before the yā', and then both were treated as mentioned.

﴿And We will increase the reward of the good-doers﴾ — in reward. He made compliance a repentance for the wrongdoer and a cause for increased reward for the good-doer. He brought it out of the form of a response into that of a promise, to give the impression that the good-doer is poised for this even if he has not yet done it, so how much more so when he has done it, and that God, Exalted, will certainly do it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 59:

﴿So those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been said to them.﴾ They substituted, in place of what they had been commanded to do of repentance and seeking forgiveness, the pursuit of what they desired of the transient goods of this world.

﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong﴾ He repeated it (the sending down) as an intensification in condemning their affair, and as an indication that the sending down upon them was because of their wrongdoing, by placing what was not commanded in its place, or (it was sent down) upon themselves, in that they abandoned what would bring about their salvation for what would bring about their destruction.

(p-83) ﴿a plague from the heaven because they were defiantly disobedient﴾ a punishment decreed from the heaven because of their defiant disobedience (fisq). The rijz (plague, abomination) in origin is that which is loathed, and likewise the rijs (filth). It has also been read with a damma (rujz), and this is a dialect form of it. What is meant by it is the plague (ta'un).

It is narrated that there died in a single hour twenty-four thousand of them.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 60:**

﴿And when Moses prayed for water for his people﴾ when they became thirsty in the wilderness (al-tih).

﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff.﴾ The definite article in "al-hajar" (the rock) is for specificity (al-'ahd), according to what is related: that it was a Tur stone (hajaran tawriyyan), cube-shaped, which he carried with him, and from each of its faces three springs would gush forth, each spring flowing in a stream to one tribe. They were six hundred thousand, and the width of the encampment was twelve miles. Or it was a stone that Adam brought down from Paradise, which came to Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), who gave it to Moses along with the staff. Or it was the stone that fled with his garment when he placed it upon it to bathe, and God cleared him by means of it of what they had accused him of, namely the defect of the testicles (al-udrah); so Gabriel (peace be upon him) gestured to him to carry it. Or the article is for the genus (lil-jins), and this is more evident in the argument. It has been said that he was not commanded to strike a particular stone; rather, when they said: "What will become of us if we arrive at a land with no stones in it?", he carried a stone in his saddlebag, and he would strike it with his staff when he dismounted, and it would gush forth, and he would strike it with it when he departed, and it would dry up. They said: "If Moses loses his staff, we will die of thirst." So God revealed to him: "Do not knock the stone; speak to it, and it will obey you, that perhaps they may take heed." It has also been said that the stone was of marble, one cubit by one cubit, and the staff was ten cubits, matching the height of Moses (peace be upon him), made of myrtle (as) of Paradise, and it had two branches that would shine in the darkness.

﴿Then there gushed forth from it twelve springs.﴾ It is related to an omitted element, its estimated sense being: "If you strike, then it has gushed forth," or "He struck, and it gushed forth," as was mentioned in His saying: ﴿So He turned to you﴾. It has been read as "ashrata" with the shin vowelled with kasra and with fatha, and both are dialectal forms of it.

﴿Each group knew its drinking place.﴾ "Kull unas" means each tribe; "mashrabahum" means their spring from which they drink.

﴿"Eat and drink"﴾ with an implied "saying" (qawl) understood.

﴿"of God's provision."﴾ By this he means what God provided for them of manna, quails and the water of the springs. It has been said that it refers to water alone, because it is drunk and eaten from what grows by it.

﴿And do not act wickedly in the land, causing corruption.﴾ Do not transgress while you are causing corruption. He restricted it this way because, although it predominates in corruption, there may be among it what is not corruption, such as retaliating against the oppressive transgressor with his own act; and among it what includes a greater good, such as al-Khidr (peace be upon him) killing the boy and damaging the ship. Close to it is "'ayth" (wicked action), except that it predominates in what is perceived by the senses. As for whoever denies the likes of these miracles, it is due to the extreme of his ignorance of God and his little reflection on the wonders of His creation. For since it is possible that there are stones which shave hair, repel vinegar, and attract iron, it is not impossible that God should create a stone which He subjects to drawing water from beneath the earth, or to drawing air from the surroundings and turning it into water by the power of cooling, and the like.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 61:

﴿And when you said: "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food."﴾ They meant by it what they were provided with in the wilderness (al-tih) of manna and quail (al-salwa).

By its oneness is meant that it does not vary and does not change, like their saying "the food of the banquet of the commander is one (ṭaʿām māʾidah al-amīr wāḥid)," meaning that its kinds do not change. And by this they were unanimous, or it was one kind, because both are the food of people of luxury. They were farmers, so they turned back to their former condition (ʿakar) and craved what they had been accustomed to. ﴿So call upon your Lord for us﴾ (p-84) ask Him for us by your supplication to Him, ﴿that He may bring forth for us﴾ that He may make manifest and bring into existence. Its jussive form (jazm) is because it is the answer (jawab) to "call upon," for his supplication is the cause of the answer.

﴿from what the earth grows﴾ is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi) and the placing of the recipient in the position of the agent (iqamat al-qabil maqam al-fa'il), and min is partitive (lil-tab'id). ﴿of its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions﴾ is an explanation and clarification that stands in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it has been said it is an apposition (badal) by repeating the preposition. Al-baql is what the earth brings forth of greens, and what is meant by it is its good edible parts. Al-fum is wheat, and it is said of bread, and from it comes "fawwimu lana" (make bread for us). It has been said it means garlic. It is also read "qiththa'iha" with a ḍammah, which is a dialectal form of it. (He said), i.e., God, or Moses, peace be upon him. ﴿Would you exchange that which is lower?﴾ nearer in rank and lower in worth. The original meaning of dunuw is nearness in place, and it is borrowed for baseness, just as bu'd (distance) is borrowed for nobility and elevation, so it is said "far in station, far in aspiration." It is also read "adna'" from al-dana'a (baseness). ﴿for that which is better﴾ he means by it the manna and quail, for it is better in pleasure, benefit, and freedom from the need to strive. ﴿Go down to a city﴾ descend to it from the wilderness. It is said habata al-wadi when one descends into it, and habata minhu when one comes out of it. It is also read with a ḍammah. Al-misr is a great city, and its origin is a boundary between two things. It has been said that he intended it as a proper name, and he made it diptote (ṣarafahu) because its middle is quiescent, or on the interpretation of "city" (al-balad). This is supported by its being without tanwin in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. It has been said its origin is Misraim, and it was arabized. ﴿For you there is what you asked, and humiliation and wretchedness were struck upon them﴾ they were surrounded by it as a dome surrounds whoever is beneath it, or they were stuck to them, from the striking of mud upon a wall, as a recompense to them for ingratitude for blessing. The Jews, for the most part, are humiliated and wretched, either in reality or by affectation, out of fear that their poll-tax (jizya) would be increased. ﴿And they returned with wrath from God﴾ they came back bearing it, or they became deserving of His wrath, from "fulan ba fulan" when he deserves to be killed for him, and the root of bawʾ is equality. ﴿That﴾ is a reference to what preceded: the striking of humiliation and wretchedness and the returning with wrath. ﴿Because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right﴾ because of their disbelief in the miracles, among which are what was counted against them: the splitting of the sea, the shading by clouds, the sending down of manna and quail, and the gushing of springs from the rock. Or [it refers to] the revealed books, such as the Gospel, the Furqan, the verse of stoning, and what in the Torah describes Muhammad (ﷺ), and their killing of the prophets, for they killed Shaʿya, Zakariyya, Yahya, and others without right according to them, since they did not see from them anything by which they believed killing them to be permissible. What moved them to that was following desire and love of the world, as He indicated by His words: ﴿That is because they disobeyed and were transgressing﴾ that is, disobedience, persistence, and transgression in it led them to disbelief in the signs and killing of the prophets. For the minor sins are a cause leading to the commission of the major ones, just as minor acts of obedience are causes leading to pursuing the major ones. It has been said He repeated the reference to show that what befell them, just as it was due to disbelief and killing, was also due to their committing sins and transgressing the limits of God, exalted is He. It has been said the reference is to disbelief and killing, and the bi' means "with." The reference to a singular for two or more things is permitted on the interpretation of "what has been mentioned or preceded," for brevity. Its parallel in pronouns is the verse of Ru'ba describing a cow:

"In it are lines of black and white, as if on its hide is the pattern of vitiligo."

What made that acceptable is that the dual, plural, and feminine forms of pronouns and indefinites are not literal, and for that reason alladhi came with the meaning of the plural.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 62:

﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ with their tongues. He means by this those who adhere to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), both the sincere among them and the hypocrites. It is also said that the hypocrites are meant, because they were enrolled in the ranks of the disbelievers. ﴿And those who were Jews﴾ (alladhina hadu), that is, those who became Jews (tahawwadu). One says hada and tahawwada when one enters Judaism. As for "Yahud" (Jews), it is either an Arabic word, from hada meaning "he repented," and they were so named when they repented of worshipping the calf; or it is an arabicized form of Yahudha (Judah), and it is as if they were named after the eldest of the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob), peace be upon him. ﴿And the Christians﴾ (al-nasara) is the plural of nasran, like nadama and nadman (companions). The yaʼ in nasrani (Nasrani, singular) is for intensification, as in ahmariyy. They were named so because they helped (nasaru) the Messiah, peace be upon him; or because they were with him in a village called Nasran or Nasirah, so they were named after it, or after its name. ﴿And the Sabians﴾ are a people between the Christians and the Magians. It is also said that the origin of their religion is the religion of Noah (ﷺ)... (p-85) peace be upon him. It is also said that they are worshippers of the angels. It is also said that they are worshippers of the stars, and if it is an Arabic word, it is from sabaa, meaning "he went out." Nafi' alone read it with a yaʼ (Sabiyyin), either because he eased the hamza and replaced it with a yaʼ, or because it is from sabaa meaning "he inclined," since they inclined away from all other religions toward their religion, or from the truth to falsehood.

﴿Whoever believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds﴾: whoever among them was in his religion before it was abrogated (nuskh), affirming with his heart the origin and the return, acting in accordance with the requirements of his law. It is also said: whoever among these disbelievers believes with sincere faith and enters Islam with true entry, ﴿for them is their reward with their Lord, who has promised them for their faith and their deeds.﴾ ﴿And no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ at the time when disbelievers fear punishment, and those who fall short grieve over wasting their lifetime and missing the reward. ﴿Whoever﴾ (man) is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is ﴿for them is their reward﴾, and the clause is the predicate of inna; or it is an apposition (badal) to the subject of inna, whose predicate is ﴿for them is their reward﴾. The fa' (fa) is there because the subject contains the meaning of a condition. Sibawayh prohibited its entry into the predicate of inna, on the grounds that it does not enter a conditional clause, and he refuted this with the words of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women and then did not repent, for them is the punishment of Hell﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 63–64:

﴿And when We took your covenant﴾ to follow Musa and to act by the Torah. ﴿And We raised the mountain above you﴾ until you gave the covenant. It is narrated that when Musa, peace be upon him, brought them the Torah and they saw the arduous obligations in it, they found them hard and refused to accept it. So he ordered Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, who uprooted the mountain and held it over them until they accepted. ﴿Take﴾, with the implied sense of saying: ﴿what We have given you﴾ of the Book, ﴿with strength﴾, with earnestness and resolve. ﴿And remember what is in it﴾: study it and do not forget it, or reflect upon it, for it is remembrance by the heart, or act upon it. ﴿So that you may be mindful﴾: so that you may guard against sins, or as a hope from you that you will be among the mindful. It is permissible according to the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) that this be connected to the omitted verb, meaning: "We said: take, and remember, with the intention that you may be mindful."

﴿Then you turned away after that﴾: you turned away from fulfilling the covenant after taking it. ﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ by enabling you to repent, or by Muhammad ﷺ who calls you to the truth and guides you to it. ﴿You would have been among the losers﴾, those defrauded by persisting in sins, or by going astray and being lost during a gap between the messengers.

Originally, لَوْ (law, "if/had") indicates the non-occurrence of one thing due to the non-occurrence of another. When it is preceded by لا (la, "not"), it conveys affirmation, namely the non-occurrence of a thing due to the occurrence of another. The noun that follows it is, according to Sibawayh, a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) must be omitted because the context indicates it and the response clause (jawab) takes its place. According to the Kufans, it is the agent (fa'il) of an omitted verb.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 65–66:

﴿And certainly you know those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath.﴾ The *lam* is *lam muwatti'a* (the lam that prepares for an oath), indicating an oath. *As-sabt* is the verbal noun of your saying *sabatat al-yahud* (the Jews "observed the Sabbath"), when they magnified the day of Saturday. Its root meaning is cutting off. They were commanded to devote it to worship, but some of them transgressed concerning it in the time of Dawud (peace be upon him), and they occupied themselves with hunting. That was because they lived in a village on a coast called Ayla. When the Sabbath came, no fish remained in the sea without appearing there and extending its snout. When it passed, they dispersed. So they dug pools and ran channels to them, and the fish would enter them on the Sabbath, and they would catch them on Sunday.

﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, rejected."﴾ Combining the form of apes and *khusu'*, which is humiliation and expulsion. Mujahid said: "Their forms were not transformed, but their hearts were. So they were likened to apes, just as they were likened to a donkey in His saying: ﴿like the example of a donkey carrying books﴾." His saying *"Kun"* ("Be") is not a command, since they have no capacity to do it. Rather, what is meant by it is the swiftness of the bringing into being, and that they became such just as He willed for them. It is read *"qarideh"* (with a fatha on the qaf and a kasra on the ra), and *"khasin"* without a hamza.

(p-86) ﴿So We made it﴾, that is, the transformation or the punishment, ﴿a deterrent﴾, an example that restrains the one who takes heed from it, that is, prevents him. From this comes *an-nikl* for the shackle (*an-nikl li-l-qayd*).

﴿as a warning for what lay before it and what lay after it﴾, for the nations before it and after it, since their condition was mentioned in the scriptures of the earlier ones, and their story became well known among the later ones. Or it is for their contemporaries and those after them. Or it is for the villages near it and those far from it. Or it is for the people of that village and those around it. Or it is because of the sins that preceded it and those that followed it. ﴿and an admonition for the God-fearing﴾, among their people, or for every God-fearing person who heard it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 67:

﴿And when Moses said to his people: "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow"﴾ The beginning of this story is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾ It was separated from it and placed before it because it stands on its own with another kind of their faults, which is mockery of the command, excessive questioning, and failing to hasten to comply. Its story is that among them there was an elderly man of wealth, whose nephews killed his son out of greed for his inheritance, and they threw him at the gate of the city. Then they came demanding his blood. So Allah commanded them to slaughter a cow and strike him with a part of it, so that he would come to life and tell them who his killer was. ﴿They said: "Do you take us for a laughing-stock?"﴾ That is, a place of mockery, or its people, or ones mocked by us, or the mockery itself out of extreme derision, considering what he said far-fetched and treating it lightly. Hamzah, Isma'il (from Nafi') and Hafs (from 'Asim) recited it with ḍamma and conversion of the hamza into a waw. ﴿He said: "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant"﴾ Because mocking in such a matter is ignorance and foolishness. He negated from himself what was attributed to him by way of proof, and expressed that in the form of seeking refuge, to magnify its enormity.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 68:

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what she is."﴾ That is, what her state and attribute are. Their proper question would have been: "Which cow is it?" or "How is it?", because what is asked about with "mā" (what) is usually the genus (jins). However, when they saw that what they had been commanded was in a condition in which nothing of its genus was found, they treated it as what they did not know the reality of and had not seen the like of.

﴿He said: "Indeed He says she is a cow neither aged (fāriḍ) nor virgin (bikr)"﴾, that is, neither past-prime (musinnah) nor young (fatiyyah). It is said: "faraḍat al-baqaratu furūḍan," from al-farḍ, meaning al-qaṭʿ (cutting), as if she had cut off her teeth (sinn). The root of bikr (virgin) denotes priority (al-awwaliyyah), and it is derived from al-bukrah (early morning) and al-bākūrah (early fruit).

﴿ʿAwān﴾ means middle (niṣf). A poet said: "Tender ones between virgins and ʿawān."

﴿Between that﴾, that is, between what was mentioned, the aged and the virgin. For this reason "bayn" is attached to "dhālik," since "bayn" is only attached to a plural (mutaʿaddid). The return of these pronouns and the application of these attributes to "a cow" indicates that what is meant is a specific cow, and this entails the delay of clarification (ta'khīr al-bayān) beyond the time of address. Whoever denies this claims that what is meant is a cow from the category of cows, not specified, and then it became specified by their question; this entails abrogation (naskh) before the act, for specification is the nullification of the choice (takhyīr) established by the text, while the truth is that both are permissible. The second opinion is supported by the apparent wording and by what is narrated from him, upon him be prayers and peace: "If they had slaughtered any cow they wished, it would have sufficed them, but they made it hard upon themselves, so God made it hard upon them." Their rebuke for persisting and their restraint for returning to questioning is in His saying: ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, that is, what you are commanded (tu'marūnahu), in the sense of "you are commanded with it," from their saying: "amartuka al-khayra" (I commanded you the good), so do what you were commanded with; or "amrukum" means "al-ma'mūrukum" (what you are commanded).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 69:

﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a yellow cow, intensely yellow in its color."﴾ Al-fuqu' (intensity, pure brightness) is the purity of yellowness. For this reason it is used as an emphasis, and it is said: "aṣfar fāqi'" (intensely yellow), just as it is said: "aswad ḥālik" (intensely black). Ascribing it (fāqi') to the color, while it is an attribute of the cow, because it is associated with her, adds emphasis, as if it were said: "a yellow cow, intensely yellow in her yellowness." It is narrated from al-Ḥasan (al-Basri): "black, intensely black," and it is in this sense that His statement, exalted is He, ﴿Yellow camels﴾ is explained. Al-A'sha said:

"Those are my horses from it, and those are my riding-camels... they are yellow, their young ones like raisins."

Perhaps he expressed blackness by yellowness because yellowness is among its preliminaries, or because the blackness of camels is overlaid with yellowness. But there is a problem with this, because yellowness in this sense is not emphasized by fuqu'. ﴿That pleases the onlookers﴾, i.e., it delights them. Surur (joy) originally is a pleasure in the heart upon the attainment of a benefit, or the anticipation of it, and it is derived from sirr (secret, inner concealment).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 70:

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what she is."﴾ This is a repetition of the first question, with an additional seeking of clarification. His saying: ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confused to us﴾ is an excuse for it, meaning: the cow described as being of middling age and yellow is numerous, so it has become confused for us. It is also read "Inna al-Baqir" (إنَّ الباقِرَ), and al-Baqir is a collective noun for the cattle, and for the plural forms al-abaqir and al-bawaqir. "Yatashabahu" and "tatashabahu" are read with the ya and the ta; "tashabaha," "yushabihu," and "tashshabaha" are read with the ta dropped and assimilated into the shin, in the masculine and feminine forms; "tashabahat" and "tashshabahat" are read both lightened and doubled; "tashabbaha" carries the meaning of "tatashabbahu," and "tashabbaha" is in the masculine; and there are the forms "mutashabih," "mutashabihah," "mutashabbih," and "mutashabbihah."

﴿And indeed, if Allah wills, we will surely be guided﴾ to the intended one, its slaughter, or to the killer. In the hadith: "Had they not made the exception, they would never have been shown it until the end of time." Our companions (the Ash'aris) used this as evidence that events occur by the will of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and that a command may be separated from the will, for otherwise the condition after the command would have no meaning. The Mu'tazilah and the Karramiyyah hold that the will is newly created. It was answered that the conditionality is by way of the connection (ta'alluq).

He said: "Indeed, He says: It is a cow that is neither trained to plough the earth nor to water the tilled field" ﴿قالَ إنَّهُ يَقُولُ إنَّها بَقَرَةٌ لا ذَلُولٌ تُثِيرُ الأرْضَ ولا تَسْقِي الحَرْثَ﴾. That is, it has not been made tame for ploughing the land or for watering the crops. ﴿لا ذَلُولٌ﴾ is an attributive (ṣifah) of ﴿بَقَرَةٌ﴾, meaning "not tame" (ghayr dhalūl). The second ﴿لا﴾ is redundant, serving to emphasise the first. The two verbs ﴿تُثِيرُ﴾ and ﴿تَسْقِي﴾ are attributes of ﴿ذَلُولٌ﴾, as if it were said: "not tame, ploughing and watering." It is also read as ﴿لا ذَلُولَ﴾ with a fatḥah, meaning "wherever it is," as in your saying "I passed by a man who is neither miserly nor cowardly" (لا بَخِيلَ ولا جَبانَ), meaning "wherever he is." And ﴿تَسْقِي﴾ means "it waters" (man asqā). ﴿مُسَلَّمَةٌ﴾ means that God has preserved it from defects; or that its owners were spared from labour; or that its colour was made pure, from the phrase "salima lahu kadha" meaning it became free of it for him. ﴿لا شِيَةَ فِيها﴾ means there is no colour in it that differs from the colour of its hide. Shiyah is originally a verbal noun: "shāha, shiyan, shiyah" means he mixed one colour with another colour. They said: ﴿الآنَ جِئْتَ بِالحَقِّ﴾, meaning: you have now brought the truth, namely the true description of the cow, and you have made it clear to us. It is also read as ﴿الآنَ﴾ with a madd, as an interrogative, and as ﴿لانَ﴾ with the hamzah omitted and its vowel placed on the lām. ﴿فَذَبَحُوها﴾ contains an ellipsis; the implied meaning is: so they obtained the cow with that description, and then they slaughtered it. ﴿وَما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ is due to their prolonged questioning and their many repeated objections, or out of fear of exposure when the killer would be revealed, or because of the high price of the cow. It is narrated that a pious old man among them had a young calf, and he brought it to the thicket and said: "O God, I entrust it to You for my son until he grows up." It grew and became unique with those attributes. They bargained with the orphan and his mother until they bought it for a full hide of gold, while at that time the cow was worth three dinars. Kāda (كادَ) is one of the verbs of approximation (af'āl al-muqārabah), placed to indicate that the predicate is near to occurring. When negation enters upon it, it is said that its meaning becomes affirmation absolutely. It is also said that it is a past-tense verb. The correct view is that it is like the other verbs. His saying ﴿وَما كادُوا يَفْعَلُونَ﴾ does not conflict with ﴿فَذَبَحُوها﴾, because the two refer to different times. The meaning is that they did not come close to doing it until their questions ended and their excuses ran out, and then they acted like one compelled and forced into action.

(p-88) ﴿وَإذْ قَتَلْتُمْ نَفْسًا﴾ is an address to all of them, because the killing existed among them. ﴿فادّارَأْتُمْ فِيها﴾ means you disputed concerning its matter, since each of the two disputants pushes the other away. Or it means you blamed one another, each one casting the killing off from himself onto his companion. Its root is تَدارَأْتُمْ (*tadara'tum*), in which the ت was assimilated into the د and a hamzat al-wasl (the connecting hamza, a hamza pronounced only when a word is begun) was prefixed to it, giving ادّارأتم (*iddara'tum*). ﴿واللَّهُ مُخْرِجٌ ما كُنْتُمْ تَكْتُمُونَ﴾ means God will undoubtedly bring to light what you were concealing. The participle مُخْرِجٌ (*mukhrijun*) governs its object in the accusative (أُعْمِلَ, *u'mila*, "was made to act"), because it narrates a future event, just as باسِطٌ in ﴿باسِطٌ ذِراعَيْهِ﴾ governs its object, because it narrates a past state.

﴿فَقُلْنا اضْرِبُوهُ﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ادّارأتم, and what lies between them is an interjected parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ). The pronoun in ﴿اضْرِبُوهُ﴾ refers to the soul (النَّفْسِ), and the masculine form is used in view of the meaning of "person" (الشَّخْصِ) or "the slain one" (القَتِيلِ). ﴿بِبَعْضِها﴾ means with some part of it, whichever part it was. It has been said: with its smaller part; it has been said: with its tongue; it has been said: with its thigh, the right one; it has been said: with its ear; and it has been said: with its coccyx (العَجْب). ﴿كَذَلِكَ يُحْيِي اللَّهُ المَوْتى﴾ indicates what has been omitted, which is: so they struck it and it came to life. The address is to those present, (witnessing) the slain man's revival, or to (those at the time of) the revelation of the verse. ﴿وَيُرِيكم آياتِهِ﴾ means His signs, that is, His proofs of the perfection of His power. ﴿لَعَلَّكم تَعْقِلُونَ﴾ means so that He may perfect your intellect, and that you may know that whoever is able to bring one soul back to life is able to bring all souls back to life; or that you may act according to its ruling.

It may be that God, exalted is He, did not revive him directly and made the condition what it was because of what this contains of drawing near to Him, fulfilling an obligation, benefiting the orphan, alerting to the blessing of trust in God and of compassion toward children, and that it is proper for the seeker to offer a act of devotion, and for the one seeking nearness (to God) to choose the best and pay a high price for it. This is as is reported from ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, that he sacrificed a noble she-camel which he had bought for three hundred dinars. Also (it alerts to) that the true agent is in reality God, exalted is He, and that means are mere signs without any real effect. And whoever wishes to know his most hostile enemy, the one striving to cause him the true death, the way to do so is to slaughter the cow of his own self, which is the appetitive power, once the excess of youthful vehemence has left it and the weakness of old age has not yet reached it; a cow that is pleasing to behold, of fine appearance, not subjugated in the pursuit of this world, free of its filth and of any mark of its ugliness, such that its effect reaches his soul, whereupon it lives a good life and manifests what reveals the true state of affairs, and what lies between intellect and imagination of dispute and contention is removed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 74:

﴿Then your hearts hardened after that⁠﴾. Qaswah (hardness) is an expression for harshness together with firmness, as in stone. The hardness of the heart is a metaphor for its refusal to take heed (i'tibar, reflection on lessons). The word "thumma" (then) here indicates the remoteness of such hardness ﴿after that⁠﴾, meaning the revival of the slain man, or all the signs that were enumerated, for these are of the kind that necessitate softness of heart. ﴿Yet they are like stones⁠﴾ in their hardness ﴿or even harder⁠﴾ than them. The meaning is that in hardness they are like stones or more intense than them; or that they are like them, or like something harder than them in hardness, such as iron. The genitive noun (mudaf) has been omitted and the genitive complement (mudaf ilayhi) put in its place. This is supported by the reading of al-Hasan in the genitive case, in coordination with "al-hijara" (stones). The reason it does not say "aqsa" (harder) is the emphasis conveyed by "ashadd" (more intense) and the indication of the intensification of both hardnesses, and because the comparative includes an additional quality. "Aw" (or) here is for choice, or for uncertainty, in the sense that whoever knows their state would liken them to stones or to what is harder than them.

﴿And indeed among stones there are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed among them there are those that split open so that water comes out of them, and indeed among them there are those that fall down out of fear of Allah⁠﴾. This is a justification (ta'lil) for the preference. The meaning: stones are affected and respond, for among them are those that split and water springs from them, and rivers burst forth from them, and among them are those that tumble down from the top of a mountain, submitting to what Allah the Exalted wills for them. The hearts of these people are not affected and do not respond to His command, exalted is He. Tafajjur (gushing) is opening up with abundance and quantity. Khashyah (fear) is a metaphor for submission. It is read "in" (indeed) as the lightened form of the heavy "inna", and it is necessarily followed by the distinguishing lam (lam al-farq) between it and the negative "in". "Yahbitu" is read with a damma (yahbutu).

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do⁠﴾. This is a threat for that. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ya'qub, Khalaf and Abu Bakr read it with the letter ya' (yaʿmalūna, third person), joining it to what follows it, while the rest read it with the letter ta' (second person).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 75:

﴿Do you then hope﴾ The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers. ﴿that they will believe for you﴾, that is, that they will confirm you (as truthful), or that they will believe because of your call (da'wah). Here "they" means the Jews. ﴿And there was a group among them﴾, a party from among their predecessors, ﴿who heard the speech of Allah﴾, meaning the Torah, ﴿and then distorted it﴾, such as the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the verse of stoning (al-rajm). Or (it means) their interpretation (ta'wil), so they explained it according to their desires. It was also said that these were from the seventy chosen men who heard the speech of Allah the Exalted when Musa (peace be upon him) was spoken to at Mount Tur, and then they said, "We heard Allah the Exalted say at its end: If you are able to do these things, then do them, and if you wish, do not do them." ﴿after they had understood it﴾, that is, they comprehended it with their minds, and no doubt remained for them concerning it. ﴿while they knew﴾ that they were fabricators and falsifiers. The meaning of the verse is that the rabbis (ahbar) of these people and their leaders were in this condition, so what then is your assumption about their lowly ones (saflah) and their ignorant ones (juhhal)? And that if they disbelieved and distorted, they have a precedent in that matter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 76–77:

﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾, meaning their hypocrites. "[We believe] that you are upon the truth, and that your Messenger is the one foretold in the Torah." ﴿But when they are alone with one another, they say﴾, that is, those among them who did not hypocritize, rebuking those who did: ﴿"Do you tell them what Allah has disclosed to you?"﴾, namely what He has made clear to you in the Torah of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). Or it means those who were hypocritical toward their own kind, displaying firmness in Judaism and preventing them from revealing what they found in their Book, so that they would be hypocritical toward both groups. The interrogative in the first reading is a reproach, and in the second it is a denial and prohibition. ﴿So that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, that is, that they may argue against you with what your Lord has sent down in His Book. They made their argument with the Book of Allah and His judgment an argument "before Him," just as one says "before Allah such-and-such," meaning that it is found in His Book and His judgment. It has also been said: "before the mention of your Lord," or "in the presence of the Messenger of your Lord." And it has been said: "before your Lord on the Day of Resurrection," but this is open to question, since concealment does not prevent it. ﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ This is either a continuation of the speech of the blamers, its sense being: "Will you not then reason that they will argue with you about it and so defeat you?" Or it is an address from Allah Most High to the believers, connected to His words ﴿Do you then hope...﴾, and the meaning is: "Will you not then understand their condition and that there is no hope for you in their faith?"

﴿Do they not know﴾, meaning these hypocrites, or the blamers, or both, or them and the distorters. ﴿That Allah knows what they conceal and what they disclose﴾. Among what is included in these two is their concealing of disbelief and their proclaiming of faith, and their concealing of what Allah disclosed to them, and their showing of other than it, and the distortion of words from their places and their meanings.
