﴿And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book﴾: ignorant folk who cannot write, so they cannot read the Torah and verify what is in it. Or, [the meaning is] the Torah itself, ﴿except wishful fancies﴾. This is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*). The word *amani* is the plural of *umniyyah*, which in its original sense is what a person conjures in his mind as a wish when he is able to fulfil it. For this reason it is used for falsehood, for what is wished for, and for what is recited. The meaning is: "Rather, they hold to lies that they took on by blind imitation (*taqlid*) of the distorters (*muharrifin*), or to empty promises that they heard from them, such as that no one will enter Paradise except those who are Jews, and that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days." It has also been said that the meaning is: "except what they recite as a recitation devoid of knowledge of its meaning and reflection upon it," from the verse of the poet:

*He longed for the Book of God at the start of his night,*
*longing as David longed for the Psalms at his leisure.*

But this does not fit the description of them as *ummiyyun*. ﴿And they are only conjecturing﴾: they are only a people who conjecture and have no knowledge. The term *zann* (conjecture) is used in contrast to knowledge (*'ilm*) for every opinion and belief that is not certain, even if its holder asserts it firmly, such as the belief of the blind imitator (*muqallid*) and of one who deviates from the truth because of a doubt.

﴿So woe﴾: that is, regret and destruction. As for one who says it is a valley or a mountain in Hell, its meaning is that there is in it a place where whoever is assigned woe will dwell. Perhaps he named it this by way of metaphor (*majaz*). Originally it is a verbal noun (*masdar*) with no verb of its own, and it was permissible to begin a sentence with it in indefinite form because it is a supplication (*du'a'*). ﴿For those who write the Book﴾: meaning the distorters, and perhaps he intended by this what they wrote of corrupt interpretations. ﴿With their own hands﴾: an emphasis, like your saying, "I wrote it with my right hand." ﴿Then they say, "This is from God," to exchange it for a small price﴾: so that they may obtain by it some worldly good, for even if it is a great deal (*ju'l*), it is small in comparison with the eternal punishment they have deserved. ﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written﴾: meaning the distortion. ﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾: he means by this the bribes.

﴿وَقالُوا لَنْ تَمَسَّنا النّارُ﴾ ("They said: The Fire will not touch us"). **المَسُّ** (*al-mass*, touching) is the contact of a thing with the skin, such that the sense is affected by it. **اللَّمْسُ** (*al-lams*, feeling or touching) is like seeking that contact, which is why one says *almisuhu fala ajiduhu* ("I feel for it but do not find it").

﴿إلا أيّامًا مَعْدُودَةً﴾ ("except for a few counted days"): limited and few. It is narrated that some of them said: "We will be punished for the number of days during which the calf was worshipped, forty days." Others said: "The duration of the world is seven thousand years, and we will be punished for one day for every thousand years."

﴿قُلْ أتَّخَذْتُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ عَهْدًا﴾ ("Say: Have you taken a covenant from God?"): **عَهْدًا** means a report or a promise concerning what you claim.

Ibn Kathir and Hafs recited **إظْهارِ** (*idhhar*, clear pronunciation) of the **الذّالِ** (*dhal*), while the rest recited **إدْغامِهِ** (*idgham*, assimilation, the merging of one letter into the next).

﴿فَلَنْ يُخْلِفَ اللَّهُ عَهْدَهُ﴾ ("then God will not break His covenant"): this is the response (*jawab*) to a hypothetical condition (*shart muqaddar*, an implied condition), meaning: if you have taken a covenant with God, then God will not break His covenant. This indicates that failing to fulfil His report is impossible.

﴿أمْ تَقُولُونَ عَلى اللَّهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("Or do you say about God what you do not know?"): **أمْ** is *mu'adilah* (equivalent, connected) to the interrogative **الهَمْزَةِ** (*hamza*, the interrogative particle), meaning "which of the two matters is the case," as an affirmation of knowledge of the occurrence of one of them. Alternatively, it is *munqati'ah* (disconnected), meaning "rather, do you say," for rebuke and reproach.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 81–82:

﴿Bala﴾ (Yes, indeed) is an affirmation of what they denied: that the Fire would touch them for a long, lengthy span of time, and in a more general sense, so that it serves as a proof against the invalidity of their claim. It is specifically the answer to a negation. ﴿Whoever earns an evil deed﴾, ugly in nature. The difference between it (sayyi'ah) and khati'ah (sin) is that sayyi'ah may be said of what is intended in essence, whereas khati'ah predominates over what is intended incidentally, because it derives from khata' (error). Kasb (earning) is the seeking of benefit. Its connection to sayyi'ah follows the pattern of His saying: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾.

﴿And his sin has encompassed him﴾, meaning it has overpowered him and enveloped the totality of his states, until he is as one encompassed by it, such that nothing of him from any side is free of it. This applies properly only to the disbeliever, for the other, even if he has nothing but the confirmation of his heart and the acknowledgment of his tongue, is not encompassed by sin. For this reason the early scholars (al-salaf) explained khati'ah as kufr (disbelief). The realization of this is that whoever commits a sin and does not desist from it, it draws him to repeat its like, to be absorbed in it, and to commit what is greater than it, until sins take control over him and seize the core of his heart, so that by his nature he inclines toward acts of disobedience, regards them as good, believes there is no pleasure other than them, hates whoever prevents him from them, and denies whoever advises him concerning them, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst, that they denied the signs of Allah﴾. Nafi' read khati'atuhu (singular).

It is also read as khatiyyatuhu and khatiyyatuhu (khaṭiyyātuhu), with metathesis (al-qalb) and idgham (assimilation) in both. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide in it forever﴾ in the Hereafter, just as they are bound to its causes in this world. ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾, meaning perpetually, or remaining for a long duration. As you see, the verse contains no proof for the eternal abiding of the one guilty of a grave sin, and likewise the preceding verse.

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds, those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever﴾. It is His customary practice, glory be to Him and exalted is He, to couple His promise with His threat, so that His mercy may be hoped for and His punishment feared. The conjunction of deeds with faith indicates that they are outside its definition (musammah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 83:

﴿And [remember] when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Do not worship except Allah"﴾. This is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾. And it is more eloquent than an explicit prohibition, because it gives the impression that the one being prohibited hastened to desist, so it reports about him and reinforces it. The reading "Do not worship" (lā taʿbudū) supports this. He also conjoined "say" (qūlū) to it, so it is on the basis of the intention of saying. It was also said: its estimate is "that they not worship," and when "an" (that) was omitted, it was put in the nominative, like the poet's words:

"Ala ayyuhadha al-zajiri ahḍura al-waghā... wa an ashhada al-ladhdhāti hal anta mukhlidī"

It is indicated by the reading "Lā taʿbudūna" (that you not worship), so it is either a substitute (badal) for "the covenant," or an object of purpose (maʿmūl lahu) with the preposition omitted. It was also said that it is the answer to an oath which the meaning indicates, as if he said: "We made them swear that they would not worship." Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim and Yaʿqūb read with the "t" (tā'), relating what they were addressed with, while the rest read with the "y" (yā'), because they are third-person.

﴿And to parents, kindness﴾: it is connected to an implied verb whose estimate is: "And you shall be kind," or "Be kind." ﴿And to near kin, orphans and the needy﴾: conjoined to "parents." "Yatāmā" is the plural of "yatīm" (orphan), like "nadīm" and "nadāmā," and this is a rare pattern. "Miskīn" (needy) is on the pattern "mifʿīl" from "sukūn" (stillness), as if poverty had made him still.

﴿And speak to people kindly﴾: that is, a good speech; he called it "kindness" (ḥusn) for emphasis. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb read "ḥasanan" with two fatḥas. It was also read "ḥusunan" with two ḍammas, and this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz; and "ḥusnā" on the pattern of a verbal noun, like "bushrā." What is meant by it is that which contains good moral conduct and guidance.

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾: he means by them what was prescribed for them in their religion.

﴿Then you turned away﴾: in the manner of iltifāt (a shift of address). It is likely that the address is to those present among them in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and those before them, by way of predominance (taghlīb), that is: you turned away from the covenant and rejected it.

﴿Except a few of you﴾: he means by it those who maintained Judaism in its proper form before the abrogation, and those among them who embraced Islam.

﴿And you are averse﴾: a people whose habit is aversion from fidelity and obedience. The original sense of iʿrāḍ (aversion) is going away from confrontation toward the side of the breadth (al-ʿarḍ).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 84:

﴿And when We took your covenant: You shall not shed your blood, nor expel your own people from your homes.﴾ This is in the same manner as what preceded, and what is meant is that some of them should not attack others by killing or by driving them out of their homeland. He made the killing of a man of another people as the killing of his own self (nafs) because of his connection to him through lineage (nasab), or religion (din), or because it necessitates retaliation (qisas). It has also been said that its meaning is: do not commit what would make your blood and your expulsion from your homes permissible; or: do not do what ruins you and turns you away from eternal life, for that is death in reality; and do not commit what keeps you from Paradise, which is your abode, for that is true exile. ﴿Then you affirmed﴾ the covenant and acknowledged its binding obligation ﴿and you were witnesses﴾. This is an emphasis, like your saying: "So-and-so affirmed, as a witness against himself." It has also been said that the meaning is: and you, who are present, are witnesses to the affirmation of your forefathers, so the attribution of the affirmation to them is metaphorical (majaz).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 85:

(p-92)﴿Then you are these [people]﴾ is an expression of astonishment at what they committed after the covenant, after their acknowledgment of it and their bearing witness to it. "Antum" is the subject (mubtada') and "haulaa'" is its predicate (khabar), with the meaning: "You, after that, are these ones, the ones who fall short," like your saying: "You are that man who did such-and-such." He treated the change of attribute as the change of essence. He addressed them in the second person in view of what was attributed to them, as present, and referred to them in the third person in view of what he is about to narrate about them, as absent. As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿you kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes﴾, it is either a circumstantial clause (hal), whose governing element is the meaning of the demonstrative (ishara), or an elaboration (bayan) of this sentence. It has been said: "haulaa'" is an emphatic (ta'kid), and the predicate is the sentence. It has also been said: it means "alladhina" (those who), the sentence following it is its relative clause (silah), and the whole is the predicate. "Tuqattiluna" has been read with intensification (al-takthir). ﴿You support one another against them in sin and enmity﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "takhrujun," or from its object, or from both. Tazahur means mutual cooperation, derived from "zahr" (back). Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with one of the two taa' elided. It has also been read with both taa's pronounced, and "tuzhirun" with the meaning of "tatazahharun."

﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾. It is related that the Qurayzah were allies of the Aws, and the Nadir were allies of the Khazraj. When the two clashed, each party aided its allies in killing, in destroying homes, and in expelling their people. And when one of the two sides took a captive, they gathered together to ransom him. It has been said that its meaning is: if they come to you as captives in the hands of the devils, you strive to rescue them through guidance and admonition, while you neglect your own selves, like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon people and forget yourselves?﴾. Hamzah read "asra," which is the plural of "asir" like "jarih" and "jarha," and "usara" is its plural, like "sakran" and "sukara." It has also been said that it too is the plural of "asir," as if it were likened to "kaslan" and the plural of its plural.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read "tafduhum." ﴿And it was forbidden to you to expel them﴾ is related to His saying ﴿and expel a group of you from their homes﴾, and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiradh). The pronoun refers to the matter (li-al-sha'n), or it is undefined (mubham) and is explained by "ikhrajuhum," or it refers to what is indicated by "tukhrijun" of the verbal noun. "Ikhrajuhum" is either an apposition (badal) or an elaboration (bayan). ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book?﴾ meaning the ransom.

﴿And you disbelieve in part﴾ meaning the prohibition of fighting and expulsion. ﴿So what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the life of this world﴾ such as the killing and enslavement of the Qurayzah, the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, and the imposition of the jizyah upon others. The root of khizy is a humiliation that causes shame, and for this reason it is used for each of the two. ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment﴾ because their disobedience is greater. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ is an emphasis of the threat, meaning: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is on watch and does not neglect their deeds. Asim, in the narration of al-Mufaddal, read "turaddun" in the second person, in reference to His saying ﴿among you﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr, Khalaf and Ya'qub read "ya'malun," taking the pronoun to refer to "man" (those).

These are those who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter (who have 'bought' the life of this world in exchange for the Hereafter); they have preferred the life of this world over the Hereafter. ﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them﴾ by way of reducing the jizya (poll tax) in this world, or the torment in the Hereafter. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾ by having either of them averted from them.

And We certainly gave Moses the Book, meaning the Torah. ﴿And We followed him up with messengers﴾, meaning We sent messengers in his wake, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. It is said *qaffāhu* when one follows someone, and *qaffāhu bihi* when one makes someone follow another, derived from *al-qafā* (the nape), like *dhanabahu* (he made him follow his tail) from *al-dhanab* (the tail). ﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear proofs﴾, meaning the manifest miracles, such as raising the dead, healing the blind and the leper, and informing people of unseen matters. Or it means the Gospel. Jesus in Hebrew is *Abshū'*. Maryam means "servant," and in Arabic it is for women what *al-zīr* is for men. Ru'ba said:

"I said to a *zīr* whom *Maryamah* did not reach."

Its weight is *maf'al*, since *fa'īl* is not attested.

﴿And We strengthened him﴾, meaning We supported him. It was also read *āyadnāhu* with a long vowel. ﴿With the holy spirit﴾, meaning with the holy spirit, as in your saying *ḥātim al-jūd* (the paragon of generosity) and *rajul ṣidq* (a man of truth). By it he meant Gabriel.

It is also said that it refers to the spirit of Jesus, peace be upon him. It was described as holy because of its purity from the touch of Satan, or because of its honor before God, which is why He attributed it to Himself. Or because the spirit was not contained by the loins and the wombs that were menstruating. Or it refers to the Gospel. Or to the Greatest Name of God, by which he used to revive the dead. Ibn Kathīr read *al-Qudus* with a sukūn (silent) in all of the Qur'an.

﴿Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls do not desire﴾, meaning with what they do not love. It is said *hawiya* (with kasra) *hawan* when one loves, and *hawā* (with fatḥa) *huwiyyan* (with ḍamma) when one falls. The hamza (interrogative) was placed between the *fā'* (and) and what it is connected to, as a rebuke to them for following that with this, and as an expression of wonder at their state. It is possible that it is a new sentence (*isti'nāf*), and the *fā'* is for coordination with an implied preceding clause. ﴿You became arrogant﴾ toward faith and following the messengers. ﴿A group you denied﴾, like Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them, and the *fā'* indicates causation or detail. ﴿And a group you kill﴾, like Zechariah and John, peace be upon them. It was mentioned in the present tense to narrate a past situation, to make it vivid in people's minds, since the matter is appalling. Or to observe the rhyme endings (*fawāṣil*). Or to indicate that you are still engaged in it, for you are circling around killing Muḥammad (ﷺ), were it not that I protect him from you. For this reason you bewitched him and poisoned a sheep for him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 88:

﴿And they say, "Our hearts are wrapped."﴾ Veiled with innate coverings, so that what you have brought does not reach them, and they do not comprehend it. It is a metaphor taken from the uncircumcised (aghlaf), the one who has not been circumcised. It is also said that its origin is ghulufun, the plural of ghilaf (covering), which was lightened (to ghulf). The meaning is that their hearts are receptacles for knowledge that do not hear any knowledge without retaining it, yet they do not understand what is said. Or: we are self-sufficient with what is in us, and have no need of anything else. ﴿Nay, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief.﴾ This is a refutation of what they said. The meaning is that their hearts were created upon the natural disposition (fitrah) and the capacity to accept the truth, but Allah forsook them for their disbelief, and so nullified their readiness. Or: their hearts did not refuse to accept what he (the Prophet) had said because of any flaw in it, but rather because Allah the Exalted forsook them for their disbelief, as the Exalted said: ﴿And He made them deaf and blinded their eyes.﴾ Or: they are disbelievers and accursed, so from where do they have the claim of knowledge and of being independent of you? ﴿So little is it that they believe.﴾ That is, they believe with a little faith. The word "ma" (mā) is an intensifier for emphasis on the paucity, and it refers to their belief in part of the Book. It is also said: by "little" he meant "none."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 89:

﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what is with them﴾, i.e. their own Book. It is also read in the accusative (muṣaddiqan) as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of "kitāb", since it is specified by the qualifier. The response (jawāb) of the first "lammā" is omitted, indicated by the response of the second "lammā".

﴿And previously they had been seeking victory (yastaftiḥūna) over those who disbelieved﴾, i.e. they would seek help against the polytheists and say: "O Allah, help us through the Prophet of the last age, described in the Torah." Or they would open up (to them) and inform them that a prophet would be sent from among them, and that his time had drawn near. The sīn (in yastaftiḥūna) is for emphasis (mubālagha) and to indicate that the agent is asking for this for himself.

﴿So when there came to them what they recognised﴾ of the truth, ﴿they disbelieved in it﴾ out of envy and fear for their leadership (riyāsa). ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾, i.e. upon them. The explicit noun was used to indicate that they were cursed for their disbelief, so the lām is for prior reference (ʿahd). It is also permissible that it be for the class (jins), and they enter into it primarily, since the discourse is about them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 90:

﴿Wretched is that for which they have sold their souls﴾ (mā is an indefinite noun meaning "a thing," functioning as a specifying accusative (tamyīz) for the hidden subject (fā'il) of bi'sa (wretched/evil is), and ishtaraw is its description (ṣifa). Its meaning is "they sold." Or, [ishtaraw is understood] according to their assumption, for they assumed that by what they did they had saved their souls from punishment.) ﴿that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down﴾ is the thing specified for blame (al-makhṣūṣ bi'l-dhamm). ﴿out of insolent envy (baghy)﴾ meaning seeking what was not theirs, and envy (ḥasad). It is the cause (ʿilla) of ﴿they disbelieve﴾, not of ﴿they sold﴾, because of the separation (li'l-faṣl). ﴿that Allah should send down﴾ meaning "because Allah sends down," i.e., they envied him over Allah's sending down. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Sahl, and Yaʿqūb read it with the lightened form (takhfīf). ﴿of His bounty﴾ means revelation (al-waḥy). ﴿upon whomever of His servants He wills﴾ upon whomever He has chosen for the message (al-risāla). ﴿So they returned with anger upon anger﴾ for disbelief and for envy of the one who is the best of creation. It has also been said: for their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ) after ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), or after their saying "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah." ﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾ meaning their humiliation is intended by it, unlike the punishment of the disobedient believer, which is a purification for his sins.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 91:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down,"﴾ this covers all the revealed books in their entirety. ﴿They say, "We believe in what was sent down to us,"﴾ i.e., in the Torah. ﴿And they disbelieve in what is beyond it,﴾ a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "they say." The word warā' (beyond, behind) was originally made into an adverb of place. It may be annexed to the subject, in which case it means that which conceals a thing, namely what is behind it; or it may be annexed to the object, in which case it means that which conceals something, namely what is in front of it. For this reason it is counted among the words with contrary meanings (al-adhdād). ﴿While it is the truth,﴾ the pronoun refers to "what is beyond it," and what is meant by it is the Qur'an. ﴿Confirming what is with them,﴾ a emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah) that contains a rejection of their claim, for when they disbelieved in what agrees with the Torah, they had in fact disbelieved in the Torah itself. ﴿Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?"﴾ This is an objection directed at them concerning the killing of the prophets, despite their claim to believe in the Torah, while the Torah does not permit it. It was ascribed to them because it was the deed of their forefathers, and because they were content with it and determined upon it.

Nafi' alone read "anbi'a'a Allah" with hamza throughout the whole Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 92:

﴿And indeed Moses came to you with clear proofs﴾. He means the nine signs mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses nine clear signs﴾. ﴿Then you took the calf﴾, i.e., as a god, ﴿after him﴾, after Moses' coming, or his departure to the Mount (al-Tur), ﴿while you were wrongdoers﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: you took the calf as a god while being wrongdoers, by worshipping it, or by neglecting the signs of God exalted is He; or it is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad), meaning: and you are a people whose habit is wrongdoing. The purpose of the verse is also to refute their saying ﴿We believe in what was sent down to us﴾, and to alert that their conduct toward the Messenger is the conduct of their forebears toward Moses, peace be upon them both, not to repeat the story, and likewise what follows it.

﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you: take what We have given you with strength, and listen.﴾ That is, We said to them: take what you were commanded in the Torah with earnestness, and listen with the listening of obedience. ﴿They said: We have heard﴾ your word ﴿and we disobey﴾ your command. ﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ its love permeated them and its image became firmly fixed in their hearts, owing to the excess of their infatuation with it, just as dye permeates cloth and drink permeates the depths of the body. "In their hearts" explains the place of the drinking, like His saying ﴿They only eat fire into their bellies﴾ (2:174). ﴿Because of their disbelief﴾ on account of their unbelief. This is because they were anthropomorphists (mujassima) or incarnationists (hulūliyya), and they did not see any body more wondrous than it, so what the Samiri embellished for them took firm hold in their hearts. ﴿Say: Wretched is what your faith enjoins upon you﴾ That is, the Torah. The object of the censure is omitted, as in "this command," or it covers this and other of their enormities mentioned in the three verses, as a reproach against them. ﴿If you are believers﴾ is an affirmation that rebukes their claim to faith in the Torah. Its implied sense: if you are believers in it, it would not have commanded you these abominations nor permitted them to you. Or: if you are believers in it, then wretched is what your faith in it enjoins upon you, because the believer should not pursue anything except what his faith requires, but faith in it does not command this; therefore you are not believers.

(p-95)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 94–95:

﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is yours exclusively, to the exclusion of the people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾ "Exclusively" means specifically for you, just as you have claimed: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews.﴾ He put it in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the Abode." ﴿To the exclusion of the people﴾ means the rest of them. The lam (al-lam) here is for the genus (li-l-jins), or, if it refers to the Muslims, it is for a previously known group (li-l-'ahd). ﴿Then wish for death, if you are truthful﴾ because whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise longs for it and loves to be freed from this abode of impurities, just as 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: (I do not care whether I fall upon death, or death falls upon me).

'Ammar, may Allah be pleased with him, said at Siffin:

(Now I shall meet the beloved, Muhammad, and his party.)

Hudhayfah, may Allah be pleased with him, said when he was near death: (A beloved has come upon poverty; he who regrets has not prospered.) That is, regarding wishing [for death], especially when he knows that it is entirely his, with no one else sharing in it.

﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward﴾ of things that necessitate the Fire, such as disbelief in Muhammad ﷺ, in the Qur'an, and the distortion of the Torah. Since the working hand is specific to the human being, being the instrument of his power by which he performs most of his crafts and most of his benefits, he has used it to express the self at one time and power at another. This statement is a report of the unseen, and it came to pass as he reported, for if they had wished for death it would have been transmitted and widely known, since wishing is not an act of the heart that could remain hidden; rather, it is to say: "Would that I had such-and-such." Had it been in the heart, they would have said: "We wished." It is related from the Prophet ﷺ: "If they had wished for death, every person would have choked on his saliva and died in his place, and not a Jew would have remained on the face of the earth."

﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ a warning to them and an alert that they are wrongdoers in claiming what is not theirs, and in denying it to those to whom it truly belongs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 96:

﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾. The verb "wajada" (found), used here in the sense of "knowledge" (ʿilm), takes two objects: "them" (hum) and "the most eager of people" (aḥraṣa al-nās). The indefinite form of "ḥayah" (life) is used because what is intended by it is one particular instance of it, namely a long-extended life. It is also read with the definite article (al-ḥayah). ﴿And of those who associated partners [with God]﴾ is governed by the sense: it is as if he said, "more eager than people for life, and more eager than those who associated partners." Its being singled out for mention is for emphasis, for their eagerness is intense, since they knew only the present life; and for the intensification of rebuke and reproach, since their eagerness increased even though they affirm the recompense, which indicates that they know they are destined for the Fire. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is "and more eager than those who associated partners," so "aḥraṣa" is omitted because the first one indicates it. It is also possible that it is the predicate of an omitted subject whose description is ﴿each one of them wishes﴾, on the basis that by "those who associated partners" the Jews are meant, because they said, ﴿ʿUzayr is the son of God﴾; that is, "and among them are people, each one of whom wishes..." This, according to the first view, is an explanation of the increase in their eagerness, by way of resumption. ﴿If he were given a life of a thousand years﴾ is a report of their wish, and "law" (lau) here has the meaning of "layta" (would that). Its original form was "law uʿammiru" (if I were given life), but it was shifted to the third person in accordance with "yawaddu" (wishes), like your saying "he swore by God that he would certainly do it." ﴿And he is not one to remove him from the punishment by being given life﴾: the pronoun refers to one of them, and "an yuʿammar" (being given life) is the agent of "muzahzihihi" (one who removes him), meaning: none of them is one whom his being given life would remove from the punishment. Alternatively, it refers to what is indicated by "yuʿammar." "An yuʿammar" may be a substitute for it, or it may be ambiguous with "an yuʿammar" clarifying it. The original form of "sanah" (year) is "sanawah," as in their saying "sanawat," and it has been said it is "sanhah," like "jabhah," as in their saying "sanahathu" and "tasannahat al-nakhlah" (the palm tree aged, when the years passed over it). Zahzahah (removing) means distancing. ﴿And God is seeing of what they do﴾, so He will recompense them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 97:

﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel﴾. It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Suriya, who asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the one who brings down revelation to him. He said: "Gabriel." He said: "That is our enemy. He has been hostile to us repeatedly, and the worst of it is that he brought down to our Prophet that Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) would be ruined by Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar). So we sent someone to kill him, and he saw him in Babil (Babylon), and Gabriel repelled him from him. He said: 'If your Lord commanded him to destroy you, then He would not give him power over you. Otherwise, why do you kill him?'"

It is also said: "One day Umar, may God be pleased with him, entered the schools of the Jews and asked them about Gabriel. They said: 'That is our enemy. He informs Muhammad of our secrets, and he is the one in charge of every collapse and punishment, while Mika'il is in charge of fertility and peace.' He said: 'And what is their station with God?' They said: 'Gabriel is on His right and Mika'il is on His left, and between them there is enmity.' He said: 'If they are as you say, then they are not enemies, and you are more disbelieving than donkeys. Whoever is an enemy of either of them is an enemy of God.' Then Umar returned and found that Gabriel had preceded him with the revelation, so the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'Your Lord has agreed with you, O Umar.'"

There are eight dialects (lughat) of the name Jibril, by which recitation (qira'a) has been performed. Four are well known: Jabra'il, like Salsabil, is the recitation of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i; Jibril, with a kasra on the ra and the hamza omitted, is the recitation of Ibn Kathir; Jabra'il, like Jahmarish, is the recitation of 'Asim according to the transmission of Abu Bakr; and Jibril, like Qindil, is the recitation of the rest. Four are irregular (shadhdh): Jabra'il-l and Jabra'il, like Jabra'il, and Jibril, and Jibrin. Its diptote status (not taking nunation) is due to its foreignness (ajamiyya) and definiteness (ta'rif), and its meaning is "servant of God."

﴿Indeed, it is He who has brought it down﴾. The first pronoun refers to Gabriel, and the second to the Qur'an. Leaving its referent unmentioned indicates the magnitude of his status, as if, because he is so specific and so famous, he needed no prior mention.

﴿upon your heart﴾. The heart is the first receptacle of revelation and the seat of understanding and memorization. The proper form would have been "upon my heart," but it came in the form of quoting the words of God Most High, as if He had said: "Say: what you have spoken."

﴿by the permission of God﴾: by His command, or by His facilitation. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to its agent, who is the one who brought it down.

﴿confirming what is before it, and as guidance and good tidings for the believers﴾: these are circumstantial clauses (ahwal) referring to its object. The apparent view is that the answer to the conditional is ﴿indeed, it is He who has brought it down﴾. The meaning is: whoever among them is hostile to Gabriel has cast off the bond of fairness, or has disbelieved in the scripture that is with him, by opposing him for his bringing down revelation to you, since it is the descent of a scripture confirming the earlier books. The answer is omitted and its cause is put in its place. Alternatively: whoever is hostile to him, the reason for his hostility is that he brought it down upon you. It is also said that the answer is omitted, like: "let him die of rage," or "then he is an enemy to Me, and I am an enemy to him."

As he said:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 98:

﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, Jibril, and Mika'il, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾ He intended by enmity to Allah opposing Him out of obstinacy, or opposing His close servants. He began the statement with mention of Him to magnify their status, as in His saying, ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾. He singled out the two angels for mention because of their excellence, as though they were of another kind. This alerts that opposing one or all of them is equal in disbelief and in drawing enmity from Allah, Exalted is He, and that whoever opposes one of them has in effect opposed all of them, since the factor that truly necessitates enmity toward them and love for them is one. Also, the argument (with the Jews) concerned these two. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that He, Exalted is He, opposed them because of their disbelief, and that enmity toward the angels and messengers is disbelief.

Nafi' read مِيكائِلَ as مِيكاعِلَ (like "Mika'il" with the pattern of مِيكاعِلَ), Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and 'Asim in the narration of Hafs read مِيكالَ as مِيعادٍ (the pattern of "Mi'ad"), and the rest read مِيكائِيلَ with a hamza and a yā' after it. It was also read مِيكِئْلَ like مِيكِعْلَ, مِيكَئِيلَ like مِيكَعِيلَ, and مِيكايِلَ.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 99–100:

﴿And indeed, We have sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾. Ay, the rebellious ones among the disbelievers. When fisq (depravity, transgression) is used for a category of sins, it indicates its gravity, as if it had exceeded its limit. It was revealed concerning Ibn Suriya when he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "You have brought us nothing that we recognize, and no sign has been sent down to you that we would follow you."

﴿Is it not that whenever they make a covenant﴾. The hamzah is for denunciation, and the waw is for conjunction with an elided element, the estimated meaning being: "Did they disbelieve in the signs, and whenever they make a covenant?" It is also read with the waw sukūn, on the basis that the estimate is "except those who transgressed," then "whenever they make a covenant." It is also read as ʿūhidū and ʿahidū. ﴿a party of them threw it aside﴾: they broke it. The root meaning of nabdh (throwing aside) is casting off, but it is predominantly used for what is forgotten. He said "a party" (farīq) because not all of them were in breach. ﴿Rather, most of them do not believe﴾: a refutation of the supposition that "the party" refers to the minority, or that whoever did not openly throw it aside is secretly a believer in it.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 101:**

﴿When there came to them a messenger from Allah, confirming what they already had,﴾ such as Jesus and Muhammad, upon them both be blessings and peace. ﴿a party of those who had been given the Scripture threw away the Book of Allah﴾, meaning the Torah, because their disbelief in the Messenger who confirmed it was disbelief in it as far as he confirmed it, and a rejection of what it contains concerning the obligation to believe in the messengers supported by signs. It has also been said that what was with the Messenger (ﷺ) is the Qur'an.

﴿behind their backs﴾ is a parable for their turning away from it entirely, by turning away from what is cast behind the back, since it receives no attention.

﴿as if they did not know﴾ that it is the Book of Allah, meaning that their knowledge of it is firm, but they feign ignorance out of obstinacy. Know that by these two verses, Allah, exalted is He, indicates that the generation of the Jews consisted of four groups. One group believed in the Torah and upheld its rights, like the believers among the People of the Book, and they are the minority, indicated by His saying: ﴿Rather, most of them do not believe﴾. A second group openly cast off its covenants and transgressed its limits, out of rebellion and wickedness, and they are the ones referred to by His saying: ﴿a party of them threw it away﴾. A third group did not openly reject it, but was cast aside because of their ignorance of it, and they are the majority. A fourth group held to it outwardly but secretly rejected it while knowing the truth, out of insolence and obstinacy, and they are the feigned ignorers.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 102:

﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾ is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*, conjunction) with *nabadha* (threw away), meaning: they threw away the Book of God and followed the books of magic that the devils recite or follow, whether the devils of the jinn, of mankind, or of both. ﴿Over the kingdom of Solomon﴾ means in his time (*ʿahd*). *Tatlū* (recite) expresses a description of a past state (*ḥikāyat ḥāl*, narrative of a circumstance). It is said: they used to eavesdrop (*yastariqūna al-samʿ*) and add to what they heard lies, and they would throw these to the soothsayers (*kahana*), who would record them and teach them to people. This spread in the time of Solomon, peace be upon him, to the point that it was said that the jinn know the unseen, that Solomon's kingdom was achieved through this knowledge, and that through it the jinn, mankind and the wind were subjected to him.

﴿And Solomon did not disbelieve﴾ is a refutation of whoever claims that. He expressed magic by the term *kufr* (disbelief) to indicate that it is disbelief, and that whoever is a prophet is protected from it. ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾ by using it. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *lākin* (but) with light stress and with *al-shayāṭīn* in the nominative. ﴿Teaching people magic﴾ as seduction and misguidance. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun. By magic is meant that which is sought to be attained by drawing near to Satan, in matters that a human cannot accomplish alone. This is not achieved except by one who is suited to it in wickedness and corruption of soul, for suitability is a condition for association and cooperation. By this, the magician is distinguished from the prophet and the saint (*walī*). As for what amazes people, such as what the practitioners of tricks do with the aid of instruments and drugs, or what the one of nimble hand (*khiffat al-yad*, sleight of hand) displays, this is not blameworthy. Calling it magic is a figurative usage (*ʿamal al-tajawwuz*), or because of its subtlety, since originally it refers to that whose cause is hidden.

﴿And what was sent down to the two angels﴾ is coordinated with *al-siḥr* (magic), and both refer to one thing, the coordination being due to difference of consideration. Or it means a stronger kind of it, or it is coordinated with *mā tatlū*. They are two angels sent down to teach magic as a trial from God for people, and to distinguish it from the miracle. As for what is related, that they were fashioned as two humans and were given desire, and they encountered a woman called Zuhra, who led them into sins and polytheism, then she ascended to heaven with what she had learned from them, this is related from the Jews. Perhaps it is one of the symbols of the ancients, and its solution is not hidden from people of insight. It is also said: they were two men called angels because of their righteousness, and this is supported by the reading *al-Malikayn* with a kasra. It is also said: *mā unzila* is a negation coordinated with *mā kafara Sulayman*, a refutation of the Jews in this story.

﴿At Babylon﴾ is an adverbial complement (*ẓarf*), or a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the two angels, or from the pronoun in *unzila*. The well-known view is that it is a town in the countryside of Kufa. ﴿Harut and Marut﴾ is an explicative apposition (*ʿaṭf bayān*) for the two angels. Their diptote status (not taking nunation) is due to being proper nouns and being non-Arabic (*ʿujma*). If they were derived from *al-hart* and *al-mart*, meaning breaking, they would take nunation.

Whoever makes *mā* a negation makes them a partial substitute (*badal al-baʿḍ*) for the devils, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (*iʿtirāḍ*). It is also read with *Harutu wa Marutu* in the nominative, as their predicate. ﴿And they did not teach anyone until they said: We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾. Its meaning according to the first view is: they did not teach anyone until they advised him and said to him: We are only a trial from God. Whoever learns from us and acts upon it disbelieves, and whoever learns and avoids acting upon it remains firm in faith. So do not disbelieve by believing it permissible and acting upon it. In this is evidence that learning magic and what it is not permissible to follow is not forbidden, and the prohibition applies only to following it and acting upon it. According to the second view, they do not teach it until they say: We are only afflicted, so do not be like us.

﴿So they learn from them﴾: the pronoun refers to what is indicated by *min aḥad* (from anyone). ﴿What they use to cause separation between a man and his wife﴾, that is, of magic, that which is the cause of separating the two. ﴿Yet they could not harm anyone with it except by God's permission﴾, because it and other causes do not have effect in themselves, but only by His command and His making. It is read *bi-ḍārrī* (with the genitive) as an annexation to *aḥad*, taking the preposition as part of it, with separation by the adverbial phrase.

﴿And they learn what harms them﴾ because they intend to act upon it, or because knowledge generally leads to action, and it does not benefit them, since mere knowledge of it is not intended nor beneficial in either abode. In this is evidence that avoiding it is better. ﴿And they had certainly known﴾, that is, the Jews. ﴿That whoever purchases it﴾, that is, who exchanges what the devils recite for the Book of God, Most High. The more apparent view is that the *lām* is the *lām* of initiation (*lām al-ibtidāʾ*), which suspends *ʿalimū* (they knew) from operating. ﴿Has no share in the Hereafter﴾, that is, no portion (*khalāq*). ﴿And wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾, which admits of both meanings as explained. ﴿If only they knew﴾, that is, reflected upon it, or knew its ugliness specifically, or the reality of the punishment that follows it. The affirmed knowledge given to them first, by way of emphatic oath (*taʾkīd qasamī*), is innate reason or general knowledge, which deems the act ugly, or the consequence of punishment without verification. It is also said: its meaning is, if only they acted upon their knowledge, for whoever does not act upon what he knows is like one who does not know.

(p-98)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 103:

﴿And if they had believed﴾ in the Messenger and the Book, ﴿and feared Allah﴾ by abstaining from acts of disobedience, such as rejecting the Book of Allah and following sorcery, ﴿a reward from Allah would have been better﴾ — this is the answer to "law" (law, "if"). Its original form was: "they would have been rewarded with a reward from Allah that is better than what they sold their souls for." The verb was omitted, and the remainder was constructed as a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya) to indicate the permanence of the reward and the certainty of its being better. The comparative's object was omitted out of reverence for the one who is preferred, lest it be attributed to him. The word "reward" (mathuba) is indefinite because the meaning is "some of the reward is better." It has also been said: "law" here is for wishing (li-l-tamanni), and "la-mathuba" is the beginning of a new sentence (kalam mubtada'). 

It is read as "lamathuba" with the pattern of "mashura" (lamathūbatun, as in mashūratin). The reward is called thawab and mathuba because the doer of good "returns" (yathūb) to it. ﴿If only they knew﴾ that Allah's reward is better than what they are in; they did know, but he made them ignorant by their neglect of reflection or of acting on knowledge.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 104:

﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina," but say "Unzurna," and listen.﴾ Ra'y (ر ع ي, "watching over") means guarding another's interest. The Muslims used to say to the Messenger (ﷺ), "Ra'ina," meaning: "Watch over us and be patient with us in what you teach us until we understand it." The Jews heard this, seized upon it, and addressed him with it, intending to attribute to him foolishness (ra'n), or to revile him with the Hebrew word they used to curse one another, which was "ra'ina." So the believers were forbidden to say it and were commanded to use a phrase that conveys the same meaning without admitting such distortion, namely "unzurna," which means "look upon us" (unzur ilayna). It may also mean "wait for us," from the sense of nazara when one waits for something.

"Unzirna" (from in-zar, "give us respite") was also read, meaning: "Grant us a delay so that we may preserve (what you say)." "Ra'unā" was also read in the plural form as a mark of honour. "Ra'inan" with tanwin was read, meaning a statement containing ra'n, which is foolishness (al-hawaj), since it resembled their saying "ra'ina" and was a means to reviling. "Wa-asma'u" and "ahsinu" (listen and listen well) means: listen attentively so that you do not need to ask for consideration. Or: "listen" with the listening of acceptance, not like the listening of the Jews. Or: listen to what you have been commanded with earnestness, so that you do not return to what you have been forbidden. ﴿And for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment.﴾ That refers to those who treated the Messenger (ﷺ) with contempt and reviled him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 105:

﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not love that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord.﴾ It was revealed as a refutation of a group of Jews who showed affection (mawaddah) toward the believers and claimed that they wished them well. Al-wadd (love) is the love of a thing together with wishing for it, and for this reason it is used for each of the two. Min (from) here is for specification (li-l-tabyin), as in His Exalted saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to be [free from disbelief] until there came to them clear evidence﴾ and ﴿that there should be sent down upon you any good from your Lord﴾. It is the object of yawaddu. The first min is extra (mazidah) for generality (li-l-istighraq), and the second is for commencement (li-l-ibtida'). "Good" has been interpreted as revelation. The meaning is that they envy you because of it, and they do not love that anything from it should descend upon you, nor [that anything of] knowledge or victory [should descend upon you]. Perhaps what is intended by it is that which encompasses all of that. ﴿But Allah specifies for His mercy whom He wills﴾: He makes him a prophet, teaches him wisdom, and grants him victory; nothing is obligatory upon Him, and no one has any right over Him. ﴿And Allah is the Owner of great bounty﴾: an indication that prophethood is among the bounty, and that the deprivation of some of His servants is not due to the narrowness of His bounty, but to His will and to the wisdom known in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 106–107:

﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾. It was revealed when the polytheists, or the Jews, said: "Do you not see how Muhammad orders his companions to do one thing and then forbids them from it, and orders the opposite?" Naskh (abrogation) in linguistic usage means removing the form of a thing and establishing it in something else, like the shadow's abrogation (naskh) of the sun and transference (naql), and from it comes metempsychosis (tanasukh). Then the term was used for each of these two, as in your saying: "The wind abrogated the trace," and "I copied (nasakhtu) the book."

The abrogation of a verse is the declaration that the obligation of reciting it, or of the ruling derived from it, or of both together, has ended. Its causing to be forgotten (insa') is its removal from the hearts. Ma is a conditional particle in the jussive mood, governing nansakh in the accusative as its object. Ibn ʿAmir read mā nunsikh, from ansakha, meaning: We command you, or Jibril, to abrogate it, or We find it abrogated. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read nunsi'hā, meaning: We postpone it, from al-nasʾ (postponement). It was also read nunsihā, meaning: We cause someone to forget it; and nunsihā, meaning: you (plural) cause it to be forgotten; and tunsaha, in the passive; and nunsikaha, with both objects elided.

﴿We bring a better one than it or its like﴾, meaning: something better for the servants in benefit and reward, or ﴿its like﴾ in reward. Abu ʿAmr read the hamza as an alif (nansa). ﴿Do you not know that God has power over everything?﴾ So He is able to abrogate and to bring something like the abrogated or something better than it. The verse indicates the permissibility of abrogation and of delaying the revelation, since the original principle is that inna and what it contains is restricted to matters that are possible, because the rulings were legislated and the verses were revealed for the welfare of the servants and the perfection of their souls, as a bounty and mercy from God, and this varies with the variation of eras and individuals, like the means of livelihood, for what is beneficial in one era may be harmful in another.

Those who forbid abrogation without a substitute, or with a heavier substitute, have argued with this verse. The abrogation of the Book by the Sunnah is also (disputed), since the abrogating text is the one brought as a substitute, and the Sunnah is not like that; but all of these are weak, since the absence of a ruling or a heavier one may be more beneficial. Abrogation may be known by other means, and the Sunnah is among what God the Exalted has brought; and "better" and "its like" do not mean what is so in wording. The Mu'tazilah hold that the Qur'an is created, since change and variation are among its necessary attributes. It is answered: these are among the accidents of matters related to the meaning subsisting in the eternal Essence.

﴿Do you not know﴾: the address is to the Prophet ﷺ, and what is meant is he and his community, as in His saying: ﴿and what do you have﴾. He addressed him singularly because he is the most knowledgeable of them and the source of their knowledge. ﴿That God—to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾: He does what He wills and decides what He intends. It is like a proof for His saying (p-100): ﴿that God has power over everything﴾, or for the permissibility of abrogation; and for this reason the conjunction was omitted. ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides God﴾: it is He who owns your affairs and directs them in what benefits you. The difference between wali (protector) and nasir (helper) is that a protector may be weak in giving help, while a helper may be a stranger to the one helped, so that between them there is a generality from one aspect.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 108:

﴿Do you desire to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ "Am" (or) is an equivalent (mu'adilah) to the hamza (interrogative particle) in ﴿Did you not know﴾; that is: Did you not know that He is the Owner of affairs, capable of all things, Who commands and forbids as He wills? Or do you know and yet propose, by asking, as the Jews proposed to Moses, peace be upon him? Or it is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the meaning is to enjoin them to place their trust in Him and to abandon making proposals to him. It was said: it was revealed concerning the People of the Book when they asked that God send down upon them a Book from heaven. And it was said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists when they said, ﴿We will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a Book we can read﴾, and ﴿Whoever exchanges disbelief for belief has indeed strayed from the right way﴾. Whoever abandons trust in the clear signs, doubts them, and proposes others instead, has strayed from the straight path, until he falls into disbelief after belief. The meaning of the verse is: do not make proposals, lest you stray from the middle of the way, and straying leads you away from the goal and to the exchange of belief for disbelief.

It is read ﴿yubdil﴾ (with the form of abdala).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 109–110:

﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after you have believed, out of envy﴾ — that is, their rabbis (aḥbār). ﴿Wish they could turn you back﴾ — that is, that they would turn you back. The particle law (lau) here stands in the place of an (that) in meaning, not in wording. ﴿Into disbelievers after your belief﴾ — apostates (murtaddīn). The word "disbelievers" (kuffāran) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) referring to the pronoun of the addressees. ﴿Out of envy﴾ — this is the cause (ʿillah) of "wish" (waddа).

﴿From their own selves﴾ — this may be connected to "wish," meaning: they wished this from their own selves and their own desires, not from any religious conviction or inclination toward the truth. Or it may be connected to "envy," meaning: a great envy arising from the very core of their souls. ﴿After the truth has become clear to them﴾ — through the miracles and the descriptions mentioned in the Torah. ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ — ʿafw (pardon) is abandoning the punishment of the wrongdoer, and ṣafḥ (overlooking) is abandoning his reproach. ﴿Until Allah brings His command﴾ — which is the permission to fight them and to impose the jizya (poll-tax) upon them, or the killing of the Banū Qurayẓa and the expulsion of the Banū al-Naḍīr. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that this verse was abrogated (mansūkh) by the verse of the sword; but there is room for examination in this, since the command is not absolute. ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾ — so He is able to take vengeance on them.

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ — this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "pardon," as if He commanded them to patience, to opposition, and to seeking refuge in Allah the Exalted through worship and righteousness. ﴿And whatever good you send forth for yourselves﴾ — such as prayer and charity. It is also read tuqdimū (from aqdama). ﴿You will find it with Allah﴾ — that is, its reward.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ — no deed is lost in His sight. It is also read with the letter yāʾ (yaʿmalūna), in which case it is a warning (waʿīd).

(p-101) ﴿And they say﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿wadda﴾ (they wish), and the pronoun refers to the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ is a lafʿ (a rhetorical device in which two statements are interwoven and each is left to be understood from the other) between the two groups' statements, as in His saying, ﴿And they say: Be Jews or Christians﴾ (2:135). This relies on the listener's understanding. The word hūd is the plural of hāʾid (Jew, one who repents), like ʿūdh, the plural of ʿāʾidh. The singular pronoun in kāna (was) and the plural predicate are used in view of the wording (lafẓ) and the meaning (maʿnā).

﴿Those are their wishful fancies﴾: the demonstrative refers to the wishes mentioned, namely that no good from their Lord should descend upon the believers, that they should turn them back into disbelievers, and that no one other than them should enter Paradise. Alternatively, it refers to what is in the verse with an omitted modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), meaning: the likes of that wish are their wishful fancies. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ). The word umniyya (wish) is of the pattern ufʿūla from tamannī (wishing), like uḍḥūka (a joke) and uʿjūba (a marvel). ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾ of your exclusive entry into Paradise, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in your claim, for every claim without evidence is unestablished.

﴿Yes﴾ is an affirmation of what they denied, namely that others than them enter Paradise. ﴿Whoever submits his face to God﴾: he sincerely devotes himself to Him, or directs his intention to Him; its root meaning is the organ (the face). ﴿And he is a doer of good﴾ in his deed. ﴿For him is his reward﴾, which was promised to him for his deed, ﴿with his Lord﴾, established from his Lord, neither lost nor diminished. The sentence is the response (jawāb) to man if it is conditional, and its predicate if it is a relative construction. The fāʾ (so) in it is there because it contains the meaning of a condition, so the reply is with His word "Yes" alone, and it is good to pause upon it. It is also permissible that ﴿whoever submits﴾ is the subject of an implied verb, like "Yes, there enters it whoever submits." ﴿No fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ in the Hereafter.

Alternatively, it refers to what is in the verse with an omitted modifier (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), meaning: the likes of that wish are their wishful fancies. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ). The word umniyya (wish) is of the pattern ufʿūla from tamannī (wishing), like uḍḥūka (a joke) and uʿjūba (a marvel). ﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾ of your exclusive entry into Paradise, ﴿if you are truthful﴾ in your claim, for every claim without evidence is unestablished.

﴿Yes﴾ is an affirmation of what they denied, namely that others than them enter Paradise. ﴿Whoever submits his face to God﴾: he sincerely devotes himself to Him, or directs his intention to Him; its root meaning is the organ (the face). ﴿And he is a doer of good﴾ in his deed. ﴿For him is his reward﴾, which was promised to him for his deed, ﴿with his Lord﴾, established from his Lord, neither lost nor diminished. The sentence is the response (jawāb) to man if it is conditional, and its predicate if it is a relative construction. The fāʾ (so) in it is there because it contains the meaning of a condition, so the reply is with His word "Yes" alone, and it is good to pause upon it. It is also permissible that ﴿whoever submits﴾ is the subject of an implied verb, like "Yes, there enters it whoever submits." ﴿No fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 113:

﴿And the Jews say, "The Christians are not based on anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not based on anything," while they recite the Book.﴾ That is, not based on anything that is sound and counts for anything. It was revealed when the delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the rabbis of the Jews came to them, and they debated and quarrelled over this.

﴿While they recite the Book﴾: the wa (and) is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and "the Book" is generic (li-l-jins), meaning: they said this while they were among the people of knowledge and of the Book. ﴿Thus﴾: like that, ﴿said those who do not know, the like of their saying﴾: such as the idol-worshippers and the Mu'attilah (those who deny the divine attributes). He rebuked them for obstinacy and for imitating the ignorant.

If it is asked: why did He rebuke them when they spoke the truth, since both religions are, after abrogation (naskh), indeed "nothing"? I say: they did not intend that. Rather, each group intended by this the invalidation of the other's religion from its root, and disbelief in its Prophet and its Book, even though whatever has not been abrogated of the two is a truth that must be accepted and acted upon. ﴿So Allah will judge﴾, that is, will decide ﴿between them﴾, between the two groups, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection concerning that about which they used to differ﴾, by apportioning to each group the punishment appropriate to it. It has also been said that His judgment between them is that He will declare them liars and cause them to enter the Fire.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 114:

﴿And who is more unjust than those who prevent the mosques of Allah﴾ is general, applying to everyone who ruins a mosque or strives to render idle a place set aside for prayer. It is said that it was revealed concerning the Romans when they invaded Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), ruined it, and killed its people. Or it was revealed concerning the polytheists when they prevented the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from entering al-Masjid al-Haram in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. ﴿from having His name mentioned therein⦆ is the second object of "prevent" (manaʿa). ﴿and strives for their ruin⦆ by demolition or by rendering them idle. ﴿Those⦆, that is, those who prevent, ﴿it was not for them to enter them except in fear⦆: it was not fitting for them to enter them except with awe and humility, let alone that they should dare to ruin them. Or the meaning is: it was not right for them to enter them except in fear of the believers, lest the believers seize them, let alone that they should prevent them from it. Or the meaning is: it was not for them in the knowledge and decree of Allah, so this is a promise to the believers of victory and of the recovery of the mosques from them, and Allah has fulfilled His promise. It is also said: the meaning is a prohibition against enabling them to enter the mosque. The jurists differed on this: Abu Hanifah permitted it, Malik prohibited it, and al-Shafiʿi distinguished between al-Masjid al-Haram and other mosques. ﴿For them in this world is disgrace⦆: killing and captivity, or humiliation through the imposition of the jizyah. ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment⦆ because of their disbelief and their wrongdoing.(p-102)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 115:

﴿To Allah belong the east and the west﴾. He means by them the two sides of the earth, i.e., the whole earth belongs to Him; no place is specifically His to the exclusion of another. ﴿So wherever you turn﴾, if you are prevented from praying in the Sacred Mosque or the Farthest Mosque, then the earth has been made a place of prostration for you. ﴿Wherever you turn﴾ means: in whatever place you make the turning toward the qibla, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾, i.e., His direction which He has commanded, for the possibility of turning is not restricted to a mosque or a place. Or it means: there is His Essence, i.e., He is All-Knowing, aware of what you do there. ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Encompassing﴾ by His encompassing of things, or by His mercy, He intends to grant ease to His servants. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their interests and their deeds in all places.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning the prayer of the traveller on his mount. It was also said: concerning a people for whom the qibla was obscured, so they prayed facing different directions, and when they woke up they realised their error. On this basis, if a mujtahid errs and then the error becomes clear to him, he is not obliged to make up the prayer. It was also said: it is a preparation for the abrogation of the qibla, and a declaration that the Worshipped should not be confined to a particular direction.

﴿They say: God has taken a son.﴾ It was revealed when the Jews said: ﴿Ezra is the son of God﴾, the Christians said: ﴿The Messiah is the son of God﴾, and the idolaters of the Arabs said: the angels are the daughters of God. Its conjunction (ʿaṭf) is to "The Jews said," or [it is to] "prevented" (manaʿa), or to the implied meaning of His words ﴿And who is more wrong﴾.

Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ without the wāw (بِغَيْرِ واوٍ). ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ is a declaration of tanzih (God's freedom from such attributes), for taking a son implies likeness (tashbih, resemblance to created things), need, and swift perishing. Consider that the celestial bodies, despite their possibility and their perishing, have remained in existence as long as the world lasts, yet they have not taken what comes from them as a child, as animals and plants take offspring, either by choice or by nature. ﴿Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a rejection of what they said and an argument against its corruption. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, is the Creator of whatever is in the heavens and the earth, of which the angels, Ezra and the Messiah are part. ﴿All are obedient to Him﴾, submissive, not refusing His will and His bringing into being. Whatever has this attribute does not share the nature of its Originator, who is necessary in His essence, so He has no son, because it is required of a son that he share the nature of his father. The word used is مَا (mā), which is used for non-rational beings (بِما الَّذِي لِغَيْرِ أُولِي العِلْمِ), and He said قانِتُونَ (qānitūn), using the masculine plural for rational beings (ʿalā taghlīb, by grammatical precedence of the rational), to belittle their status. The tanwīn of kull is a substitute ('iwaḍ) for the genitive noun that follows it, meaning: all that is in them both. It is also possible that what is meant is: all whom they have made a son of Him are obedient and acknowledge servitude, and this would be an obligation after the establishment of proof. The verse indicates the corruption of what they said in three ways. The jurists (fuqahāʾ) have used it as evidence that whoever owns his child is freed from slavery (ʿitq) by that ownership, because God negated the son by affirming ownership, and this requires that the two are mutually exclusive.

﴿Badi' al-samawati wal-ard﴾ (the Originator of the heavens and the earth): its meaning is the one who brings them into being (mubdi'uhuma). Its counterpart is al-Sami' (the All-Hearing) in the saying of the poet:

"Does the sweet basil of the caller who hears keep me awake, while my companions sleep?"

Or it means the Originator of His heavens and His earth, from "bad'a," so that "badi'" is an intensive form. This is the fourth argument. Its explanation is that the father is the element of the child, which is affected by the separation of its substance from him, whereas Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the Originator (mubdi') of all things, the absolute Agent, exempt from being affected. Therefore He is not a father. Ibda' (origination, the bringing of a thing into existence not from a thing, all at once) is more fitting to this subject than sun' (fashioning, the composing of forms not from a substance), and than takwin (creation, which occurs through change and generally over time). It is read as "badi'in" in the genitive, as a substitution (badal) for the pronoun in "lahu," and as "badi'a" in the accusative, as a expression of praise (madh).

﴿Wa-idha qada amran﴾ (and when He decrees a matter): that is, when He wills something. The basic meaning of qada' (decree) is the completion of a thing, either in potential, as in His saying, ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ [17:23], or in act, as in His saying, ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens﴾ [41:12]. It is applied to the connection of the divine will to the existence of a thing insofar as it necessitates it.

﴿Fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fa-yakun﴾ (He only says to it, "Be," and it is): kana here is the complete (tamma) verb, meaning "come into being," so "fa-yahduth" (it comes into being). It does not mean a real command and obedience, but an illustration of the occurrence, without delay, of what His will has been connected to, like the obedience of a commanded servant who obeys without hesitation. This contains a confirmation of the meaning of origination and a hint toward the fifth argument, which is that taking a child is something that happens through stages and a lapse of time, whereas His action, exalted is He, is independent of that. Ibn 'Amir read "fa-yakuna" with a fatha on the nun. Know that the cause of this error is that the adherents of the earlier religious laws used to call God "Father," considering Him the first cause, to the extent that they said the father is the lesser lord (al-Rabb al-Asghar) and Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the greater Lord (al-Rabb al-Akbar). Then the ignorant among them thought that the intended meaning was that of begetting, and they believed this by blind imitation (taqlid). For this reason whoever says it is an unbeliever, and it is forbidden absolutely, to cut off the root of corruption.

**﴿And those who do not know say: Why does Allah not speak to us, or a sign come to us?﴾** That is, the ignorant among the polytheists, or the wilfully ignorant among the People of the Scripture (Ahl al-Kitab). **﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾** Why does Allah not speak to us as He speaks to the angels, or reveal to us that you are His Messenger? **﴿Or a sign come to us?﴾** A proof of your truthfulness. The first demand is arrogance, and the second is denial, because the signs of Allah that had already come to them were met with contempt and obstinacy. **﴿Thus said those before them﴾** from the past nations, **﴿the same as their words﴾**, when they said: **"Show us Allah openly."** **"Can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?"** **﴿Their hearts are alike﴾**: the hearts of these people and of those before them are alike in blindness and obstinacy. It is also recited with the shadda on the shin (tashdid al-shin), as tashabbahat. **﴿We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain﴾**, that is, who seek certainty, or who are certain of the realities, with no doubt or obstinacy afflicting them. This implies that they did not make these demands because the signs were unclear, nor out of a desire for more certainty, but said it out of insolence and obstinacy.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 119–120:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾, being clothed in it and supported by it. ﴿as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾. So there is no fault on you if they persist and act arrogantly. ﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, [i.e.,] what is their state that they did not believe after the message had reached them. Nafi' and Ya'qub recited ﴿لا تَسْألُ﴾ (*la tas'al*, "you shall not ask"), as a prohibition to the Messenger (ﷺ) from asking about the state of his parents. Or it is an exaggeration of the punishment of the unbelievers, as if its severity is such that he cannot be told about it. Or the listener cannot endure hearing its report, so he (ﷺ) was forbidden from asking. *Al-Jahim* means the blazing fire of the Fire.

﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion﴾. This is an intensification of despair for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding their acceptance of Islam, for if they will not be pleased with him until he follows their religion, then how could they follow his religion? Perhaps they said something similar, so God related it, and for this reason He said: ﴿Say﴾, teaching him the answer. ﴿Indeed, the guidance of God is the [true] guidance﴾, i.e., the guidance of God, which is Islam, is the guidance to the truth, not what you call to. ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾, meaning their false opinions. *Al-millah* (religion) is what God Most High has legislated for His servants through the tongues of His prophets, from *amlaltu al-kitab* (I dictated the book), when you dictate it. *Al-hawa* (desire) is an opinion that follows lust. ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, i.e., the revelation, or the religion whose soundness is known. ﴿you would have no protector or helper from God﴾ who could ward off His punishment from you. This is the answer to *la'in* (if).
