Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 121:

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ He means by this the believers among the People of the Book. ﴿Who recite it with its true recitation﴾ by observing the wording against distortion, reflecting on its meaning, and acting in accordance with what it requires. This is a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah), and the predicate is what follows. Or it is a predicate, on the basis that what is meant by the relative pronoun is the believers among the People of the Book (p-104). ﴿Those believe in it﴾ in their Book, not the distorters. ﴿And whoever disbelieves in it﴾ by distortion and by disbelieving in what confirms it, ﴿those are the losers﴾, since they have exchanged disbelief for faith.

O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds. And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another in anything, nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.

When he began their story with the command to remember the blessings, to fulfill their rights, to beware of neglecting them, and to fear the Hour and its terrors, he repeated that and concluded his address to them with it, emphasizing the advice, and signaling that it is the summary (fadhlakah) of the matter and the purpose of the narrative.

O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds. And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another in anything, nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.

When he began their story with the command to remember the blessings, to fulfill their rights, to beware of neglecting them, and to fear the Hour and its terrors, he repeated that and concluded his address to them with it, emphasizing the advice, and signaling that it is the summary (fadhlakah) of the matter and the purpose of the narrative.

﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words﴾: He assigned him commands and prohibitions. Al-ibtila' (trial, testing) originally means assigning a hard task, from bala' (affliction). But since it entails testing with regard to one who does not know the outcomes, it was thought that the two terms are synonymous. The pronoun refers to Abraham. It is permissible because it precedes in wording, though it is later in rank, since the conditional particle is one of those that take precedence. The "words" (kalimat) may be applied to meanings, so it has been explained as the thirty praiseworthy qualities mentioned in His saying: ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ up to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ up to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ up to His saying: ﴿those are the inheritors﴾. It has also been explained by these in His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. It has been explained as the ten [practices] which are among the sunan (natural practices) of the prophets, and as the rites of the Hajj, the stars, the two moons, circumcision, the sacrifice of the son, the fire, and the migration. Moreover, God dealt with him by means of them as one who tests by them and by what the verses following it contain.

It was read as "Ibrahimu rabbahu" [with Abraham as the subject and his Lord as the object], meaning that Abraham asked his Lord with words such as ﴿Show me how You give life to the dead﴾ and ﴿Make this city secure﴾, to see whether He would respond to him. Ibn 'Amir read "Ibrāhām" with an alif throughout this surah.

﴿Then he fulfilled them﴾: He performed them completely and carried them out with their due observance, in accordance with His saying: ﴿And Abraham, who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾. In the last reading, the pronoun refers to his Lord, meaning He gave him everything he asked for.

He said: ﴿Indeed, I will make you a leader for the people﴾. This is a resumptive statement if you assume a verb governing "idh" (when); it is as if it were said: "What did his Lord say when he fulfilled them?", and it was answered with this. Or it is an explanation of His saying "tried", so the words would be what He mentioned of leadership, the purification of the House, the raising of its foundations, and Islam. If you take it as governed [in the accusative], then it is said that the whole is a sentence conjoined to what precedes it; or it is a verb derived from ja'ala (to make), which has two objects. The imam (leader) is a noun for one who is followed, and his leadership is general and everlasting, since no prophet was sent after him except that he was from his descendants and commanded to follow him.

He said: ﴿And of my descendants?﴾ This is a conjunction with the kaf (pronoun "you"), meaning "and [make leaders] some of my descendants", as you would say, "and Zayd," in answer to "I will honor you." Al-dhurriyyah (offspring) is the progeny of a man; it is of the form fu'livyah or fa'ulah, whose second rā' was changed to yā', as in taqaddaytu. It is from al-dharr (scattering), meaning dispersal; or it is of the form fa'ulah or fi'liyyah, whose hamzah was changed, from al-dharrah (creation). It was read "dhirriyyati" with a kasrah, and this is a dialect.

He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. This is a response to his request, and an indication that some of his descendants may be wrongdoers, and that they will not attain leadership, because it is a trust from God Most High and a covenant, and the wrongdoer is not fit for it; rather, only the righteous and God-fearing among them attain it. In this is evidence for the infallibility of the prophets from major sins before prophethood, and that the sinner is not fit for leadership. It was read "al-zalimun" (the wrongdoers) [in the nominative], and the meaning is one, since whatever reaches you, you have reached it.

﴿And when We made the House﴾, meaning the Ka'bah, it became distinguished by it as a star is distinguished over the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). ﴿A place of return for the people﴾, a place to which the individuals of the visitors return, or their likes, or a place of reward through which they are rewarded for its Hajj and 'Umrah. It is also read «مَثاباتٍ» (mathabat, plural), meaning that it is a place of return for every person.

﴿And a sanctuary﴾, a place of security in which its inhabitants are not molested, as in His saying, ﴿a sacred, secure sanctuary﴾. ﴿And people are snatched away from around them﴾, or the one who performs the Hajj is secure from the punishment of the Hereafter, because the Hajj erases what came before it; or the offender who takes refuge in it is not punished until he leaves it. This is the view of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him. ﴿And take the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer﴾ is either on the assumption of a verb of saying (qawl), or it is a conjunction with what is implied as the governing element of "idh" (when), or it is a parenthetical clause conjoined with an implied element whose sense is: "Repent to Him and take," with the address being to the Ummah of Muhammad ﷺ, and it is a command of recommendation (istihbab). The Station of Ibrahim is the stone on which the mark of his foot is, or the place where the stone was when he stood on it and called the people to the Hajj, or the place where he raised the building of the House, which is its place today.

It is related that he, peace be upon him, took the hand of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said, "This is the Station of Ibrahim." 'Umar said, "Shall we not take it as a place of prayer?" He said, "I have not been commanded with that." Then the sun had not set until this was revealed.

It has also been said: what is meant by it is the command to the two rak'ahs of the Tawaf, because Jabir related that when he, peace be upon him, had finished his Tawaf, he went to the Station of Ibrahim, prayed two rak'ahs behind it, and recited, ﴿And take the Station of Ibrahim as a place of prayer﴾.

For al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, there are two opinions on whether these two are obligatory. It has also been said: the Station of Ibrahim is the whole Haram (sacred precinct). It has also been said: the standing places of the Hajj, and taking them as a place of prayer means that supplication is made in them and nearness to Allah, the Exalted, is sought. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read «واتَّخَذُوا» (wa-ittakhadhu) in the past tense, conjoined to ﴿We made﴾, meaning: and the people took his (Ibrahim's) station, which is marked by it, namely the Ka'bah, as a qiblah toward which they pray.

﴿And We covenanted with Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾, We commanded them, ﴿that purify My House﴾, by "that purify My House." It is permissible that "an" be explanatory (mufassirah), because the covenant includes the meaning of saying. He means: purify it from idols, impurities, and whatever is not fitting for it; or make it sincere. ﴿For those who circle around it﴾, around it. ﴿And those who stay there﴾, those who reside near it, or those who seclude themselves in retreat (i'tikaf) in it. ﴿And those who bow and prostrate﴾, meaning those who pray, the plural of "raki'" (bowing) and "sajid" (prostrating).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 126:

﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this⁠﴾ refers by it to the city (balad) or the place (makan). ﴿a city secure⁠﴾ meaning possessing security (dhā amn), like His saying ﴿in a life of good pleasure⁠﴾. Or "secure" may describe its people, like your saying: "a night sleeping" (layl nā'im). ﴿And provide its people with fruits, such of them as believe in God and the Last Day⁠﴾: "such of them as believe" is substituted from ﴿its people⁠﴾ as a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd) for specification (li'l-takhsis). ﴿He said: "And whoever disbelieves⁠﴾ is conjoined (ma'tūf) upon "believes", and the meaning is: "and provide for whoever disbelieves." Abraham, upon him be peace, analogized provision to leadership (al-imāma), so God, glorified is He, drew attention to the fact that provision is a worldly mercy that encompasses both believer and disbeliever, unlike leadership and precedence in religion. Or it is a subject (mubtada') containing the meaning of a conditional (shart), ﴿then I will give him enjoyment for a little⁠﴾ is its predicate (khabar). Although disbelief is not a cause of enjoyment, it is a cause of its diminishing, by making it confined to the portions of this world, not used as a means to attaining reward. For this reason it is conjoined to it: ﴿then I will drive him to the punishment of the Fire⁠﴾, that is, I will compel him toward it with the compulsion of one under duress, because of his disbelief and his squandering of the blessings with which I granted him enjoyment. "Little" (qalīlan) is in the accusative as an infinitive (maṣdar) or as an adverb of time (ẓarf). It has been read in the imperative form in both verbs, on the basis that it is part of Abraham's supplication, and the pronoun in "he said" refers to him. Ibn 'Āmir read ﴿fa-amta'ahu⁠﴾ from the form amta'a. It has been read ﴿fa-numatti'uhu⁠﴾ and ﴿thumma naḍṭarruhu⁠﴾, and ﴿iḍṭarruhu⁠﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, according to the dialect of those who vowel the prefixed letters of the imperfect with kasra, and ﴿iṭṭarruhu⁠﴾ with the ḍād assimilated, which is weak, because the letters of "ḍamm shafr" are the ones into which what is adjacent to them is assimilated, not the reverse.

﴿And wretched is the destination⁠﴾: the object specified by the dispraise is omitted, and it is the punishment.

And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House, and Ishmael with him, saying: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us; indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [2:127].

Wait, I need to translate only the passage given, so here is the faithful translation:

"﴿And when Abraham was raising the foundations of the House﴾ is a narration of a past state. ﴿The foundations﴾ is the plural of qā'ida (foundation), which is a predominantly used attribute derived from qu'ud (sitting), in the sense of steadiness; perhaps it is a metaphor from the opposite of standing, and from it comes the expression qi'dak Allah (may God keep you seated/steadfast). ﴿Raising﴾ them means building upon them, for it transfers them from a state of lowness to a state of height. It is possible that by them is meant the levelled surfaces of the building, since every levelled surface is a foundation upon which something is placed, and its building raises it. It has also been said that what is meant is raising his station and manifesting his nobility by honoring him and calling people to his pilgrimage. The vagueness of ﴿the foundations﴾ and then their specification serves to magnify their status. ﴿And Ishmael﴾ used to hand him the stones, but since he had a part in the building he was joined to him in the verb. It has also been said: they were building at two ends, or in turns. ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾ means: they were saying, "Our Lord, accept from us," and it has been read this way; the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to both of them. ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing﴾ of our supplications ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of our intentions."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 128–129:

﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You (muslimayn laka)﴾ — mukhlisayn laka (sincere to You), from aslama wajhahu (he submitted his face), or mustaslimayn (surrendering), from uslima, meaning when he surrendered and yielded. The intent is to seek an increase in sincerity and submission, or steadfastness in it. It is also read "muslimin" (in the plural), on the basis that the intended meaning is themselves and their progeny, and that the dual is among the degrees of the plural (in the sense of inclusion). ﴿And from our descendants, a Muslim community (ummah muslimah) submissive to You﴾ — i.e., make some of our descendants so. They singled out the descendants in the supplication because they are most deserving of compassion, and because if they are righteous, their followers are made righteous through them. They singled out some of them because they were informed that among their descendants there would be wrongdoers. They also knew that divine wisdom does not necessitate that everyone agree on sincerity and full devotion to God the Exalted, for that would disrupt livelihood; for this reason it is said: "Were it not for fools, the world would be ruined." It is also said that by the ummah is meant the ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is permissible that min (from) be explanatory, as in His saying: ﴿God has promised those among you who believe﴾. It is placed before the explained term and separates the conjunction from what is conjoined, as in His saying: ﴿He created seven heavens and of the earth the like thereof﴾. ﴿And show us﴾ — from ra'a in the sense of "saw" or "knew"; for this reason it does not take two objects. ﴿Our rites (manasikana)﴾ — our acts of worship in the Hajj, or our places of sacrifice. Nusk originally means the utmost degree of worship, and it became prevalent for the Hajj because of the hardship and departure from habit that it involves. Ibn Kathir, al-Susi on the authority of Abu 'Amr, and Ya'qub read "arina" (with a kasra on the ra), by analogy with "fakhdh" → "fakhidh"; but this involves a flaw, because the kasra is transferred from the dropped hamza, which is evidence for it. al-Duri on the authority of Abu 'Amr read with ikhtilas (a brief, rapid vowel). ﴿And turn to us in forgiveness﴾ — a request for repentance for their descendants, or for what slipped from them through forgetfulness. Perhaps they said this out of humbling themselves and as guidance for their descendants. ﴿Indeed You are the Ever-Returning, the Most Merciful﴾ — toward whoever repents.

﴿Our Lord, and send among them﴾ — among the Muslim community — ﴿a messenger from among them﴾. He did not send from their descendants anyone other than Muhammad (ﷺ), so he is the one through whom their supplication was answered, as the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him said: "I am the answer to the supplication of my father Abraham, the glad tidings of Jesus, and the vision of my mother." ﴿Who recites to them Your verses﴾ — reads to them and conveys to them what You reveal to him of the proofs of monotheism and prophethood. ﴿And teaches them the Book﴾ — the Qur'an.

﴿And the wisdom﴾ — that by which their souls are perfected, of knowledge and rulings. ﴿And purifies them﴾ — from polytheism and sins. ﴿Indeed You are the Mighty﴾ — who is not overpowered or defeated in what He wills — ﴿the Wise﴾ — who makes His handiwork firm.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 128–129:

﴿Our Lord, and make us submissive to You (muslimayn laka)﴾ — mukhlisayn laka (sincere to You), from aslama wajhahu (he submitted his face), or mustaslimayn (surrendering), from uslima, meaning when he surrendered and yielded. The intent is to seek an increase in sincerity and submission, or steadfastness in it. It is also read "muslimin" (in the plural), on the basis that the intended meaning is themselves and their progeny, and that the dual is among the degrees of the plural (in the sense of inclusion). ﴿And from our descendants, a Muslim community (ummah muslimah) submissive to You﴾ — i.e., make some of our descendants so. Nusk originally means the utmost degree of worship, and it became prevalent for the Hajj because of the hardship and departure from habit that it involves. Perhaps they said this out of humbling themselves and as guidance for their descendants. ﴿Indeed You are the Ever-Returning, the Most Merciful﴾ — toward whoever repents.

﴿Our Lord, and send among them﴾ — among the Muslim community — ﴿a messenger from among them﴾. He did not send from their descendants anyone other than Muhammad (ﷺ), so he is the one through whom their supplication was answered, as the Prayer and Peace of God be upon him said: "I am the answer to the supplication of my father Abraham, the glad tidings of Jesus, and the vision of my mother." ﴿Who recites to them Your verses﴾ — reads to them and conveys to them what You reveal to him of the proofs of monotheism and prophethood. ﴿And teaches them the Book﴾ — the Qur'an.

﴿And the wisdom﴾ — that by which their souls are perfected, of knowledge and rulings. ﴿And purifies them﴾ — from polytheism and sins. ﴿Indeed You are the Mighty﴾ — who is not overpowered or defeated in what He wills — ﴿the Wise﴾ — who makes His handiwork firm.

﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham?﴾ This is a rejection and a denial that anyone would turn away from his clear and luminous religion. That is, no one turns away from his religion. ﴿Except one who makes a fool of himself﴾, that is, except one who debases himself, humiliates himself and makes light of himself. Al-Mubarrad and Tha'lab said: *safiha* with a kasra (*safiha*) is transitive, and with a damma (*safuha*) is intransitive. A hadith supports this: "Pride is to reject the truth (*tusaffiha al-haqq*) and to look down upon people." It was also said that the original is *safuha nafsuhu* with the subject in the nominative, and then the noun was put in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification, an accusative that clarifies the ambiguity of the verb), like *ghabuna ra'yuhu* ("his opinion was deceived") and *alima ra'suhu* ("his head ached"), and like the line of Jarir:

"And after him we take up the tail of a life, its back bare, having no hump."

Or it was *safiha fi nafsihi*, and the noun was put in the accusative by removing the preposition (*naza' al-khafid*, the dropping of the preposition). The exception clause is, according to the preferred view, in the nominative position as a *badal* (substitute) for the pronoun in *yarghabu* (the pronoun subject of the verb), because it carries the sense of negation. ﴿And We certainly chose him in this world, and he in the Hereafter is surely among the righteous﴾. This is a proof and an explanation of that. For whoever was the chosen one of the servants in this world, and is witnessed on the Day of Resurrection to be upright and righteous, is worthy of being followed, and no one turns away from him except a fool, or one who makes himself appear foolish, having debased himself through ignorance and by turning away from reflection.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 131:

﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds."﴾ It is an adverbial clause (zarf) governed by ﴿chose him﴾ (iṣṭafaynāhu), or it gives the reason for it (ta'līl), or it is in the accusative by an implied verb, "remember" (idhkur). As if it were said: "Remember that time, so that you may know that he was the chosen, righteous one deserving of imamate (leadership) and precedence, and that he attained what he attained by hastening to submission and sincerity of heart when his Lord called him and brought to his mind the proofs leading to knowledge, which summon to Islam."

It is narrated that it was revealed when ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām called his two nephews, Salama and Muhājir, to Islam; Salama embraced Islam, and Muhājir refused.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 132:

﴿And Abraham charged his sons with it﴾. The tawsiyah (charge, bequest) is advancing to another a matter in which there is goodness and nearness to God. Its root meaning is connection: one says wassaahu (he charged him) when he connected him, and fassaahu when he separated him, as if the one who charges connects his act with the act of the one charged. The pronoun in bihā refers either to the religion (millah), or to his saying "I have submitted" (aslamtu), taking the word or the sentence as its referent. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-wassā" (with the doubled sad), and the first reading is more eloquent. Ya'qub (Jacob) is coordinated with Ibrahim, meaning: and he too charged his sons with it. It was also read in the accusative (wa-wassā with a different construction), as being among those whom Abraham charged: ﴿Ya banī﴾ ("O my sons"). It is in the accusative by the elision of the verb of saying according to the Basrans, and it is connected to wassā according to the Kufans, since it is a kind of it. Its parallel is the line of verse:

"Two men from Dabba informed us... that we saw a man naked"

with the genitive (bi-l-kasr), and the sons of Ibrahim were four: Isma'il, Ishaq, Madyan and Madan. It has been said they were eight, and it has been said fourteen:

And the sons of Ya'qub were twelve: Ruwbil, Sham'un, Lawi, Yahudha, Yashsukhur, Zabulun, Naftuni, Dun, Kudha, Ushir, Binyamin and Yusuf. ﴿Indeed God has chosen for you the religion﴾, the religion of Islam, which is the choicest of religions, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾. Its apparent meaning is a prohibition against dying in a state other than Islam, while the intended meaning is a prohibition against their being in a state other than that when they die, and a command to remain steadfast upon Islam, like your saying: "Do not pray except while you are humble." The change of expression indicates that their dying not upon Islam is a death in which there is no good, and that it is due to them that it not befall them. Its counterpart in the imperative is "Die while you are a martyr."

It is related that the Jews said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Do you not know that Ya'qub charged his sons with Judaism on the day he died?" So this was revealed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 133:

﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ Am (or) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the meaning of the interrogative hamzah in it is denial (inkar), i.e., you were not present when death approached Ya'qub and he said to his sons what he said, so why do you claim Jewishness for him? Or it is connected (muttasilah) to an omitted element, its estimated form being: "Were you absent, or were you witnesses?" It has been said: the address is to the believers, and the meaning is: you did not witness that, and you only know it through revelation. It was also read "ḥaḍira" with a kasra.

﴿When he said to his sons﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿when death approached﴾. ﴿What will you worship after me?﴾ That is, what thing will you worship? He intended by it to make them affirm monotheism (tawhid) and Islam, and to take their covenant to remain steadfast in both. The word "ma" is used to ask about anything whose nature is not yet known; once it is known, it is restricted to rational beings when one asks about its identity, while if one asks about its attribute it is said: "What is Zayd, a jurist or a physician?" (p-108) ﴿They said: We shall worship your God and the God of your fathers, Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac﴾: the One whose existence, divinity and the obligation of worshipping Him are agreed upon. He counted Ishmael among his fathers by way of giving precedence to the father and grandfather, or because he was like a father, due to his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "A man's paternal uncle is the twin of his father." As he, peace and blessings be upon him, said about al-'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "This is the remainder of my fathers." It was also read "God of your father" (ilaha abika), on the basis that it is a plural formed with the waw and nun, as the poet said:

"When our voices became distinct to them, they wept and ransomed us with our fathers."

Or it is singular, and Abraham alone is an explicative apposition ('atf bayan).

﴿One God﴾ is a substitute for "God of your fathers," like the Almighty's saying: ﴿by the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock﴾. Its benefit is the explicit statement of monotheism, and it negates the misconception arising from repeating the annexed noun, since coordination with the genitive and emphasis are impossible. Or it is put in the accusative by way of exclusivity (ikhtisas). ﴿And to Him we are submitting﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "we worship" or its object, or to both, and it may be an interjected clause (i'tiraḍ).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 134:

﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ meaning Ibrahim, Ya'qub and their descendants. The word ummah (community) originally means the intended goal, and the group is called by it because the sects aim at it (yaummuha, "they make for it"). ﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you have earned﴾: each has the reward of his own deed. The meaning is that your affiliation to them does not necessitate your benefiting from their deeds; you benefit only by agreeing with them and following them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "People will not come to me with their deeds while you come to me with your lineages."

﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾ meaning you will not be held accountable for their misdeeds, just as you will not be rewarded for their good deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 135:

﴿And they say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided."﴾ The pronoun of absence refers to the People of the Book, and "aw" (or) is for diversification (tanwi'), and the meaning is that their statement is one of these two sayings. The Jews said, "Be Jews," and the Christians said, "Be Christians." ﴿Tahtadu﴾ (you will be guided) is the response to the imperative. ﴿Say: "Nay, [we follow] the millata (creed/religion) of Ibrahim"﴾ That is: "Nay, let there be the millata of Ibrahim," i.e., the people of his millah (religion), or: "Nay, we follow the millata of Ibrahim." It is also read in the nominative (millatu), meaning his millah is our millah, or the reverse, or "we are his millah," in the sense of "we are the people of his millah." ﴿Hanifan﴾ (upright), inclining away from falsehood toward truth. It is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the mudaf (the governed noun) or the mudaf ilayhi (the governing noun), like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, [making them] brothers﴾. ﴿And he was not of those who associate others with Allah﴾ is an indirect rebuke (ta'ridh) directed at the People of the Book and others, for they claim to follow him while they are polytheists.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 136:

﴿Say: "We believe in God"﴾ The address is to the believers, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they believe in the like of what you believe in⁠—﴾. ﴿And what has been sent down to us﴾ refers to the Qur'an; He mentioned it first because it is the first in terms of its being sent down to us, or because it is the cause of belief in what is other than it. ﴿And what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the tribes﴾ refers to the scriptures (suhuf). Although they were sent down to Abraham, yet, since they (his descendants) were obligated to worship according to their details and were included under their rulings, they too were sent down to them, just as the Qur'an was sent down to us. "Al-asbat" is the plural of "sibt," which means grandson. By it he means the grandsons of Jacob, or his sons and offspring, for they are the grandsons of Abraham and Isaac. ﴿And what was given to Moses and Jesus﴾ refers to the Torah and the Gospel. He singled out these two for mention with a more emphatic ruling, because their matter, with regard to being ascribed to Moses and Jesus, differs from what preceded, and the dispute arose concerning them. ﴿And what was given to the prophets﴾ refers to the totality of those mentioned among them and those not mentioned. ﴿From their Lord﴾: sent down to them from their Lord. ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾, as the Jews do, believing in some and disbelieving in others. Since "aḥad" (any one) occurs in a negative context, it is general, and so it was permissible for "bayn" (between) to be attached to it. ﴿And to Him we are Muslims﴾: i.e., to God; ﴿Muslims﴾ means submitting and sincere (mukhliṣun).(p-109)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 137:

﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe, then they have been guided﴾ is of the category of challenge and rebuke (al-ta'jiz wal-tabkit), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then bring a surah like it﴾, since there is no like of what the Muslims believe in, nor a religion like the religion of Islam. It has been said: the ba' (in bimithli) is for instrumentality (al-alah) and not for transitivity (al-ta'diyah), and the meaning is: if they seek faith by a path that leads to the truth, like your path, then the unity of the aim does not preclude the multiplicity of paths. Or it is emphatic (za'idah li-l-ta'kid), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The recompense of an evil is an evil like it﴾. The meaning is: if they believe in Allah with a faith like your faith in Him. Or "like" (al-mithl) is inserted (muqhamun), as in His saying: ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾, meaning "to it". This is supported by the reading of those who read bima amantum bihi or bi-alladhi amantum bihi. ﴿And if they turn away, then they are only in opposition﴾, meaning: if they turn away from faith, or from what you tell them, then they are only in opposition to the truth, which is hostility and contrariety, for each of two opponents is in a side other than the side of the other. ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ is consolation and tranquilization for the believers, and a promise to them of protection and victory over those who oppose them. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: either it is part of the promise, meaning that He hears your words and knows your sincerity, and He will surely recompense you; or it is a threat to those who turn away, meaning that He hears what they display and knows what they conceal, and He will punish them for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 138:

﴿The dye of Allah﴾. That is: Allah has dyed us with His dye, and this is the innate nature (fitrah) of Allah with which He created mankind, for it is the adornment of the human being, just as dye is the adornment of what is dyed. Or: Allah guided us with His guidance and showed us His proof. Or: He purified our hearts with faith in a purification of His. He called it "dye" because its effect appeared upon them in the way dye appears upon what is dyed, and it penetrated their hearts as dye penetrates cloth. Or it is by way of harmonizing the expression (al-mushakalah), for the Christians used to immerse their children in yellow water which they called the baptism (al-ma'mudiyyah), and they would say: it is a purification for them, and by it their Christianity is realized. Its being in the accusative is as an emphatic infinitive (masdar mu'akkid) for His saying ﴿We believe﴾. It was also said that it is in the accusative as an incitement (al-igra'), and it was also said that it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for ﴿the religion of Abraham﴾, peace be upon him.

﴿And who is better than Allah in dye?﴾ There is no dye better than His dye. ﴿And we are worshippers of Him﴾: an allusion against them, that is, we do not associate partners with Him as you do. This is a conjunction upon ﴿We believe﴾. That requires that His saying ﴿the dye of Allah﴾ falls under the object of ﴿Say﴾. As for those who read it in the accusative as an incitement or as a substitute, they may posit an implied ﴿say﴾ conjoined to ﴿Adhere﴾, or ﴿Follow the religion of Abraham﴾ with ﴿Say: We believe﴾ as a substitute for ﴿Follow﴾, so that there is no disruption of the composition nor poor arrangement.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 139:

﴿Say: Do you argue with us about Allah?﴾ That is, do you dispute with us. ﴿Concerning Allah﴾ concerning His affair and His choosing a prophet from among the Arabs, rather than you. It is related that the People of the Book said: "All the prophets are from among us; if you were a prophet, you would be from among us." So this was revealed: ﴿while He is our Lord and your Lord﴾, meaning He is not restricted to one people over another; He bestows His mercy on whomever He wills of His servants. ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾. So it is not far-fetched that He should honour us for our deeds. It is as if He obliged them, on every creed they profess, to be silenced and confounded. For the honour of prophethood is either a bounty from Allah bestowed upon whomever He wills, in which case all are equal in it, or it is the outpouring of a right upon those who are prepared for it through persistence in obedience and adorning oneself with sincerity. Just as you have deeds which Allah may take into account in bestowing them, so too do we have deeds. ﴿And we are sincere to Him﴾, monotheists who devote worship and obedience to Him exclusively, to the exclusion of you.

(p-110) ﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians?﴾ Here "am" (أم) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the hamzah is for denial (lil-inkar). According to the reading of Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs with the "ta'" (i.e., ﴿Do you dispute with us﴾ read as "tuhajjuna"), it is possible that it is equivalent (mu'adilah) to the hamzah in ﴿Do you dispute with us﴾, meaning: which of the two matters do you undertake, disputation, or the claim of Judaism or Christianity against the prophets? ﴿Say: Are you more knowing, or is God?﴾ He has negated both matters regarding Abraham by His saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian﴾, and He argued against them with His saying: ﴿And the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him﴾. Those who are mentioned alongside him are his followers in religion, by consensus (wifaqan). ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?﴾ meaning the testimony of God to Abraham as a ḥanīf and of his disassociation from Judaism and Christianity. The meaning is: no one is more unjust than the People of the Book, because they concealed this testimony; or [than] us, if we concealed this testimony. In this there is an allusion to their concealment of God's testimony to Muhammad (ﷺ) concerning prophethood in their books and elsewhere. Min here is for origin (li-l-ibtida'), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿A disavowal from God and His Messenger﴾. ﴿And God is not unaware of what you do﴾ is a warning to them. It is also read with the "ya'" (yaʿmaluna).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 141:

﴿That is a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾ This is a repetition, for the sake of emphasis in warning and restraining against what has become firmly entrenched in human nature: boasting of one's forefathers and relying upon them. It is said: the address in what preceded was to them, and in this verse there is a warning for us against imitating them. It is also said: what is meant by "community" (ummah) in the first instance is the prophets, and in the second instance it is the ancestors of the Jews and the Christians.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 142:

﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ those whose intellects are light, who make a trade of it by blind imitation (taqlid) and by turning away from reflection (nazar). By this he means those who denied the change of the qibla from among the hypocrites (munafiqun), the Jews and the polytheists (mushrikun). The benefit of announcing it in advance is to settle the soul (tawtin al-nafs), to prepare the answer (i'dad al-jawab), and to manifest the miracle (i'jaz). ﴿What turned them﴾ means what diverted them ﴿from their qibla which they were upon﴾, that is, Bayt al-Maqdis. The qibla, in origin, is the state in which a person is while facing (the direction), and it became by convention the name of the place toward which one turns in prayer. ﴿Say: to God belong the east and the west﴾: no particular place is restricted to Him by an intrinsic property that prevents another place from standing in its stead; rather, what matters is the implementation of His command, not the specific place itself. ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾, and this is what wisdom approves and what the public interest requires, namely turning at one time toward Bayt al-Maqdis and at another toward the Ka'bah.

﴿And thus﴾ refers to the meaning of the preceding verse, that is: just as We guided you to the straight path, or: We made your qibla the best of qiblas. ﴿We made you a community of the middle way (ummah wasatan)﴾, that is, the best, or the just, those who are made pure through knowledge and action. Originally, wasat is a noun for the place to which the sides of an area are equal in distance, and then it was borrowed for praiseworthy qualities because they lie between two extremes of excess and deficiency, such as generosity between extravagance and miserliness, and courage between recklessness and cowardice. Then it was applied to the one characterized by these qualities, with the singular and plural, and the masculine and feminine, being the same, like the rest of the adjectives used in this way. It has been cited as evidence that ijma' (scholarly consensus) is a proof, since if there were falsehood in what they agreed upon, their uprightness (adalah) would be compromised by it. ﴿So that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾ is the reason (illah) for the making, that is: so that you may know, by reflecting on the proofs set up for you and the Book sent down to you, that He, exalted is He, did not withhold from anyone and did not wrong anyone, but rather He made the ways clear and sent the messengers, and they conveyed and gave sincere counsel. ﴿But those who disbelieved﴾, wretchedness drove them to follow their desires and turn away from the signs, so you will bear witness to that concerning your contemporaries and those before you or after you.

It has been narrated: "On the Day of Resurrection the nations will deny that the prophets conveyed (the message), so God will demand from them evidence of the conveyance, though He knows them better, to establish the proof against those who deny. The community of Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and they will testify. The nations will say, 'How do you know?' They will say, 'We know this through God's informing us in His Book, which speaks through the tongue of His truthful Prophet.' Then Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and asked about the state of his community, and he will testify to their uprightness."

This testimony, although it is for them, when the Messenger, upon him be peace, is like the watchful guardian over his community, the verb is construed with ʿalā (over), and the prepositional phrase is placed first to indicate their exclusivity: the Messenger will be a witness over them. ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you were facing﴾, that is, the direction that you were facing, which was the Kaʿbah. For he, upon him be prayer and peace, used to pray toward it in Mecca. Then when he emigrated, he was commanded to pray toward the rock (of Jerusalem) in order to win over the Jews. Or the rock is what is meant, according to the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "His qibla in Mecca was Bayt al-Maqdis, but he would place the Kaʿbah between himself and it." So what is informed about, on the first view, is the making (jaʿl) that abrogates (al-jaʿl al-nasikh), and on the second view, what is abrogated (al-mansukh). The meaning is that the origin of your command was that you should face the Kaʿbah, and We did not make your qibla Bayt al-Maqdis.

﴿Except that We might know who follows the Messenger from those who turn back on their heels﴾, that is: except that We might test the people by it and know who follows you in praying toward it, from among those who apostatize from your religion out of attachment to the qibla of their fathers. Or: so that We might now know who follows the Messenger from those who do not follow him, and this was for a cause that ends with its ending. According to the first view, its meaning is: We did not return you to the one you were facing except that We might know the one who stands firm in Islam from the one who turns back on his heels because of his unease and weakness of faith. If it is said: how can His knowledge be the goal of the making when He has always been knowing? I say: this and similar expressions are with regard to the present attachment (al-taʿalluq al-ḥālī), which is the basis of the recompense, and the meaning is that Our knowledge may become attached to it as existing. It has also been said: so that His Messenger and the believers may know, but He attributed it to Himself because they are His elect. Or it means the distinguishing of the steadfast from the wavering, like His saying, ﴿So that God may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾. Thus knowledge is placed in the position of the distinguishing that results from it. This is supported by the recitation liyuʿlama (with the verb in the passive voice). Knowledge is either in the sense of recognition (maʿrifah), or it is suspended (muʿallaq) by what is in man of the sense of interrogation, or its second object is "from those who turn back," that is: so that We might know who follows the Messenger distinguished from those who turn back.

﴿And indeed it would have been difficult﴾: in is the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy (thaqilah), and the lam is the separating lam (al-lam al-fasilah).

The Kufans said: in is negating, and the lam means illa (except). The pronoun refers to what the saying of God, exalted is He, ﴿And We did not make the qibla which you were facing﴾ indicates, namely the making (al-jaʿlah), or the turning back (al-ridda), or the turning (al-tawliyah), or the change (al-tahwilah), or the qibla. It is read as lakabīrah (with the predicate in the nominative) with the verb kāna being extra (zāʾidah). ﴿Except for those whom God has guided﴾ to the wisdom of the rulings, those who are firm in faith and following. ﴿And God would never make your faith go to waste﴾, that is, your steadfastness in faith. It has also been said: your faith in the abrogated qibla, or your prayer toward it. This is because it was narrated that when he, upon him be peace, was turned toward the Kaʿbah, they said: "What about someone who died before the change from our brethren, O Messenger of God?" Then this was revealed: ﴿Indeed God is Kind and Merciful toward the people﴾, so He does not waste their rewards and does not leave off their welfare. Perhaps He placed al-raʾūf (the Kind) first, and it is more emphatic in preserving the rhyme-endings (al-fawasil). The two Ḥaramayn, Ibn ʿAmir, and Ḥafs read la-raʾūfun with the long vowel (al-madd), and the rest read it with the short vowel (al-qaṣr).

﴿We have certainly seen﴾ meaning "perhaps We see" ﴿the turning of your face toward the sky﴾, meaning the fluctuation of your face toward the direction of the sky, looking eagerly for revelation. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would have this in his mind, and he would expect from his Lord that He would turn him to the Ka'bah, because it was the qiblah (direction of prayer) of his father Ibrahim (Abraham), the earlier of the two qiblahs, and more likely to draw the Arabs to faith, and to oppose the Jews. This indicates the perfection of his good manners, in that he waited and did not ask. ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah﴾, meaning We will enable you to face it. From your saying "wallaytuhu kadha" (I made him such-and-such), when you make him a governor (wali) over it; or, "We will make you take charge of its direction" ﴿that you will be pleased with﴾, meaning you will love it and long for it, for religious purposes that accord with the will and wisdom of Allah. ﴿So turn your face﴾, meaning direct your face

(p-112) ﴿toward the Sacred Mosque﴾, meaning toward it. It has been said: the word shatr originally refers to that part which separates from a thing when it is separated, and a house is called shutur, meaning separated from the other houses; then it was used for its side, even if it is not separated, as in qatr (side). The word haram means "forbidden", i.e., fighting is forbidden in it, or it is protected from the oppressors so that they cannot harm it. The Mosque is mentioned rather than the Ka'bah itself because he (peace be upon him) was in Madinah, and the distant person is sufficed by facing the general direction, since facing its exact point would be a hardship for him, unlike the one who is near.

It is narrated that: "When he (peace be upon him) arrived in Madinah, he prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen months. Then he was directed to the Ka'bah in Rajab, after midday, two months before the battle of Badr."

He had led his companions in the mosque of Bani Salamah in two rak'ahs of Dhuhr, and during the prayer he turned and faced the mizab (spout), and the men and women exchanged their rows, so the mosque was named the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs. ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾. He addressed the Messenger specifically as an honour to him and to make his desire binding, then he generalised explicitly, to affirm the generality of the ruling, to emphasise the matter of the qiblah, and to urge the Ummah (community) to follow. ﴿Indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾. This is a sentence, because of their knowledge that it is Allah's custom to assign each law a qiblah, and as a detail, because their books include that he (ﷺ) would pray toward the two qiblahs. The pronoun refers to the turning or to the facing. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾, a promise and a warning to both groups. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the letter ya' (yaʿmalūna).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 145:

﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾: this is a proof and an argument that the Ka'bah is the qibla. The lam is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatta'ah lil-qasam, the lam that prepares for an oath). ﴿They would not follow your qibla﴾ is the answer to the implied oath, and the oath with its answer takes the place of the answer to the conditional clause. The meaning is: they did not abandon your qibla due to a doubt that you could remove with proof; rather, they opposed you out of obstinate arrogance and stubborn denial. ﴿And you are not one who follows their qibla﴾ is a cutting off of their hopes, for they used to say: "If he remained upon our qibla, we would hope that he is our companion whom we await," seeking to honour him and hoping for his return. Their qiblas, although multiple, are united in falsehood and opposed to the truth. ﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾: the Jews face the rock, and the Christians face the rising place of the sun. Their agreement is not to be expected, just as their agreement with you is not to be expected, because each group is firm in what it is upon. ﴿And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you﴾ is on the basis of supposition and assumption, meaning: if you were, hypothetically, to follow them after the truth has become clear to you and revelation has come to you concerning it. ﴿Indeed, you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾. He emphasised this warning and intensified it in seven respects:

First: the bringing of the preparatory lam for the oath.

Second: the implied oath.

Third: the particle of affirmation, which is inna.

Fourth: its composition of a verbal clause and a nominal clause.

Fifth: the bringing of the lam in the predicate.

Sixth: making him one of "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin), and he did not say "you are a wrongdoer," because joining them carries the implication of the occurrence of all kinds of wrongdoing.

Seventh: the restriction by the arrival of knowledge, magnifying the known truth, urging its pursuit, warning against following desire, and expressing horror at the commission of sin by the prophets.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 146–147:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾ means their scholars. ﴿recognize him﴾: the pronoun refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), even though he has not been mentioned before, because the context points to him. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the knowledge, or to the Qur'an, or to the change of qibla. ﴿as they recognize their own sons﴾ supports the first view. That is, they recognize him by his attributes, as they recognize their sons, without confusing them with others. It is reported from ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, that he asked ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, may God be pleased with him, about the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He said: "I know him better than I know my son." ʿUmar said: "And why?" He said: "Because I have no doubt about Muhammad, that he is a prophet. As for my son, perhaps his mother has been unfaithful." ﴿And indeed a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ is a specification of those who were stubborn, and an exception for those who believed.

﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ is a new (independent) sentence. ﴿The truth﴾ may be the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), whose predicate (khabar, the grammatical predicate) is ﴿from your Lord﴾, and the lam on "al-haqq" is for a known referent (lam al-ʿahd, the definite article used for something already known). The reference is to what the Messenger (ﷺ) is upon, or to the truth they are concealing, or the lam is for the genus (lam al-jins, the definite article denoting the category as a whole). The meaning is that the truth is that which is established as being from God, like that which you (the Prophet) are upon, not what has not been established, like that which the People of the Book hold. Or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is ﴿the truth﴾. ﴿From your Lord﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a phrase describing the state of the subject at the time of the action), or a predicate following another predicate. It has also been read in the accusative (naṣb), on the basis that it is a substitute (badal, a word that replaces the preceding noun in the sentence) for the first word, or the object (mafʿūl, the direct object) of ﴿they know﴾.

﴿So do not be among the doubters (al-mumtarīn, those who harbour doubt)﴾: doubting that it is from your Lord, or doubting their concealment of the truth while knowing it. The intended meaning is not a prohibition to the Messenger (ﷺ) from doubt, because that is not expected of him, and it is not something done by deliberate choice. Rather, it is either an affirmation of the matter, that it is such that no observer could doubt it, or a command to the community to acquire knowledge that removes doubt in the most eloquent manner.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 148:

﴿And for each there is a direction﴾ For each nation there is a qibla (direction of prayer), or: for each group of the Muslims there is a direction and side of the Ka'bah. The tanwin (nunation) in "likullin" is a substitute for the idafa (genitive construction). ﴿He is turning towards it﴾ One of the two objects is omitted, meaning: He is turning it (i.e., His own face) towards it, or Allah Most High is turning them towards it (i.e., towards that direction). It was also read: "wa-li-kulli wijhatin" with the idafa, and the meaning is: "every direction of Allah is one towards which its people turn." The lam is added for emphasis, to compensate for the weakness of the governing element (al-'amil).

Ibn 'Amir read: "mawlaha," meaning: He is the one who holds that direction, i.e., He has taken charge of it. ﴿So race to the good works﴾ concerning the matter of the qibla and other things by which the happiness of both abodes is attained; or, "the superior directions," which are those that align with the Ka'bah. ﴿Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together﴾ That is: wherever you are, whether among those in agreement or disagreement, whether your parts are gathered or scattered, Allah will gather you to the place of assembly for recompense. Or: wherever you are, from the depths of the earth to the peaks of the mountains, He will take your souls. Or: wherever you are from the opposing directions, Allah will bring you all together and will make your prayers as if they were directed toward one direction. ﴿Indeed Allah is competent over all things﴾, so He is able to cause death, to give life, and to gather.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 149–150:**

﴿And from wherever you set out﴾, that is, from whatever place you set out for travel, ﴿turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque﴾ when you pray. ﴿And indeed it﴾, that is, this command, ﴿is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾. Abu 'Amr read it with the *ya'* (third person), while the rest read it with the *ta'* (second person) (qira'a, a recognised variant recitation).

﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face towards the Sacred Mosque, and wherever you are, turn your faces towards it﴾. He repeated this ruling because of the multiplicity of its causes (*'ilal*, reasons), for He, exalted is He, mentioned three reasons for the change (of qibla). The first is the honouring of the Messenger (ﷺ) by seeking his good pleasure. The second is the divine custom that every community and every bearer of a call should have a direction (*wijha*) that it faces and by which it is distinguished. The third is the repelling of the arguments of the opponents, as we will explain. He attached to each reason its effect, as the indicated meaning is attached to each of its indications, for the sake of bringing it near and establishing it, although the qibla (direction of prayer) has its own importance.

Abrogation (*naskh*, the replacement of one ruling by another) is among the places where doubt and confusion arise, so it is fitting that its command be emphasised and its mention repeated again and again. ﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾ is the reason for His saying ﴿turn﴾. The meaning is that turning away from the Rock (Bayt al-Maqdis) towards the Ka'ba repels the argument of the Jews, that the one described in the Torah has the Ka'ba as his qibla, and that Muhammad denies our religion and follows us in our qibla. It also repels the argument of the polytheists, that he claims the religion of Abraham yet opposes his qibla. ﴿Except those of them who did wrong﴾ is an exception from "the people": that is, so that no one among the people has an argument, except the obstinate among them, for they say: "He only turned to the Ka'ba out of inclination towards the religion of his people and love of his city," or "it occurred to him, so he returned to the qibla of his fathers, and he is about to return to their religion." He called this an "argument" as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿their argument is void in the sight of their Lord﴾ (42:16), because they put it forward in that manner. It is also said that "argument" here means the act of arguing. It is also said that the exception is for emphasis in negating argument altogether, as in the verse:

*"There is no fault in them, except that their swords*
*are notched by the clashing of the battalions."*

This is because it is known that the wrongdoer has no argument. It is also read: *"Alā"* (with the interrogative/alerting particle), ﴿those of them who did wrong﴾, as a resumed statement introduced by the particle of alerting. ﴿So do not fear them﴾, that is, do not be afraid of them, for their criticisms will not harm you. ﴿But fear Me﴾, that is, do not oppose what I have commanded you. ﴿And that I may complete My favour upon you and that you may be guided﴾: this is a reason for something omitted, meaning: "And I have commanded you for the completion of My favour upon you and My desire for your guidance." Or it is coordinated with an implied reason, such as: "fear Me, that I may protect you from them, and that I may complete My favour upon you," or "so that [you may be guided]."

There is a hadith: "The completion of the favour is entry into Paradise."

And it is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "The completion of the favour is death upon Islam."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 151–152:

﴿As We have sent among you a messenger from among you﴾ is connected to what precedes it, meaning: "and that I may complete My favour upon you in the matter of the qiblah, or in the Hereafter, just as I completed it by sending a messenger from among you; or it is connected to what follows it, as I mentioned you by sending [the messenger], so remember Me." ﴿He recites to you Our signs and purifies you﴾: He leads you to that by which you become pure (zakiyy, pl. azkiya'). He placed it first with regard to intention, and placed it later in the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, with regard to the act. ﴿And teaches you the Book and wisdom and teaches you what you did not know﴾ by reflection and contemplation (fikr wa-nazar), since there is no way to know it except through revelation. He repeated the verb to indicate that it is a different kind [of teaching].

﴿So remember Me﴾ through obedience. ﴿I will remember you﴾ with reward. ﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ for the favours I have bestowed upon you. ﴿And do not deny Me﴾ by rejecting the blessings and disobeying the command.

﴿So remember Me﴾ through obedience. ﴿I will remember you﴾ with reward. ﴿And be grateful to Me﴾ for the favours I have bestowed upon you. ﴿And do not deny Me﴾ by rejecting the blessings and disobeying the command.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 2, verses 153–154:

﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience﴾ from disobedience and the desires of the self, ﴿and prayer﴾ which is the mother of acts of worship (*umm al-'ibadat*) and the ascent (*mi'raj*) of the believers, and the intimate conversation (*munajat*) with the Lord of the worlds. ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ with victory and the answering of supplication. ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead."﴾ That is, they are dead. ﴿Rather, they are alive﴾ That is, rather, they are alive. ﴿But you do not perceive﴾ their condition. This is an admonition that their life is not of the body, nor of the kind perceived by the senses as animals are. Rather, it is a matter not grasped by reason but by revelation. And it is reported from al-Hasan: "The martyrs are alive with their Lord; their provision is presented to their spirits, so that joy and delight reach them, just as the Fire is presented to the spirits of Pharaoh's family morning and evening, so that pain and agony reach them." The verse was revealed concerning the martyrs of Badr, who were fourteen. In it is evidence that the spirits are substances subsisting by themselves, distinct from the body that is perceived, and that they remain after death, aware and perceiving. This is the position of the majority of the Companions (*sahabah*) and the Successors (*tabi'un*), and the verses and the Sunnah speak to it. On this basis, the specification of the martyrs is due to their special nearness to Allah, the Exalted, and their greater delight and honour.

(p-115) ﴿And We will surely test you﴾: We will surely afflict you in the manner of one who tests your conditions, to see whether you will be patient in trials and submit to the decree. ﴿with something of fear and hunger﴾: that is, with a little of that. He made it little in comparison with what He protected them from, to lighten it for them and to show them that His mercy does not leave them. Or it is in relation to what He will inflict on their opponents in the Hereafter. He informed them of it before it occurred so that they might prepare their souls for it. ﴿and loss of wealth, lives and fruits﴾: the phrase is coordinated (ʿaṭf, a conjunction) with "something" (shayʾ) or with "fear" (khawf).

It is narrated from al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that the fear is the fear of Allah; the hunger is the fasting of Ramadan; the loss of wealth is the voluntary charities and the zakat (obligatory almsgiving); the loss of lives is illnesses; and the loss of fruits is the death of children.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the child of a servant dies, Allah, exalted is He, says to the angels: 'Have you taken the soul of the child of My servant?' They say: 'Yes.' He says: 'Have you taken the fruit of his heart?' They say: 'Yes.' Allah, exalted is He, says: 'What did My servant say?' They say: 'He praised You and said the words of istirjaʿ (Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un).' Allah says: 'Build for My servant a house in Paradise and name it the House of Praise.'"

﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 156–157:

﴿Those who, when a calamity afflicts them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return."﴾ The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to whoever is fit to be given good news. The word muṣība (calamity) encompasses whatever befalls a person of hardship, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «Everything that harms the believer is a calamity for him.» Patience is not merely saying the istirjaʿ (the formula of returning to Allah) with the tongue; rather, it is with the tongue and the heart together, by contemplating that for which one was created, and that one is returning to one's Lord, and by remembering the blessings of Allah upon him, so that he sees that what remains with him is many times what has been taken from him, whereupon it becomes easy for his soul and he submits to Him. The good news referred to is omitted, indicated by what has been mentioned.

﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy.﴾ Ṣalawāt (blessings) originally means supplication, and from Allah Most High it means purification and forgiveness. He used the plural form to draw attention to its abundance and its variety. By raḥma (mercy) is meant kindness and beneficence.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): «Whoever says the istirjaʿ at the time of a calamity, Allah will repair his calamity, make his outcome good, and give him a righteous successor whom he will be pleased with.» ﴿And it is they who are the guided﴾ to the truth and the right course, in that they said the istirjaʿ and submitted to the decree of Allah Most High.

Al-Baydawi, *Anwar al-Tanzil*, commentary on Surah 2, verse 158:

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah﴾ are two named mountains in Makkah. ﴿Among the symbols (sha'a'ir) of Allah﴾, that is, among the markers (a'lam) of His rites (manasik). Sha'a'ir is the plural of sha'irah, which means a sign or marker. ﴿So whoever performs the Hajj to the House or the 'umrah﴾: hajj linguistically means intending or heading toward something, and i'timar means visiting. These terms became established in the Shari'ah for intending the House and visiting it in the two specific forms. ﴿There is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾. Isaf was on al-Safa and Na'ilah was on al-Marwah, and when the people of the Jahiliyyah performed the sa'y, they would rub (masah) the two of them. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims felt uneasy about going back and forth between them for that reason, so this verse was revealed.

There is consensus (ijma') that the sa'y is prescribed in the Hajj and the 'umrah. The disagreement concerns whether it is obligatory (wujub). According to one report from Ahmad, it is a sunnah (recommended practice), and this was the view of Anas and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, based on His saying ﴿there is no blame upon him﴾, since this implies optional choice (takhyir). This view is weak, because the negation of blame indicates permissibility, which falls within the meaning of obligation and therefore does not rule it out. According to Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, it is obligatory and can be compensated for by a sacrifice (dam). According to Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on both of them, it is a pillar (rukn) of the Hajj, based on the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Perform the sa'y, for Allah has prescribed the sa'y for you."

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾, that is, performs an act of obedience, whether obligatory or voluntary, or exceeds what Allah has obligated upon him of Hajj or 'umrah, or of tawaf, or performs the sa'y voluntarily, if we say that it is a sunnah. The word ﴿khayran﴾ (in Arabic, *khayran*) is in the accusative case (nasb) either as an adjective of a deleted verbal noun (masdar mahdhuf), or by deleting the preposition and making the verb reach it directly, or by making the verb transitive because it includes the meaning of "to bring" (ata) or "to do" (fa'ala). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read *yatatawwa'* (in Arabic, *yattawwa'*). Its original form is *yatatawwa'*, and it was assimilated (idghам) like *yattawwaf*. ﴿Indeed Allah is Appreciative (shakir), All-Knowing﴾: He rewards the obedience, and nothing of it is hidden from Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 159–160:

(p-116) ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ like the rabbis of the Jews. ﴿what We have sent down of the clear proofs﴾ like the verses testifying to the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿and the guidance﴾ and that which guides to the obligation of following him and believing in him. ﴿after We have made it clear to the people﴾ We have explained it. ﴿in the Book﴾ in the Torah. ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah curses, and the cursers curse them﴾ i.e., those from whom cursing upon them can come from the angels and the two species (jinn and humankind).

﴿Except those who repent﴾ of the concealment and of everything else that must be repented of, ﴿and reform﴾ what they corrupted by making amends, ﴿and make clear﴾ what Allah has made clear in their Book, so that their repentance may be complete. It has also been said: what they have produced of repentance, so that they may erase by it the mark of disbelief from themselves and their like may follow their example. ﴿Those, I accept their repentance﴾ by acceptance and forgiveness. ﴿And I am the Ever-Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful﴾, the one who exceeds in accepting repentance and bestowing mercy.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 161–162:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾ That is, and whoever among the concealers does not repent until he dies. ﴿Upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of the people, all together﴾ The curse has become firmly established upon them from Allah, and [also] from whoever among His creation takes his curse into account. It has been said: the first (curse) is their being cursed while alive, and this is their being cursed after death. It has also been recited, "and the angels and the people, all together" (al-malā'ikatu wa-l-nāsu ajma'ūna), in coordination with the place of the noun Allah, since it is the agent in meaning, as in your saying, "The striking of Zayd and 'Amr amazed me" (a'jabanī ḍarbu Zaydin wa-'Amrin); or [it is] in the nominative as the agent of a verb implied, such as "and the angels curse them" (wa-talʿanuhumu al-malā'ikatu).

﴿Abiding therein﴾ That is, in the curse, or in the Fire. Its pronoun being mentioned before any explicit reference is for the sake of magnifying its matter and striking awe, or because the meaning of "curse" points to it. ﴿Their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be respited﴾ That is, they will not be given a reprieve; or they will not be awaited so that they may make excuses; or no merciful glance will be cast upon them.
