Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 163:

﴿And your God is One God.﴾ This is a general address: the one who is deserving of worship from you is One, having no partner, such that He is fit to be worshipped or to be called a god. ﴿There is no god but He.﴾ This is an affirmation of (al-wahdaniyya) the oneness of God, and a removal of the notion that there might be a god in existence who is nonetheless not deserving of worship from them.

﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.﴾ These serve as a proof for this, for since He is the Master of all blessings, both their roots and their branches, and everything other than Him is either a blessing or one who has been blessed, no one other than Him deserves to be worshipped. These two are (two further predicates) of His statement "your God," or (they are predicates) of an omitted subject. It was said: when the polytheists heard it, they were amazed and said, "If you are truthful, then bring a sign by which we may recognize your truthfulness," and so it was revealed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 164:

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ He used the plural for "heavens" and the singular for "earth," because the heavens are layers that are separate in their essence and different in their reality, unlike the earths. And "the alternation of the night and the day" refers to their succession, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He made the night and the day as a succession (khilfah)﴾. ﴿And the ship that runs in the sea with what benefits people﴾, meaning with their benefit, or with that which benefits them. The purpose of this is to draw inference from the sea and its conditions. The ship is singled out for mention because it is the means of plying the sea and becoming acquainted with its wonders. For this reason it was placed before the mention of rain and clouds, because their origin in most cases is the sea. The feminine form of "ship" (al-fulk) is because it has the meaning of "vessel" (safinah).

It was also read with two dammas, on the basis of the original form, or as a plural; and the damma of the plural is different from the damma of the singular according to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun).

﴿And what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾: the first "min" (from) indicates the starting point, and the second "min" indicates explanation. "Sky" (al-sama') may refer to the celestial sphere or to the clouds, or to the direction of height.

﴿And with it He gives life to the earth after its death﴾, by means of vegetation. ﴿And He scattered throughout it every kind of moving creature﴾ is coordinated with "sent down" (anzala), as though He were inferring from the descent of rain, the growth of plants through it, and the dispersal of living creatures upon the earth; or it is coordinated with "gives life" (ahya), since the creatures grow through fertility and live through life. "Al-batth" means spreading out and scattering. And the directing of the winds in their directions and their conditions. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the singular (ar-riyh). ﴿And the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth﴾ that neither descend nor disperse, although nature would require one of these two until the command of Allah, exalted is He, comes.

It was said: the subjection of the clouds is their being moved about in the atmosphere by the will of Allah, exalted is He, and its derivation is from "al-sahb" (dragging), because some of it drags others along. ﴿Surely there are signs for a people who use their reason﴾: they reflect upon them and look at them with the eyes of their intellects. And from him (ﷺ): "Woe to the one who recites this verse and passes over it (famajja bi-ha)," meaning he did not reflect upon it.

Know that the indication of these verses upon the existence of God and His oneness is from many aspects, whose detailed explanation would be lengthy. The summary statement is that these are possible things, each of which came into existence in a specific way from among many possible ways and different modes. For it is permissible, for example, that the heavens should not move, or some of them, like the earth, and that they should move in the reverse of their motions, and in such a way that the zodiac becomes a circle passing through the two poles, and that they should have no apogee or perigee at all. Given this manner, on account of their simplicity and the equality of their parts, there must be a creator who is powerful and wise, who brings them into being according to what His wisdom requires and His will necessitates, exalted above the opposition of any other. For if there were with Him another god who is capable of what the other is capable of, then if their wills agree: the act, if it is for both of them, necessitates two influencers on a single effect; and if it is for one of them, it necessitates the preponderance of the agent without a preponderant cause, and the negation of the other, which contradicts his divinity. And if their wills differ, it necessitates mutual opposition and mutual exclusion, as He indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾. In the verse there is an alert to the nobility of the science of kalam (theology) and its people, and an exhortation to inquiry and reflection in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 165:

﴿وَمِنَ النّاسِ مَن يَتَّخِذُ مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ أنْدادًا﴾ [i.e., rivals (andad)] from among the idols. It is also said: from among the leaders whom they used to obey, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إذْ تَبَرَّأ الَّذِينَ اتُّبِعُوا مِنَ الَّذِينَ اتَّبَعُوا﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah 2:166: "when those who were followed disown those who followed"]. Perhaps the intended meaning is more general than both of these, namely whatever distracts one from Allah. ﴿يُحِبُّونَهُمْ﴾ [they love them] means they revere them and obey them. ﴿كَحُبِّ اللَّهِ﴾ [as the love of Allah] means like their reverence of Him and their inclination to obey Him; that is, they make equal between Him and them in love and obedience. Al-mahabbah (love) is the inclination of the heart from hubb (love), a term borrowed for the heart's love, and then hubb was derived from it, because it reached the heart and settled in it. The servant's love for Allah is the desire to obey Him and to be solicitous in attaining His pleasure, and Allah's love for the servant is the desire to honor him, to employ him in obedience, and to preserve him from sins. ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أشَدُّ حُبًّا لِلَّهِ﴾ [but those who believe are stronger in love for Allah], because their love for Allah, exalted is He, never ceases, unlike the love for rivals, which is for corrupt, imagined purposes and vanishes at the slightest cause. For this reason they used to turn away from their gods to Allah, exalted is He, in times of hardship, and would worship an idol for a time and then abandon it for another.

﴿وَلَوْ يَرى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ [And if those who did wrong could see], that is, if those who did wrong by taking rivals would know ﴿إذْ يَرَوْنَ العَذابَ﴾ [when they see the punishment], that is, when they witness it on the Day of Resurrection. The future has been treated as though it were past, for its certainty, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَنادى أصْحابُ الجَنَّةِ﴾ [Surah al-A'raf 7:44: "and the companions of the Garden will call out"].

﴿أنَّ القُوَّةَ لِلَّهِ جَمِيعًا﴾ [that power belongs entirely to Allah] serves as the substitute for the two objects of ﴿يَرى﴾ [see], and the answer of (law) [if] is omitted. That is: if they knew that power belongs entirely to Allah when they witness the punishment, they would regret with the utmost regret. It is also said that it is the complement of the answer, with both objects omitted, and the estimated meaning is: if those who did wrong saw that their rivals do not benefit them, they would know that power belongs wholly to Allah, and that none other than Him benefits or harms. Ibn 'Amir, Nafi' and Ya'qub read ﴿لَوْ تَرى﴾ [if you [O Prophet] could see], as an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: if you could see that, you would see a tremendous matter. Ibn 'Amir read ﴿إذْ يُرَوْنَ﴾ [when they are shown] in the passive form (al-bina' lil-maf'ul). Ya'qub read ﴿إنَّ﴾ [indeed] with a kasrah (إنَّ instead of أنَّ), and likewise ﴿وَأنَّ اللَّهَ شَدِيدُ العَذابِ﴾ [and that Allah is severe in punishment], as a resumed clause (al-isti'naf) or with a suppressed verb of saying (idmar al-qawl).(p-118)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 166–167:

﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ is a substitution (badal) for ﴿when they see﴾; that is, when those who were followed disown their followers. It is also read in the reverse, that is, the followers disown the leaders. ﴿And they see the punishment﴾, that is, seeing it, and the waw is for the circumstantial clause (hal), and a verb is implied. It is said it is conjoined (ʿatf) to "disown". ﴿And their means (asbab) are cut off from them﴾: it is possible that it is conjoined to "disown" or to "they see", with the waw being for the circumstantial clause, and the first is more apparent. The asbab are the ties that existed between them, of following and agreement upon the religion, and the motives that called to that. The original meaning of sabab is the rope by which a tree is climbed. It is also read "wa-tuqqattiʿat" in the passive voice.

﴿And those who followed will say: "If only we had a return (karrah), so that we might disown them as they have disowned us."﴾ The ﴿law﴾ (if only) is for wishing, and that is why it is answered with the fa' (so); that is, "would that we had a return to the world, so that we might disown them in the same way, like that dreadful sight." ﴿God will show them their deeds as regrets (hasarat) upon them﴾: regrets (nadamat), and it is the third object of "to show" (yura) if it is from the sight of the heart; otherwise it is a circumstantial clause (hal). ﴿And they will not be coming out of the Fire﴾: its original form was "and they will not come out," but it was turned to this expression for emphasis on eternal abiding and for despair of deliverance and of return to the world.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 168:

﴿O mankind, eat of what is in the earth, lawful and good﴾. It was revealed concerning a people who forbade themselves the choicest foods and clothing. "Halalan" (lawful) is the object of "kulu" (eat), or an adjective of a omitted verbal noun (masdar), or a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "what is in the earth." The particle "min" (of) is partitive (li-l-tab'id), since not everything in the earth is eaten that is good, as judged good by the Sharia (al-shar'), or by upright desire (al-shahwa al-mustaqima), since "lawful" points to the first meaning.

﴿And do not follow the steps (khutuwat) of Satan﴾: do not take him as a model in following desire, so that you forbid what is lawful and make lawful what is forbidden. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Bazzi and Abu Bakr, wherever it occurs, read "khutuwat" with a sukun on the "ta'" (khutwat). Both are dialectal forms (lughatan) of the plural of "khutwa," which is the space between the two feet of the one who strides. It was also read with two dammas and a hamza, the damma of the "ta'" being made as if it were upon it, and with two fathas, as the plural of "khatwa," which is a single instance of striding (al-khaṭw).

﴿Indeed he is to you a clear enemy﴾: evident in enmity to those of insight, even though he shows friendship to those whom he misleads. For this reason he called him a "walī" (protector) in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Their protectors are the Taghut﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 169:

﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ This explains his enmity and the obligation to guard against following him. The word "command" is used figuratively for his adorning wrongdoing for them and urging them toward evil, in order to show the foolishness of their opinion and belittle their standing. "Evil" (al-su') and "immorality" (al-fahsha') are what reason rejects and the Sharia (divine law) finds repugnant. They are joined by a conjunction because the two descriptions differ: it is "evil" because it distresses the rational person, and "immorality" because the rational person finds it repugnant. It has been said: "evil" (al-su') encompasses all ugly deeds, while "immorality" (al-fahsha') is what exceeds the limit of ugliness among the major sins. It has also been said: the first is what has no prescribed penalty (hadd) attached to it, and the second is what has a prescribed penalty (hadd) legislated for it. ﴿And that you say about God what you do not know﴾, such as ascribing equals to Him, declaring the forbidden lawful, and prohibiting the good things. In this is evidence for the absolute prohibition of following conjecture (zann). As for a mujtahid (a qualified jurist who exercises independent legal reasoning) following what his conjecture has led him to, when that conjecture rests on a valid legal proof (mudrak shar'i), its obligation is definite, and the conjecture is valid as a path to it, as we have explained in the books of legal theory (usul).

(p-119) ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down," the pronoun refers to the people, and the address was turned away from them to call attention to their misguidance, as if he turned to the intelligent ones and said to them: "Look at these fools, see how they answer."﴾ ﴿They say, "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon"﴾, meaning what we found them upon. It was revealed concerning the polytheists, who were commanded to follow the Qur'an and the rest of what God sent down of proofs and signs, but they inclined toward taqlid (blind imitation). It is also said that it was revealed concerning a group of the Jews whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) invited to Islam, and they said: "Rather we follow what we found our fathers upon, for they were better than us and more knowledgeable." In this case, "what God has sent down" is general and includes the Torah, since it too calls to Islam. ﴿Even though their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?﴾ The waw is for the circumstantial state or for conjunction, and the hamzah is for rebuke and wonder. The response of "law" (law) is omitted, meaning: even if their fathers were ignorant, not reflecting on matters of religion, and not guided to the truth, they would still have followed them. This is evidence for the prohibition of taqlid for one who is able to reflect and exercise independent judgment (ijtihad). As for following another in religion when it is known by some evidence that he is right, such as the prophets and mujtahids in legal rulings, this is in reality not taqlid but rather following what God has sent down.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 171:

﴿And the likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and a cry﴾. This is by elision of a modifier (mudaf), its estimated form being: "And the likeness of the caller of those who disbelieve is like the likeness of the one who shouts (yan'iq)," or "the likeness of those who disbelieve is like the likeness of the cattle of the one who shouts." The meaning is that the disbelievers, because of their total immersion in taqlid (blind imitation), do not direct their minds to what is recited to them, nor do they reflect on what is set forth before them. In this they are like the beasts at which one shouts: they hear the sound but do not grasp its purport, and they perceive the call but do not understand its meaning. It has also been said that it is an image of their following their forefathers in their outward condition, while ignorant of its reality, by the likeness of beasts that hear a sound but do not understand what lies beneath it. Or it is an image of their calling upon the idols, by the likeness of the one who shouts (al-na'iq) in his shouting (na'q), which is vocalizing to beasts. This would dispense with the supposed elision, but the phrase "nothing but a call and a cry" does not support it, since idols do not hear, unless this is taken as a case of compound imagery (al-tamthil al-murakkab).

﴿Deaf, dumb, blind﴾: raised (marfu') by way of censure (al-dhamm). ﴿So they do not understand﴾: that is, in actuality, owing to their neglect of reflection (al-nazar).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 172:

﴿O you who have believed, eat from the good things with which We have provided you﴾. When He had extended the matter to all people and permitted them what is on the earth, except what He had forbidden them, He commanded the believers among them to seek out the good things they have been provided with and to fulfill their rights, so He said:

﴿And be grateful to Allah﴾ for what He has provided you and made lawful for you. ﴿if you are indeed worshipping Him﴾, if it is true that you single Him out for worship and acknowledge that He is the master of blessings, for His worship, exalted is He, is not complete except with gratitude. Thus, what is dependent on the act of worship is the command to be grateful, for its completion, and it is absent when it is absent.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "God Most High says: Indeed, I and mankind and jinn are in a great news. I create, and another than Me is worshipped; I provide sustenance, and another than Me is thanked."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 173:

﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only carrion﴾, i.e., eating it, or benefiting from it. It is that which died without slaughter (dhakah). The hadith (tradition) has been attached to it: whatever is cut off from a living animal. Fish and locusts have been excluded from it by custom ('urf), or the Law (shar') has made an exception for them. The prohibition ascribed to a thing (al-hurmah al-mudafah ila al-'ayn) conveys by custom the prohibition of any disposal of it in an absolute sense, except what the evidence has specified, such as the disposal of a tanned hide (al-madbugh). ﴿And blood, and the flesh of swine﴾. He singled out the flesh for mention because it is the main part of what is eaten from animals, and the rest of its parts follow it. ﴿And that over which other than God has been invoked﴾, i.e., the voice was raised over it at its slaughter for an idol. Al-ihlal (invocation) originally means the sighting of the crescent (hilal); it is said: "the crescent appeared (ahalla al-hilal)" and "I sighted it (ahlaltuhu)." But when it became customary to raise the voice with takbir (proclaiming God's greatness) upon sighting it, that was called ihlal, then it was said of raising the voice even when it was for other than that. ﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾, i.e., by monopolizing (food) against another person who is compelled. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah read the nun with a kasrah (al-nun bi-kasr). ﴿Nor exceeding﴾, i.e., beyond the amount that sustains life (sadd al-ramaq), or the satisfying of hunger. It has been said: "neither desiring" means against the ruler, and "nor exceeding" means by highway robbery. Accordingly, it is not permitted for one who is disobedient by travel, and this is the apparent position of the school of al-Shafi'i and the view of Ahmad, may God have mercy on them both. ﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾ in consuming it. ﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving﴾ of what he did ﴿Merciful﴾ in granting the concession for it. If it is said: [the restriction] only conveys the limitation of the ruling to what was mentioned, and how many prohibited things were not mentioned? I say: what is meant is the limitation of the prohibition to what was mentioned among what they had deemed lawful, not in an absolute sense; or the limitation of its prohibition to the state of choice, as if it were said: "Indeed, He has forbidden you these things, so long as you are not compelled to them."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 174–175:

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book and exchange it for a small price﴾: a paltry return.

﴿Those – they consume nothing into their bellies except the Fire﴾: either immediately, because what they consumed was something associated with fire, since it is its punishment; so it is as if they ate the Fire, like the words of the poet:

"I have eaten blood, if I do not cause you distress with a co-wife... far-reaching in the place of the earring, fragrant in her scent"

meaning the blood-money (diyah). Or in the outcome, i.e. on the Day of Resurrection they will consume nothing but the Fire. The meaning of "in their bellies" is: filling their bellies. It is said: "he ate in his belly" and "he ate in part of his belly," like his saying:

"Eat in some of your bellies, you will be pardoned"

﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾: an expression of His anger toward them, and an implicit indication of their being deprived, in contrast to those who are honoured and brought near to Allah. ﴿Nor will He purify them﴾: He will not praise them. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾: causing pain.

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance﴾ in this world, ﴿and punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾ in the Hereafter, by concealing the truth for the sake of greed and worldly aims. ﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾ He marvels at their condition in engaging in things that bring about the Fire without any concern. Here "mā" is a complete (ta"ammah) noun in the nominative, functioning as the subject of the sentence (mubtada'), and its specification is like the specification in their saying:

"An evil that baring its fangs..."

Or it is an interrogative (istifhamiyyah), with what follows it being the predicate (khabar); or it is a relative (mawsulah), with what follows it being its relative clause, and the predicate being omitted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 176:

﴿That is because Allah has sent down the Book with truth.﴾ That is, that punishment is because Allah sent down the Book with truth, but they rejected it, either by denying it or by concealing it. ﴿Indeed, those who differ concerning the Book﴾ The definite article in "al-Kitab" (the Book) may be for the genus (kind), and their differing would then be their believing in some of the books of Allah the Exalted and disbelieving in others. Or it may be for a specific reference (al-'ahd), and the reference is either to the Torah, where "ikhtalafu" (they differed) is understood in the sense of "takhallafu" (they deviated) from the straight path in interpreting it, or "khallafu" (they substituted) in the midst of what Allah the Exalted sent down a replacement for it, meaning they altered what was in it. Or the reference is to the Qur'an, and their differing concerning it is their saying: it is magic, and it is fabrication, and it is words taught by a human being, and it is the fables of the ancients. ﴿Are in extreme dissension﴾ That is, they are in a dissension far removed from the truth.

(p-121)﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west.﴾ *Al-birr* is every good action that is pleasing (to God). The address is to the People of the Book, for they excessively debated the matter of the *qiblah* (direction of prayer) when it was changed, and each group claimed that righteousness was facing their own *qiblah*. So God, exalted be He, refuted them and said: "It is not righteousness that you are upon," for it is *mansukh* (abrogated, a term meaning its ruling has been superseded). "But righteousness is what God has explained and what the believers follow." It has also been said that the statement is general, applying to them and to the Muslims, meaning: righteousness is not confined to the matter of the *qiblah*, or: it is not the great righteousness for which it is fitting that you be so absorbed in its affair as to neglect other matters.

Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ read *al-birra* with the accusative (*naṣb*), ﴿But righteousness is [that of] one who believes in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets.﴾ That is: "But the righteousness that ought to be cared for is the righteousness of one who believes in God," or: "But possessor of righteousness is one who believes." This is supported by the reading of one who read *wa-lakinna al-bārr* (with *al-bārr* in the nominative). The first is more suitable and better. By "the Book" is meant the genus, or the Qur'an. Nāfi' and Ibn ʿĀmir read *walākin* with the lightened particle and the nominative *al-birru* (*rafʿ*).

﴿and gave wealth, despite love for it﴾: that is, despite love of wealth.

The Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, said when he was asked which charity is best: «That you give while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for prosperity and fearing poverty.» It has also been said that the pronoun refers to God, or to the verbal noun (*maṣdar*). The prepositional phrase and what it governs are in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*).

﴿to relatives, orphans﴾: he means those among them who are in need. He did not restrict it, due to the absence of ambiguity. He placed "relatives" first because giving to them is more excellent, as the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, said: «Your charity to a poor person is charity, and to a kinsperson it is two: charity and maintaining kinship.»

﴿and the needy﴾: the plural of *miskīn*, which is one whom need has made still (i.e., destitute). Its origin is one who is constantly still, like *miskīr* for one who is constantly drunk.

﴿and the traveler﴾: the wayfarer. He was so named because of his staying on the road (*al-sabīl*), just as the highwayman is called "son of the road." It has also been said that it means the guest, because the road is where one is hosted.

﴿and those who ask﴾: those whom need has compelled to ask.

He, upon him peace, said: «The one who asks has a right, even if he comes on a horse.»

﴿and for freeing slaves﴾: for their liberation through assisting those in a contract of manumission (*mukātabīn*), or ransoming captives, or purchasing slaves to free them.

﴿and established prayer﴾: the obligatory prayer.

﴿and gave zakah﴾: it is possible that what is intended by this and by His saying ﴿and gave wealth﴾ is the obligatory zakah, but the purpose of the first is to explain its recipients, and the purpose of the second is its payment and urging upon it.

It is also possible that what is meant by the first is voluntary charities, or rights that exist in wealth besides zakah.

It is related in a hadith: «Zakah has abrogated every (other) charity.»

﴿and those who fulfill their covenant when they make one﴾: a conjunction upon ﴿those who believe﴾.

﴿and the patient in suffering and adversity﴾: he put it in the accusative by way of praise, and did not conjoin it, because of the excellence of patience over all other deeds. It is related from al-Azharī: *al-basā'* (suffering) is in wealth, like poverty, and *al-ḍarrā'* (adversity) is in the self, like sickness.

﴿and in time of battle﴾: at the time of fighting the enemy.

﴿Those are the ones who are true﴾: in religion, in following the truth, and in seeking righteousness.

﴿And those are the God-fearing﴾: who guard against disbelief and all other vices.

As you see, the verse encompasses all human perfections in their entirety, indicating them explicitly or implicitly, for with its multiplicity and diversity it is confined to three things: soundness of belief, goodness of social conduct, and refinement of the soul. The first is indicated by His saying ﴿who believes in God﴾ up to ﴿and the prophets﴾; the second by His saying ﴿and gave wealth﴾ up to ﴿and for freeing slaves﴾; and the third by His saying ﴿and established prayer﴾ to its end. Therefore, the one who combines them is described as "true," in view of his faith and belief, and as "God-fearing," in view of his social dealings with creation and his conduct with the Truth. To this he alluded, upon him peace, when he said: «Whoever acts upon this verse has perfected faith.»

﴿O you who believe, retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female.﴾ In the Pre-Islamic period (al-Jahiliyya), there was bloodshed between two of the tribes of the Arabs, and one of them had superiority over the other. So they swore that they would kill the free man among you for the slave, and the male for the female. When Islam came, they brought their dispute to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed, and he commanded them to make it equal (yatabawa'u). It does not indicate that a free man is not to be killed for a slave, or a male for a female, just as it does not indicate the opposite. For the implication (mafhum, the meaning understood by implication) is not valid where no purpose for specification (takhsis, restricting a ruling to a particular category) has become apparent beyond the restriction of the ruling itself, and we have already explained what the purpose was. Malik and al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with them both, prohibited the killing of a free man for a slave, whether it was his own slave or the slave of another, based on what has been narrated from Ali, may God be pleased with him: "That a man killed his slave, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) flogged him and banished him for a year, and did not subject him to retaliation for it."

And it has been narrated from him that he said: "It is part of the Sunnah that a Muslim is not to be killed for one under a covenant, nor a free man for a slave."

Also, Abu Bakr and Umar, may God be pleased with them both, used not to kill a free man for a slave among the Companions, without any objection.

And by analogy with the limbs (qiyas 'ala al-atraf, reasoning by analogy from the lesser injuries). Whoever's implication is sound has no claim that it has been abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one) by His saying: ﴿a life for a life﴾, because it is a narration of what is in the Torah, and so it does not abrogate what is in the Qur'an. The Hanafis used it as evidence that the requirement for deliberate killing is retaliation alone, but this is weak, since the obligatory (wajib) under option (takhyir) truly fits the description that it was made obligatory and prescribed, and for this reason it has been said that choice between an obligation and something else is not an abrogation of its obligation. It has been read "kutiba" (was prescribed) in the active form (the verb read as ka-tabe, with the subject understood as God), and "al-qisas" (retaliation) in the accusative, and likewise every verb that occurs in the Qur'an in this way.

﴿So whoever is pardoned by his brother in anything﴾: that is, anything of the pardon, because "'afa" (to pardon) is intransitive (lazim, not taking a direct object). Its benefit is to indicate that a part of the pardon is like the complete pardon in dropping retaliation. It has been said that "'afa" means "taraka" (to leave), and that "shay'" (anything) is its object, but this is weak, since it has not been established that "'afa al-shay'" means "taraka al-shay'"; rather it is "a'faahu" (he excused it). "'Afa" is transitive with "'an" to the offender and to the sin. God, Exalted, said: ﴿God has pardoned you﴾ and He said: ﴿God has pardoned what has passed﴾. When it is transitive to the sin, it is transitive to the offender with the preposition "li-" (for), and the verse is to be understood accordingly, as if it were said: "So whoever is pardoned for his offence on behalf of his brother," meaning the guardian of the blood. He mentioned him with the term "brotherhood" that exists between them through common humanity and Islam, so that he may be softened towards him and incline to him.

﴿Then there should be following with fairness and payment to him with good conduct﴾: that is, let there be following, or the matter is following. What is meant by it is the instruction to the one who pardons, that he should demand the blood-money (diyya) with fairness, and not be harsh. And to the one pardoned, that he should pay it with good conduct, which is that he should not delay or diminish it. In this there is evidence that the blood-money is one of the requirements of deliberate killing, for otherwise the command to pay it would not have been ordered upon mere pardon. Al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, has two opinions on this question.

﴿That﴾: that is, the ruling mentioned concerning the pardon and the blood-money. ﴿is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy﴾ because of the ease and benefit in it. It has been said that retaliation alone was prescribed for the Jews, and pardon absolutely for the Christians. This nation was given the choice between both of them and the blood-money, as facilitation for them and as an appropriate ruling according to their ranks.

﴿So whoever transgresses after that﴾: that is, kills after the pardon and the taking of the blood-money, ﴿for him is a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter. It has also been said that it is in this world, by his being killed without fail, based on his peace be upon him saying: "I shall not pardon anyone who kills after accepting the blood-money."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 179:

﴿And for you in retaliation there is life﴾. This is a statement of the utmost eloquence and rhetorical power, in that it places a thing in the position of its opposite. He made "retaliation" definite and "life" indefinite, so as to indicate that in this category of ruling there is a kind of life that is great. This is because knowledge of it deters the killer from killing, and so it becomes the cause of the life of two souls. Also, because they used to kill someone other than the killer, and a group for one person, so strife would erupt among them. When retaliation is exacted from the killer, the rest are safe, and that becomes a cause of their life. According to the first explanation, there is an implied element (idmar); according to the second, there is a restriction (takhsis). It has also been said: the intended meaning is the life of the Hereafter, for when retaliation is exacted from the killer in this world, he is not held accountable for it in the Hereafter. ﴿And for you in retaliation﴾ may be two predicates for "life," or one of them may be a predicate and the other a complement to it, or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed within it. It has also been read as "al-qasas" (in the "qasas" reading), meaning: in what has been related to you of the ruling on killing there is life; or: in the Qur'an there is life for the hearts. ﴿O people of understanding﴾: possessors of perfect intellects. He addressed them so that they would reflect on the wisdom of retaliation, namely the preservation of souls and the safeguarding of lives. ﴿so that you may be God-conscious﴾: in upholding retaliation, enforcing it, and submitting to it, or by refraining from killing out of fear of retaliation.

(p-123) ﴿It is prescribed for you, when death approaches any of you, if he leaves behind wealth, that he make a bequest to the parents and the near relatives, in a fair manner; this is a duty upon the God-fearing.﴾ That is, its causes have arrived and its signs have appeared. ﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾ — that is, property; it is said, much property, based on what is narrated from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: that a client of his wished to make a bequest while he had seven hundred dirhams, and he forbade him, saying: God Most High says: ﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾, and wealth is much property.

And from ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her: that a man wished to make a bequest, so she asked him: "How much is your wealth?" He said: "Three thousand." She said: "How many are your dependants?" He said: "Four." She said: "God Most High only said: ﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾, and this is a small amount, so leave it for your dependants."

﴿The bequest to the parents and the near relatives﴾ is in the nominative case as the subject of ﴿It is prescribed﴾ (kutiba). The verb's gender is masculine due to the separation (between the verb and its subject), or it is interpreted as "that he make a bequest" or "the making of a bequest"; for this reason the pronoun referring back is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Then whoever alters it﴾. The operative element in idhā (when) is the meaning of kutiba, not the bequest (waṣiyyah), since the bequest comes after it. It is also said that it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is ﴿to the parents﴾, and the sentence is the response of the conditional, with the particle fāʾ (then) omitted, as in his saying:

*Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them… and evil with evil is equal in the sight of God.*

This was refuted: even if it is authentic, it is one of the necessities of poetry. This ruling was in the early days of Islam, and it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance and by his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "Indeed God has given every person with a right his right; no bequest is valid for an heir." There is a problem with this: the verse of inheritance does not contradict it but rather confirms it, insofar as it indicates the priority of the bequest in general; and the hadith is from the solitary reports (āḥād), and the community's acceptance of it does not elevate it to the level of the mass-transmitted (mutawātir). Perhaps whoever interpreted the bequest as what God had bequeathed concerning the inheritance of parents and near relatives, by His saying ﴿God enjoins upon you﴾, avoided this problem. Or [interpreted it as] the dying person's bequest to them of providing what God has enjoined upon them ﴿in a fair manner﴾, meaning with justice, so that he does not favor the wealthy and does not exceed one-third. ﴿A duty upon the God-fearing﴾ is an emphatic infinitive, meaning: that is a duty, indeed.

﴿So whoever alters it﴾, meaning changes it, namely the executors and the witnesses, ﴿after he has heard it﴾, that is, after it has reached him and he has become certain of it, ﴿then its sin is only upon those who alter it﴾. So the sin of the altered bequest, or of the alteration itself, rests only upon those who alter it, because they are the ones who feared and opposed the divine law (al-shar').

﴿Indeed Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾: a threat (wa'id) to the one who alters without right.

﴿And whoever fears from a testator﴾, that is, expects and knows, from their saying "akhaafu an tursala al-sama'" ("I fear that the sky will send down rain"). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr read "Mūṣin" with a shaddah (doubled letter), i.e., "mussin" (from the form of wasiyyah, bequest). ﴿Deviation﴾, meaning an inclination into error in the bequest. ﴿Or sin﴾, meaning deliberate injustice. ﴿Then he makes peace between them﴾, between those to whom the bequest is made, by bringing them back to the course of the divine law. ﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾ in this alteration, because it is an alteration from falsehood to truth, unlike the first. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾: a promise (wa'd) to the one who makes peace. He mentioned forgiveness to match the mention of sin, and because the act is of the same kind as what would incur sin.

So the sin of the altered bequest, or of the alteration itself, rests only upon those who alter it, because they are the ones who feared and opposed the divine law (al-shar').

﴿Indeed Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾: a threat (wa'id) to the one who alters without right.
