O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, meaning the prophets and the nations from the time of Adam (peace be upon him). In it there is emphasis on the ruling, encouragement to act upon it, and consolation for the self.

Ṣawm (fasting) linguistically means abstaining from what the soul longs for, and in the Sharia it means abstaining from the things that break the fast from the break of dawn until the day's end, since these are the greatest of what the soul desires.

﴿So that you may become righteous﴾ — that is, that you may guard against sins, for fasting breaks the desire which is their origin. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you can marry, let him marry; and whoever cannot, let him fast, for fasting is a shield for him" (wijā’, a protection or shield). Or [the purpose is] that one should not neglect its performance, because of its antiquity and its being ancient.

﴿Days numbered﴾: limited to a known number, or a few. A small amount of wealth is counted one by one, while a large amount is poured out in heaps (hayl). Its accusative case is not governed by al-siyam (fasting), because of the separation between them. Rather, it is governed by an implied "fast" (sumu), indicated by al-siyam. What is meant by these days is Ramadan, or what was obligatory to fast before its obligation and was abrogated (naskh, abrogation) by it. That is the day of Ashura, or three days of every month. It may also be governed by ﴿as it was prescribed﴾ as an adverbial of time (zarfiyya), or be a second object (maf'ul thani) of ﴿it has been prescribed for you﴾, in the sense of latitude (si'a). It has been said that its meaning is: your fasting is like their fasting in the number of days, based on what is reported: that Ramadan was prescribed for the Christians, and it fell in a severe cold or heat, so they moved it to spring and added twenty days of expiation (kaffara) for changing it. It has also been said that they added those days because of a plague (mawtan) that afflicted them. ﴿Whoever among you is ill﴾: an illness that the fast harms or makes difficult. ﴿Or on a journey﴾, or a traveller. This implies that whoever travels during the day does not break his fast. ﴿Then a number of other days﴾: that is, he must fast the number of days of the illness or journey on other days, if he breaks his fast. The condition, the genitive-governing word and the word governed by it have been omitted, because they are known.

It was read in the accusative (naṣb), meaning: then let him fast a number (of days). This is by way of concession (rukhsa). It has been said that it is obligatory, and this is the view of the Zahiriyya (the Literalist school), and Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said so. ﴿And for those who are able to endure it﴾: and for those who are able to fast, if they break their fast. ﴿A ransom: feeding a poor person﴾: half a ṣāʿ of wheat, or a ṣāʿ of other grain, according to the jurists of Iraq, and a mudd according to the jurists of the Hijaz. This was permitted for them at the beginning of the matter, when they were commanded to fast and it was hard for them because they were not accustomed to it. Then it was abrogated. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, read ﴿fidya﴾ as an annexation to ﴿ta'am﴾ (food) and the plural ﴿al-masakin﴾. Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of Hisham, read ﴿masakin﴾ without annexing the ransom to the food, and the rest read it without annexation and with the singular ﴿miskin﴾. It was also read ﴿yuṭawwiqūnahu﴾, meaning they impose it upon him and put it on him as a collar (ṭawq), in the sense of capacity (ṭāqa) or a necklace (qilāda). And ﴿yataṭawwaqūnahu﴾, meaning they bear its burden. And ﴿yuṭīqūnahu﴾ and ﴿yaṭīqūnahu﴾, on the basis that their original forms are ﴿yuṭayyūqūnahu﴾ and ﴿yataṭawwaqūnahu﴾, from the patterns fa'ala and taf'īl, with the meaning of ﴿yuṭawwiqūnahu﴾ and ﴿yataṭawwaqūnahu﴾. On these readings, there is a second meaning, which is the concession for one whom fasting tires and exhausts. These are the elderly men and women, regarding breaking the fast and the ransom. So this would be established, and the well-known reading has been interpreted in this sense, meaning: they fast with their utmost effort and capacity. ﴿Whoever volunteers good﴾: so he adds to the ransom. ﴿It is better for him﴾: so the volunteering or the good is better for him. ﴿And that you fast﴾, O you who are able, or you who are made to bear it and exert your capacity. Or you who grant concession in breaking the fast, so that the ill and the traveller are included under it. ﴿Is better for you﴾ than the ransom, or than volunteering good, or than both, and than postponing to make up the days. ﴿If you know﴾ the virtue of fasting and the clearing of one's obligation. Its response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, meaning: you would choose it. It has been said that its meaning is: if you are among the people of knowledge and reflection, you know that fasting is better for you than that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 185:

﴿The month of Ramadan﴾ is a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence) whose predicate (khabar) is what follows it. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimated form is "That is the month of Ramadan." Or it is an apposition (badal, a substitute noun) for "the fasting," with an omitted modifier (mudaf, the first term of an idafa construction), meaning: "Fasting is prescribed for you, the fasting of the month of Ramadan." It has also been read with the accusative (naṣb), either by supposing an implied verb, "fast" (ṣūmū), or as an object (maf'ul bihi). ﴿And that you fast﴾ is also read this way, though this reading is weak. Or it is an apposition for "a certain number of days" (ayyaman ma'dudat).

"Al-shahr" (month) comes from "shuhra" (fame, renown). "Ramadan" is a verbal noun (maṣdar) from "ramiḍa," meaning "to be scorched," and the word "month" was attached to it and made a proper name. It is treated as indeclinable (mamnu' min al-ṣarf), because of its status as a proper noun (ʿalamiyya) and its ending in -an. This is like the word "daʾya," which in "Ibn Daʾya" became a proper name for the crow, and is indeclinable because of its status as a proper noun and its feminine form.

The saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, "Whoever fasts Ramadan," is an example of an omitted modifier (mudaf), omitted because there is no risk of confusion. They named it so either because they were scorched in it by the heat of hunger and thirst, or because sins were burned away in it, or because it fell in the days of the scorching heat (ramḍ al-ḥarr), when they transferred the names of the months from the ancient language.

﴿Which the Qur'an was sent down in﴾: that is, the beginning of its descent occurred in it, and this was the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr). Or the Qur'an was sent down in it all at once to the lowest heaven, and then it was sent down piecemeal to the earth. Or the Qur'an was sent down concerning its matter, which is His saying: ﴿Fasting is prescribed for you﴾.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The scrolls of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) were sent down on the first night of Ramadan. The Torah was sent down on the sixth night (of it), the Gospel on the thirteenth, and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth."

The relative clause with its complement is the predicate of the subject, or its descriptor (ṣifa), and the predicate is the following ﴿so whoever witnesses﴾. The fa' (so) is for describing the subject with what includes the meaning of a conditional (shart). In this there is an indication that the descent of the Qur'an in it is the reason for its specific obligation of fasting. ﴿A guidance for mankind, and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (ḥālān) referring to the Qur'an, when it was sent down: it is guidance for mankind through its inimitability, and clear verses that guide to the truth and distinguish between it and falsehood through its wisdoms and rulings.

﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾: whoever is present in the month and is not a traveler, let him fast in it. The original form is "whoever witnesses it, let him fast in it," but the apparent noun was placed in the position of the first pronoun, for glorification. The word is put in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf), the preposition is omitted, and the second pronoun is put in the accusative by extension (ittisā'). It has also been said: ﴿whoever of you witnesses﴾ the crescent (hilāl) of the month, let him fast it, taking it as a direct object, as in your saying: "I witnessed the Friday," meaning "its prayer." In that case ﴿and whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾ specifies it, because the traveler and the sick person are among those who witness the month. Perhaps its repetition is for this reason, or so that it is not supposed to be abrogated (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one), as its counterpart was abrogated.

﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾: that is, He intends to make things easy for you and not to make them difficult for you. For this reason He permitted breaking the fast during travel and illness.

﴿And that you complete the period, and that you glorify Allah for having guided you, and that you may be grateful﴾: these are causes (ʿilal) for an omitted verb indicated by what came before, meaning: and He legislated the whole of what has been mentioned, namely the command to the witness to fast the month, the permission to make up missed days, and the observance of the number of days in which one broke the fast. The permission ﴿and that you complete the period﴾ to the end is according to a method of wrapping (laff), so that His saying ﴿and that you complete the period﴾ is the cause of the command to observe the number of days; ﴿and that you glorify Allah﴾ is the cause of the command to make up missed days and explain how; and ﴿and that you may be grateful﴾ is the cause of the permission and facilitation. Or each verb has its own cause. Or they are conjoined to an estimated cause, such as "so that He may make it easy for you," or "so that you may know what you know, and so that you may complete the period." It is also permissible for them to be conjoined to "ease," meaning: and He intends for you to complete the period, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They intend to extinguish the light of Allah﴾.

By glorification (al-takbir) is meant magnifying Allah through praise and commendation of Him, which is why it takes the preposition "ʿalā" (upon). It has been said that it refers to the glorification on the day of Fitr (the feast at the end of Ramadan), and it has been said that it refers to glorification at the sighting of the new moon. The word may also be a verbal noun (maṣdar). The predicate here is ﴿that to which He guided you﴾. It is narrated from ʿĀṣim, through the transmission of Abu Bakr, that the reading is "wa-li-tukammilū" with the doubled letter (tashdīd).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 186:

﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾. That is, say to them: "Indeed I am near." This is an illustration of the completeness of His knowledge of the deeds and words of the servants, and of His awareness of their states, by way of the likeness of one whose place is near to them.

It is narrated: "A Bedouin said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Is our Lord near, so that we may speak to Him in private, or far, so that we must call out to Him?' Then this was revealed: ﴿I answer the prayer of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾." This confirms nearness, and is a promise to the supplicant of a response.

﴿So let them respond to Me﴾: when I call them to faith and obedience, just as I respond to them when they call upon Me for their needs. ﴿And let them believe in Me﴾: a command to steadfastness and persistence in it. ﴿That they may be guided﴾: hoping to attain rushd (right guidance), which is reaching the truth. It is also read with the shin vowelled with fatha and with kasra.

Know that when He, exalted is He, commanded them to fast the month and to observe the prescribed number of days, and urged them to perform the duties of glorifying (takbir) and thanking (shukr), He followed this with this verse, which indicates that He is aware of their states, hears their words, answers their supplications, and recompenses them for their deeds, as an emphasis on this and an incitement to it. Then He explained the rulings of fasting, saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 187:

(p-126) ﴿It is made lawful for you, on the night of the fast, to go in unto your wives﴾. It is narrated that when the Muslims broke their fast at sunset, eating, drinking and intercourse became lawful for them until they performed the late night prayer (al-'isha') or went to sleep. Then: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, had intercourse after the 'isha' prayer, then regretted it, came to the Prophet ﷺ and apologized to him. Some men then stood up and confessed what they had done after the 'isha' prayer, and the verse was revealed.

"The night of the fast" means the night after which you wake up fasting. "Al-rafath" (intercourse, lit. obscene speech) is a metaphor for intercourse, because it is hardly free of "rafath", which is the explicit expression of what ought to be veiled by euphemism. It is construed with "ila" because it includes the sense of "ifda'" (reaching or going unto). It is chosen here to censure what they had committed, and for this reason God called it "khiyana" (betrayal). It is also read as "al-rufuth". ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾: this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining the reason for the permission, which is the difficulty of abstaining from them and the hardship of avoiding them because of constant mixing and close contact. Since a man and a woman embrace and each wraps around the other, they are likened to garments. al-Ja'di said:

"When the bedfellow bends her side, she bends and becomes a garment over him."

Or because each of them covers the state of the other and protects them from immorality. ﴿God knows that you were betraying yourselves﴾: wronging them by exposing them to punishment and diminishing their share of reward. "Ikhtiyan" is more intensive than "khiyana", as "iktisab" is more intensive than "kasb".

﴿So He turned to you﴾: when you repented from what you had committed. ﴿and pardoned you﴾: and erased its trace from you. ﴿So now, go in unto them﴾: since He abrogated the prohibition for you (naskh, abrogation). This contains evidence for the permissibility of abrogating the Sunna by the Qur'an. "Mubashara" means the contact of skins, used as a metaphor for intercourse. ﴿And seek what God has prescribed for you﴾: seek what He has decreed for you and recorded for you in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) of offspring. The meaning is that the one who has intercourse should intend offspring, since that is the wisdom behind creating desire, and marriage was legislated for this and not merely for satisfying desire. It is said that the prohibition here refers to 'azl (coitus interruption), and it is said that it refers to intercourse in the wrong place. The implied meaning is: seek the place which God has prescribed for you.

﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of the dawn﴾: He likened the first appearance of the dawn that stretches across the horizon, and the darkness of the night that extends along with it, to two threads, one white and one black. He mentioned the white thread by saying ﴿of the dawn﴾ and did not explain the black thread, since that is indicated by it. By this they move from metaphor (isti'ara) to simile (tamthil). It is also possible that "min" is partitive, since what appears is part of the dawn. It is narrated that when this verse was revealed, the dawn had not yet appeared, so some men took a black thread and a white thread and kept eating and drinking until they could distinguish them, and then this verse was revealed. If this report is authentic, it may have been before the beginning of Ramadan, and delaying clarification until the time of need is permissible. Or he first relied on the two threads being well known for this purpose, and then explicitly clarified it because it had become unclear to some of them. The permission for intercourse until dawn indicates that delaying the ritual bath (ghusl) until then is permissible, and that the fast of one who enters the morning in a state of major impurity (junub) is valid.

﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾: a clarification of its last time, which is night. This negates continuous fasting (sawm al-wisal), without eating between days.

﴿And do not go in unto them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques﴾: that is, while you are performing i'tikaf (seclusion) in them. "I'tikaf" is staying in the mosque with the intention of drawing near to God. "Mubashara" here means sexual intercourse. It is narrated from Qatada that a man would be in seclusion, then go out to his wife, have intercourse with her, and then return, so they were forbidden from this. This contains evidence that i'tikaf is to be performed in a mosque and is not restricted to a particular mosque. It also indicates that intercourse is prohibited during it and invalidates it, because a prohibition in acts of worship necessitates invalidity.

﴿These are the limits of God﴾: that is, the rulings that have been mentioned. ﴿So do not approach them﴾: He forbade approaching the limit that separates truth from falsehood, lest one come close to falsehood, let alone cross over it. As the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed every king has a sanctuary (hima), and the sanctuary of God is His prohibitions. Whoever grazes around the sanctuary is near to falling into it."

This is more emphatic than His saying ﴿So do not transgress them﴾. It is also possible that by ﴿the limits of God﴾ He means His prohibitions and His forbidden things.

﴿Thus﴾: like that clarification, ﴿God makes His signs clear to the people, so that they may be mindful﴾: of opposing the commands and prohibitions.

(p-127) ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾, i.e., let not some of you consume the property of others by a means that Allah, exalted is He, has not permitted.

"Bayn" (among) is in the accusative as an adverb of place or as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "amwāl" (wealth). ﴿And [do not] send it [i.e., its dispute] to the rulers (ḥukkām)﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the prohibited verb, or it is in the accusative by the implied "an" (that). "Idlāʾ" means casting or throwing, i.e., do not cast its litigation before the rulers. ﴿That you may consume﴾ through litigation. ﴿A portion﴾ (farīqan), a group. ﴿Of the wealth of people through sin﴾, by that which entails sin, such as false testimony and a false oath, or while you are entangled in sin. ﴿While you know﴾ that you are wrongdoers (mubṭilūn), for committing disobedience while knowing it is more heinous.

It is narrated that ʿAbdān al-Ḥaḍramī claimed against Imruʾ al-Qays al-Kindī a piece of land, and he had no proof. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled that Imruʾ al-Qays should swear an oath. He intended to do so, whereupon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price…﴾ until the end of the verse. He then refrained from the oath and handed over the land to ʿAbdān, and this verse was revealed.

In this is evidence that a judge's ruling does not take effect inwardly (bāṭinan), and this is supported by his statement, upon him be blessings and peace: "I am only a human being, and you bring your disputes to me. Perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I judge for him according to what I hear from him. Whoever I give him something from the right of his brother, I am only giving him a piece of Fire."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 189:

﴿They ask you about the new moons.﴾ Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah ibn Ghanm asked him, and they said: ("What is the matter with the crescent? It appears thin like a thread, then it grows until it becomes full, then it keeps decreasing until it returns as it began.") ﴿Say: they are timekeeping markers for people and for the pilgrimage.﴾ They asked about the wisdom behind the variation of the moon's state and the change of its condition, so God commanded him to answer that the apparent wisdom in this is that it serves as markers for people by which they fix their affairs, and as markers for the appointed acts of worship, by which their times are known, especially the pilgrimage, since the time is observed in it for performance (adda') and for making up (qada') a missed performance. Mawaqit (plural of miqat, an appointed time or place) derives from waqt (time). The difference between it and mudda (duration) and zaman (time): absolute duration is the extension of the movement of the celestial sphere from its beginning to its end; zaman is a divided duration; and waqt is the time appointed for a matter.

﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs.﴾ Abu 'Amr, Warsh and Hafs recited the word al-birr with a ḍamma on the bāʾ (البُيُوتَ, al-buyūt, read as above), and the rest read it with a kasra (البِرُّ, al-birr).

﴿But righteousness is in one who fears God.﴾ Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited the word lakin with a lighter pronunciation (لَكِنْ) and read al-birr in the nominative (البِرُّ). The Ansar (the Helpers of Medina), when they entered into the state of ihram, would not enter a house or a tent through its door; rather, they would enter through a hole or an opening behind it, and they considered that to be righteousness. So he made clear to them that it is not righteousness, and that righteousness is the righteousness of one who guards against what is forbidden and against desires. The connection of this to what precedes it is that they asked about both matters. Or, since he had mentioned that these are the markers of the pilgrimage, and this is also one of their practices in the pilgrimage, he mentioned it by way of digression (istitrad). Or, when they asked about what did not concern them and was not related to the knowledge of prophethood, and left off asking about what concerned them and was specific to the knowledge of prophethood, he followed up with mention of it, after answering what they had asked, to alert them that it is fitting for them to ask about such matters and to be concerned with knowing them. Or the purpose of it is to alert them to the inversion of their questioning, by likening their state to that of one who leaves the door of the house and enters from behind it. The meaning is: it is not righteousness that you invert your questions, but righteousness is the righteousness of one who guards against that and does not dare to do the like.

﴿And enter houses by their doors.﴾ Since there is no righteousness in deviating, go about affairs by their proper ways.

﴿And fear God﴾ in changing His rulings and in objecting to His acts.

﴿That you may prosper.﴾ So that you may attain guidance and righteousness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 190:

﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ strive to raise high His word and to strengthen His religion. ﴿those who fight you﴾ It is said: this was before they were commanded to fight all the polytheists, both those who fight and those who hold back. And it is said that its meaning is: those who make war upon you and from whom such fighting is expected, to the exclusion of others such as the elderly, the children, the monks and the women; or, all the disbelievers, for they are poised to fight the Muslims and intent upon it. What supports the first view is what has been related: that the polytheists barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and they made a treaty with him that he would return the following year and they would vacate Makkah for him, may Allah ennoble it, for three days. So he returned for the ʿUmrat al-Qadaʾ (the make-up ʿumrah), and the Muslims feared that they would not honour the terms for them and would fight them in the Sanctuary (al-Ḥaram), or in the sacred month, and they disliked that. So it was revealed: ﴿And do not transgress﴾ by initiating the fighting, or by fighting one who has a covenant, or by surprising them with it without a summons, or by mutilation, or by killing those whom you have been forbidden to kill. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾ He does not will good for them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 191:

﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ wherever you find them, whether within the sacred territory (ḥill) or within the Sacred Precinct (ḥaram). The root of thaqaf (to find, to overtake) is skill in attaining a thing, whether in knowledge or in action. Thus it carries the meaning of dominance, and for this reason it is used in that sense. He said:

"If you overtake me, then kill me... but whoever is overtaken, there is no eternity for him."

﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾ that is, from Makkah. This was done to those who did not embrace Islam on the day of the Conquest. ﴿And persecution (fitnah) is worse than killing﴾ that is, the trial by which a person is put to the test, such as expulsion from one's homeland, which is harder than killing because its hardship lasts and the soul suffers pain from it. It is also said: its meaning is their polytheism within the Sacred Precinct and their barring you from it is worse than your killing them in it. ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾ until they fight you in it, that is, do not initiate fighting with them and violate the sanctity of the Sacred Mosque. ﴿But if they fight you, then kill them﴾ so do not concern yourselves with fighting them, then, for it is they who violated its sanctity. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited, "And do not kill them until they kill you in it; but if they kill you..." The meaning is: until they kill some of you, as in their saying, "Banu Asad killed us." ﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ such is their recompense; they are dealt with in the same way as they dealt.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 192–193:

﴿And if they desist﴾ from fighting and disbelief, ﴿then indeed Allah is Ever-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾; He will forgive them what has passed. ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾, i.e., shirk, ﴿and religion is for Allah﴾, sincerely devoted to Him, with nothing of it belonging to Satan. ﴿And if they desist﴾ from shirk. ﴿Then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾. That is: do not transgress against those who have desisted, since it is not fitting that anyone be wronged except one who has wronged. He placed the cause (ʿillah) in the position of the ruling (ḥukm). The recompense for wrongdoing is named by its name for the sake of parallelism (mushakalah), as in His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾. Or, it means: if you assail those who have desisted, you will become wrongdoers, and the matter will be reversed upon you. The first fa' (in ﴿fa-in﴾ and ﴿fa-la﴾) indicates sequence (taʿqib), and the second fa' indicates the apodosis (jaza').

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 192–193:

﴿And if they desist﴾ from fighting and disbelief, ﴿then indeed Allah is Ever-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾; He will forgive them what has passed. ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾, i.e., shirk, ﴿and religion is for Allah﴾, sincerely devoted to Him, with nothing of it belonging to Satan. ﴿And if they desist﴾ from shirk. ﴿Then there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾. That is: do not transgress against those who have desisted, since it is not fitting that anyone be wronged except one who has wronged. He placed the cause (ʿillah) in the position of the ruling (ḥukm). The recompense for wrongdoing is named by its name for the sake of parallelism (mushakalah), as in His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾. Or, it means: if you assail those who have desisted, you will become wrongdoers, and the matter will be reversed upon you. The first fa' (in ﴿fa-in﴾ and ﴿fa-la﴾) indicates sequence (taʿqib), and the second fa' indicates the apodosis (jaza').

The sacred month for the sacred month, and the sacred things (are subject to) retaliation. [Al-Baydawi] Al-Mushrikun (the polytheists) fought them in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, in Dhu al-Qa'da, and it so happened that their departure for ʿUmrat al-Qada' (the "make-up" ʿumra) fell in that month. They disliked fighting them in it because of its sanctity, so it was said to them: this month is (answered) with that month, and its violation is (answered) with its violation, so do not be concerned about it. ﴿And the sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾ is an argument against them. That is, every sacred thing, which is what must be preserved, is subject to qisas (the law of equal retaliation). When they violated the sanctity of your month by obstructing you, then do to them the same, enter upon them by force, and kill them if they fight you. As He said: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾, and this is the summary of the affirmation. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding the helpers, and do not exceed what has not been permitted to you. ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾, so He will guard them and set their affairs right.

(p-129) ﴿And spend in the cause of God﴾, and do not hold back completely. ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾, by extravagance and by neglecting the means of livelihood; or by withholding from fighting (jihad) and from spending on it, for that strengthens the enemy and empowers them to destroy you. This is supported by what is reported from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "When God honored Islam and its adherents multiplied, we returned to our families and property, staying there and attending to them, and then this verse was revealed." Or it means by withholding and loving wealth, for that leads to everlasting destruction; and for this reason stinginess was called destruction. Originally, "halak" (destruction) means a thing reaching its end in corruption. Al-ilqa' (casting) means throwing a thing down, and it is followed by "ila" because it implies the sense of reaching an end; the "ba'" (in bi-aydikum) is extra, and "al-aydi" (hands) here means the selves. "Al-tahlukah," "al-halak," and "al-halak" are one and the same; thus it is a verbal noun like "al-tadirrah" and "al-tasirrah." The meaning is: do not bring your selves into destruction. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not make them (the hands) grasp the destruction, or: do not cast your selves into it with your own hands, so the object has been omitted. ﴿And do good﴾ in your deeds and your character, or show bounty to the needy. ﴿Indeed, God loves the good-doers﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 196:

﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah﴾. That is: perform both complete, fulfilling their rites, seeking the Face of Allah, the Exalted. On this reading it indicates that both are obligatory. This is supported by the recitation of those who read "وأقِيمُوا الحَجَّ والعُمْرَةَ لِلَّهِ" (and establish the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah), and by what Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, related: "It was said, 'O Messenger of Allah, is the ʿUmrah obligatory like the Hajj?' He said: 'No, but if you perform it, it is better for you.'"

This is opposed by what has been related: "A man said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, 'I found the Hajj and the ʿUmrah written upon me, so I entered into the state of ihram (ritual consecration) for both together.' He said: 'You have been guided to the sunnah of your Prophet.'" It cannot be said that he explained "found written" by his saying "I entered into ihram for both," so that obligation would be due to his entering ihram for them, because he placed the entering into ihram upon the finding, and that indicates that the finding is the cause of entering into ihram, not the reverse. It has been said that completing them means that you enter into ihram for both from the dwelling of your family, or that you make a separate journey for each of them, or that you devote the intention purely to them without mixing them with a worldly purpose, or that the expenditure be lawful.

﴿But if you are prevented﴾: that is, if you are hindered. It is said: "ḥaṣarahu al-ʿaduww" and "aḥṣarahu" when he confines him and prevents him from proceeding, like "ṣaddahu" and "aṣadda." The intended meaning is the enemy's blockade, according to Malik and al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on them both, because of His saying: ﴿But when you are secure﴾, and because of its revelation concerning al-Hudaybiyyah, and because of the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "There is no blockade except the blockade of the enemy." Every prevention by an enemy, or by illness, or by other than these, is included according to Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, based on what has been related from him, upon him be prayers and peace: "Whoever is injured by a break or a limp has been released, and upon him is the Hajj in the following year."

This is weak, and it is interpreted as applying when the release by it was made a stipulation, based on his saying, upon him be prayers and peace, to Dubaʿah bint al-Zubayr: "Perform the Hajj, and make a stipulation, and say: 'O Allah, my place of release is where You hold me back.'"

﴿Then whatever sacrificial offering (hady) is feasible﴾: then upon you is what is feasible, or then what is obligatory is what is feasible, or then offer what is feasible. The meaning is: if the muḥrim (one in ihram) is blockaded and wishes to release himself from ihram, he is released by slaughtering a sacrificial animal (hady) that is available to him, a camel, a cow, or a sheep, wherever he is blockaded, according to the majority. This is because he, upon him be prayers and peace, slaughtered animals in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, and that place was outside the sacred precinct (ḥill). According to Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, he sends it, and he sets for the one sent with it a day of appointment. When the day comes and he thinks that it has been slaughtered, he is released, based on His saying: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial offering reaches its place of sacrifice (maḥill)﴾. That is: do not release yourselves until you know that the offering sent to the sacred precinct has reached its place, that is, the place where it must be slaughtered. The earlier scholars interpreted the reaching of the offering to its place of release as its slaughter wherever slaughter is permitted, whether in the non-sacred area or in the sacred precinct. Restricting it to the offering indicates that there is no obligation of qaḍāʾ (making up). Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, said: qaḍāʾ is obligatory.

The word maḥill, with a kasra, is used for both a place and a time. Hady is the plural of hadyah, like jadiyy and jadyah. It has also been read as "al-hadiyy," the plural of hadiyyah, like maṭiyy for maṭiyyah.

﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾: an illness that compels him to shave.

﴿Or has an injury upon his head﴾, such as a wound or lice. ﴿Then a compensation (fidyah)﴾: then upon him is a compensation if he shaves. ﴿Of fasting, or charity, or sacrifice (nusuk)﴾ is an explanation of the kind of fidyah. As for its amount, it has been related that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said to Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah: "Perhaps your vermin have harmed you?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Shave, and fast three days, or give charity of a farq to six needy persons, or sacrifice a sheep."

The farq is three ṣāʿs.

﴿But when you are secure﴾ from the blockade, or you were in a state of ease and safety. ﴿Then whoever performs tamattuʿ (combining ʿUmrah with Hajj) until the Hajj﴾: whoever takes enjoyment and benefit by drawing near to Allah through the ʿUmrah before benefiting by drawing near through the Hajj in its months. It has been said: whoever takes enjoyment after release from his ʿUmrah, by making lawful the prohibitions of ihram, until he enters into ihram for the Hajj.

﴿Then whatever sacrificial offering is feasible﴾: then upon him is a sacrifice that he can afford, because of the tamattuʿ. It is a blood-sacrifice for compensation (damm jabr), which he slaughters when he enters into ihram for the Hajj, and he may not eat from it. Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, said that it is a blood-sacrifice of worship (nusk), so it is like the udhiyah (sacrifice of Eid).

﴿But whoever does not find﴾, that is, the offering, ﴿then a fast of three days during the Hajj﴾: during the days of occupation with it after entering into ihram and before release. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "during its months, between the two ihrams." It is preferable to fast the seventh, eighth, and ninth of Dhu al-Hijjah. Fasting on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Naḥr) and the Days of Tashriq is not permitted according to the majority.

﴿And seven when you return﴾ to your families. This is one of the two opinions of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him. Or when you depart and have finished its acts. This is his second opinion, and the position of Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him. It has been read "sabʿatan" in the accusative, as a conjunction with the position (maḥall) of "thalathat ayyam."

﴿That is ten﴾: a summation of the calculation. Its benefit is that no one should suppose that the particle "wa" means "or," as in your saying "he sat with al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin." And that the number should be known in total as it was known in detail, for most of the Arabs did not reckon well. And that by "seven" is meant the number itself, not the multitude, for it is used for both.

﴿Complete﴾ is a descriptive qualifier that emphasizes and conveys exaggeration in preserving the number. Or it clarifies the completeness of the ten, for it is the first complete number, since by it the units end and their ranks are completed. Or it restricts, specifying the completeness of its substitution for the sacrificial offering.

﴿That﴾ is a pointer to the ruling mentioned, according to us. Tamattuʿ, according to Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, is not permitted, nor is qirān (combining), for the residents of al-Masjid al-Ḥaram according to him. So whoever of them does that, that is, tamattuʿ, upon him is a blood-sacrifice for a violation (damm jināyah).

﴿For one whose family is not present at al-Masjid al-Ḥaram﴾. This refers to whoever is within the sacred precinct at the distance for shortening prayer (qaṣr), according to us, for whoever is closer than that is a resident of the sacred precinct or has the ruling of one. Whoever has his dwelling beyond the miqat (boundary point) according to him; and the people of the non-sacred area according to Tawus; and non-Meccans according to Malik.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in preserving His commands and prohibitions, especially in the Hajj. ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever does not fear Him, so that knowledge of Him may restrain you from disobedience.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 197:

﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾ meaning, its time is (these months). Like your saying, "The cold is two months." ﴿Known﴾: well-known. They are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah up to the night of sacrifice (laylat al-nahr) according to us, and the ten days according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. And all of Dhu al-Hijjah according to Malik. Based on the difference of opinion, whether what is meant by its time is the time of its ihram, or the time of its acts and rites, or what no other rites are proper in absolutely, Malik disliked performing 'umrah in the remainder of Dhu al-Hijjah. And Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, although he considered entering ihram for it before Shawwal valid, disliked it. It is called "months" though two months and part of a month, to treat the part as standing for the whole, or to apply the plural to what is more than one. ﴿Whoever undertakes the Hajj therein﴾: whoever makes it obligatory upon himself by entering ihram therein according to us, or by the talbiyah or driving the sacrificial animal according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. This is evidence for what al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, held, that whoever enters ihram for Hajj is bound to complete it. ﴿Then there shall be no obscenity (rafath)﴾: no sexual intercourse, or no vulgar speech. ﴿Nor wickedness (fusuq)﴾: nor going beyond the limits of the Shari'ah through sins and committing prohibited acts. ﴿Nor disputing (jidal)﴾: nor quarrelling with servants and companions. ﴿In the Hajj﴾: during its days. The negation of the three is in the form of a prohibition, for emphasis and to indicate that they are by nature such that they should not exist; and whatever among them is abhorrent in itself is more abhorrent during Hajj, like wearing silk in prayer. And adorning the recitation of the Qur'an with melody, because it is a departure from the demands of natural disposition and custom toward pure worship. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and the first (group) read with raising (rafʿ), in the sense: "let there be no obscenity and no wickedness." The third (group) reads with fatha, in the sense of informing that there is no dispute in the Hajj; that is because the Quraysh used to form alliances with the rest of the Arabs and would stand at the Sacred Mash'ar, so the dispute was removed by being commanded to also stand at 'Arafat. ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾: an exhortation to good, which follows the prohibition of evil so that it may replace it and take its place. ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety (taqwa)﴾: and take for your return (ma'ad) piety, for it is the best provision. It was said: it was revealed concerning the people of Yemen, who used to perform Hajj without taking provisions, saying, "We are reliant upon God," and so they became a burden upon people; so they were commanded to take provisions and to avoid burdening others and imposing upon people by begging. ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾: for the essence of intellect is the fear of Allah and His piety. He exhorted them to piety, then commanded that its object be Allah the Exalted alone, so that one disassociates from everything other than Him; and this is the demand of reason free from the taints of desire, and therefore this address is specific to "people of understanding."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 198:

﴿There is no blame upon you that you seek﴾ i.e., "in that you seek," i.e., you desire (tabtaghu, "seek," "pursue"). ﴿bounty from your Lord﴾, i.e., provision and sustenance from Him, meaning profit through trade. It was said: ʿUkaz, Majannah and Dhu al-Majaz were their markets in the Jahiliyyah, which they held during the seasons of the Hajj, and their livelihoods came from them. When Islam came, they felt sinful about it, and so this was revealed. ﴿Then when you pour forth from ʿArafat﴾, i.e., you move on from it in large numbers, from "afadtu al-ma'" ("I poured the water") when you pour it out in abundance. Its original form is "afadtum anfusakum" ("you pour forth yourselves"), and the object was omitted, just as it is omitted in "dafa'tu min al-Basrah" ("I departed from Basra"). ﴿ʿArafat﴾ is a plural that has been named as a proper noun, like Adhri'at. It is declined with tanwin and kasra, and it has both definiteness (ʿalamiyyah) and feminine form, because the tanwin of the plural is the tanwin of correspondence (muqabalah), not the tanwin of declension (tamkin); and for this reason it may be combined with the definite article (al-). The loss of the kasra follows the loss of the tanwin without compensation, due to the absence of declension (sarf); but here the situation is not like that. Or, because the feminine marker is either the ta' mentioned, and it is not a feminine ta', but rather together with the alif before it is the sign of the feminine plural; or it is a ta' that is assumed, as in "Su'ad" — and assuming it is not valid, because the mentioned ta' prevents it, inasmuch as it is like a substitute for it, being specific to the feminine, like the ta' of "bint." The site was named ʿArafah because it is an epithet of Ibrahim, peace be upon him: when he saw it, he recognized it (ʿarafahu). Or because Jibril, peace be upon him, used to go around with him among the holy sites, and when he showed him it, he said, "I have recognized (qad ʿaraftu)." Or because Adam and Eve met there and recognized one another (fa-taʿarafa). Or because people recognize one another there. ʿArafat is used for emphasis in this sense, and it is among the improvised (murtajalah) names, unless it is made the plural of ʿarif. In this is evidence for the obligation of standing there, because pouring forth is not possible except after it, and it is commanded by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then pour forth﴾. Or it is a prelude to the remembrance that is commanded, and this is open to question, since remembrance is not obligatory but recommended. And on the assumption that it is obligatory, it is a conditional obligation, not an absolute obligation, so that its preliminary is not obligatory, and the command to it is not absolute. ﴿Remember Allah﴾ by the talbiyah, the tahlil, and supplication. It was said: by the prayer of the two evening prayers. ﴿at the Sacred Monument﴾: a mountain upon which the imam stands, called "Quzah." It was said: what lies between the two passes (ma'zimayn) of ʿArafah and the valley of Muhassir. The first view is supported by what Jabir narrated: "When the Prophet, peace be upon him, prayed the dawn prayer — meaning at Muzdalifah, in the dimness — he mounted his she-camel until he reached the Sacred Monument, and he supplicated, glorified, and declared Allah's unity, and he remained standing until it became light." It was called a "mash'ar" because it is the mark of worship, and it was described as "sacred" because of its sanctity. The meaning of "at the Sacred Monument" is: from what is adjacent to it and near to it, for that is more excellent; otherwise, all of Muzdalifah is a standing place except the valley of Muhassir. ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾: as He has taught you, or remember Him with a good remembrance, as He has guided you with a good guidance to the rites and others. The "ma" is either verbal-masdariyyah or kafah. ﴿And indeed you were before it﴾: i.e., before the guidance. ﴿among those astray﴾: i.e., ignorant of faith and obedience. "In" here is the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and the "lam" is the distinguishing lam. It was said: "in" is negating and the "lam" has the meaning of "illa," like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed we think you are among the liars﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 199:

﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ That is, from ʿArafat, not from Muzdalifah. The address is to the Quraysh, who used to stand at Jamʿ (Muzdalifah) while the rest of the people stood at ʿArafat, considering this a form of superiority over them, so they were commanded to be equal to them. And ﴿then﴾ (thumma) is for the difference between the two departures, as in your saying: "Be good to people, then do not be good to someone other than the noble." It was also said: [the departure is] from Muzdalifah to Mina after the departure from ʿArafat to it, and the address is general. It is also read "an-nāsi" with a kasra, meaning "the forgetful one" (an-nāsī), referring to Adam, from the words of the Exalted and Glorified: ﴿but he forgot (fa-nasiya)﴾. The meaning is that the departure from ʿArafat is an ancient legislated practice, so do not change it. ﴿And seek forgiveness from God﴾ for your ignorance (jāhiliyyah) in altering the rites and the like. ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful﴾ — He forgives the sin of the one who seeks forgiveness and bestows His favour upon him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 200:

﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasik)﴾ i.e., when you have completed the acts of worship of the Hajj and finished with them. ﴿then remember God as you remember your fathers﴾ i.e., remember Him much and be thorough in it, just as you do when you recall your fathers in boasting. The Arabs, when they had completed their rites, would stand at Mina between the mosque and the mountain, and they would mention the glorious deeds of their forefathers and the fine days of their people. ﴿or with even greater remembrance﴾ The phrase may be in the genitive, in coordination with "remembrance" (dhikr), making the remembrance the one who remembers in a metaphorical sense; the meaning being: remember God as you remember your fathers, or as a remembrance greater than that and more eloquent. Or it is in the genitive by virtue of what is attached to it, with weakness, in the sense of "or as the remembrance of a people greater than you in remembrance." It may also be in the accusative by coordination with ﴿your fathers﴾, with "remembrance" being an action of the mentioned, in the sense: "or as your remembrance of something of greater mention than your fathers." Or it is governed by an implied verb indicated by the meaning, its estimate being: "or be more intense in remembering God than you are in remembering your fathers."

﴿Among the people there is he who says﴾ This is a division of those who remember: into one who is slight (muqill), who seeks by the remembrance of God Most High only the world, and one who is abundant (mukthir), who seeks by it the good of both abodes. The intended purpose is to encourage abundance in remembrance and to guide toward it. ﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾ i.e., make our giving and our bounty be in this world. ﴿and he has no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾ i.e., no portion or lot, because his aspiration is confined to this world; or [it means] from the seeking of a share (khalaq).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 201–202:

﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good,"﴾ meaning health, sufficiency (al-kafaf) and success in goodness. ﴿And in the Hereafter good,﴾ meaning reward and mercy. ﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire,﴾ by pardon and forgiveness. The saying of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: the good in this world is a righteous wife, and in the Hereafter it is the maiden of paradise (al-hawraʾ). The punishment of the Fire is a wicked wife. The saying of al-Hasan: the good in this world is knowledge and worship, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. ﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire,﴾ its meaning is: guard us from desires, sins, and what leads to the Fire, these being examples of what is intended.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the second group. It has been said it refers to both. ﴿For them there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ That is, of its kind, and that is its recompense; or because of it, as in His saying, ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾; or of what they asked for, We give them from it what We have decreed. Supplication is called "earning" because it is one of the deeds. ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ He reckons with His servants, despite their multitude and the multitude of their deeds, in the span of a glance; or it is imminent that He establish the Resurrection and call people to account. So hasten to the acts of obedience and earn good deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 201–202:

﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good,"﴾ meaning health, sufficiency (al-kafaf) and success in goodness. ﴿And in the Hereafter good,﴾ meaning reward and mercy. ﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire,﴾ by pardon and forgiveness. The saying of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: the good in this world is a righteous wife, and in the Hereafter it is the maiden of paradise (al-hawraʾ). The punishment of the Fire is a wicked wife. The saying of al-Hasan: the good in this world is knowledge and worship, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. ﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire,﴾ its meaning is: guard us from desires, sins, and what leads to the Fire, these being examples of what is intended.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the second group. It has been said it refers to both. ﴿For them there is a share of what they have earned.﴾ That is, of its kind, and that is its recompense; or because of it, as in His saying, ﴿Because of their sins they were drowned﴾; or of what they asked for, We give them from it what We have decreed. Supplication is called "earning" because it is one of the deeds. ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾ He reckons with His servants, despite their multitude and the multitude of their deeds, in the span of a glance; or it is imminent that He establish the Resurrection and call people to account. So hasten to the acts of obedience and earn good deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 203:

﴿And remember God during the appointed days.﴾ Glorify Him (takbir) after the prayers, at the slaughtering of the sacrificial animals, at the stoning of the pillars (al-jimar), and at other times during the days of tashriq (the days of drying meat, the 11th to 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah). ﴿Whoever hastens in two days﴾: whoever hastens the departure (al-nafr). ﴿In two days﴾: the Day of al-Qarr and the day after it, meaning that whoever departs on the second day of tashriq after stoning the pillars, according to us, and before the dawn breaks according to Abu Hanifa. ﴿There is no sin upon him﴾ for his hastening. ﴿And whoever delays, there is no sin upon him﴾: whoever delays the departure until he stones on the third day after the decline of the sun (al-zawal). Abu Hanifa said: it is permissible to perform the stoning before the decline of the sun. The meaning of negating sin from both hastening and delaying is giving the choice between them, and a refutation of the people of the pre-Islamic era (jahiliyya), for among them were those who considered the one who hastens sinful, and among them were those who considered the one who delays sinful. ﴿For the one who fears God﴾: that is, the choice mentioned, or the rulings mentioned, are for the one who fears God, because he is truly the pilgrim (al-hajj) and the one who benefits from it, or for his sake, so that he is not harmed by abandoning what concerns him of the two. ﴿And fear God﴾ in all matters of your affairs, so that He may take account of you. ﴿And know that you will be gathered to Him﴾ for recompense after resurrection. The origin of al-hashr is gathering and joining what is scattered.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 204:

﴿And among the people is one whose speech impresses you in the life of this world﴾ it pleases you and becomes great in your estimation. Ta'ajjub (wonder, astonishment) is a bewilderment that comes over a person due to his ignorance of the cause of what he marvels at. ﴿In the life of this world﴾ is connected to the speech, meaning: what he says concerning the affairs of this world and the means of livelihood. Or, it is in the sense of "the world," since it is intended for claiming love and displaying faith. Or, "impresses you" means: his speech impresses you in this world with its sweetness and eloquence, but does not impress you in the Hereafter, because of the bewilderment and speechlessness that seize him, or because he will not be permitted to speak. ﴿And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ he swears and calls upon Allah as witness that what is in his heart agrees with his words. ﴿Yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾ the most intense in enmity and contention against the Muslims. Khisam (contention) is the act of disputing, and it may be the plural of khasm (opponent), like sa'b and si'ab, meaning the most fierce of adversaries in hostility.

It was said that this was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq al-Thaqafi, who had a handsome appearance and sweet speech, who professed loyalty to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and claimed to be Muslim.

It was also said that it refers to the hypocrites in general.

﴿And when he turns away﴾ he withdraws and departs from you. It is also said: when he prevails and becomes a ruler (wali). ﴿He strives in the land to spread corruption therein and destroy the crops and the livestock﴾, as al-Akhnas did to the tribe of Thaqif, when he attacked them by night, burned their crops and destroyed their livestock. Or it is like what bad rulers (wulat al-su') do through killing and destruction, or through injustice, such that God withholds the rain because of their wickedness, and the crops and livestock perish. ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾: He does not approve of it, so beware of His anger for it.

﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear God," arrogance takes hold of him to sin﴾: pride and the zealotry of the Days of Ignorance (hamiyyat al-jahiliyyah) carry him to the sin which he is commanded to avoid, out of obstinacy. It derives from your saying "akhadhtuhu bi-kadha" (I held him to such-and-such), when you compel him to it and bind him to it. ﴿Hell will suffice him﴾: it is sufficient for him as recompense and punishment. Jahannam (Hell) is a proper name for the abode of punishment, and in origin it is synonymous with "al-nar" (the Fire). It is also said to be an arabized (mu'rab) word. ﴿And how wretched is the resting-place﴾: this is the answer to an implied oath (qasam muqaddar), and the one singled out for censure is omitted, since it is known. Al-mihad means the bed, and it is also said to be what one lies down upon for the side.

﴿And when he turns away﴾ he withdraws and departs from you. It is also said: when he prevails and becomes a ruler (wali). ﴿He strives in the land to spread corruption therein and destroy the crops and the livestock﴾, as al-Akhnas did to the tribe of Thaqif, when he attacked them by night, burned their crops and destroyed their livestock. Or it is like what bad rulers (wulat al-su') do through killing and destruction, or through injustice, such that God withholds the rain because of their wickedness, and the crops and livestock perish. ﴿And God does not love corruption﴾: He does not approve of it, so beware of His anger for it.

Al-mihad means the bed, and it is also said to be what one lies down upon for the side.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 207:

﴿And among the people is one who sells his soul⁠﻿ seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ — he sells it, i.e., he expends it in jihad, or he enjoins what is good and forbids what is evil, even to the point of being killed. ﴿Seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ — desiring His good pleasure. It is said: this verse was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinan al-Rumi, whom the polytheists seized and tortured in order to make him apostatize. He said: "I am an old man; I shall be of no benefit to you if I am with you, nor any harm to you if I am against you. So leave me alone with what I am upon, and take my wealth." They accepted this from him, and he went to Medina. ﴿And Allah is Compassionate toward the servants﴾ — in that He guided them to such a sale and obligated them to jihad, thereby exposing them to the reward of the warriors and the martyrs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verses 208–209:

﴿O you who believe, enter into submission (al-silm) completely.﴾ *Al-silm*, with a kasra or a fatha on the sin, means submission and obedience, and for this reason it is also used for reconciliation (*sulh*) and for Islam. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha, and the rest read it with a kasra. *Kaffatan* is a noun for the whole (*ism li-l-jumlah*), because it restrains the parts (p-134) from dispersion. It is a circumstantial (*hal*, the accusative of state) from the pronoun or from *al-silm*, because *al-silm* is feminine like *al-harb* (war). The poet said:

*Of peace, take from it what pleases you,*
*and of war, a few sips of its breaths suffice you.*

The meaning is: submit to God and obey Him wholly, outwardly and inwardly. The address is to the hypocrites. Or it means: enter into Islam with your entirety and do not mix anything else with it. Or the address is to believers among the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*), for after their conversion to Islam they still glorified the Sabbath and forbade camels and their milk. Or it means: enter into all of God's laws by believing in all the prophets and books, and the address is to the People of the Book. Or it means: enter into all the branches and rulings of Islam, so do not neglect anything, and the address is to the Muslims.

﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ by dispersion and division. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, manifest in enmity.

﴿And if you slip﴾ away from entering into submission ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾, the signs and arguments that testify that it is the truth, ﴿then know that God is Mighty﴾, whom retribution cannot overpower, ﴿Wise﴾, who does not take retribution except with right.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verses 208–209:

﴿O you who believe, enter into submission (al-silm) completely.﴾ *Al-silm*, with a kasra or a fatha on the sin, means submission and obedience, and for this reason it is also used for reconciliation (*sulh*) and for Islam. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha, and the rest read it with a kasra. *Kaffatan* is a noun for the whole (*ism li-l-jumlah*), because it restrains the parts (p-134) from dispersion. It is a circumstantial (*hal*, the accusative of state) from the pronoun or from *al-silm*, because *al-silm* is feminine like *al-harb* (war). The poet said:

*Of peace, take from it what pleases you,*
*and of war, a few sips of its breaths suffice you.*

The meaning is: submit to God and obey Him wholly, outwardly and inwardly. The address is to the hypocrites. Or it means: enter into Islam with your entirety and do not mix anything else with it. Or the address is to believers among the People of the Book (*Ahl al-Kitab*), for after their conversion to Islam they still glorified the Sabbath and forbade camels and their milk. Or it means: enter into all of God's laws by believing in all the prophets and books, and the address is to the People of the Book. Or it means: enter into all the branches and rulings of Islam, so do not neglect anything, and the address is to the Muslims.

﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ by dispersion and division. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾, manifest in enmity.

﴿And if you slip﴾ away from entering into submission ﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾, the signs and arguments that testify that it is the truth, ﴿then know that God is Mighty﴾, whom retribution cannot overpower, ﴿Wise﴾, who does not take retribution except with right.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 210:

﴿Are they waiting﴾ is a question with the meaning of negation (istifham fi ma'na al-nafy), and for this reason what follows it is introduced with ﴿except﴾. ﴿That Allah should come to them﴾, i.e., that His command (amr) or His punishment (ba's) should come to them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or that the command of your Lord should come﴾ [16:33] and ﴿Then Our punishment came upon them﴾ [7:4]. Or it means that Allah Himself should come to them with His punishment, and the thing brought is omitted because it is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: (Indeed, Allah is Mighty and Wise). ﴿In canopies﴾, plural of ẓullah (canopy), like qullah and qulal, meaning that which shades you. It has been read as ẓilal, like qilal. ﴿Of the clouds﴾, the white clouds. The punishment comes to them within them because the cloud is the place where mercy is expected (maẓinnat al-raḥmah); so when punishment comes from it, it is more dreadful, for evil that comes from where one does not expect it is harder to bear, so how much more when it comes from where one expects good. ﴿And the angels﴾: they are the intermediaries in bringing His command, or they are those who literally bring His punishment. It has also been read in the genitive (bi'l-jarr), in coordination with ﴿ẓulal﴾ or ﴿al-ghamam﴾. ﴿And the matter is decided﴾: the matter of their destruction is completed and finished with, the past tense being used in place of the future because it is near and its occurrence is certain. It has also been read as ﴿qaḍā'u al-amr﴾ (the decree of the matter) in coordination with ﴿the angels﴾. ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read it in the passive voice, as being from al-rāji' (returned); the rest read it in the active voice with the feminine form, except Ya'qub, as being from al-ruju' (return). It has also been read with the masculine form and the passive voice.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 211:

﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾ — an imperative addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone. The purpose of this question is to rebuke them. ﴿How many a clear sign have We given them﴾ — a manifest miracle, or a sign in the Books bearing witness to the truth and rightness through the hands of the prophets. "Kam" (how many) is either a declarative (khabariyyah) or an interrogative (istifhamiyyah) used for affirmation (muqarrirah), and its place in the sentence is either the accusative, as a direct object, or the nominative, as a subject (mubtada'), with the returning pronoun (a'id) from the predicate to the subject omitted. "Ayah" is its specifier (tamyiz). "Min" is for emphasis (lil-fasl). ﴿And whoever substitutes the blessing of God﴾ — that is, the signs of God, for they are the cause of guidance, which is the greatest of blessings; he makes them a cause of misguidance and an increase in filth (rijs), or by distortion (tahrif) and deviant interpretation (ta'wil za'igh). ﴿After it has come to him﴾ — after it has reached him and he has been able to know it. This contains an implied reproach that they altered it after they had understood it, and for this reason it has been said that its implied reading is: "So they altered it, and whoever alters..." ﴿Indeed, God is severe in punishment﴾ — so He will punish him with the most severe punishment, because he committed the gravest of crimes.

(p-135) ﴿The life of this world has been made alluring to those who disbelieve﴾. It has been made beautiful in their eyes and its love has been infused into their hearts, to the point that they grow greedy for it and turn away from anything else. The one who truly makes it alluring is God Most High, since there is nothing but that He is its doer. This is confirmed by the reading "zayyana" (with the verb in the active voice). Both Satan and the animal faculty (al-quwwa al-hayawaniyya), together with the splendid qualities and desirable things that God has created within it, are made alluring by way of presentation (bi-al-'ard).

﴿And they mock those who believe﴾. He means the poor among the believers, such as Bilal, 'Ammar and Suhayb; that is, they belittle them and ridicule them for their rejection of this world and their devotion to the next. The particle "min" here marks the starting point (li-al-ibtida'), as if they had made the mockery originate from themselves. ﴿But those who are God-fearing will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, because they are in the highest ranks ('illiyyun) while those others are in the lowest of the low (asfal al-safilin); or because they are in honor while those others are in humiliation; or because those who mocked them in this world will be looked down upon by them and mock them as they mocked them in this world. The phrase "and those who are God-fearing" follows "those who believe" to indicate that the believers are God-fearing and that their being elevated is due to their piety.

﴿And God provides for whom He wills﴾ in both abodes, ﴿without reckoning﴾, that is, without measure. He thus widens provision in this world at times as a gradual lure (istidraj) and at other times as a trial (ibtila').

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 213:

﴿Mankind were one community﴾, agreed upon the truth between Adam and Idris, or Noah, or after the Flood; or agreed upon ignorance and disbelief in the interval (fatrah) between Idris or Noah [and the following period]. ﴿So Allah sent forth the prophets as bearers of good tidings and as warners﴾, i.e., they differed, so Allah sent forth [the prophets]; the verb is elided because of the indication of His saying "concerning that over which they differed." It is related from Ka'b (who said): "What I know of the number of the prophets is one hundred and twenty-four thousand, and the messengers among them are three hundred and thirteen, and those mentioned in the Qur'an by name are twenty-eight." ﴿And He sent down with them the Book﴾, meaning by it the genus (i.e., the books collectively), and not meaning that a separate book was sent down with each one of them, for most of them did not have a book specific to them; rather, they would follow the books of those before them. ﴿With the truth﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the Book," i.e., accompanied by the truth and bearing witness to it. ﴿That He might judge between the people﴾, i.e., Allah, or the prophet who was sent, or His Book. ﴿Concerning that over which they differed﴾: concerning the truth over which they differed, or concerning that which had become confused for them. ﴿And none differed concerning it﴾: concerning the truth, or the Book. ﴿except those who were given it﴾, i.e., the Book revealed to remove disagreement; that is, they reversed the matter, making what was sent down, which was meant to remove disagreement, a cause of its entrenchment. ﴿After clear proofs had come to them, out of envy among themselves﴾: out of mutual jealousy among them and injustice, due to their greed for worldly things. ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth over which they differed﴾, i.e., to the truth about which whoever differed had differed. ﴿By His permission﴾ is an explanation of "over which they differed"; ﴿by His leave﴾: by His command, or by His will and gentleness. ﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾: whoever travels it does not go astray.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 214:

﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise﴾ He addressed this to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers after mentioning the disagreement of the nations over the prophets after the signs had come, as encouragement for them to remain steadfast despite their opponents. The ﴿Or (am)﴾ is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and the meaning of the interrogative hamzah in it is denial. ﴿And not yet has come to you﴾ meaning: and there has not come to you. The origin of "lamma" (not yet) is "lam" with "ma" added to it, and it carries the sense of expectation; for this reason it is considered the counterpart of "qad" (already). ﴿The example of those who passed away before you﴾ their condition, which is an example of severity. ﴿Misfortune and adversity touched them﴾ is an explanation of it, in the form of a resumption (isti'naf). ﴿And they were shaken﴾ and were driven into a violent state of agitation by what befell them of hardships. ﴿Until the Messenger and those who believed with him said﴾ because the severity had reached its extreme and the period had stretched on, to the point that the cords of patience were cut. Nafi' read "yaqulu" (says) in the nominative, on the basis that it is a narration of a past state, like your saying "he fell ill, to the point that they had no hope for him." ﴿When will the help of God come?﴾ as a request for its hastening, because of its delay. ﴿Surely the help of God is near﴾ is a resumption on the assumption of a saying, meaning: they were told this as a kindness to them, to bring them to their request for the swift help. In this is an indication that reaching God Most High and attaining honor in His presence is through renouncing desire and pleasures, and enduring hardships and disciplines, as the prayer and peace of God be upon him said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires."

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 215:**

﴿They ask you what they should spend.﴾ «From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh al-Ansari was an aged, decrepit man of great wealth, and he said, "O Messenger of Allah, what should we spend of our wealth, and where should we place it?" So it was revealed: ﴿Say: whatever good you spend is for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer.﴾» The questioner asked about the one who spends, but he was answered by explaining the recipients, because the reckoning of expenditure is based upon them, and because the question of ʿAmr was in view even though he is not mentioned in the verse. He limited the explanation of the spender to what is contained in His saying ﴿whatever good you spend﴾. ﴿And whatever good you do﴾ carries the sense of a conditional. ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾ is its response (jawab), meaning: if you do good, Allah knows its reality and will fully repay its reward. There is nothing in the verse that contradicts the obligation of zakat (obligatory alms), such that it would be abrogated (naskh) by it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 216:

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, while it is hateful to you.﴾ It is burdensome for you and naturally disliked. (Karh) is a verbal noun (masdar) used as an adjective for emphasis, or it is an form (fi'l) with the meaning of a passive participle (maf'ul), like (khayr). It was also read with a fatha (kaŕh) as a dialectal variant (lughah) of it, like (ḍa'f) and (ḍu'f), or it means compulsion (ikrah) in a metaphorical sense, as if they were compelled to it because of its severity and the greatness of its hardship, like the words of God Most High: ﴿His mother bore him with hardship, and gave birth to him with hardship﴾. ﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing while it is good for you﴾, which is all that they were charged with, for the nature dislikes it, and it is the criterion of their welfare and the cause of their success. ﴿And it may be that you love a thing while it is bad for you﴾, which is all that they were forbidden from, for the soul loves it and desires it, and it leads them to ruin. He mentioned (it may be) because when the soul is trained, the matter is reversed for it. ﴿And God knows﴾ what is good for you. ﴿And you do not know﴾ that. In this is evidence that the rulings follow the predominant benefits even if their specific nature is not known.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 217:

﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it.﴾ It is related that (ﷺ) the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, sent ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh, the son of his paternal aunt, at the head of a military expedition (sariyya) in Jumada al-Akhirah, two months before Badr, to lie in wait for a caravan of the Quraysh, in which were ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Hadrami and three others with him. They killed him, took two prisoners, and seized the caravan, which contained merchandise from al-Ta'if. This occurred on the first day of Rajab, while they thought it was from Jumada al-Akhirah. The Quraysh said: "Muhammad has made lawful the sacred month, a month in which the fearful is secure and people go out to their livelihoods." This grieved the companions of the expedition, and they said: "We will not depart until our repentance is revealed." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned the caravan and the captives.

And on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, "When this was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the spoils, and it was the first spoil in Islam." The ones asking were the polytheists, who wrote to him about this as a means of reproach and censure. It is also said that the ones asking were the companions of the expedition.

﴿Fighting in it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from ﴿the sacred month﴾. It has also been read as ʿan qitalin (عَنْ قِتالٍ) with the governing particle repeated.

﴿Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾, i.e., a grave sin. Most scholars hold that it has been abrogated (mansukh) by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾, contrary to ʿAta'. This is the abrogation of the specific by the general (naskh al-khass bil-ʿamm), concerning which there is disagreement. The preferable view is to deny that the verse indicates the absolute prohibition of fighting in the sacred month, for ﴿fighting in it﴾ is an indefinite noun (nakira) within an affirmative context, and therefore does not generalize.

﴿And hindering﴾ means turning away and preventing. ﴿From the way of God﴾, i.e., Islam, or whatever brings the servant to God, exalted is He, of acts of obedience. ﴿And disbelief in Him﴾, i.e., in God. ﴿And the Sacred Mosque﴾ is by the implication of an omitted noun, i.e., and the hindering of the Sacred Mosque, like the verse of Abu Du'ad:

Do you suppose every man is a man... and a fire kindled at night is a fire?

It is not good to conjoin it to ﴿from the way of God﴾, because conjoining ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾ to ﴿hindering﴾ prevents it, since the conjunction cannot precede the relative pronoun over the conjunction to the relative clause, nor over the pronoun in ﴿in Him﴾, for conjunction to a genitive pronoun occurs only by repeating the preposition.

﴿And expelling its people from it﴾, the people of the Sacred Mosque, who are the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers. ﴿Is greater in the sight of God﴾ than what the expedition did by mistake and on the basis of supposition. It is a statement about the four matters counted among the major sins of the Quraysh. The elative form (afʿal) is used in a way where singular, plural, masculine and feminine are alike.

﴿And persecution is greater than killing﴾, i.e., what you commit of expulsion and polytheism is more atrocious than what they committed in killing al-Hadrami.

﴿And they will not cease to fight you until they turn you back from your religion﴾: an announcement of the continuance of the enmity of the disbelievers toward you, and that they will not desist from it until they turn you back from your religion. Here "until" (hatta) expresses causation, like your saying: "I worship God until I enter Paradise."

﴿If they are able﴾: this is a statement of improbability regarding their ability, like the saying of one confident of his strength over his opponent: "If you overcome me, do not spare me," and an indication that they will not turn you back.
