﴿Have you not considered the chiefs (al-Mala'), the group of people who gather for consultation and have no singular form, like qawm (people), of the Children of Israel?﴾ Min (مِن) here is partitive (lil-tab'id), indicating a part of them. ﴿After Musa (Moses)﴾ meaning after his death, and min (مِن) here indicates a starting point (lil-ibtida'). ﴿When they said to a prophet of theirs﴾ he was Yusha' (Joshua), or Shamun (Simeon), or (p-150) Shamwil (Samuel), peace be upon them. ﴿Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah﴾ meaning, establish for us a commander whom we may rise up with to fight, who will manage his affairs, and whose opinion we will follow. The verb ﴿nuqatil﴾ (نُقاتِلْ) is in the jussive mood as an answer to the imperative (jawab). It is also read in the nominative, as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "appoint him for us while we are determined to fight." It is also read as ﴿yuqatil﴾ (يُقاتِلُ) with the yā' prefix, either jussive or nominative, as an answer or as a descriptor of the word "malikan" (a king). ﴿He said: Is it possible that if fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight?﴾ He placed the conditional clause between ʿasā (عَسى, "perhaps") and its predicate. The meaning is: I expect your cowardice from fighting if it is prescribed for you. He introduced hal (هَلْ, interrogative particle) before the verb of expectation, asking about what is expected, to confirm and establish it. Nafi' read ﴿ʿasitum﴾ (عَسِيتُمْ) with a kasra on the sīn. ﴿They said: What reason do we have not to fight in the way of Allah, when we have been expelled from our homes and our children?﴾ meaning, what purpose do we have in abandoning fighting, when there has befallen us what requires it and urges it, namely expulsion from our homelands and separation from our children? This happened because Jalut (Goliath) and those with him from the Amalekites lived on the coast of the Roman Sea between Egypt and Palestine. They overpowered the Children of Israel, seized their homes, captured their children, and took four hundred and forty sons of kings as captives. ﴿When fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except a few of them﴾ they were three hundred and thirteen, corresponding to the number of the people of Badr. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ a warning to them for their wrongdoing in abandoning jihad.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 247:

﴿Their prophet said to them, "Indeed God has sent Ṭālūt (Saul) to you as king."﴾ Ṭālūt is a proper name in Hebrew (ʿIbrī), like Dāwūd (David). It is of the pattern *faʿalūt*, derived from *al-ṭawl* (height). To read it as derived in this way is a forced reading, since what repels it is that it is not given tanwīn (ṣarf), the nunation that marks declension. It is reported that when their prophet (ﷺ) asked God to make a king over them, he was brought some rods by which the man who would be made ruler over them would be measured, and none matched them except Ṭālūt. ﴿They said, "How can he have kingship over us?"﴾ That is, from where could he have this, and how is he fit for it? ﴿"And we have more right to kingship than he does, and he has not been given abundant wealth."﴾ That is, the situation is that we have more right to kingship than he does, by inheritance and by capacity, and he is a poor man with no wealth to support him. They said this because Ṭālūt was a poor man, a shepherd, a water-carrier, or a tanner, from the descendants of Binyamin (Benjamin), and prophethood and kingship were not among them. Prophethood was among the descendants of Lāwī ibn Yaʿqūb (Levi son of Jacob), and kingship among the descendants of Yahūdhā (Judah), and among the two tribes there were many people. ﴿He said, "Indeed God has chosen him over you and increased him in knowledge and physique. And God gives His kingship to whom He wills, and God is all-encompassing and all-knowing."﴾ When they regarded his becoming king as unlikely because of his poverty and the lowliness of his lineage, he answered them. First, the essential matter is that God, glorified and exalted, chose him, and He chose him over you, and He knows the interests better than you do. Second, the condition for it is abundance of knowledge, so that he can know political affairs, and bodily largeness, so that he will be greater in awe in hearts and stronger in resisting the enemy and enduring wars, not what you mentioned. God increased him in both of these, and a standing man would reach up and touch his head. Third, God, exalted, is the absolute owner of kingship, so He may give it to whomever He wills. Fourth, He is vast in bounty, who enriches the poor and makes him wealthy, and He is all-knowing of who is fit for kingship, whether of noble lineage or otherwise.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 248:

﴿And their prophet said to them﴾ when they asked him for a proof that God, glory be to Him and exalted, had chosen Talut (Saul) and made him king over them. ﴿Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that there will come to you the chest (al-tabut)﴾. Al-sunduq (the chest, box) is on the pattern fa'ut from al-tawb, which means return, for it constantly returns to what comes out of it. It is not on the pattern fa'ul, because such forms are rare, like salis and qalaq. As for the one who reads it with a ha' (al-tabuh), he perhaps substituted the ha' for the taa' (taa' of tabut), as the taa' of the feminine was substituted, because the two share the qualities of hams (breathiness) and augmentation. By it is meant the chest of the Torah, which was made of shimshad wood, overlaid with gold, roughly three cubits in length and two cubits in breadth. ﴿In it is tranquility (sakina) from your Lord﴾. The pronoun refers to the coming, meaning that in its coming there is calm and reassurance for you; or it refers to the chest, meaning that in it is deposited ﴿what you find tranquility in﴾ (p-151), namely the Torah. Moses, upon him be peace, used to place it at the front when he fought, so the souls of the Children of Israel would be at rest and would not flee. It is also said that it contained an image of emerald or ruby, having a head and tail like the head and tail of a cat, and two wings; it would hum, and the chest would be driven toward the enemy while they followed it. When it came to rest, they stood firm, became calm, and victory descended. It is also said that the image in it was the likenesses of the prophets from Adam to Muhammad, upon them be peace. It is also said that the chest is the heart, and the tranquility is the knowledge and sincerity within it; its coming means that his heart becomes a settled place for knowledge and dignity after it had not been so. ﴿And a remnant of what the family of Moses and the family of Aaron left behind﴾: the fragments of the tablets, the staff of Moses, his garments, and the turban of Aaron. Their family (al-al) means their sons or themselves. The word al is inserted to magnify their status. Or it means the prophets of the Children of Israel, because they were the sons of their paternal uncle. ﴿Carried by the angels﴾. It is said that God lifted it after Moses, and the angels descended with it while they watched it. It is also said that after him it remained with their prophets, who sought victory through it, until they corrupted, and the unbelievers overcame them and seized it, and it was in the land of Jalut, until God made Talut king; then a calamity befell them, until five cities were destroyed, so they regarded the chest as a bad omen. They placed it on two oxen, and the angels drove them to Talut.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾. It is possible that this is part of the speech of the Prophet, upon him be peace, and it is possible that it is the beginning of an address from God, glory be to Him and exalted.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 249:

﴿When Talut set out with the troops﴾ he departed with them from his land to fight the Amalekites. Its original form is فَصَلَ نَفْسَهُ عَنْهُ (fasala nafsahu 'anhu, "he separated himself from it"), but because it was used so often, its object was dropped and it came to function as an intransitive verb.

It is reported that he said to them: "None shall go out with me except a young man who is vigorous and free [of other commitments]." So there gathered to him, from among those he had chosen, eighty thousand. The time was the height of summer, so they took his route through the desert and asked him to make God cause a river to flow for them. ﴿He said: Indeed God will test you with a river﴾, meaning: your treatment will be the treatment of one who tests, in response to what you have proposed. ﴿Whoever drinks from it is not of me﴾, meaning he is not among my partisans, or he is not united with me. ﴿And whoever does not taste it, he is of me﴾, meaning whoever has not tasted it. ṭa'ima al-shay' means to taste something, whether food or drink. The poet says:

"And if I wish, I do not taste sweet fresh water nor cold water."

God knew this by revelation, if he was a prophet, as has been said, or through the report of the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿Except one who scoops a handful with his hand﴾ is an exception to his saying "whoever drinks from it." The second clause was placed before it for emphasis, just as al-Sabi'un was placed before the predicate in His saying: ﴿Indeed those who believe and those who are Jews﴾. The meaning is a concession for a small amount, not a large one. Ibn 'Amir and the Kufans read غُرْفَةً (ghurfatan) with a ḍamma on the ghayn.

﴿So they drank from it, except a few of them﴾, meaning they plunged into it (kara'a fihi), since the normal way of drinking from it is not to immerse oneself. The first clause is generalized so that the exception connects, or it means they drank to excess, except a few of them. It is also read with raf' (nominative, إلا قَلِيلٌ), taking the meaning into account, since His saying فَشَرِبُوا مِنهُ ("so they drank from it") has the sense of "so they did not obey him." The few numbered three hundred and thirteen men. It has also been said three thousand, and it has been said one thousand. It is reported that whoever confined himself to a handful was sufficient for his drinking and for his waterskin, but whoever did not confine himself was overcome by it, his lip turned black, and he could not continue. Likewise is the world for one who seeks the Hereafter.

﴿When he crossed it, he and those who believed with him﴾, meaning the few who did not oppose him. ﴿They said﴾, meaning some of them said to others: ﴿We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops﴾, because of their great number and power. ﴿Those who thought that they would meet God said﴾, meaning the sincere ones among them, who were certain of meeting God and expected His reward, or who knew that they would soon be martyred and would therefore meet God the Exalted. It has also been said that they are the few who stood firm with him. The pronoun in ﴿They said﴾ refers to the many who withdrew from him, as an excuse for their staying behind and as a way of discouraging the few. It is as if they were arguing with one another while the river lay between them.

﴿How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's permission﴾ (p-152), meaning by His decree and facilitation. كَمْ (kam, "how many") may carry the sense of a statement or of a question. مِن (min) is either explanatory or superfluous. Fi'ah (فِئَةٌ) means a group of people, derived either from fa'wtu ra'sahu, meaning "I split his head," or from fa'a, "he returned," so its pattern is fi'ah or filah. ﴿And God is with the patient﴾, that is, with help and reward.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 250–251:

﴿When they came out against Jalut (Goliath) and his hosts﴾: that is, they became visible to them and drew close to them. ﴿They said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ They sought refuge in Allah, glorified and exalted is He, through supplication. In it there is an eloquent sequence, for they first asked that patience be poured into their hearts, which is the foundation of the matter; then the steadiness of the feet in the slippery places of battle, which is caused by it; then victory over the enemy, which generally follows from both of these.

﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah﴾: that is, they broke them by His help, or they were accompanied by His help against them in answer to their supplication. ﴿And David killed Jalut (Goliath).﴾ It is said: Iyasha (Jesse) was in the army of Talut (Saul) with six of his sons, and David was the seventh of them. He was young and used to tend the sheep. Allah revealed to their prophet that it was he who would kill Jalut. So [Saul] asked for him from his father, and he came, and on the way three stones spoke to him and said: "Verily, by us you will kill Jalut." So he carried them in his shepherd's pouch (mikhlah) and threw them at him, and he killed him. Then Talut married him to his daughter. ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom﴾: that is, the kingship of the Children of Israel, for they had not been united under one kingship before David. ﴿And wisdom﴾: that is, prophethood. ﴿And taught him of what He willed﴾: such as the craft of coat-of-mail (al-sard) and the speech of animals and birds. ﴿And had it not been for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted; but Allah is full of bounty toward the worlds.﴾ Had it not been that He, glorified and exalted, repels some people by others, grants victory to the Muslims over the disbelievers, and restrains their corruption through them, they would have prevailed and spread corruption in the earth; or the earth would have been corrupted by their wickedness. Nafi' recited here and in (surah) al-Hajj: "Difa' Allah" (the repelling of Allah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 250–251:

﴿When they came out against Jalut (Goliath) and his hosts﴾: that is, they became visible to them and drew close to them. ﴿They said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make firm our feet, and help us against the disbelieving people."﴾ They sought refuge in Allah, glorified and exalted is He, through supplication. In it there is an eloquent sequence, for they first asked that patience be poured into their hearts, which is the foundation of the matter; then the steadiness of the feet in the slippery places of battle, which is caused by it; then victory over the enemy, which generally follows from both of these.

﴿So they routed them by the permission of Allah﴾: that is, they broke them by His help, or they were accompanied by His help against them in answer to their supplication. ﴿And David killed Jalut (Goliath).﴾ It is said: Iyasha (Jesse) was in the army of Talut (Saul) with six of his sons, and David was the seventh of them. He was young and used to tend the sheep. Allah revealed to their prophet that it was he who would kill Jalut. So [Saul] asked for him from his father, and he came, and on the way three stones spoke to him and said: "Verily, by us you will kill Jalut." So he carried them in his shepherd's pouch (mikhlah) and threw them at him, and he killed him. Then Talut married him to his daughter. ﴿And Allah gave him the kingdom﴾: that is, the kingship of the Children of Israel, for they had not been united under one kingship before David. ﴿And wisdom﴾: that is, prophethood. ﴿And taught him of what He willed﴾: such as the craft of coat-of-mail (al-sard) and the speech of animals and birds. ﴿And had it not been for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted; but Allah is full of bounty toward the worlds.﴾ Had it not been that He, glorified and exalted, repels some people by others, grants victory to the Muslims over the disbelievers, and restrains their corruption through them, they would have prevailed and spread corruption in the earth; or the earth would have been corrupted by their wickedness. Nafi' recited here and in (surah) al-Hajj: "Difa' Allah" (the repelling of Allah).

﴿Those are the verses of God﴾: a reference to what was narrated of the story of the thousands, the appointment of Talut (Saul) as king, the coming of the Ark (al-Tabut), the defeat of the tyrants, and the killing of Jalut (Goliath) by Dawud (David). ﴿We recite them to you in truth﴾, in the accurate manner that the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab) and the masters of histories (arbab al-tawarikh) have no doubt about.

﴿And indeed you are among the messengers﴾, because of what you have related of these events without having learned them or heard them from anyone.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 253:

﴿Those messengers﴾ is a reference to the group whose stories were mentioned in the surah, or to those known to the Messenger ﷺ, or to the group of messengers in general, with the definite article (al-lam) denoting totality (al-istighraq). ﴿We made some of them exceed others﴾ by singling out one of them with a distinction not granted to anyone else. ﴿Among them are those to whom Allah spoke﴾ is a specification of his excellence, and he is Musa (Moses), peace be upon him. It is said: Musa and Muhammad, peace be upon them both, were spoken to by Allah: Musa on the night of the hayra (bewilderment) and at the Tur (Mount Sinai), and Muhammad ﷺ on the night of the Mi'raj (Ascension), when he was at two bow-lengths or nearer, and between them is a great distance. It has also been recited as "kallama Allaha" and "kalama Allaha" with the accusative case, meaning that he spoke to Allah just as Allah spoke to him; for this reason he was called Kalim Allah, in the sense of one who converses with Him. ﴿And He raised some of them in rank﴾ by favouring him over others in many respects, or in several distinct degrees. He is Muhammad (p-153) ﷺ, for He singled him out with the general call (to mankind), abundant proofs, continuous miracles, signs succeeding one another with the passing of time, and scholarly and practical virtues too numerous to be counted. The vagueness (of the reference) is to magnify his station, as if he were the one specific knowledge fit for this description, which needs no specification. It is said: Ibrahim (Abraham), peace be upon him, was singled out by the friendship (khullah), which is the highest of ranks. It is said: Idris (Enoch), peace be upon him, on account of the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾. It is said: they are the Ulu al-Azm (steadfast messengers) among the messengers. ﴿And We gave Isa (Jesus), son of Maryam, the clear signs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit﴾: He singled him out by name because the Jews and Christians excessively belittled and exalted him, and He made his miracles the cause of his excellence, for they were manifest signs and great miracles which no one else combined. ﴿And if Allah had willed﴾, that is, had guided all people together. ﴿Those who came after them would not have fought one another﴾, after the messengers. ﴿After clear proofs had come to them﴾, that is, manifest miracles, because of their disagreement in religion and their misguiding one another. ﴿But they differed, so some of them believed﴾ by His granting them success in adhering to the religion of the prophets out of grace. ﴿And some of them disbelieved﴾ by His forsaking them for their turning away from it. ﴿And if Allah had willed, they would not have fought﴾: He repeated it for emphasis. ﴿But Allah does what He intends﴾: so He grants success to whom He wills out of grace, and forsakes whom He wills out of justice. The verse is evidence that the prophets, peace be upon them, differ in their ranks, and that it is permissible to prefer some of them over others, but on the basis of a definitive proof, since consideration of conjecture is for matters related to action; and that events are in the hand of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, following His will, whether good or evil, faith or disbelief.

O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you. That is, from what I have made obligatory upon you to spend.

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, no friendship, and no intercession.﴾ That is, before there comes a Day on which you will be unable to make up for what you neglected, or to escape its punishment. There is no trade in it, by which you could obtain what you spent, or ransom yourselves from the punishment. There is no friendship, through which your friends could help you or grant you leniency. And there is no intercession, ﴿except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and whose word He approves.﴾ This is so that you do not rely on intercessors who would intercede to remove what is upon your obligations (dhimam, obligations or liabilities). The three negations were given the nominative (raf') together with the intent of generality, because in meaning they answer the question: Is there trade in it? Or friendship? Or intercession? Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read them with the fath (the vowel of the accusative), in accordance with the original (al-asl, the basic reading).

﴿And it is the disbelievers who are the wrongdoers.﴾ He means: those who withhold zakat (obligatory alms) are the wrongdoers, who wronged themselves, or who placed wealth in other than its proper place and spent it in other than its proper manner. The word "disbelievers" was placed in the position of the wrongdoers in order to intensify the rebuke and warn them, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ in place of "and whoever does not perform Hajj." It also signals that withholding zakat is among the attributes of disbelievers, according to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And woe to the polytheists, ﴿who do not give zakat﴾.

﴿Allah, there is no god but He﴾. This is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar) construction, and the meaning is that He alone deserves worship, not anyone else. The grammarians (al-nuhat) differ over whether the predicate of the second term is to be understood as implied, meaning "there is no like of Him in existence," or whether it is valid for the term to exist.

﴿The Ever-Living﴾: the one who can know and have power. Everything that is valid for Him is necessary and does not cease, because He is free from potentiality and contingency.

﴿The Sustainer﴾: the one who is always standing in managing and preserving creation. It is a pattern (fay'ul) from "qama bil-amr," meaning he preserved it. It has also been read as "al-Qayyam" and "al-Qayyim."

﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾. Sinah (drowsiness) is a lethargy that precedes sleep. Ibn al-Raqqa' said:

"A drowsy one whom slumber overcame, and a haze of sinah settled over his eye, yet he is not asleep."

Sleep (nawm) is a state that comes over living beings from the relaxation of the nerves of the brain due to moisture from rising vapours, such that the outward senses completely stop perceiving. Mentioning sinah before sleep, and the intensive form being the reverse of this, follows the natural order of existence. The sentence is a negation of anthropomorphism and an affirmation that He is Living and Sustainer. For whoever is seized by drowsiness or sleep is deficient in life and lacking in preservation and management. For this reason the conjunction is omitted here and in the sentences that follow it.

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. This confirms His self-subsistence and argues from it for His uniqueness in divinity. What is meant by "what is in them" is either what is inside their reality or what is outside them but established within them. This is more emphatic than His saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them﴾.

﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ This is an explanation of the greatness of His majesty, glory be to Him and exalted, and that no one equals Him or approaches Him, such that one could independently repel what He wills by intercession and humble entreaty, let alone obstruct Him out of stubbornness or opposition (munasaba), that is, by contention.

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾: what is before them and what is behind them, that is, what came before them and what comes after them. Or it is the reverse, because you face the future and turn your back on the past. Or it is the affairs of this world and the affairs of the Hereafter, or the reverse. Or it is what they perceive by the senses and what they understand by reason, or what they apprehend and what they do not apprehend. The pronoun refers to what is in the heavens and the earth, because among them are rational beings, or to what is indicated by ﴿who is it﴾, namely the angels and prophets, peace be upon them.

﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾: of what is known to Him.

﴿except what He wills﴾ that they should know. It is conjoined to what precedes it because together the two phrases indicate His unique possession of perfect essential knowledge, which indicates His oneness, glory be to Him and exalted.

﴿His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾. This is a depiction of His greatness and a pure figurative representation, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾. In reality there is no kursi (seat or footstool) and no one sitting. It has been said that His kursi is a metaphor for His knowledge or His dominion, taken from the kursi of the scholar and of the king. It has also been said that it is a body before the Throne ('arsh), and for this reason it is called a kursi, encompassing the seven heavens, because of the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The seven heavens and the seven earths, compared to the Kursi, are nothing but a ring thrown in a desert, and the excellence of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excellence of that desert over that ring."

Perhaps this is the well-known sphere called the falak of the zodiacal constellations (falak al-buruj). Originally kursi is the name for what is sat upon and does not exceed the seat of the one sitting. It seems to be related to the kursi, which is the padded cushion.

﴿And it does not weary Him﴾, that is, it does not burden Him. It is taken from al-awd, which means crookedness.

﴿The preserving of them﴾, that is, His preserving of the heavens and the earth. The agent is omitted and the verbal noun is annexed to the object.

﴿And He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾: He is exalted above rivals and likenesses.

﴿Al-'Azim (the Mighty)﴾: everything other than Him is belittled in comparison to Him.

This verse includes the foundational principles of divine matters, for it indicates that He, exalted is He, is one in divinity, characterized by life, necessarily existent in His essence, and the originator of everything else. Al-Qayyum is the one who stands by Himself and sustains others. He is exalted above being localized or indwelling, free from change and lethargy. He is not like bodies, and what befalls souls does not befall Him. He is the owner of dominion and sovereignty, the originator of roots and branches, the one of severe seizing, from whom none intercedes except one whom He permits. He is the knower of all things, the manifest and the hidden, the universal and the particular. He has vast dominion and power over everything that can be owned or be subject to power. No hardship wearies Him and no affair occupies Him. He is exalted above what can be perceived, and He is the Great whom no understanding can encompass.

For this reason the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed the greatest verse in the Qur'an is the Verse of the Kursi. Whoever recites it, Allah sends an angel who writes down good deeds for him and erases his bad deeds until the morning from that hour."

And he said: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Kursi after every obligatory prayer, nothing prevents him from entering Paradise except death, and none is constant in it except a truthful one (siddiq) or a worshipper. Whoever recites it when he takes his bed, Allah keeps him safe for himself, his neighbour, his neighbour's neighbour, and the houses around him."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 256:

﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ For compulsion, in reality, is forcing another to do an act for which he sees no good that would move him to it. But ﴿the right course has become clearly distinct from error﴾: faith has been distinguished from disbelief by the clear signs, and the proofs have indicated that faith is right guidance which leads to everlasting happiness, while disbelief is error which leads to everlasting misery. When this has become clear to the rational person, his soul hastens to faith, seeking success and salvation, and he has no need of compulsion or coercion. It has also been said that it is a report with the meaning of a prohibition, i.e., do not be compelled in religion. It is either general, abrogated by His saying ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them﴾, or specific to the People of the Book, on account of what has been related: "(That an Ansari man had two sons who had become Christians before the mission (of the Prophet), then they came to Medina, and their father clung to them and said: 'By God, I will not leave you until you become Muslims.' They refused, so they brought their dispute to the Messenger of God ﷺ. The Ansari said: 'O Messenger of God, shall they enter the Fire while I am watching?') So it was revealed, and he let them go." ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the Taghut﴾: the Taghut is the Satan, or the idols, or everything that is worshipped besides God, or whatever turns away from the worship of God, the Most High. It is on the pattern of fa'lut from tughyan (transgression), its 'ayn and lam having been transposed. ﴿and believes in God﴾: in the Oneness (tawhid) and in confirming the messengers.

﴿He has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾: he has sought to hold fast to the most trustworthy handhold, from a firm rope. It is used metaphorically for one who holds fast to the truth, through correct reasoning and sound opinion. ﴿There is no breaking of it﴾: there is no severance of it. It is said: "fasamtuhu, fa-nfasama," when you break it.

﴿And God is All-Hearing﴾ of the sayings, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intentions. Perhaps this is a warning against hypocrisy.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 257:

﴿Allah is the Protector (walī) of those who believe﴾: their beloved (muḥibbuhum), or the one who manages their affairs (mutawallī umūrihim). What is meant by them is those whom He wills to have faith, and whose faith He has known in His knowledge to be fixed. ﴿He brings them out﴾ by His guidance and enabling success (tawfīq). ﴿From the darknesses﴾, the darknesses of ignorance (jahl), following desire (hawā), accepting whisperings (waswasa) and doubts (shubah) that lead to disbelief. ﴿Into the light﴾: into the guidance (hudā) that leads to faith. The clause is a predicate following a predicate, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in the predicate, or from the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl), or from both of them, or a resuming clause (isti'nāf) that explains, or one that confirms the guardianship (walāya). ﴿As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are the false deities (ṭāghūt)﴾, that is, the devils (shayāṭīn), or the misleading things from desire, Satan and others. ﴿They bring them out from the light into the darknesses﴾: from the light that they were given by innate nature (fiṭra), into disbelief, the corruption of readiness (fasād al-istiʿdād) and absorption in desires; or from the light of clear proofs (al-bayyināt) into the darknesses of doubts and suspicions. It has been said: it was revealed concerning a people who apostatized from Islam. Attributing the bringing out to the false deities, on the basis of causation (tasabbub), does not preclude the connection of His power and will (taʿalluq qudratihi wa irādatihi) to it, exalted is He. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever﴾: a threat and a warning. Perhaps the absence of its being paired with a promise for the believers is an exaltation of their station.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 258:**

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at the argumentation of Nimrod and his foolishness. ﴿Because God had given him dominion.﴾ Because "ātāhu" means that God made him haughty by giving him dominion, and this drove him to argue. Or he argued on account of it, as thanks to Him by way of inversion, like your saying "you were hostile to me because I did you a kindness." Or "when God gave him dominion," and this is a proof against the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school), who deny that God gives dominion to an unbeliever.

﴿When Abraham said﴾ is a temporal adverbial complement (*zarf*) of "argued," or, on the second reading, an apposition (*badal*) to "because God had given him dominion." ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾ by creating life and death in bodies. Ḥamzah read "Rabb" with the yā' omitted. ﴿He said: I give life and cause death﴾ by pardoning from killing and by killing. Nāfi' read "anā" without an alif.

﴿Abraham said: Indeed God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west.﴾ Abraham, upon him be peace, turned away from objecting to Nimrod's corrupt counter-argument and moved to an argument in which Nimrod could not produce such a deception, in order to stop the disputation. In reality this is a shift from a hidden example to a clear example from among His powers, which no one else can accomplish, not a shift from one argument to another. Perhaps Nimrod claimed that he could do every kind of thing that God does, so Abraham refuted him with this. What drove him to it was the haughtiness and foolishness of the king, or his belief in incarnation (*ḥulūl*). It was said that when Abraham, upon him be peace, broke the idols, Nimrod imprisoned him for some days, then brought him out to burn him, and said to him: "Who is your Lord to whom you call?" and he argued with him about it.

﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded.﴾ He became bewildered. It is also read "fabuhita," meaning Abraham overcame the unbeliever. ﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ (p-156) who wronged themselves by refusing to accept guidance. It was also said: He does not guide them to the path of argument, or the way of salvation, or the road to Paradise on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾: its implied construction is "Or have you seen the likeness of the one who..." The word "the likeness" was omitted because the phrase "Have you not seen" (﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾) indicates it. Its specification with the particle of comparison (ḥarf al-tashbīh, the particle of comparison) is because those who deny resurrection are many, and those ignorant of its manner are more than can be counted, unlike the claimant to lordship. It is also said that the kāf (the particle "like") is extra (zā'idah), and the sense of the speech is: "Have you not seen the one who argued, or the one who passed by?" It is also said that it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) carried over to the meaning, as if it were said: "Have you not seen like the one who argued, or like the one who passed by?" It is also said that it is from the speech of Abraham, mentioned as a reply to his opponent, and its sense is: "Or if you give life, then give life as God, exalted is He, gives life," referring to the one who passed by a town. He is ʿUzayr ibn Sharḥiyā, or al-Khiḍr, or an unbeliever in resurrection. The context in which he is placed with Nimrod supports this. The town is Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) when Bukhtanasr (Nebuchadnezzar) destroyed it. It is also said that the town is the one from which the thousands went out. It is also said to be something else, and its derivation is from qurā (gatherings), which means collecting.

﴿And it was fallen down upon its roofs﴾: empty, its walls fallen down upon its roofs.

﴿He said: "How will God give life to this after its death?"﴾: as an acknowledgment of inability to know the way of giving life, and as a glorification of the power of the Giver of life if the speaker was a believer, and as a denial if he was an unbeliever. The word ﴿أنّى﴾ (anná, "how/when") is in the position of an accusative, either as an adverb of time in the sense of "when," or as a circumstantial accusative in the sense of "how."

﴿So God caused him to die for a hundred years﴾: so He caused him to remain dead for a hundred years, or God caused him to die, and he remained dead for a hundred years.

﴿Then He raised him﴾: by giving life.

﴿He said: "How long have you remained?"﴾: the speaker is God, and it was permissible for Him to speak to him even if he was an unbeliever, because he believed after being raised, or he was about to believe. It is also said that the speaker was an angel or a prophet.

﴿He said: "I have remained a day or part of a day"﴾: like the saying of one who supposes. It is also said that he died in the forenoon and was raised after a hundred years, shortly before sunset. So he said, before looking at the sun, "a day," then he turned and saw some of it remaining, so he said ﴿or part of a day﴾ as a correction (ʾiḍrāb, retraction).

﴿He said: "Nay, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink, it has not spoiled﴾: it had not changed with the passage of time. Its derivation is from the word sanah (year). The hāʾ (the final letter of the verb) is original if the third radical of sanah is taken as hāʾ, and a silent hāʾ (hāʾ al-sakt) if it is taken as wāw. It is also said that its origin is lam yatasannan, from ḥamaʾ masnūn (black, moulded clay), so the third nūn was changed to a weak letter (ḥarf ʿillah), as in taqaḍḍā al-bāzī (the falcon's "taqaḍḍā"). The pronoun is singular because food and drink are like one kind. It is also said that his food was figs and grapes and his drink was juice or milk, and all of it remained in its state. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read "lam yatasannah" without the hāʾ in continuous recitation (waṣl).

﴿And look at your donkey﴾: how its bones were scattered, or look at it whole in its place as you tied it. We preserved it without water or fodder, just as we preserved the food and drink from change. The first is more evident for the state and more fitting for what follows.

﴿And that We may make you a sign for the people﴾: that is, and Our doing that is so that We may make you a sign.

It is narrated that he came to his people on his donkey and said, "I am ʿUzayr," and they denied him. Then he recited the Torah from memory, which no one before him had memorised, so they recognised him by that and said, "He is the son of God." It is also said that when he returned to his home he was young while his children were old, so when he related a story to them they said, "A story of a hundred years."

﴿And look at the bones﴾: meaning the bones of the donkey, or the dead whose revival you wonder at.

﴿How We raise them﴾: how We give them life, or We raise some of them upon others and assemble them. "How" (kayfa) is in the accusative, governed by nunshiruhā (We raise them), and the clause is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the bones, meaning: look at them as revived.

Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb read ﴿nunshiruhā﴾ from anshara Allāh al-mawtā (God raised the dead). It is also read ﴿nanshuruhā﴾ from nashara, with the same meaning as anshara.

﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾. When it became clear to him, the subject of "became clear" (tabayyana) is a hidden pronoun explained by what follows. Its sense: "When it became clear to him that God is over all things capable."

﴿He said: "I know that God is over all things capable"﴾: the first (verb) is omitted because the second indicates it. Or what precedes explains it, meaning: when there became clear to him what had been unclear to him. Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿qāla iʿlam﴾ ("He said: 'Know!'") in the imperative, and the imperative is an address, either addressed to himself, or he addressed himself with it by way of rebuke.(p-157)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 260:

﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾ He asked this only so that his knowledge would become direct observation ('iyan). It is said that when Nimrod said, ﴿"I give life and cause death,"﴾ Abraham told him: indeed, God's giving of life is by returning the soul to its body. Nimrod said, "Have you seen Him?" and Abraham could not say "yes." He moved on to another argument. Then he asked his Lord to show him, so that his heart would be at rest with the answer should he be asked about it again. ﴿He said, "Do you not believe?"﴾ That is, that I am able to give life by restoring the composition and life. He said this to him, although he knew that Nimrod had drowned the people in belief, so that Nimrod would answer as he did and the listeners would understand his purpose. ﴿He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."﴾ That is, yes, I believe, but I asked this in order to increase my insight and the tranquility of my heart by combining direct observation with revelation or reasoning. ﴿He said, "Take four birds."﴾ It is said they were a peacock, a rooster, a crow and a dove; and some mentioned the eagle in place of the dove. In this there is an allusion that the living of the soul through eternal life is only achieved by causing the death of love of desires and adornments, which is the attribute of the peacock; the boldness for which the rooster is known, the baseness of the soul and long hope, which the crow is characterized by; and the haughtiness and haste toward desire, which the dove is marked by. He specified birds because they are closest to man and most comprehensive of the properties of animals. "Birds" (al-tayr) is either a verbal noun used as a name, or a plural like ṣaḥb. ﴿"Then bring them close to you."﴾ That is, incline them and gather them to you, so that you may examine them and know their markings, lest they become confused for you after being brought back to life. Hamzah and Ya'qub read ﴿fa-ṣurhunna﴾ with a kasra, and both are dialects. The poet said:

"And the seizing of necks among them is not innate, but the tips of spears shape them."

And he said:

"And a branch that bends the neck, a cluster, as if it were over the lion, the heavy grape clusters."

It was also read "fa-ṣurhunna" with a damma and kasra on the ṣad, and both are dialects, with the rā' doubled, from ṣarrahu yaṣurruhu and yaṣirru, meaning he gathered it. And "fa-ṣurhunna" is from al-taṣriyah, which also means gathering. ﴿"Then set on every mountain a portion of them."﴾ That is, then divide them and spread their parts over the mountains that are in your presence. It is said there were four, and it is said seven. Abu Bakr read "juz'an" and "juz'un" with a damma on the zay wherever it occurs. ﴿"Then call them."﴾ Say to them, "Come, by God's leave." ﴿"They will come to you running."﴾ Hastening, flying swiftly or walking.

It is narrated that he was commanded to slaughter them, pluck their feathers, cut them up, hold their heads, mix the rest of their parts, and distribute them over the mountains, then call them. He did so, and each part flew toward another until they became bodies, then they came and joined themselves to their heads. In this there is an indication that whoever wishes to give life to his soul with eternal life must turn to the bodily powers, kill them, and mix some of them with others until their fierceness is broken, so that they obey him swiftly whenever he calls them with the call of reason or the Law. Sufficient as evidence of the excellence of Abraham, peace be upon him, and the blessing of humble supplication and the goodness of manners in asking, is that God showed him what he wished to be shown immediately, in the easiest manner, and showed him 'Uzayr after He had caused him to die for a hundred years. ﴿"And know that God is Mighty"﴾ He cannot be incapacitated from what He wills. ﴿"Wise"﴾ possessing perfect wisdom in all that He does and leaves undone.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 261:

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain﴾ That is, the likeness of their spending is like the likeness of a grain, or their likeness is like the likeness of one who sows a grain, with the noun elided (ʿalā ḥadhf al-muḍāf, i.e., the omission of a governed noun). ﴿It grows seven ears; in every ear is a hundred grains﴾ He attributed the growing (al-ināt) to the grain because it was one of the means (al-asbāb), just as growth is attributed to the earth, the water and the place of growth, while in truth the one who causes it is Allah, exalted is He. The meaning is: a stalk emerges from it (p-158) that branches out, and from each branch come seven shoots, each with an ear containing a hundred grains. This is an illustrative parable (tamthīl) that does not require that it actually occur, though it may occur in millet and sorghum in fertile lands (al-arāḍī al-maghillah). ﴿And Allah multiplies﴾ that multiplication ﴿for whom He wills﴾ by His bounty, and in accordance with the state of the spender in his sincerity (ikhlāṣ) and his exertion (taʿab). For this reason, deeds differ in the measures of their reward. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, whose bounty is not restricted by any increase He grants. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intention of the spender and the measure of his expenditure.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 262–263:

﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury﴾ It was revealed concerning ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, for he equipped the army of hardship (jaysh al-ʿusrah) with a thousand camels, with their saddles and their saddle-cloths; and concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, for he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with four thousand dirhams as charity. Al-mann (reminding of favour) is to count one's kindness against the one to whom one has done good; al-adha (injury) is to be overbearing toward him on account of what one has bestowed upon him. And thumma (then) indicates the gap between spending and abandoning mann and adha. ﴿For them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾. Perhaps he did not introduce the fa' (so) here, although what is attributed to them includes the meaning of a condition, giving the impression that they are people worthy of this, and that if they do not do it, how much more so when they do. ﴿A kind word﴾: a gracious response. ﴿And forgiveness﴾: an overlooking of the beggar and the one in need; or the attainment of forgiveness from Allah through the gracious response; or a pardon from the beggar, in that he excuses and his refusal is overlooked. ﴿Better than charity followed by injury﴾: a predicate concerning both of them; and the beginning with an indefinite noun (nakirah) was valid because it is specified by its qualifying attribute. ﴿And Allah is Free of need﴾ from spending accompanied by reminder and injury. ﴿Forbearing﴾: He defers punishment for one who reminds and injures.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 262–263:

﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury﴾ It was revealed concerning ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, for he equipped the army of hardship (jaysh al-ʿusrah) with a thousand camels, with their saddles and their saddle-cloths; and concerning ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf, for he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with four thousand dirhams as charity. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 264:

﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders [of your generosity] or injury﴾ Do not nullify their reward by either of these.

﴿like one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ Like the nullification of the hypocrite who shows off with his spending, not intending thereby the pleasure of Allah the Exalted nor the reward of the Hereafter. Or [the meaning is]: "being like those who spend to be seen by the people." The kaf (ka) is in a position of nasb (accusative), as a adverbial of manner (maṣdar) or a circumstantial state (ḥāl). And ﴿ri'a'a﴾ (to be seen) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) or as a circumstantial state, in the sense of "showing off" (muraʾiyan), or as a verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: spending ﴿to be seen﴾.

﴿So his example﴾ That is, the example of the one who shows off in his spending.

﴿is like the example of a smooth stone﴾ Like a smooth rock.

﴿upon which is dust; then a heavy rain strikes it﴾ Rain of great heavy drops.

﴿and leaves it bare⁠﴾ Smooth, clean of dust.

﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ They gain nothing from what they did for show, and they find no reward for it. The pronoun refers to "the one who spends" according to meaning, since what is intended by it is the category, or the plural, as in the line of poetry:

؎ Indeed, those whose blood was spilled at Falj... they are the people, all of the people, O Umm Khalid.

﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ to goodness and right guidance. In this there is an implicit indication that showing off, reminding of favours, and injuring others through charity are among the attributes of disbelievers, and the believer must necessarily avoid them.

﴿وَمَثَلُ الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ أمْوالَهُمُ ابْتِغاءَ مَرْضاتِ اللَّهِ وتَثْبِيتًا مِن أنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the approval of Allah and firmly establishing their souls. "Tathbitan min anfusihim" means: some of their souls are made firm in faith (al-iman). Wealth is the sibling of the soul (shaqiq al-ruh), so whoever gives away his wealth for the sake of Allah has made some part of his soul firm, and whoever gives away both his wealth and his soul has made all of it firm. Or the meaning is: confirming Islam and realizing the reward, a mubtada' (subject of a nominal sentence) that comes from the origin of their souls. This contains an alert that the wisdom of spending for the spender is the purification of the soul (tazkiyat al-nafs) from miserliness (bukhl) and love of wealth. ﴿كَمَثَلِ جَنَّةٍ بِرَبْوَةٍ﴾ That is, the example of the spending of these people in zakat (zakah, obligatory alms) is like the example of a garden on an elevated place, whose trees are more beautiful in appearance and more pure in fruit. Ibn Amir and Asim read "bi-rabwatin" (بِرَبْوَةٍ) with fatha, and it was also read with kasra; all three forms are dialectal variants (lughat) of the word. ﴿أصابَها وابِلٌ﴾ A heavy rain with large drops. ﴿فَآتَتْ أُكُلَها﴾ Its fruit. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "ukulaha" (أُكُلَها) with sukun for lightness. ﴿ضِعْفَيْنِ﴾ Twice the amount it used to yield because of the heavy rain. By "double" (di'f) is meant "equal" (mithl), just as "pair" (zawj) is used to mean one in His words, exalted is He: ﴿مِن كُلٍّ زَوْجَيْنِ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ (from every kind, two pairs). It is also said: four times its equivalent. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial (hal) meaning "doubled." ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ يُصِبْها وابِلٌ فَطَلٌّ﴾ That is, then it is struck (by something), or what strikes it is a light rain (tall), or a light rain suffices for it because of the nobility of its planting and the coolness of its air due to the height of its place. A tall is a rain of small drops. The meaning is that the spending of these people is pure (zakiyah) in the sight of Allah and never goes to waste in any state, even though it varies according to what accompanies it of their circumstances. It is also permissible that the illustration of their state in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, is a garden on an elevation, with their abundant and scanty spending increasing their nearness (zulfa) to Him, like heavy rain and light rain. ﴿واللَّهُ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ بَصِيرٌ﴾ A warning against showing off (riya') and an encouragement toward sincerity (ikhlas).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 266:

﴿Would any one of you wish﴾ The hamza (interrogative particle) here is for denunciation (inkar). ﴿that he should have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, beneath which rivers flow, and in which he has every kind of fruit﴾ He made the garden consist of these two, together with the rest of the trees in it, by giving precedence to them (taghlib) because of their nobility and the abundance of their benefits. Then he mentioned that in it there is "every kind of fruit," to indicate that it contains all types of trees. It is also possible that what is meant by "fruits" is benefits. ﴿And old age has overtaken him﴾ That is, the age of old age, for poverty and dependence are harder in advanced years. The waw is either for the circumstantial clause (hal) or for coordination (atf), taking the meaning into account, so it is as if it were said: "Would any one of you wish that he had a garden and old age had overtaken him?" ﴿And he has offspring, weak﴾ young, having no ability to earn. ﴿Then a fiery whirlwind strikes it, and it is burned﴾ This is coordinated with "overtaken him," or it is so in terms of meaning.

Al-i'sar (whirlwind) is a violent wind that rises from the earth toward the sky, rotating like a pillar. The meaning is an illustration of the state of one who performs good deeds but attaches to them what nullifies them, such as showing off and harming others, in regret and sorrow. When the Day of Resurrection comes and his need for them becomes intense, he finds them annulled, in the condition of one with this kind of attitude. The most fitting comparison for him is one who wandered with his inner self in the realm of the dominion (malakut), ascended with his thought to the presence of the Omnipotent (jabarut), and then turned back on his heels to the world of falsehood, looking toward what is other than the Truth, and made his striving "scattered dust." ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you the signs, that you may reflect﴾ That is, that you may reflect upon them and thereby take lesson from them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 267:

﴿O you who believe, spend of the good things you have earned﴾, that is, of what is lawful (ḥalāl) or of what is excellent (jiyād). ﴿And of what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾, meaning: and of the good things of what We have brought forth for you of grains, fruits and minerals; the modified noun (al-muḍāf, "good things") has been omitted because it was mentioned earlier. ﴿And do not aim at the bad of it﴾, that is, do not intend the inferior of it, namely of the wealth, or of what We have brought forth for you. Its restriction to this is because the variation in it is greater. It was also read as "wa-lā tuʼammimū" and "wa-lā tuyammimū" with a ḍammah on the tā'. ﴿While you spend from it﴾ is a presumed circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah) from the subject of tayammamū; it is permissible that min-hu be connected to it, and the pronoun then refers to the bad, and the clause is a circumstantial clause from it. ﴿And you would not take it﴾, that is, while your state is that you would not take it in your own rights because of its inferiority. ﴿Except that you overlook in it﴾, that is, except that you be lenient in it; it is a metaphor from "aghmaḍa baṣarahu" when he lowered his gaze. It was also read (p-160) "tughmiḍū", that is, you are compelled to overlook it, or you find yourselves overlooking it. It is narrated from Ibn ʻAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that they used to give in charity the shriveled dates and the worst of them, so they were forbidden from that. ﴿And know that Allah is Free of need﴾ from your spending, and He only commands you to it for your own benefit. ﴿Praiseworthy﴾ in accepting it and rewarding it.

Al-Baydawi, Anwar al-Tanzil, on surah 2, verse 268:

﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty﴾ in spending, and the wa'd (promise, threat) is in origin common to good and evil. The word al-faqr (poverty) has been read with a single ḍammah and with sukūn, and with two ḍammahs and with two fatḥahs.

﴿And commands you to indecency﴾, that is, incites you to stinginess. The Arabs call a miser fāḥish (indecent, foul).

It has been said that the indecency means the sins. ﴿But Allah promises you forgiveness from Him﴾, that is, He promises you, in spending, forgiveness for your sins. ﴿And bounty﴾, a replacement better than what you have spent in this world, or in the Hereafter. ﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾, that is, abundant in bounty for whoever spends. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of his spending.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 269:

﴿He gives wisdom﴾ (al-hikmah): the verification of knowledge (tahqiq al-'ilm) and the perfecting of knowledge (itqan al-'ilm). ﴿to whom He wills﴾ (man yasha'): the first object (maf'ul awwal), placed later for the sake of giving attention to the second object. ﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾: its verb is in the passive voice, because it is the intended meaning. Ya'qub read it with a kasra, i.e., "and whoever He gives wisdom to" (wa man yu'tihi Allah al-hikmah). ﴿then he has been given much good﴾: i.e., what great good? For he has been granted the good of both abodes (khayr al-darayn). ﴿And none will be reminded﴾ (wa ma yadhdhakkaru): none will take heed (yatta'izu) from what has been related of the verses, or none will reflect (yatafakkaru), for the one who reflects is like the one who remembers, regarding the knowledge that Allah has deposited in his heart in potential form (bil-quwwah). ﴿except those of understanding﴾ (ulu al-albab): those of pure intellects (dhawu al-'uqul al-khalisah), free from the impurities of illusion and from inclining to the pursuit of desire.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verses 270–272:

﴿And whatever expenditure you spend, or whatever vow you vow﴾: whether little or much, secretly or openly, in what is right or what is wrong. ﴿Or whatever vow you vow﴾: with a condition or without a condition, in obedience or in disobedience. ﴿Indeed, Allah knows it﴾: so He will recompense you for it. ﴿And for the wrongdoers﴾: those who spend in sins and vow in them, or who withhold the charities and do not fulfill the vow. ﴿There are no helpers﴾: anyone who would help them against Allah and protect them from His punishment.

﴿If you disclose your charities, then how excellent they are﴾: how excellent a thing their disclosure is. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "fa-ni'imma" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the 'ayn, according to the original form (al-asl). Abu Bakr, Abu 'Amr and Qalun read it with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the 'ayn, and it is also related from them with a kasra on the nun and the vowel of the 'ayn being suppressed (ikhfa'), which is the more analogical reading (aqyas). ﴿And if you conceal them and give them to the poor﴾: meaning, you give them while concealing them. ﴿Then it is better for you﴾: so concealment is better for you. This applies to voluntary charity, and to one who is not known to be wealthy, for disclosing an obligatory (fard) charity to others is more excellent, in order to negate suspicion of him.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, [the Prophet] said: "The charity of secrecy in voluntary giving surpasses its open form by seventy times, and the charity of obligation, its open form is better than its secret form by twenty-five times." ﴿And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾: Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read it with a ya' (yukaffiru), meaning, Allah removes, or the concealment does. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Ibn 'Ayyash, and Ya'qub read it with a nun in the nominative, as a verbal sentence beginning a new clause (mubtada'ah) or a nominal sentence conjoined to what follows the fa', meaning: "and We remove." Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the jussive, on the locus of the fa' and what follows it. It is also read with a ta' in the nominative and the jussive, with the verb referring to the charities. ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾: an encouragement toward secrecy.

﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾: it is not obligatory upon you to make people guided; rather, upon you is guidance and urging toward good deeds, and forbidding ugly deeds, such as reminding of favors, harm, and spending what is corrupt. ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾: an explicit statement that guidance is from Allah, the Exalted, and by His will, and that it is specific to some people over others. ﴿And whatever you spend of good﴾: from a known expenditure. ﴿Then it is for yourselves﴾: it is for your own selves; no one other than you benefits from it, so do not remind [others] of it, and do not spend what is corrupt. ﴿And you spend not except seeking the Face of Allah﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (hal), as if he said: "And whatever you spend of good, it is for yourselves, while you are not spending except seeking the Face of Allah and desiring its reward." Or it is conjoined to what precedes it, meaning: "Your expenditure is not except seeking His Face, so what is the matter with you that you remind [others] of it and spend what is corrupt?" It has also been said that this is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition. ﴿And whatever you spend of good will be repaid to you in full﴾: its reward multiplied manifold. This is a confirmation of the earlier conditional clause, or it is what is replaced for the one who spends, in response to the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: "O Allah, give a replacement to the one who spends, and destruction to the one who withholds."

It is related that some Muslims had in-laws and foster-relations among the Jews, and they used to spend upon them. When they embraced Islam, they disliked benefiting them, so this was revealed. This applies to what is not obligatory; as for the obligatory, it is not permissible to direct it to the disbelievers. ﴿And you will not be wronged﴾: meaning, your reward for your expenditures will not be diminished.
