Abu Bakr, Abu 'Amr and Qalun read it with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the 'ayn, and it is also related from them with a kasra on the nun and the vowel of the 'ayn being suppressed (ikhfa'), which is the more analogical reading (aqyas). ﴿And if you conceal them and give them to the poor﴾: meaning, you give them while concealing them. ﴿Then it is better for you﴾: so concealment is better for you. This applies to voluntary charity, and to one who is not known to be wealthy, for disclosing an obligatory (fard) charity to others is more excellent, in order to negate suspicion of him.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, [the Prophet] said: "The charity of secrecy in voluntary giving surpasses its open form by seventy times, and the charity of obligation, its open form is better than its secret form by twenty-five times." ﴿And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾: Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim, in the narration of Hafs, read it with a ya' (yukaffiru), meaning, Allah removes, or the concealment does. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the narration of Ibn 'Ayyash, and Ya'qub read it with a nun in the nominative, as a verbal sentence beginning a new clause (mubtada'ah) or a nominal sentence conjoined to what follows the fa', meaning: "and We remove." Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it in the jussive, on the locus of the fa' and what follows it. It is also read with a ta' in the nominative and the jussive, with the verb referring to the charities. ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾: an encouragement toward secrecy.

﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾: it is not obligatory upon you to make people guided; rather, upon you is guidance and urging toward good deeds, and forbidding ugly deeds, such as reminding of favors, harm, and spending what is corrupt. ﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾: an explicit statement that guidance is from Allah, the Exalted, and by His will, and that it is specific to some people over others. ﴿And whatever you spend of good﴾: from a known expenditure. ﴿Then it is for yourselves﴾: it is for your own selves; no one other than you benefits from it, so do not remind [others] of it, and do not spend what is corrupt. ﴿And you spend not except seeking the Face of Allah﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (hal), as if he said: "And whatever you spend of good, it is for yourselves, while you are not spending except seeking the Face of Allah and desiring its reward." Or it is conjoined to what precedes it, meaning: "Your expenditure is not except seeking His Face, so what is the matter with you that you remind [others] of it and spend what is corrupt?" It has also been said that this is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition. ﴿And whatever you spend of good will be repaid to you in full﴾: its reward multiplied manifold. This is a confirmation of the earlier conditional clause, or it is what is replaced for the one who spends, in response to the saying of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace: "O Allah, give a replacement to the one who spends, and destruction to the one who withholds."

It is related that some Muslims had in-laws and foster-relations among the Jews, and they used to spend upon them. When they embraced Islam, they disliked benefiting them, so this was revealed. This applies to what is not obligatory; as for the obligatory, it is not permissible to direct it to the disbelievers. ﴿And you will not be wronged﴾: meaning, your reward for your expenditures will not be diminished.

﴿For the poor﴾ is connected to an implied verb, meaning: "Direct (your charity) to the poor," or "Make what you spend go to the poor," or "Your charities are for the poor."

﴿Who are restricted in the way of Allah﴾: jihad has restricted them. ﴿They cannot﴾ because they are occupied with it. ﴿Go about in the land﴾: traveling in it to earn a living. It was also said that they are the People of the Bench (Ahl al-Suffa), about four hundred of the poor among the emigrants (muhajirun), who lived in the bench of the mosque and devoted their time to learning and worship. They used to go out with every expedition (sariyya) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dispatched. ﴿The ignorant one thinks them﴾ wealthy because of their condition. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza read the sin with a fatha (yahsabuhum).

﴿Wealthy because of their restraint﴾: because of their abstaining from asking. ﴿You recognize them by their mark﴾: from their weakness and shabby state. The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone.

﴿They do not ask people persistently﴾: "ilhaf" means insistence, that one keeps pressing the one asked until he gives. It comes from their saying, "lahafani min fadli lihafihi," meaning he gave me from the surplus of what he had. The meaning is that they do not ask, and even if they ask out of necessity, they do not press. It was also said that it is a negation of both matters, as in his saying:

"Over a faint road, guided by its landmark"

It is put in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is a kind of asking, or as a circumstantial accusative (hal).

﴿And whatever good you spend, indeed Allah is Knowing of it﴾: an exhortation to spending, especially upon these people.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 274:

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾, that is, they cover the times and the states with good. It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), who gave in charity forty thousand dinars: ten by night, ten by day, ten in secret and ten openly.

It was also said concerning the Commander of the Faithful, Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), that he owned nothing but four dirhams, so he gave one dirham by night, one dirham by day, one dirham in secret and one dirham openly.

It was also said: it was revealed concerning tying horses in the way of Allah and spending on them. ﴿Their reward is with their Lord, and there is no fear for them, nor do they grieve﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of ﴿Those who spend﴾, and the fa' (in fa-lahum) indicates causation (al-sababiyyah). It was also said that it is for coordination (al-'atf), and the predicate is omitted, meaning: and among them are those who... For this reason, stopping (waqf) on ﴿and openly﴾ was permitted.

(p-162) ﴿Those who consume riba﴾, i.e., those who take it. He mentioned "consuming" because it is the greatest benefit of wealth, and because riba is common in foodstuffs. Riba (the unlawful excess in a transaction) is an increase in the term, such as when one foodstuff is sold for another foodstuff, or cash for cash on credit, or an increase in the exchange, such as when one of the two items is sold for more than the same kind. It was written with a waw, as in الصَّلاة (al-salah, "prayer"), for emphasis according to one dialect, and an alif was added after it to resemble the waw of the plural. ﴿Will not rise﴾ when they are raised from their graves. ﴿Except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch﴾, i.e., except rising like the one who has been struck down (مَصْرُوع, "epileptic" or "struck down"). This is in accordance with what they claim: that Satan strikes a person and he is thrown down. Al-khabt (الخَبْط) is striking without order, like the khabt of the 'ashwa' (a blind she-camel that strikes about aimlessly).

﴿From the touch﴾, i.e., madness. This too is one of their claims, that a jinn touches a person and his intellect becomes confused; for this reason it is said: "the man has become possessed (جُنَّ)."

It is connected to ﴿will not rise﴾, meaning: they will not rise from the touch that is upon them because of consuming riba. Or it is connected to يَقُومُ (will rise) or يَتَخَبَّطُ (is driven), so that their rising and falling is like that of the struck-down, not because their intellects are disordered, but because God increased in their bellies what they had consumed of riba, so it weighed them down. ﴿That is because they said: "Trade is only like riba"﴾, i.e., that punishment is due to the fact that they equated riba and trade in one category, because both lead to profit, so they deemed it lawful just as they deemed trade lawful. The original form would have been "riba is only like trade," but it was reversed for emphasis, as if they made riba the principle and measured trade by it. The difference: whoever gives two dirhams for one dirham loses one dirham, whereas whoever buys a commodity worth one dirham for two dirhams perhaps the need for it, or the expectation of its selling, compensates for this loss. ﴿But God has permitted trade and forbidden riba﴾: a denial of their equating them, and the nullification of analogy (qiyas, "analogical reasoning") by the opposition of the text (nass). ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾: whoever is reached by an admonition and warning from God Most High, such as the prohibition of riba. ﴿And desists﴾: heeds the advice and follows the prohibition. ﴿He shall have what has passed﴾: what he took before the prohibition, and it shall not be reclaimed from him. The words مَا (what) in the position of the nominative are governed by the adverbial phrase if مَن is taken as a relative pronoun, or by the subject if it is taken as a conditional, according to the view of Sibawayh, since the adverbial phrase does not depend on what precedes it. ﴿And his affair is with God﴾: He will reward him for his desisting, if it was from accepting the admonition and sincerity of intention.

It is also said: He will judge concerning his case, and there is no objection from you against Him.

﴿And whoever returns﴾ to permitting riba, since the discussion concerns that. ﴿Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾, because they have disbelieved in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 276:

﴿Allah destroys usury﴾ He takes away its blessing and ruins the wealth into which it enters. ﴿And He causes charities to increase﴾ He multiplies their reward and blesses what is given out of them. It is related from him, upon him be prayers and peace: «Indeed Allah accepts charity and nurtures it just as one of you nurtures his foal.»

And from him, upon him be prayers and peace: «Zakat has never diminished any wealth.» ﴿And Allah does not love﴾ He does not approve, and He does not love with the love He has for those who turn in repentance (tawwabin). ﴿every ungrateful sinner﴾ one who persists in declaring the forbidden lawful (kaffar, the one who persists in making lawful what is unlawful). ﴿sinful (athim)﴾ one who is immersed in committing it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 277:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ in Allah and His Messenger, and in what came to them from Him. ﴿and do righteous deeds, establish the prayer, and give the zakah﴾ — they are conjoined to what encompasses them both, because of their excellence over the rest of the righteous deeds. ﴿For them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them﴾ of what is to come. ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over what has passed.

**(p. 163)** ﴿O you who believe, fear God and give up what remains of the riba (usury/interest)﴾, and leave off what is still owed of the riba that you stipulated from people. ﴿If you are believers﴾ in your hearts, for its proof is complying with what you have been commanded.

It is narrated that the tribe of Thaqif had money owed to them by some of Quraysh, and when the due date arrived they demanded the principal and the riba. So this was revealed.

﴿But if you do not do so, then be informed of a war from God and His Messenger﴾. That is, know of it, from *adhina bi-al-shay'* (to know something), when one knows of it. Hamzah and Asim, in the transmission of Ibn Ayyash, read *fa-ādhinū*, meaning inform others of it, from *al-udhun* (listening), since it is one of the means of knowledge. The indefinite *harb* (war) is for emphasis, and this implies that the one who practices riba is to be fought after he is asked to repent, until he returns to the command of God, just as with a rebel, and this does not imply his disbelief. It is narrated that when this was revealed, Thaqif said, "We have no power to wage war against God and His Messenger." ﴿Then you have your capital﴾ from the *irtibā'* (taking riba) and believing it to be lawful. ﴿You will not wrong [others] by taking extra﴾, ﴿nor will you be wronged﴾ by delay or reduction. From this it is understood that if they do not repent, they have no right to their principal, and this is sound according to what we have said, since one who persists in declaring it lawful is an apostate, and his property is *fay'* (property taken by the public treasury).

**(p. 163)** ﴿O you who believe, fear God and give up what remains of the riba (usury/interest)﴾, and leave off what is still owed of the riba that you stipulated from people. ﴿If you are believers﴾ in your hearts, for its proof is complying with what you have been commanded.

It is narrated that the tribe of Thaqif had money owed to them by some of Quraysh, and when the due date arrived they demanded the principal and the riba. So this was revealed.

﴿But if you do not do so, then be informed of a war from God and His Messenger﴾. That is, know of it, from *adhina bi-al-shay'* (to know something), when one knows of it. Hamzah and Asim, in the transmission of Ibn Ayyash, read *fa-ādhinū*, meaning inform others of it, from *al-udhun* (listening), since it is one of the means of knowledge. The indefinite *harb* (war) is for emphasis, and this implies that the one who practices riba is to be fought after he is asked to repent, until he returns to the command of God, just as with a rebel, and this does not imply his disbelief. It is narrated that when this was revealed, Thaqif said, "We have no power to wage war against God and His Messenger." ﴿Then you have your capital﴾ from the *irtibā'* (taking riba) and believing it to be lawful. ﴿You will not wrong [others] by taking extra﴾, ﴿nor will you be wronged﴾ by delay or reduction. From this it is understood that if they do not repent, they have no right to their principal, and this is sound according to what we have said, since one who persists in declaring it lawful is an apostate, and his property is *fay'* (property taken by the public treasury).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 280:

﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾: if a debtor who is in hardship (ʿusrah) befalls you. It is also recited as "dhā ʿusrah" (with dhā as the nominative), meaning: "and if the debtor is in hardship."

﴿then [let there be] postponement﴾: the ruling is postponement (naẓirah), or upon you is postponement, or let there be postponement; and it is al-inẓār (granting respite). It is also recited as "fa-nāẓiruh" in the indicative mood, meaning: then the one who is entitled to it is his creditor (nāẓiruh), in the sense of "his awaiter" (muntaẓiruh), or "the one who holds his respite" (ṣāḥib naẓratih), by way of attribution. And it is recited as "fa-nāẓirhu" in the imperative, meaning: so grant him respite (fa-sāmiḥhu bil-naẓrah).

﴿until a time of ease﴾: a time of affluence (yasār). Nāfiʿ and Ḥamzah read the sīn with a ḍammah, and both are dialects, like mashraqah and mashruqah. It is also recited with both forms in construct (muḍāfayn), with the tā' dropped in the construct state, as in the poet's line: "And they broke with you the promise of the matter which they had promised."

﴿And that you remit [it] as charity﴾: by granting remission (al-ibrāʾ). ʿĀṣim reads the ṣād with lightening (takhfīf). 

﴿is better for you﴾: greater in reward than granting respite; or better than what you take, because of the multiplication of its reward and its permanence. It has been said: the intended meaning of "charity" here is granting respite, based on his saying, upon him be blessings and peace: "The debt of a Muslim man who postpones it does not become due except that he will have for every day a charity."

﴿if you knew﴾: what is in it of fine and abundant remembrance.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 281:

﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ — the Day of Resurrection, or the Day of Death, so prepare yourselves for your destination toward Him. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it as "turja'un" with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the jim (i.e., "tarji'una" would be the reading with the ta' open and the jim kasra; here the verb is read with the first letter open and the jim kasra, so that the subject is the one returning). ﴿Then every soul will be paid in full for what it earned﴾ — the recompense for what it did of good or evil, ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ — by a reduction in reward or an increase in punishment.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that (it was the last verse that Jibril (peace be upon him) brought down, and he said: "Place it at the head of the two hundred and eightieth verse of al-Baqarah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) lived after it twenty-one days, and it was said eighty-one days. It was also said seven days, and it was said three hours.)

(p-164)﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt with one another﴾, i.e., when some of you deal with others on credit. One says "dayantuhu" (I dealt with him on credit) when one deals with someone on deferred terms, whether giving or taking. The purpose of mentioning "debt" is to exclude the understanding that "tadayun" means reciprocal recompense, to make known that it has varieties (deferred and immediate), and that it is what prompts the writing. The referent of the pronoun in "fa-ktubuhu" (then write it down) is a specified term, known by days and months, not by the harvest or the arrival of the pilgrims.

﴿Then write it down﴾, for it is more trustworthy and more effective in preventing dispute. The majority hold that this is recommendation (istihbab). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the intended meaning is salam (advance sale), and he said: "When Allah forbade riba, He permitted salam."

﴿And let a scribe write it down between you justly﴾: one who writes evenly, neither adding nor subtracting. In reality this is a command to the contracting parties to choose a pious jurist-scribe, so that what he writes is trustworthy and certified by the Shari'ah.

﴿And let no scribe refuse﴾, i.e., let no one refuse to write, ﴿to write as Allah has taught him﴾, i.e., in the manner Allah taught him, of the writers of documents; or, let him not refuse to benefit people by his writing, as Allah has benefited him by teaching it, like His saying: ﴿And do good as Allah has done good to you﴾. ﴿So let him write﴾ that taught writing. He commanded it after forbidding refusal, for emphasis. It is also possible that the kaf (as) is connected to the command, so that the prohibition on refusing is absolute and the command to write is then restricted.

﴿And let the one upon whom the right is due dictate﴾: let the dictator be the one who owes the right, because he is the one acknowledging and the one testified against. "Imlal" and "imla'" are the same. ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, i.e., the dictator, or the scribe. ﴿And let him not diminish from it anything﴾, i.e., from the right, or from what was dictated. ﴿If the one upon whom the right is due is foolish﴾, deficient in intellect and wasteful; ﴿or weak﴾, a child or a senile old man who is impaired; ﴿or unable to dictate himself﴾, or unable to dictate by himself, because of muteness or ignorance of the language. ﴿Then let his guardian dictate justly﴾, i.e., the one who manages his affairs and stands in his place, such as a custodian if he is a child or mentally impaired, or an agent or translator if he is unable. This is evidence that representation is valid in acknowledgment, though perhaps it is restricted to what the custodian or agent has undertaken.

﴿And call to witness two witnesses﴾: seek that two witnesses testify to the debt. ﴿From your men﴾, i.e., from among the Muslim men. This is evidence for the requirement that witnesses be Muslims, and the general body of scholars went this way. Abu Hanifah said: the testimony of unbelievers against one another is accepted. ﴿And if they are not two men﴾, i.e., if the two witnesses are not two men, ﴿then one man and two women﴾, i.e., let a man and two women testify. This is restricted to property matters according to us, and according to Abu Hanifah to matters other than hudud (fixed penalties) and qisas (retaliation). ﴿From among those you approve as witnesses﴾, because of your knowledge of their uprightness. ﴿So that if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾. This is the reason for considering the number: if one of them forgets the testimony, the other reminds her. In reality the reason is the reminding, but since error is its cause, it takes its place, as in their saying: "I prepared the weapon so that if an enemy comes I may repel him." It is as if it were said: "for the purpose that one of them reminds the other should she err." Within this is an indication of the deficiency of their intellect and the weakness of their retention. Hamzah read "an tadilla" as a conditional with "fatudhakkiru" in the nominative. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read "fatudhkira," from idhkar.

﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾, for giving testimony or for bearing it. They were called "witnesses" before bearing it, treating what is about to be the case as though it were the case; and "ma" is extra (zaidah).

﴿And do not be weary of writing it﴾, i.e., do not tire from the frequency of your dealings, of writing the debt, or the right, or the document. It was said that "sa'am" (weariness) is a figure for laziness, since it is a trait of the hypocrite; hence the prayer and peace of Allah be upon him said: "The believer should not say, 'I am lazy.'" ﴿Whether small or large﴾, whether the right is small or large, or whether the document is brief or detailed. ﴿To its term﴾, i.e., to the time of its falling due, which the debtor acknowledged.

﴿That﴾ refers to writing it down. ﴿Is more just in the sight of Allah﴾, i.e., more equitable. ﴿And more upright for testimony﴾, i.e., firmer for it and more helpful in establishing it. Both words are formed from "aqsata" and "aqama," irregularly, or from "qasit" in the sense of one possessing justice, and "qawim." The waw in "aqwam" was kept as it was in the comparative of wonder, because that form is fixed. ﴿And nearer to preventing doubt﴾, i.e., closer to ensuring you do not doubt the kind of debt, its amount, its term, the witnesses, and the like. ﴿Except that it is a present trade which you conduct among yourselves, then there is no blame upon you that you do not write it﴾. This is an exception to the command to write. "Present trade" covers exchange for a debt or for goods, and "conducting it among them" means their handling of it hand to hand; that is, unless you trade hand to hand, in which case there is no harm in not writing, since that is far from dispute and forgetfulness. 'Asim read "tijaratan" as the predicate, with an implied subject, its estimate being: "unless the trade is a present trade," like the poet's words:

"O Banu Asad, do you know our affliction
when there is a day of stars, most dreadful?"

The rest read it in the nominative, as subject and predicate, "tudirunaha," or as the complete verb "kana."

(p-165)﴿And call witnesses when you trade﴾, this trade, or in general, since that is more cautious. The commands in this verse are for recommendation according to most of the imams. It was said that they are for obligation, and then scholars differed over whether they are upheld (muhkam) or abrogated (naskh).

﴿Let neither scribe nor witness be harmed﴾. The verb admits both readings, and what indicates this is that it was read "wa-la yudarra" with kasra and with fatha. It is a prohibition on both of them against refusing to respond, distorting, or altering the documents and the testimony; or a prohibition against harming them, such as hurrying them away from an important matter and requiring them to go beyond what is set for them, or the scribe not being given his fee, or the witness not being given the cost of his journey wherever he is. ﴿And if you do﴾ harm, or what you have been forbidden. ﴿Then indeed it is a transgression in you﴾, a departure from obedience that attaches to you.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in opposing His command and prohibition. ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾ His rulings, which contain your interests. ﴿And Allah is Knower of all things﴾. He repeated the word "Allah" in the three clauses because each stands on its own: the first is an urging to piety, the second a promise of His favour, and the third an exaltation of His majesty. And because the name was used in the exaltation by way of allusion.

﴿And if you are on a journey﴾, i.e., travelling, ﴿and you find no scribe, then a pledge taken in possession﴾. What serves as security is a pledge (*rihan*), or [the meaning is] "then upon you is a pledge," or "then let a pledge be taken." This conditional does not make travel a requirement for taking a pledge, as Mujahid and al-Dahhak, may Allah have mercy on them both, supposed. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) pledged his coat of mail in Medina to a Jew for twenty *sa'* of barley that he took for his family. Rather, the condition is to establish security for the pledge in place of security through writing, during travel, which is the situation where writing is likely to be unavailable. The majority of scholars require taking possession (*qabd*) in pledging, and Malik does not. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *"fa-rahnun"* (with the vowel pattern of *saqf*). Both forms are the plural of *rahn*, meaning *marhun* (that which is pledged). It was also read with the *ha'* sukun, for lightening the pronunciation. ﴿Then if some of you trust others﴾, i.e., some of the creditors trust some of the debtors and are content with their trustworthiness in place of a pledge. ﴿then let him who is entrusted discharge his trust﴾, i.e., his debt. He called it a trust (*amanah*) because the creditor has entrusted him with it by forgoing a pledge against it. It was read *"alladhi aytumina"* with the hamzah changed to a *ya'*, and *"alladhi utumina"* with the *ya'* assimilated into the *ta'*, which is an error, because the letter that has been converted from a hamzah is governed by its rule and so is not assimilated. ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾, regarding betrayal and denial of the right. There are intensifications in this. ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾, O witnesses, or the debtors, and the testimony is their testimony against themselves. ﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾, i.e., his heart commits sin, or his heart is sinful. The clause is the predicate of *inna*, and the attribution of sin to the heart is because concealment is committed by it. A parallel is: "The eye commits adultery and the ear commits adultery." Or it is for emphasis, since it is the chief of the organs and its acts are the greatest acts. It is as if it were said: sin has taken hold of his soul and seized its noblest part, and has surpassed all his other sins.

It was also read *"qalbahu"* in the accusative, like *husna wajhihi* (the beauty of his face). ﴿And Allah is Knowing of what you do﴾, a warning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 2, verse 284:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, in creation and in dominion. ﴿And whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it﴾, meaning the evil within them and the resolve upon it, since forgiveness and punishment are consequent upon it. ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾ on the Day of Resurrection. This is a proof against those who deny the reckoning, such as the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) and the Rafidah (the Shi'ite extremists). ﴿So He forgives whom He wills﴾ His forgiveness, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾ His punishment. This is explicit in negating the obligation of punishment. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub read both verbs in the nominative, as a resumptive clause (isti'naf). The rest read them in the jussive, as coordinated with the apodosis of the conditional. Whoever reads them in the jussive without the particle fa' makes them a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in the apodosis, either as a substitute of part for whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull) or as a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), as in the verse:

"Whenever you visit us, you will visit us at our abodes, and you will find firewood, thick and blazing fire."

Idgham of the ra' into the lam is a grammatical error (lahn), since the ra' is only assimilated into a letter of its own kind. ﴿And Allah is over all things Competent﴾, so He is able to give life and to call to account.

The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord. ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been revealed to him from his Lord﴾ is a testimony and an explicit statement from God, Exalted, confirming the soundness of his faith and its acceptance, and that he is certain of his matter, not doubting it. ﴿And the believers, each one believes in God, His angels, His books, and His messengers﴾: the believers may be taken as conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "the Messenger," so that the pronoun replaced by the tanwin (nunation) of "kullun" refers to both the Messenger and the believers; or "al-mu'minun" may be made the subject (mubtada'), in which case the pronoun refers to the believers. On this reading it is valid for "kullun" to be the subject whose predicate is its predicate (khabar), and the singling out of the Messenger for the ruling is either to honour him, or because his faith is based on direct witnessing and observation, whereas theirs is based on reflection and inference. Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī recited:

« wa-kitābihi » meaning the Qur'an or the category (of scripture). The difference between it and the plural is that the singular is used generically for the category, while the plural is used for its multiple collections; for this reason it was said: "al-kitāb (the Book) is more than al-kutub (the books)." ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾, i.e., they say, "We make no distinction." Ya'qub recited "lā yufarriqu" with the yā' (third person masculine), on the basis that the verb's subject is "kullun." It was also read "lā yufarriqūna," taking account of its meaning, as in the Most High's words: ﴿And each of them comes to Him humbled﴾, where "kullun" is singular in form but plural in meaning because it occurs in a negative context, as in His words: ﴿Then none of you could withhold him from Him﴾.

For this reason "bayna" governs it, and the intended meaning is the negation of distinction in affirming or denying (them). They said ﴿We hear﴾, meaning we respond. ﴿And we obey﴾ Your command.

﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾: grant us Your forgiveness, or we seek Your forgiveness. ﴿And to You is the final return﴾: the return after death, and this is an acknowledgement from them of the Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 2, verse 286:

﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.﴾ Beyond what its power can bear, out of bounty and mercy. Or, [He imposes] what is less than the extent of its ability, such that its capacity is broad in it and it is made easy for it, as in His saying, ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾. This indicates that taklif (divine obligation) with the impossible does not occur, but it does not indicate that it is impossible. ﴿It shall have what it earned﴾ of good. ﴿And it shall bear what it earned﴾ of evil. No one else benefits from its obedience or is harmed by its disobedience. The attribution of *kasb* (earning) to good and *iktisab* (acquiring) to evil is because *iktisab* carries an element of effort, and the soul desires evil and is drawn to it, so it is more eager to obtain it and more active in it, unlike good.

﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or err﴾, that is, do not take us to task for what led us to forgetting or error through negligence and lack of concern, or for the two themselves, since taking to task for them is not rationally impossible. Sins are like poisons: just as consuming them leads to destruction, so too the pursuit of sins is not far from leading to punishment, even if they were not intentional. But He, exalted is He, promised to overlook them out of mercy and bounty, so it is permissible for a person to supplicate with this, seeking its continuation and acknowledging the blessing in it. This is supported by the implication of the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Error and forgetting have been lifted from my community."

﴿Our Lord, and do not lay on us a burden (*isr*)﴾, a heavy load that binds its bearer, i.e., holds him in his place. He means by it arduous obligations. It has been recited as "*wa-la tuhimmil*" with shadda for emphasis.

﴿As You laid it on those before us﴾, a burden like Your laying it on those before us, or like that which You laid on them. Thus it is an attribute of *isr*. What is meant by it is what the Children of Israel were charged with: killing themselves, cutting off the place of impurity, fifty prayers in a day and night, and giving a quarter of their wealth as zakat. Or what befell them of hardships and trials.

﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾ of calamity and punishment, or of obligations which human capacity cannot fulfill. This indicates the permissibility of taklif with what cannot be borne; otherwise, they would not have asked to be freed from it. The shadda here is for transitivity of the verb to the second object (p-167).

﴿And pardon us﴾, wipe out our sins. ﴿And forgive us﴾, cover our faults and do not expose us through taking to task.

﴿And have mercy on us﴾, show compassion to us and be bountiful to us. ﴿You are our Master (*mawlana*)﴾, our lord. ﴿So help us against the disbelieving people﴾, for it is the right of a master to help his clients against enemies. Or what is meant is the disbelievers in general.

It is narrated that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, made these supplications, it was said to him after each phrase: "Done."

And from him, peace be upon him: "Allah, exalted is He, sent down two verses from the treasures of Paradise, which the Most Merciful wrote with His hand two thousand years before He created creation. Whoever recites them after the final night prayer, they will suffice him in place of the night vigil."

And from him, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever recites the two verses at the end of Surat al-Baqarah on a night, they will suffice him." This refutes the view of those who disliked saying "Surat al-Baqarah," and said it should be said "the surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned," just as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "The surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned is the tent-pole of the Qur'an, so learn it, for learning it is a blessing and abandoning it is regret, and the *batalah* will not be able to master it." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what are the *batalah*?" He said: "The sorcerers."

Completed, by the praise of Allah and the goodness of His success, the printing of the first volume of the *Tafsir* of al-Baydawi at the presses of Dar Ihya' al-Turath al-Arabi, in radiant Beirut, may Allah preserve it for the printing of more beneficial books.

And the last of our supplication is that all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
